TLB

TLB

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003

Definition and mechanism

The translation lookaside buffer caches recent address translations and relevant access metadata, not the bytes being loaded. A miss may trigger a valid page-table walk without OS fault handling. A TLB hit can coexist with a data-cache miss. Context and permissions matter; it is not just a global VPN-only dictionary.

Prerequisites

  • Page tables and MMU — Cached or faulting translation starts from the mapping/protection mechanism.

Used by

  • Huge pages and TLB reach — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites.

Recall and next depth

Distinguish a translation miss, cache miss, and page fault.

Pending: ASIDs/PCIDs, shootdowns, hierarchy, associativity, and measured reach.

Source and navigation

C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map

Reconstruction depth

The Translation Lookaside Buffer caches recent virtual-page to physical-frame translations. Without a cached translation, the processor performs a page-table walk, which itself requires memory accesses and can stall an otherwise cache-friendly loop.

TLB locality differs from data-cache locality. A traversal can touch one cache line from thousands of separate pages: each useful access is small, but the page working set can exceed TLB capacity. Huge pages increase TLB reach because one translation covers more bytes, although they introduce allocation and fragmentation trade-offs.

When profiling, do not diagnose every unexplained memory stall as a TLB problem. Hardware performance counters can separate cache misses, page walks and TLB misses on supported CPUs. Synthetic experiments should vary stride and working-set pages while keeping useful work controlled.

For engine data, dense arrays often help both cache and TLB locality; pointer-heavy structures can hurt both. NUMA adds another axis: a translation may be cached while the physical page still resides on a remote node.

Virtual and physical contiguity

Virtual and physical contiguity

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003

Definition and mechanism

Consecutive virtual addresses can map nonadjacent physical frames. Vector’s contiguous elements guarantee adjacent object storage in the process model, not one contiguous physical allocation. File offsets and storage-device placement are separate adjacency notions. Contiguity must always name the space being discussed.

Prerequisites

  • Pages and page offsets — Page identity is translated while within-page position is preserved.

Source and navigation

C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map

Reconstruction depth

A virtually contiguous array occupies one uninterrupted range of virtual addresses. The page table may map those virtual pages to physical frames scattered through RAM. Most user-space code only requires virtual contiguity because ordinary loads and stores are translated by the MMU before reaching memory.

Physical contiguity matters at different boundaries: some DMA devices, huge-page mappings, kernels or fixed hardware buffers may impose stronger requirements. Modern IOMMUs can themselves provide device-visible address translation, reducing the need for physically contiguous host memory in some designs.

This explains why a large dynamic allocation can succeed even when free physical RAM is fragmented into many regions: the operating system can assemble the virtual range from separate frames and may not commit all of them until faults occur.

For performance, virtual contiguity still does not guarantee identical locality. Page placement can span NUMA nodes, and TLB reach depends on page size and access footprint. Therefore contiguous storage is a statement about address iteration and element layout, not a complete claim about physical placement.

Huge pages and TLB reach

Huge pages and TLB reach

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003

Definition and mechanism

A larger page covers more bytes per translation. With T same-size cached entries, illustrative reach is T×P bytes. One GiB requires 262144 pages at 4 KiB versus 512 at 2 MiB. Larger pages trade flexibility, availability, fragmentation and fault granularity; the counts alone do not prove performance improvement.

Prerequisites

  • TLB — Larger pages change the amount of memory covered by cached translations.
  • Allocator fragmentation — Coarser allocation granularity introduces space/availability trade-offs.

Used by

Update downstream uses when later chunks build on this concept.

Recall and next depth

Calculate page counts without asserting a universal speedup.

Pending: Mixed page sizes, workloads, benchmarks and OS policy.

Source and navigation

C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map

Reach, fragmentation, and measurement

TLB reach is approximately the number of cached translations multiplied by the page size. If a TLB can hold NN translations, switching from 4 KiB pages to 2 MiB huge pages can increase the bytes covered by those translations by a factor of 512.

That does not make huge pages universally faster. They can increase internal fragmentation, make allocation/compaction harder, change NUMA placement behavior and waste memory when only small portions of each huge page are touched. Transparent Huge Pages may also promote or split mappings asynchronously, so an application should not infer actual page size from its allocation API alone.

The right benchmark holds the useful computation fixed while varying working-set size and access stride, then observes TLB/page-walk counters where available. A speedup from huge pages should correlate with translation pressure rather than simply with a different allocator or cache footprint.

For engines, huge pages are most plausible for stable, large, densely accessed arenas—not as a default for every allocation.

Page faults and demand paging

Page faults and demand paging

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003

Definition and mechanism

A memory fault requires OS intervention when current translation/protection state cannot satisfy access. Valid demand loading, zero-fill, or copy-on-write may install/alter mapping then retry. Invalid addresses or denied permissions may fail instead. A fault need not perform disk I/O; a TLB miss need not fault at all.

Prerequisites

  • Page tables and MMU — Cached or faulting translation starts from the mapping/protection mechanism.

Used by

  • Copy-on-write — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites.
  • Memory-mapped files — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites.

Copy-on-write

Copy-on-write

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003

Definition and mechanism

COW initially shares physical contents while deferring private copies. A permitted write to a COW-protected mapping faults; OS allocates/copies a frame, updates the writer’s mapping, and retries. Other mappings retain old contents. Not every read-only page is COW, so not every write fault is recoverable.

Prerequisites

  • Page faults and demand paging — Deferred private copying is implemented through a recoverable write fault.

Used by

Update downstream uses when later chunks build on this concept.

Recall and next depth

Show frame identity before and after one process writes.

Pending: Fork behavior, mapping flags, reference tracking and costs.

Source and navigation

C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map

Reconstruction depth

Copy-on-write delays physical copying until shared data is actually modified. At the virtual-memory level, two address spaces may initially map the same physical page as read-only. A write triggers a protection fault; the operating system allocates a private page, copies old contents, updates the writer’s page table and resumes the instruction.

The key invariant is logical independence after a write, even though physical storage was shared before it. This is why process creation can be cheap initially without eagerly duplicating every writable page.

COW has costs that disappear in a high-level description: the first write can incur a page fault and page copy, dirty-page accounting changes, and large working sets can turn an initially cheap clone into substantial later memory traffic. Huge pages and NUMA placement make those costs workload-dependent.

Do not generalize OS page COW into a recommendation for C++ value types. Library-level copy-on-write strings or containers complicate iterator/reference validity, threading and mutation semantics. The mechanism is useful when ownership and fault or copy behavior are explicit.

A file mapping makes file-backed bytes accessible through a virtual region. Fault handling can supply pages lazily; ownership, access flags, mapping length, and synchronization still matter. A mapped byte buffer is not automatically a set of live aligned C++ objects. File persistence and virtual access are separate mechanisms.

Storage duration and object lifetime

Storage duration and object lifetime

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C010

Definition and mechanism

Direct local reference binding can extend a temporary under specified rules; a returned parameter alias does not renew the deadline. A reference’s own lifetime does not prove the referent’s lifetime.

Construction and destruction can delimit an occupant while backing storage remains. The inline C++ lab uses construct_at/destroy_at in an alignas byte buffer and new/delete as the combined allocation/construction and destruction/release operations. The pointer object does not own or extend pointee life. Implicit object creation occurs only for specified operations and suitable types; a reinterpret_cast is not a universal construction operation.

Storage duration specifies how long storage is potentially available: automatic, static, thread, or dynamic. Object lifetime describes when a particular initialized object exists within it. Old bytes can remain after lifetime ends without authorizing access. const restricts mutation, not physical placement. Language categories do not dictate a universal segment map.

M010 reuses this separation for smart owners and arenas: a wrapper’s storage duration, the managed object’s lifetime, the ownership-group lifetime, and an external GPU-use interval may all end at different times. Placement construction reuses suitable live storage; object destruction alone does not return that storage to an allocator.

Prerequisites

  • Interpretation contract — Representation, type, and lifetime must identify what object exists.

  • Thread-local storage — uses this prerequisite to establish its entity, lifetime, representation or lookup contract.
  • Object construction and storage reuse — separates an occupant’s construction from backing storage availability.

Allocator fragmentation

Allocator fragmentation

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003

Definition and mechanism

Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated block, e.g. 37 bytes requested in a 48-byte class leaves 11. External fragmentation is free space split into holes incapable of satisfying one contiguous request, e.g. three separated 20-byte holes cannot supply one 60-byte block. Metadata overhead is an additional cost.

Prerequisites

  • Dynamic allocation and heap — Allocated buffers/blocks supply the storage whose ownership and fragmentation matter.

Used by

  • Huge pages and TLB reach — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites.

Source and navigation

C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map

Reconstruction depth

Fragmentation is wasted allocation capacity caused by request shapes and allocator policy. Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated block because of alignment, size classes or rounding. External fragmentation is free memory split into pieces that cannot satisfy a larger request even when total free bytes are sufficient.

A game or graphics workload amplifies the issue because lifetimes are structured: per-frame temporaries, long-lived assets, streaming resources and transient staging data behave differently. Using one general heap for all of them can mix lifetimes and make reuse less predictable.

A useful experiment records requested bytes, committed bytes, peak live bytes, largest free span, allocation count and reuse over time. Frame arenas eliminate external fragmentation inside a frame by resetting wholesale; pools trade generality for fixed-size reuse; free lists require split and coalesce policy.

Fragmentation is not measured by “the process uses a lot of memory” alone. Residency, allocator metadata, page commitment and application-owned slack must be separated before choosing a remedy.

Static storage and initialization

Static storage and initialization

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C007

Definition and mechanism

constinit requires static initialization without making an object const. Dynamic initialization across translation units requires ordering care; explicit owners or function-local statics can provide a clear dependency path. Local-static first initialization is synchronized since C++11, but later calls/mutations still require normal concurrency rules. Initialization and shutdown dependencies are distinct.

Namespace-scope/static objects have program-duration storage. Initialized writable objects commonly use data-like regions; zero-initialized objects use BSS-like zero-fill, avoiding literal zeros in the executable. Some objects require runtime dynamic initialization; cross-unit order is a distinct problem from storage allocation.

Prerequisites

  • Storage duration and object lifetime — Access requires an object and backing storage that are still valid.

ASLR

ASLR

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003

Definition and mechanism

Address-space layout randomization varies mapping locations to make fixed-address assumptions less reliable and support exploitation resistance. It does not alter C++ member offsets or grant pointer validity. A pedagogical stack/heap/data/text ordering is not a guaranteed live map.

Prerequisites

Source and navigation

C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map

Reconstruction depth

Address Space Layout Randomization changes where executable images, shared libraries, stacks, heaps and other mappings are placed between process runs. The security goal is to make an attacker’s guessed code or data address less reliable; it is not memory encryption and it does not prevent a program from using valid pointers after the loader establishes mappings.

For engine code, the important consequence is that a virtual address is process-instance state, not durable identity. Serializing a raw pointer, hashing it as an asset identifier, or expecting the same module base across runs is invalid even before ASLR is considered; ASLR makes the mistake obvious.

Position-independent code and relocation machinery allow code and data references to work when the loader chooses a different base. Debuggers and crash reports therefore resolve addresses against the exact module build and load map rather than treating an absolute address as a universal source location.

A practical test is to run a tiny program multiple times and record stack, heap, function and shared-library addresses while keeping the binary unchanged. Values may vary, while relationships required by the program remain valid. ASLR strength and platform policy are operating-system evidence, not something portable C++ can infer from one run.

Ownership and non-owning views

Ownership and non-owning views

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C010

Definition and mechanism

By-value copies use member semantics, not recursive deep cloning. Rule-Zero composition delegates ownership to members; raw owners must coordinate transfer and release. Copying a pointer/view/handle is not acquiring ownership.

Copying span/string_view or capturing a view by value copies only a descriptor. An owning string capture supplies independent storage; a view or handle does not automatically pin a deferred resource.

The inline C++ laboratory distinguishes NamedVector::to_array, which copies values into a new array, from ArrayVector::view, which aliases actual array elements without owning them. Neither span nor pointer extends backing lifetime. Ownership and RAII are introduced as next-depth connections, not yet a full exception-safety treatment.

M010 makes the distinction operational: an owner is responsible for release; a borrow only accesses. std::unique_ptr expresses exclusive ownership, std::shared_ptr retains a shared lifetime, and std::weak_ptr observes without extending that lifetime. Smart pointers do not remove the borrow/invalidation rules of raw pointers obtained from them. See RAII and resource handles and Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership.

An owner controls a resource’s validity and release; a view merely refers to it. Vector owns its element buffer; span does not copy or prolong that buffer’s life. Owner destruction or invalidating reallocation can dangle the span. A reader retaining a span needs stable live backing for every read, not only at construction.

Prerequisites

  • Storage duration and object lifetime — Access requires an object and backing storage that are still valid.
  • Dynamic allocation and heap — Allocated buffers/blocks supply the storage whose ownership and fragmentation matter.

Used by

  • Memory-mapped files — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites.
  • Atomic publication and durability — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites.
  • Deferred captures and borrowed views
  • Copy semantics and resource identity
  • Rules of Three Five and Zero
  • RAII and resource handles
  • Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership

Recall and next depth

Pending: smart owners, shared immutable data and scheduling/resource pinning.

Executed POSIX durability sequence

The durability contract now has an actual syscall-level witness in tools/labs/atomic_publication_durability_lab.cpp.

The reference creates a staging file with exclusive creation, writes the complete payload, calls fsync on the file, closes it, renames it within the same directory, opens the containing directory, and calls fsync on that directory before treating publication as complete. It then verifies the final bytes and absence of the staging name. Separate tests reject a pre-existing staging file and a traversal-style final name.

This is stronger than “write temp then rename,” because rename atomicity and durable persistence are different properties. The file sync requests persistence of file contents/metadata; the directory sync requests persistence of the directory-entry change. Successful calls on CI are evidence that the operating-system/filesystem accepted that ordering. They are not a laboratory power-cut test and cannot promise identical persistence guarantees on every filesystem, storage controller, Windows API, network filesystem or production asset pipeline.

Bit casting and representation

Bit casting and representation

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C004 · Latest development: C006

Definition and mechanism

A same-size eligible bit_cast transfers representation, not numeric value. On the checked binary32 host, bit_cast(1.0f)=3F800000, whereas a numeric cast gives 1. Pointer punning is not an equivalent legal operation.

M006 separates representation copying, numeric conversion and endian coding. Eligibility does not validate arbitrary padding/target representations or establish a typed object in file-mapped bytes. Use initialized compatible scalars and explicit external encoding.

Prerequisites

  • Fixed-width integer types — A same-size unsigned carrier holds the specified interchange representation.
  • Interpretation contract — A bit transfer and a numeric conversion interpret the same carrier differently.
  • IEEE-754 floating point — The format/arithmetic contract gives these bits their numerical domain.

Used by

  • Binary format contracts — uses this mechanism to define its representation, error or validation contract.

  • Memory dump interpretation — uses this mechanism to define its representation, error or validation contract.

Checksums CRCs and hashes

Checksums, CRCs, and hashes

Curriculum depth: Reference implemented and known-answer tested · First seen: C006 · Latest development: Phase 28 repair

A checksum or digest maps an arbitrary byte sequence to a smaller fixed-size value. Different families make different promises.

An additive checksum is mainly an accidental-error detector and is weak against structured changes such as reordering or compensating byte modifications.

A CRC interprets bits as a polynomial over GF(2)GF(2) and computes a remainder under a declared generator polynomial and parameter set. CRCs are excellent for many transmission/storage error patterns, but they are not cryptographic authenticators.

A cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 is designed so that finding collisions or preimages is computationally hard under the security assumptions of the primitive. A hash still does not authenticate a file when an attacker can replace both the file and the untrusted hash value.

SHA-256 compression structure

SHA-256 pads the message with a one bit, enough zero bits to leave 64 bits at the end of the final 512-bit block, and then the original message length modulo 2642^{64}. Each 512-bit block expands sixteen 32-bit words into a 64-word schedule and updates an eight-word chaining state through 64 rounds.

The important learning boundary is representation: message words are interpreted in the algorithm’s specified byte order. Reinterpreting native host integers without explicit conversion can produce a platform-specific hash implementation.

Known-answer evidence

tools/labs/crypto_primitives_lab.cpp implements SHA-256 directly and validates the standard digest of “abc” and the empty message. The same SHA-256 implementation is then used by HMAC, HKDF and a domain-separated Merkle tree.

This raises the evidence above “definition present,” but the implementation is educational. It is not reviewed for constant-time behavior, hardware acceleration, fault attacks, side channels or production cryptographic use.

What to use for what

Use a checksum/CRC when the threat is accidental corruption and the protocol specifies the polynomial/parameters.

Use a cryptographic hash when content identity or collision/preimage resistance is required.

Use a MAC such as HMAC when a party holding a secret key must authenticate content.

Use a digital signature when verification must be possible without sharing the signing secret.

Prerequisites

Bitwise XOR, Serialization, Endianness.

Used by

Integrity and authenticity, HMAC and HKDF, Merkle trees and authenticated structure, Production manifests and transactional publication.

Integrity and authenticity

Integrity and authenticity

Curriculum depth: Derived with executable primitive witnesses · First seen: C006 · Latest development: Phase 28 repair

Integrity means detecting unauthorized or accidental modification relative to a trusted reference. Authenticity additionally answers who or what was authorized to create the message.

Hashing a file and storing the digest beside it protects against accidental corruption only when the digest itself is trusted. An attacker able to replace both can recompute the hash.

A message authentication code solves a different problem: parties share a secret key KK and compute a tag such as

HMAC⁡K(m). \operatorname{HMAC}_K(m).

Someone without the key should not be able to forge a valid tag for a modified message under the security assumptions of HMAC and the underlying hash.

A digital signature separates signing and verification keys and supports different trust models. The choice between MAC and signature is therefore architectural, not a matter of which API call is available.

HMAC construction

For hash block size BB, normalize key KK to one block, then compute

HMAC⁡K(m)=H((K⊕opad)∥H((K⊕ipad)∥m)). \operatorname{HMAC}_K(m) = H((K\oplus opad)\,\|\, H((K\oplus ipad)\,\|\,m)).

The inner and outer domains prevent the construction from being equivalent to a naive hash of key concatenated with message.

tools/labs/crypto_primitives_lab.cpp checks HMAC-SHA256 against an RFC 4231 known-answer vector.

Key management is part of authenticity

A mathematically correct MAC does not help if:

  • the key is embedded publicly in the executable;
  • keys are reused across incompatible protocols without domain separation;
  • a compromised key is never rotated;
  • comparison leaks useful timing information in an adversarial environment;
  • replayed old authenticated messages are accepted without nonce/counter/version policy.

Cryptographic primitives are building blocks, not complete protocols.

Production boundary

The educational implementations in this repository exist to make the bytes/rounds/contracts reconstructable. Production systems should use vetted cryptographic libraries and platform key-storage facilities rather than treating a teaching SHA/HMAC implementation as hardened security code.

Related: Checksums CRCs and hashes, HMAC and HKDF, Merkle trees and authenticated structure, Shamir secret sharing.

Corrections and conventions made explicit

  • Use active right-handed rotations, column vectors, radians in code and Hamilton scalar-first quaternions. Storage order remains independent. A file/library boundary can use a different component order without changing the algebra.
  • The determinant comparison in the supplied conditioning text does not have equal determinants. The revised equal-determinant pair has determinants 10−2010^{-20} and conditions one versus 102010^{20}.
  • Diagonal matrices can represent half turns. General unit-diagonal mixing is not necessarily an elementary shear or volume preserving.
  • Pointer arithmetic starting at a separate named Mat2 member does not establish an array. The chapter uses actual arrays and logical bounds checks.
  • The source’s camera walk reaches view depth zero under the common w=−zw=-z perspective convention. The replacement uses a valid view depth −5-5, explicit projection/depth endpoints, clip coordinates and a checked divide.
  • The supplied TBN example is orthonormal with determinant −1-1. The chapter retains it with the required handedness sign rather than calling it implicitly right-handed.
  • A nonunit quaternion using its true inverse still rotates without scale. Conjugate substitution and the unit-only optimized expression have different off-unit behavior; the chapter gives explicit counterexamples.
  • Rigid dual quaternions require both unit real part and the Study constraint. TRS composition/inverse need not remain representable without shear. Euler extraction needs a singular branch and cannot recover discarded angle history.

Pedagogy and substantive corrections

The triangular workcell panel anchors a connected story: movement → coordinates → reachability and basis → measurement → decomposition → area/orientation → surfaces and optics → affine interpolation → convex collision → projective representation → dual measurements → implementation contracts.

The rewrite puts questions and ordinary meanings before terminology, defines symbols close to their equations, retains worked intermediate states, and keeps independent code examples and the runnable capstone inline. All mathematical prose uses dollar-delimited LaTeX. The token-efficiency skill constrained inspection output, not explanation depth. The Playwright skill guides local math rendering without changing Obsidian configuration.

Important clarifications include: coordinate Euclidean length assumes an orthonormal metric; squared distance is not itself a metric; a small dimensional determinant is not a universal conditioning test; zero direction is not a normalization fallback; off-plane Gram barycentrics represent a projection; projective equivalence does not license arbitrary clip-representative rescaling; a direction vector and projective point at infinity retain different information; normal/covector and cross-derived area transformations differ by determinant scaling; support functions require stated attainment assumptions; unsafe adjacent-member indexing is not rescued by apparent contiguity; NaNs must be constructed rather than obtained by reading indeterminate memory.

Twenty-eight filled reusable concept nodes, reciprocal prerequisites, keyword rows and the dependency spine were added. The existing cumulative proof, trace, coverage and provenance files were extended. No new per-part or per-chunk note files were created.

Corrections and modeling contracts

The planar display’s average PPD must not be labeled its central local density. The expanded notes derive the projection derivative: FOV47.658899degrees, average40.286285PPD, center37.936213PPD for W0.53m/D0.60m/N1920. Spectral amplitude reporting distinguishes interior one-sided amplitudes from normalized complex magnitudes; DC/Nyquist are not doubled. Balanced difference-of-Gaussian constant cancellation requires gain/normalization conditions.

Exact-Nyquist phase is a boundary hazard; post-filtering cannot generally undo alias ambiguity. A fixed display refresh rate is not a universal perceptual cutoff. Motion-vector units/direction and jitter need contracts; TAA is not exposure integration. Temporal variance benefits require stationarity, independent noise and valid alignment. Psychometric correctness differs from generic detection, curve parameters differ from a selected threshold, and nonsignificance is not equivalence. A simulated foveation filter that computes a full reference first does not prove saved shading work or human invisibility.

Primary wording and corrections

Defined user-declared versus user-provided, initializer-list syntax versus std::initializer_list, and strong/basic/non-throwing guarantees.

The raw byte owner value-initializes allocated bytes and guards empty copies before range traversal. Its copy preparation has a non-throwing byte-copy step, a non-throwing swap commit, and deterministic old-state cleanup. A deliberate failure hook tests the allocation-failure boundary; it is single-threaded instrumentation, not an allocator implementation. Self-move preserves the value under this custom contract, not a universal library promise.

Generated memberwise moves do not prove cross-member domain relationships such as extent-to-buffer consistency. A move-constructible trait can select a copy; noexcept classifications describe the usable expression, not a promised dedicated move. Move/relocation and proposal/toolchain status remain distinct; no portable C++23 trivial-relocation facility or arbitrary memmove permission is asserted. No runtime benchmark or claimed GPU clone/cleanup is implied by the numeric handle examples.

Selected book passages and primary checks

Read selected extracted passages from the local iCloud CPP/Scott_Meyers_Effective_Modern_C++.pdf: printed pages9,18,23,158–159,164 and103 (PDF pages27,36,41,176–177,182 and121); additional deduction/collapsing passages were inspected at PDF pages33,42–43,188 and221. This was selective reading, not a claim to have read the whole book. Older C++11/14 examples inform teaching, not newer language-version guarantees. Original examples/explanations were written for this vault rather than reproducing the book.

The selected passages reinforce three teaching distinctions: deduction can discard top-level const/reference information; move/forward are category casts rather than resource transfers; const cache methods still need concurrency discipline. “Universal reference” in older material is identified with the narrower current forwarding-reference mechanism, not every T&& spelling.

Primary wording checked: reference initialization, temporary lifetime, qualification conversions, delete operands, decltype, vector capacity and non-static member functions. These are living-draft pages, not a frozen C++23 publication; the notes explicitly distinguish later direct-return diagnostics and C++23 behavior. P3407R1 is provenance research discussion, not adopted C++23 wording. Core Guidelines F.16 informs parameter-design questions, not measured performance.

An attempted P2266R3 page open at the2021 path failed; that unavailable page is not treated as inspected evidence. Named rvalue-reference variables are described as lvalues in ordinary use, with move-eligible return contexts identified as a C++23 special case, not generalized.

Corrections and expanded contracts

The source’s bare delete nullptr; is ill-formed; the positive example deletes an int* whose value is null. Reference definitions versus extern declarations are distinguished. Nothrow allocation failure does not suppress constructor exceptions. A const span descriptor does not make its elements const. Pointer-difference representability and the byte-aliasing type list are stated. Provenance round trips do not revive objects.

The getter illustration includes a const-rvalue path; otherwise a const temporary can still reach a borrowed const-reference result. Pool epochs require the counter owner to survive, full invalidating-mutation coverage, wrap policy and synchronization. Cache source and cached result share protection; returned values are copied before unlocking. No sanitizer result is presented as proof against logical slot repurposing.

Corrections and explicit implementation contracts

  1. Fixed conversion rejects non-finite input before rounding/casting. The supplied range checks alone do not reject NaN.
  2. Fixed multiplication/division use proved int64 intermediates and checked destination narrowing. Negative nearest-even rescaling uses unsigned magnitudes and quotient/remainder; it never negates INT64_MIN or adds a potentially overflowing positive half-scale.
  3. C++23 signed shifting is not described as universally undefined. Instead the lab uses scaled multiplication and an explicit rounding algorithm to avoid confusing modular shift behavior, floor, truncation and desired rescaling.
  4. The source’s lrint quantizer follows the active rounding direction. The teaching quantizer declares nearest-even, validates finite samples/scales, and bounds the ratio before integer conversion. It is not represented as identical production behavior.
  5. Offset code q+8 is distinguished from two’s-complement INT4. Half-step quantization bounds exclude clipping and finite-parameter/evaluation error.
  6. Smaller groups trade adaptation for metadata, without a universal monotonic quality guarantee. Full-group asymptotic bits/sample are distinguished from exact ceiling-based storage for small/partial groups.
  7. Binary16 loss scaling is not presented as a cure for already-large values; BF16 keeps exponent width but not every FP32 endpoint or precision property.
  8. BF16/half NaNs are explicitly canonicalized in the toy converters; raw tensor words preserve bits without signaling-NaN arithmetic.
  9. Parser bounds use subtraction after offset validation; shape products are checked before multiplication; exact length and a 4096-element resource cap precede allocation.
  10. Zero-copy mapping requires representation, bounds, alignment, lifetime and permitted typed-access rules—not merely an offset divisible by four.
  11. The dump helper rejects zero/excessive row width, advances by remaining bounded length and uses a local formatting stream.
  12. Error metrics promote float operands before subtracting when evaluated in double. Scalar reconstruction error is not task-level accuracy.
  13. CRC detection, cryptographic integrity, authenticity, schema validity, publication and durability remain separate contracts. No security primitive or production format migration was implemented.

Corrections and teaching decisions

  1. The binary subtraction operands are 1753/1024 and 1751/1024, giving 2^-9; the supplied difference/exponent was incorrect.
  2. Numeric equality is not byte identity: signed zeros compare equal, while NaNs are unordered.
  3. The cross-product example loses the +1 during binary32 input conversion near 1e8, before product rounding. Later promotion cannot recover it.
  4. Distinct binary32 neighbors near 1e9 differ by 64; the source’s +32 example can round to the same input.
  5. The existing validated, widened float comparator is reused. An unchecked generic tolerance formula is not labeled production-safe.

Merge corrections and explicit policies

  1. The source’s complement-key ULP distance special-cases equal zeros but retains two zero slots for cross-zero intervals. The finite-only teaching metric collapses signed zeros in its key, rejects NaN/infinity, and verifies negative-min-subnormal to positive-min-subnormal distance 2.
  2. The supplied scalar tolerance formula rejects equal infinities but can also accept finite-versus-infinity and opposite infinities, via infinity ≤ infinity. These additional failure paths are reproduced. An alternative float-specific policy validates tolerances, handles non-finite values first, and widens finite comparisons. No production fix was made.
  3. Tiny/subnormal does not by itself mean an underflow flag; distinguish exactly representable tiny values from tininess/inexactness conditions.
  4. Raw-word quiet/signaling classification does not execute signaling-NaN arithmetic. Payload preservation through floating value transport/operations is not claimed.
  5. Rounding demonstrations check mode-setting success and restore the initial mode, rather than forcing nearest as the cleanup action. The laboratory restores direction, not all status flags.
  6. The matrix excerpt asserts before its fallback; do not describe identity return as the unconditional debug-build outcome.
  7. ULP is given an explicit local/directional convention at powers of two; finite maximum’s upward neighbor infinity is not an ordinary finite gap.

External standards-library references, checked for these points: - std::reduce explicitly permits reordering/regrouping; std::accumulate supplies the sequential left fold. - std::erase_if(std::unordered_map) is available since C++20 and removes matching entries; std::erase_if(std::vector) corresponds to erase–remove behavior on vector. - std::remove_if rearranges the retained range and requires container erasure to shrink it. - std::lower_bound, std::upper_bound, and std::equal_range require correctly partitioned ranges under their comparisons. - std::expected is standardized in C++23, not a C++20 implementation guarantee.

Translation units and linking

Translation units and linking

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C007 · Latest development: C007

Definition and mechanism

A translation unit is source after preprocessing together with its included material; module units add ownership and dependency rules. Compilation checks meaning and emits code/interface information; linking resolves implementation references. An unknown type is a frontend error, while a declared but undefined odr-used function commonly fails linking.

  • Compiler IR and machine instructions — Compilation and emitted code explain why separately translated units need a link step.

Scopes and name lookup

Scopes and name lookup

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C007 · Latest development: C008

Definition and mechanism

Lookup precedes overload resolution. A derived overload can hide base overloads; using Base::name restores candidates. A local int x=x reads the newly declared uninitialized local, not an outer integer.

Scope locates a name’s binding; lookup resolves a spelling to declarations. A local x can hide ::x without destroying it. A block-scope static has a local name but persistent storage. Qualified lookup names a namespace or class explicitly.

Prerequisites

  • Declarations and definitions — A declaration binds a name before scope and lookup can determine which binding is found.

Object construction and storage reuse

Object construction and storage reuse

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C007 · Latest development: C010

Definition and mechanism

Initialization creates an occupant whereas assignment replaces an existing occupant’s state. Ordinary constructor failure and post-target delegation failure have different complete-object cleanup behavior.

Storage needs sufficient size/alignment before object initialization can complete and start an ordinary lifetime. construct_at and destroy_at separate object life from backing storage. A cast alone does not construct arbitrary types. Some specified operations implicitly create implicit-lifetime objects; replacement and launder have additional preconditions.

M010 adds the resource-management view: placement construction or construct_at uses already-provided storage; it does not allocate that storage. destroy_at ends the occupant’s lifetime, while an arena separately decides when to reuse or release its bytes. Explicit destruction is safe only inside a protocol that prevents accidental second destruction. See Placement construction and explicit lifetime management.

Prerequisites

  • Storage duration and object lifetime — Backing-storage duration must be distinguished from the occupant’s start, destruction and replacement.

Used by

  • Object identity and generation handles — uses this prerequisite to establish its entity, lifetime, representation or lookup contract.
  • Return values and copy elision
  • Constructors and invariant establishment
  • Relocation versus move
  • Placement construction and explicit lifetime management

Standard-layout and trivial copyability

Standard-layout and trivial copyability

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C007 · Latest development: C009

Definition and mechanism

Rule-Zero composition is not itself a trivially-copyable, standard-layout or serialization promise. Hand-written/defaulted special functions can change triviality, and relocation is not generic permission to memmove a nontrivial owner.

Standard-layout is a structural language property supporting useful low-level layout reasoning; it does not promise no padding or a portable ABI. Trivial copyability permits particular byte-copy operations on valid objects/representations, not arbitrary byte validity or serialization. Aggregate, trivial and trivially-copyable are separate traits.

Prerequisites

  • ABI and object layout — ABI offsets and padding must be separated from standard-layout and byte-copy language eligibility.

Ordinary temporary destruction occurs at the full-expression’s end unless specified extension applies. Direct local binding can extend lifetime, but a returned parameter reference cannot transitively extend it. Aggregate braces and parentheses differ for reference members; new-initializer extension does not last as long as the allocated holder.

Prerequisites

  • Reference binding and converted temporaries — The chosen original or converted referent determines the destruction deadline.
  • Storage duration and object lifetime — The referent and its backing storage must survive each alias use.

Used by

  • Deferred captures and borrowed views
  • Ref-qualified accessors

Move casts and forwarding references

Move casts and forwarding references

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C008 · Latest development: C009

Definition and mechanism

Consumer constructors/assignments now distinguish the cast from actual resource transfer. Const can force copying, return std::move(local) can prevent NRVO, and move_if_noexcept selects a path based on usable construction properties.

std::move is an xvalue cast preserving constness, not a resource transfer. A deduced cv-unqualified T&& parameter can be a forwarding reference: lvalue arguments deduce T& and collapse to an lvalue reference. std::forward restores the category encoded by deduction.

Prerequisites

  • Auto decltype and reference collapsing — Deduction and collapsing encode the caller category forwarding restores.
  • Value categories and materialization — Expression category determines viable binding and whether temporary identity is needed.

Used by

Null pointers and optional access

Null pointers and optional access

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C008 · Latest development: C008

Definition and mechanism

A null pointer designates no object/function; nullptr_t converts to appropriate null pointer values without choosing an integer overload. A non-null pointer is not a lifetime or bounds proof. Deleting a typed null object pointer is valid, but bare delete nullptr is ill-formed.

Prerequisites

  • Pointer arithmetic and provenance — Storage relationships, bounds and lifetime distinguish valid access from a non-null value.

Used by

Later sources will deepen this same node; no empty dependent nodes are created.

Recall and next depth

Source and navigation

Teaching explanation and examples · Exact coverage · Dependency Map

Absence must be part of the type or contract

A null pointer represents “no object at this address-bearing interface”; dereferencing it is invalid. That makes raw pointer nullability an API question. If a parameter must always designate an object, a reference or explicitly non-null wrapper communicates more than a nullable pointer plus a comment.

Optional ownership and optional observation are different. A std::unique_ptr<T> may be empty while also owning when nonempty; T* may be nullable but usually says nothing about ownership; std::optional<T> stores an optional value without indirection. Choosing among them should follow lifetime and absence semantics rather than syntax convenience.

Null checks also do not prove lifetime. A non-null dangling pointer is still invalid, and a pointer can become logically stale even if its numeric address is later reused for a different object.

Tests for optional APIs should cover absent state, present state, transitions between them, moved-from ownership and invalid external identifiers. Avoid sentinel pointer values other than the language-defined null representation unless a low-level ABI explicitly owns that convention.

Multilevel pointer qualification

Multilevel pointer qualification

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C008 · Latest development: C008

Definition and mechanism

int** cannot implicitly become const int**: that would permit injection of an actually const object’s address into an original int*. int** can become const int* const*, whose intermediate read-only pointer blocks that assignment.

Prerequisites

  • Const qualification and shallow constness — Access-path qualification constrains nested conversions and member writes.

Used by

Later sources will deepen this same node; no empty dependent nodes are created.

Recall and next depth

Rebuild the hypothetical pointer injection step by step. Pending: qualification decomposition at further levels. Written coverage does not establish learner mastery.

Source and navigation

Teaching explanation and examples · Exact coverage · Dependency Map

Const applies at each indirection level

For a pointer chain, qualification is attached to a particular level rather than to the whole expression. const T* means the pointed-to T is not writable through that path; T* const means the pointer object itself cannot be reseated; const T* const combines both.

The distinction becomes safety-critical at multiple levels. Converting T** to const T** is not generally safe: if it were allowed, code could store a pointer-to-const object into the outer pointer and later write through the original T*, violating const protection. Qualification conversions therefore follow stricter rules than the familiar T* -> const T* case.

Engine APIs should avoid raw multi-level pointer mutation unless the ownership/indirection contract truly requires it. Spans, references to containers, output wrappers or typed handle arrays often express the real intent more clearly. A reconstruction exercise should explain each const position and demonstrate the classic unsafe hypothetical conversion.

Ref-qualified accessors

Ref-qualified accessors

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C008 · Latest development: C009

Definition and mechanism

Value-returning temporary accessors provide an owning result through direct construction or member movement. Both const and mutable rvalue policies remain required; the shorter M009 source example does not replace the four-way safe design.

Member &/&& qualifiers constrain the caller’s object category. Borrowed getters suit persistent owners; temporary getters can return owning values or be deleted. Destruction and partial construction

Destruction and partial construction

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C009 · Latest development: C010

Definition and mechanism

The destructor body precedes reverse member/base cleanup. Ordinary constructor failure destroys completed subobjects but not the incomplete whole; failure after a delegating target completed has a distinct cleanup case. RAII binds resource release to an owning object’s lifetime.

M010 extends the cleanup invariant to files, locks and native handles, and distinguishes destruction from external resource completion. A destructor can enqueue deferred release when an asynchronous user still holds the resource. Constructor failure remains safe when each acquired duty is immediately represented by a completed owner member.

Prerequisites

  • Member order and delegating constructors — Reverse cleanup depends on the order and completeness of subobject construction.
  • Storage duration and object lifetime — Cleanup belongs to an occupant’s lifetime, not merely a numeric storage address.

Used by

  • Assignment and exception guarantees
  • Move operations and moved-from states
  • RAII and resource handles

Part Supplied topic, expanded mechanism and narrative node
501 SCALARS AS ELEMENTS OF A NUMBER FIELD — Field laws make nonzero division and vector scaling meaningful; a floating type is only an approximation. Scalars fields and real-number models
502 REAL NUMBERS AND THE PROPERTIES GRAPHICS RELIES ON — Order, intervals and completeness justify real geometry; bounded machine values are not the complete number line. Scalars fields and real-number models
503 COMPLEX NUMBERS AND TWO-DIMENSIONAL ROTATION INTUITION — Unit complex multiplication rotates a plane; conjugation reverses it, and magnitude drift adds unwanted scale. Complex numbers and planar rotations
504 VECTORS AS GEOMETRIC DISPLACEMENTS — Free displacement survives translation of its starting point; location and movement are different roles. Vectors coordinates and affine points
505 VECTORS AS COORDINATE TUPLES — An ordered tuple gives components, but neither its basis nor physical role follows from storage shape. Vectors coordinates and affine points
506 THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN A VECTOR AND ITS COORDINATES — One physical vector has different coordinates in different bases; distinguish passive description from active motion. Vectors coordinates and affine points
507 VECTOR SPACES AND THEIR AXIOMS — Closure and vector-space laws enable consistent combinations; unit directions are a constrained non-example. Vector spaces subspaces and span
508 SUBSPACES — A nonempty subset closed under arbitrary two-vector combinations is a subspace; shifted planes need affine language. Vector spaces subspaces and span
509 LINEAR COMBINATIONS — Arbitrary coefficients generate movements, not necessarily averages; negative weights are valid. Vector spaces subspaces and span
510 SPAN — The span is the smallest subspace containing generators; redundant inputs do not enlarge it. Vector spaces subspaces and span
511 LINEAR INDEPENDENCE — A zero combination must have only zero coefficients for independence; near dependence is a numerical question. Basis coordinates and dimension
512 BASIS VECTORS — Spanning ensures reachability and independence ensures uniqueness; both are necessary for a basis. Basis coordinates and dimension
513 DIMENSION OF A VECTOR SPACE — Dimension counts basis elements over the selected field; a plane stored in three components still has dimension two. Basis coordinates and dimension
514 COORDINATE REPRESENTATION RELATIVE TO A BASIS — Coordinates weight an ordered basis; reconstruct the physical arrow before interpreting the tuple. Basis coordinates and dimension
515 CHANGING BASIS CONCEPTUALLY — Changing coordinates solves the new basis relation; near-parallel basis axes amplify coefficient uncertainty. Basis coordinates and dimension
516 STANDARD BASIS IN ℝ2\mathbb R^2 — The two standard unit axes reconstruct every planar coordinate; visual up/right conventions remain separate. Basis coordinates and dimension
517 STANDARD BASIS IN ℝ3\mathbb R^3 — Three standard unit axes reconstruct spatial coordinates; no universal camera forward direction follows. Basis coordinates and dimension
518 VECTOR ADDITION FROM THE PARALLELOGRAM RULE — Head-to-tail and parallelogram movement yield componentwise addition in a common basis. Vectors coordinates and affine points
519 SCALAR MULTIPLICATION OF VECTORS — Scalar scaling stretches and may reverse direction; velocity times elapsed time yields displacement with correct units. Vectors coordinates and affine points
520 VECTOR SUBTRACTION AS DISPLACEMENT DIFFERENCE — Subtraction adds the opposite vector; ordered point difference produces the displacement from one location to another. Vectors coordinates and affine points
521 AFFINE POINTS VERSUS FREE VECTORS — Affine points have no intrinsic zero; point differences and translations are valid without choosing an origin. Vectors coordinates and affine points
522 POSITION VECTORS AND WHY POINTS ARE NOT MATHEMATICALLY VECTORS — A position vector is point minus chosen origin; changing the origin cancels only in appropriate differences. Vectors coordinates and affine points
523 DIRECTION VECTORS — Direction answers which way and must be nonzero; translation does not affect it. Vectors coordinates and affine points
524 DISPLACEMENT VECTORS — Displacement records change in position and may validly be zero; units and frame must match. Vectors coordinates and affine points
525 UNIT VECTORS — Unit vectors retain direction but remove magnitude; the zero vector cannot satisfy this promise. Vectors coordinates and affine points
526 EUCLIDEAN VECTOR MAGNITUDE — Pythagoras yields Euclidean length only in orthonormal coordinates; a slanted basis needs its metric. Norms lengths and induced distances
527 SQUARED MAGNITUDE AND WHY GRAPHICS OFTEN AVOIDS SQUARE ROOTS — Squared length avoids some square roots in comparisons but is neither a norm nor a metric. Norms lengths and induced distances
528 NORMALIZING A VECTOR — Divide a nonzero vector by its length to normalize; this operation is nonlinear. Unit directions and safe normalization
529 ZERO-VECTOR NORMALIZATION AND ROBUST HANDLING — Reject zero/non-finite inputs and scale before squaring; application noise thresholds are a separate policy. Unit directions and safe normalization
530 L1 NORM — The first norm sums absolute coordinates; its unit ball is a coordinate-dependent diamond. Norms lengths and induced distances
531 L2 NORM — The second norm is Euclidean; Cauchy–Schwarz proves its triangle inequality. Norms lengths and induced distances
532 L-INFINITY NORM — The infinity norm is the maximum absolute component; its unit ball is a coordinate-dependent box. Norms lengths and induced distances
533 DISTANCE INDUCED BY A NORM — A norm induces a metric by measuring point difference; different norms can choose different nearest points. Norms lengths and induced distances
534 DOT PRODUCT ALGEBRAIC DEFINITION — The real-coordinate dot sums component products under an orthonormal metric assumption. Dot products and orthogonality
535 DOT PRODUCT GEOMETRIC INTERPRETATION — Dot measures magnitude-weighted alignment; it equals cosine only for unit inputs. Dot products and orthogonality
536 DERIVING THE COSINE-ANGLE RELATION FOR THE DOT PRODUCT — Compare an expanded squared difference with the cosine rule to derive the angle relation. Dot products and orthogonality
537 ORTHOGONAL VECTORS — Orthogonality is zero inner product; zero has no angle, and numerical tests need scale-aware criteria. Dot products and orthogonality
538 VECTOR PROJECTION ONTO ANOTHER VECTOR — Require the along-axis remainder to be orthogonal to derive the target squared-length denominator. Projection rejection and scalar components
539 VECTOR REJECTION FROM ANOTHER VECTOR — Rejection removes the projected component and enables tangent-plane movement. Projection rejection and scalar components
540 SCALAR PROJECTION — Signed scalar projection is length along a target direction, not the coefficient multiplying the target vector. Projection rejection and scalar components
541 GRAM MATRIX CONCEPT — Pairwise basis dots form a Gram metric; coordinates measure physical lengths through this matrix. Gram matrices and coordinate metrics
542 Cross product definition in ℝ3\mathbb R^3 — Reconstructed enrichment: perpendicular oriented-area vector definition precedes the supplied determinant derivation. Cross products and oriented area
543 CROSS PRODUCT DETERMINANT DERIVATION — Signed coordinate-plane minors yield the cross formula; direct expansion verifies perpendicularity. Cross products and oriented area
544 CROSS PRODUCT GEOMETRIC MEANING — Cross produces an area normal, not merely an arbitrary perpendicular direction. Cross products and oriented area
545 CROSS-PRODUCT MAGNITUDE AND PARALLELOGRAM AREA — Cross magnitude equals base times height; triangle area is half the parallelogram area. Cross products and oriented area
546 CROSS-PRODUCT ORIENTATION AND THE RIGHT-HAND RULE — Input order and a chosen positive orientation fix the cross sign; mirrored transforms add a determinant sign. Coordinate handedness and orientation
547 WHY THE CROSS PRODUCT IS SPECIAL TO THREE DIMENSIONS — Ordinary graphics cross identifies bivectors with vectors in three dimensions; higher dimensions need qualifications. Coordinate handedness and orientation
548 SCALAR TRIPLE PRODUCT — Dotting an oriented area with a third movement produces a signed scalar volume. Triple products and signed volume
549 TRIPLE PRODUCT AS SIGNED VOLUME — Triple product is parallelepiped volume; a four-point tetrahedron has one sixth of its absolute value. Triple products and signed volume
550 VECTOR TRIPLE-PRODUCT IDENTITY — Expand a nested cross into dot-weighted vectors; cross grouping is not associative. Triple products and signed volume
551 ANGLES BETWEEN VECTORS — Nonzero finite directions define an unsigned angle in the interval from zero to pi. Robust vector angles
552 ROBUST ANGLE COMPUTATION WITH atan2 — Scale first and use atan2 of cross length and dot; a signed angle additionally needs an oriented plane. Robust vector angles
553 REFLECTION OF A DIRECTION ACROSS A NORMAL — Reverse the normal component to reflect across a plane; unit-normal and general-normal formulas differ. Reflection refraction and shading directions
554 REFRACTION GEOMETRY FROM SNELL’S LAW — Snell scales the tangent component; a negative transmitted squared cosine indicates total internal reflection. Reflection refraction and shading directions
555 HALF-VECTOR CONSTRUCTION IN SHADING — Normalize the sum of unit outward light/view directions; opposite inputs have no unique half-vector. Reflection refraction and shading directions
556 TANGENT VECTORS ON A SURFACE — Surface derivatives or triangle edges span tangent movement; texture tangents may retain physical stretch. Surface tangents normals and bitangents
557 NORMAL VECTORS ON A SURFACE — Geometric normals measure perpendicularity; shading normals can differ and need their own contract. Surface tangents normals and bitangents
558 BITANGENT VECTORS — Solve edge/UV equations for a second tangent; degenerate UVs and mirrored-island signs need explicit handling. Surface tangents normals and bitangents
559 ORTHONORMAL BASES — Unit perpendicular axes give an identity Gram matrix and simple dot-based reconstruction. Orthonormal frames and Gram-Schmidt
560 CONSTRUCTING AN ORTHONORMAL BASIS FROM ONE DIRECTION — A least-aligned helper yields a nondegenerate frame from one direction, but does not ensure continuity. Orthonormal frames and Gram-Schmidt
561 GRAM-SCHMIDT ORTHOGONALIZATION — Repeated projection removal preserves span while producing perpendicular axes for independent generators. Orthonormal frames and Gram-Schmidt
562 MODIFIED GRAM-SCHMIDT AND NUMERICAL STABILITY — Measuring updated residuals changes rounding behavior; reorthogonalization cannot repair uncertain input rank. Orthonormal frames and Gram-Schmidt
563 HANDEDNESS OF COORDINATE BASES — Triple-product sign classifies an ordered basis relative to chosen orientation, not memory layout. Coordinate handedness and orientation
564 RIGHT-HANDED COORDINATE SYSTEMS — Positive frame orientation is preserved by proper rotations and cyclic axis permutations. Coordinate handedness and orientation
565 LEFT-HANDED COORDINATE SYSTEMS — A reflected frame has opposite orientation while preserving Euclidean distances; API conventions need separate statements. Coordinate handedness and orientation
566 ORIENTATION TESTS IN 2D USING SIGNED AREA — Signed doubled triangle area supplies a two-dimensional orientation predicate with a documented axis convention. Coordinate handedness and orientation
567 ORIENTATION TESTS IN 3D USING TRIPLE PRODUCTS — Four-point triple products decide plane side and coplanarity under an explicit ordering convention. Coordinate handedness and orientation
568 BARYCENTRIC COORDINATES AS AFFINE WEIGHTS — Triangle weights sum to one for affine meaning; nonnegative weights identify the convex interior. Barycentric coordinates and interpolation
569 DERIVING BARYCENTRIC COORDINATES FOR A TRIANGLE — Edge Gram solves or signed area ratios recover weights; degeneracy and off-plane residuals remain separate checks. Barycentric coordinates and interpolation
570 INTERPOLATING ATTRIBUTES WITH BARYCENTRIC COORDINATES — The same affine weights interpolate attributes; nonlinear encoding and unit length require additional policies. Barycentric coordinates and interpolation
571 AFFINE COMBINATIONS VERSUS LINEAR COMBINATIONS — Only sum-one weights preserve point translation; sum-zero weights describe a displacement. Convex combinations and convex hulls
572 CONVEX COMBINATIONS — Nonnegative affine weights produce convex mixtures; extrapolation is affine but not convex. Convex combinations and convex hulls
573 CONVEX SETS — A convex set contains every line segment between its members; a boundary need not be convex. Convex combinations and convex hulls
574 CONVEX HULL INTUITION — A convex hull is all finite convex mixtures and may fill source concavities or holes. Convex combinations and convex hulls
575 MINKOWSKI SUM INTUITION — Pairwise set-coordinate addition represents sweeps and expansions; symmetric robot dilation is a special case. Minkowski sums and support mappings
576 MINKOWSKI DIFFERENCE INTUITION — Collision difference means A plus reflected B here, not set subtraction; overlap is origin membership. Minkowski sums and support mappings
577 SUPPORT FUNCTIONS OF CONVEX SHAPES — Support scalar and support point differ; opposite-direction support queries construct difference extrema on demand. Minkowski sums and support mappings
578 HOMOGENEOUS COORDINATES AS PROJECTIVE REPRESENTATIVES — Nonzero common scale defines projective equivalence; finite representatives divide by their final coordinate. Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division
579 POINTS AND DIRECTIONS THROUGH HOMOGENEOUS ww — Homogeneous one distinguishes points from zero-tagged directions under affine translation; zero tuple is invalid projectively. Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division
580 NORMALIZED DEVICE-COORDINATE INTUITION AS A VECTOR-SPACE MAPPING — NDC standardizes device-coordinate ranges, not length; perspective division is nonlinear and follows clipping. Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division
581 DUAL VECTORS AND COVECTORS — Covectors are linear scalar measurement rules; a metric hides their distinction from ordinary vectors. Covectors linear functionals and normal transforms
582 WHY SURFACE NORMALS TRANSFORM DIFFERENTLY FROM POSITIONS — Preserve the normal’s pairing with transformed tangents to derive inverse transpose; singular cases need policy. Covectors linear functionals and normal transforms
583 LINEAR FUNCTIONALS — A linear functional distributes across weighted vector sums; its kernel contains movements it measures as zero. Covectors linear functionals and normal transforms
584 EXTERIOR-PRODUCT INTUITION — Exterior algebra retains areas and volumes without requiring a vector-valued cross in every dimension. Exterior products and geometric algebra
585 WEDGE PRODUCT AS ORIENTED AREA CONCEPT — Antisymmetric bilinear wedges encode oriented area; dependent generators have zero wedge. Exterior products and geometric algebra
586 GEOMETRIC-ALGEBRA MOTIVATION FOR GRAPHICS — The geometric product combines dot and wedge; plane elements connect to complex-like rotation structure. Exterior products and geometric algebra
587 FLOATING-POINT VECTOR STORAGE IN C++ — Floating storage has bounded precision and target layout; trivial copying does not certify external representation. Vector storage SIMD and boundary layouts
588 VEC2 DATA STRUCTURE DESIGN — A two-component value type needs initialization, safe access and explicit semantic roles. Vector value types and component access
589 VEC3 DATA STRUCTURE DESIGN — Three-component storage supports spatial operations but is not automatically a point, normal or unit direction. Vector value types and component access
590 VEC4 DATA STRUCTURE DESIGN — Four-component storage can serve distinct roles; homogeneous coordinates and quaternions require separate contracts. Vector value types and component access
591 OPERATOR OVERLOADS FOR VECTOR ARITHMETIC — Overloads should express unambiguous vector arithmetic; name dot, cross and componentwise multiplication. Vector value types and component access
592 SWIZZLES AND COMPONENT ACCESS — Read swizzles reorder components; writable swizzles need temporary-copy and duplicate-destination policies. Vector value types and component access
593 ALIGNMENT OF VECTOR TYPES — Measure alignment, size and stride; greater alignment may add padding and is not a performance guarantee. Vector storage SIMD and boundary layouts
594 PACKED VERSUS ALIGNED VEC3 REPRESENTATIONS — Compact storage and aligned compute types can coexist with explicit conversion at boundaries. Vector storage SIMD and boundary layouts
595 SIMD IMPLEMENTATION OF VECTOR ARITHMETIC — SIMD within one vector differs from SIMD across objects; layouts, reductions and FMA affect throughput and results. Vector storage SIMD and boundary layouts
596 APPROXIMATE VECTOR EQUALITY — Exact, componentwise, distance, angular and ULP comparisons answer different questions; closeness is not transitive. Vector tolerances and finite-state diagnostics
597 DEBUGGING NaN VECTORS — Catch the first invalid input or operation using finite checks; NaN propagation can silently skip decisions. Vector tolerances and finite-state diagnostics
598 VECTOR INVARIANTS IN ENGINE APIs — Validated wrappers establish finite/unit promises and operations must preserve or explicitly drop them. Coordinate-space types and validated invariants
599 DISTINGUISHING WORLD-SPACE AND LOCAL-SPACE VECTOR TYPES — Space-tagged points, vectors and transforms reject broad frame mistakes; dynamic local-frame identity remains a separate issue. Coordinate-space types and validated invariants
600 Reconstructing a Production-Ready Vec3 Library from First Principles — Reconstruct the scalar library from the mathematics, then verify contracts with edge cases and seeded properties. Inline capstone and tests

M007 - Parts 101-112

The supplied source has exactly twelve parts, 101–112. The revised M007 was integrated into the same coverage, not counted as new parts. M008 supplies 113–126, M009 supplies 127–147, and M010 supplies 148–160. Volume 02 is 4/12 accepted sources, not completed Parts 101–300.

Part Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
101 Translation units and linking — Source → preprocessing → semantic compilation → object/BMI → link. A declaration can permit compilation while an absent implementation fails linking; BMI is not object code.
102 Declarations and definitions — Every definition is a declaration, not conversely. extern int x declares; int x=0 defines. Forward class is incomplete; fixed-underlying opaque enum is complete.
103 One Definition Rule — Multiple translation units must describe coherent entities. Header guards are per-TU; ordinary external definitions and inline/template exceptions have different constraints.
104 Scopes and name lookup — Scope belongs to a name; qualified lookup selects a context; hiding changes lookup without deleting the hidden object. ADL adds associated candidates.
105 Storage duration and object lifetime — Automatic/static/thread/dynamic classify storage. A block-scope static outlives the block; a local pointer and its dynamic pointee have distinct durations.
106 Object construction and storage reuse — Sufficient aligned storage and completed initialization establish an ordinary object lifetime. destroy_at can end the object while the byte buffer remains; casts do not construct arbitrary objects.
107 Object identity and generation handles — Equal values need not be one object, and reused addresses host different occupants. A slot/generation needs live-registry validation, not merely a non-sentinel index.
108 Fixed-width integer types — sizeof(char)=1 C++ byte; CHAR_BIT≥8. int has minimum capacity, not a universal32-bit width. Exact/least/fast and size_t express different requirements.
109 Scoped enums and validated domains — Scoped enumerators and no implicit integer conversion reduce accidents. Explicit underlying width does not validate received codes; states and combinable flags need separate designs.
110 Aggregate initialization — C++20/23 aggregate criteria are not the older user-provided-constructor rule. Designators follow member declaration order. Braces may select initializer-list or ordinary constructors instead.
111 Class access and invariants — struct defaults members and bases public; class defaults them private. Both are class types. Record/invariant intent is convention, not a syntactic capability limit.
112 Standard-layout and trivial copyability — Alignment creates internal/tail padding. Traits do not imply array traversal, packing, serialization or GPU compatibility. Named x/y/z require explicit indexing or actual array storage.

M008 - Parts 113-126

All fourteen supplied parts are accepted. Source numbering audits coverage; it does not divide the teaching story. M009 now develops parameter passing and value transfer in Parts127–147.

Part Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
113 References and aliases — Binding establishes an alias; assignment acts on the referent. A reference-to-pointer can reseat that pointer, unlike a reference to its pointee.
114 Reference binding and converted temporaries — Type/category select the referent. const int& can track the original; const double& can bind a converted snapshot. Arrays keep extent through array references; bit-fields require special handling.
115 Temporary lifetime extension and Move casts and forwarding references — Direct local binding can extend a temporary, not transitive function-return aliases. Braces/parentheses/new exceptions matter; move is a cast, and deduced T&& forwarding collapses references.
116 Value categories and materialization — lvalue/xvalue identify, prvalue produces; glvalue and rvalue overlap at xvalue. A named T&& is an lvalue in ordinary use. decltype(name) differs from decltype((name)).
117 Pointer arithmetic and provenance — A pointer is an access path, not ownership. Null/object/one-past/invalid states differ; dereference requires live, aligned, type-accessible in-range storage.
118 Null pointers and optional access — nullptr distinguishes pointer absence from integer zero. Typed null deletion is valid; bare delete nullptr is ill-formed. Non-null does not prove lifetime.
119 Named members versus array elements — Array-relative positions zero through N may be formed; only zero through N-1 dereferenced. Same-array subtraction must fit ptrdiff_t. Adjacent members do not authorize array indexing.
120 Pointer arithmetic and provenance — A pointer’s storage relationship is not manufactured by a plausible integer. Specified round trips do not resurrect occupants or authorize arbitrary arithmetic; P3407 is discussion, not C++23 law.
121 Borrow invalidation and logical identity — Vector reallocation can dangle a borrow; swap assignment can leave a live slot with a different logical owner. Valid handles do not certify previous component references.
122 Deferred captures and borrowed views — Reference members, spans, string views and captured this pointers require referent lifetime. Copying a view does not own its buffer; an owning capture supplies a different contract.
123 Const qualification and shallow constness and Auto decltype and reference collapsing — Read-only access is not global immutability. Top-level const is often dropped by value deduction; actual const objects cannot be made writable by casts.
124 Multilevel pointer qualification — Separate pointer and pointee qualification. int** to const int** would enable unsafe injection; intermediate const blocks it. Const span descriptors do not imply const elements.
125 Ref-qualified accessors — const member functions restrict the object path; &/&& constrain caller category. Persistent getters can borrow; both mutable and const temporary getters need value/deleted policies.
126 Logical constness and mutable caches — Eligible mutable members permit representation changes under const access. Cache/source invariants require invalidation and synchronization; return protected snapshots. Mutable closures are not automatically thread-safe.
