M009 - Parts 127-147

The supplied source contains exactly twenty-one parts. At acceptance, it extended Volume02 to Parts101–147; M010 subsequently added Parts148–160. Teaching headings remain concept-led; exact coverage is recorded in the current ledger.

Part Definition, mechanism, and reconstruction cue
127 Parameter passing and sink contracts — Argument expressions initialize separate value-parameter objects. Lvalue/xvalue/prvalue routes differ; a sink retains/transforms a value, and copied pointer members still alias.
128 References and aliases — Mutable/const/rvalue reference parameters borrow with different access and consumption contracts. Aliased source/destination references can change a sequential update’s result.
129 Parameter passing and sink contracts — Pointer parameters copy pointer values; T*& or pointer-output protocols can reseat caller state. Null optionality must be documented; array parameters adjust to pointers without extent enforcement.
130 Return values and copy elision — Result objects can be constructed directly; NRVO is optional while appropriate same-type prvalue initialization requires no intermediate transfer. Eligible local/parameter return expressions implicitly move in C++23.
131 Ref-qualified accessors and Temporary lifetime extension — Reference/view results retain owner lifetime/invalidation obligations. Temporary getters require policies for const rvalues too; decltype(auto) can return a reference through parentheses.
132 Constructors and invariant establishment — Members/bases initialize before the body. Initializers establish state; body assignments replace it. Constructor failure and factory error results are different protocols.
133 Default and value initialization — Default, zero, aggregate and value initialization differ. First-declaration defaulting is not an empty user-provided body; braces do not universally initialize every scalar.
134 Member order and delegating constructors — Declaration order governs members regardless of colon-list spelling. Provider-before-dependent order establishes correct construction/reverse cleanup.
135 Member order and delegating constructors — Delegation centralizes a target initialization path, then runs its own body. The target is the sole initializer; cycles are ill-formed.
136 Destruction and partial construction — Destructor body precedes reverse subobject cleanup; failed ordinary construction destroys completed subobjects. Delegating-target completion changes the whole-object cleanup case.
137 Copy semantics and resource identity — New-object copying follows members’ semantic operations; equal-sign initialization is not assignment. Pointer/reference copies preserve associations rather than clone referents.
138 Assignment and exception guarantees — Existing-object replacement must handle old ownership, self-aliasing and failure. Prepare before commit; reference/const members can delete generated assignment.
139 Copy semantics and resource identity — Deep/shallow are contract choices, not good/bad labels. Pixel values may duplicate, handles identify, graph clones remap; copy-on-write adds mutation/lifetime/synchronization costs.
140 Move operations and moved-from states — New-object moves can take resources and repair source state; scalar/inline members need not become cheaper. Ordinary constructors alone do not suppress implicit move generation.
141 Move operations and moved-from states — Move assignment also handles the destination’s former resource and self-move. Allocator policy can prevent constant-time adoption.
142 Move casts and forwarding references — move changes category, not ownership itself; const remains const. Explicit local-return moves can inhibit NRVO; move_if_noexcept selects a transfer access path.
143 Move operations and moved-from states — Source lifetime continues after moving. Valid-but-unspecified is not destroyed or undefined; operation preconditions still apply. A custom empty source needs an explicit maintained invariant.
144 Return values and copy elision — Immovable types can use guaranteed direct result construction; a named-local fallback still needs usable operations. Accessible destruction remains required.
145 Rules of Three Five and Zero — Destructor/copy constructor/copy assignment are coordinated raw-owner decisions; copying may instead be deleted. It is a design heuristic, not a compiler mandate.
146 Special member generation and traits — Five adds both moves. User-declared versus user-provided matters; a defaulted destructor suppresses dedicated implicit moves, while move-constructible traits can still classify copying as viable.
147 Rules of Three Five and Zero — Compose tested member owners rather than repeat transfer/release logic. Zero does not forbid ordinary constructors or prove cross-member invariants; Relocation versus move remains a versioned research bridge.

M010 - Parts 148-160

M010 continues the same Volume 02 story from Rule-of-Zero composition into the concrete ownership and lifetime protocols underneath it. The source specifies Parts 148–160. Repository paths named in the pasted lesson are source-provided examples and remain To verify until their repositories/revisions are inspected. These entries identify coverage; the expanded teaching narrative is in Volume 02.

Part Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
148 RAII and resource handles — Bind matched acquisition/release responsibility to a live owner; scope exit handles early return and unwinding. External asynchronous use can require deferred reclamation.
149 RAII and resource handles — Each fully acquired resource must immediately enter an owner; completed subobjects clean up if construction fails. CPU ownership does not alone establish GPU completion.
150 Ownership and non-owning views — Ownership means responsibility for ending use/lifetime; a borrow provides access without extending lifetime.
151 Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership — unique_ptr is a move-only exclusive owner; get() borrows while release() transfers responsibility.
152 Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership — A custom deleter pairs a native handle with its actual release protocol; deleter state/type can affect representation and conversion safety.
153 Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership — shared_ptr copies join a control block’s strong ownership group; object and control-block lifetimes may differ.
154 Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership — Reference-count operations have costs; control-block coordination does not synchronize arbitrary pointee operations.
155 Weak observation and ownership cycles — A weak edge avoids extending object lifetime; lock() safely attempts to obtain a temporary strong owner and can break cycles.
156 Weak observation and ownership cycles — enable_shared_from_this joins an existing owner group; never build an independent shared_ptr control block from this.
157 Placement construction and explicit lifetime management — Allocation functions acquire raw storage; new-expressions combine allocation and initialization. Size, alignment, construction, failure cleanup and deallocation must match.
158 Placement construction and explicit lifetime management — Arrays require correct count-aware construction/destruction and matching new[]/delete[]; containers usually own this protocol more safely.
159 Placement construction and explicit lifetime management — Placement construction/construct_at begins an object lifetime in adequate pre-existing storage; it does not allocate that storage.
160 Placement construction and explicit lifetime management — Explicit destruction ends an occupant’s lifetime, not necessarily storage. Reuse, transparent replacement and laundering have distinct conditions.

The source discusses resource owners, smart pointers, manual allocation, placement construction, array ownership and lifetime restart. Its repository examples (KairoRenderer/VulkanBuffer.cppm, Maveb/.../MetalPtr.hpp) are not represented as live-inspected code findings here.

M011 — Parts 161–180: a request changes shape and a backend changes implementation

Source status: authored reconstruction from the canonical integrated 180-chunk / original 3,000-part curriculum contract, not a received M011 teaching transcript. Teaching placement: the continuous C++ narrative, immediately after the M010 ownership chapter and before the API-publication chapter. The concrete example follows a typed renderer request through a polymorphic backend; it does not substitute a dictionary entry for each numbered part.

Part Reason the concept appears in the request-to-backend narrative Reconstruction and evidence
161 A command record can hold overlapping alternatives but not several simultaneously active objects. Raw union active-member and lifetime rules; trivial union assignment in tested C++20 lab.
162 A request must carry its active alternative rather than guess an interpretation from bytes. std::variant, get_if, holds_alternative and visit, replacement and exceptional empty state; executable request-state checks.
163 An editor should depend on the backend’s promised operations, not the native implementation. Base/derived interface contract contrasted with composition and closed alternatives.
164 A derived object contains a base subobject with its own identity and layout constraints. Static versus dynamic object view; no invented vptr byte layout.
165 A base reference must call the selected backend’s implementation. Virtual dispatch with observable CountingBackend result in the lab.
166 Indirection has implementation and performance consequences, but no mandated vtable layout. Implementation-model explanation, devirtualization caveat and proposed measurement controls.
167 A backend contract needs operations without constructing the incomplete base. Pure virtual operation and abstract interface; concrete derived override.
168 An owner typed as base must destroy the concrete derived object correctly. Virtual destructor through std::unique_ptr<Backend>; derived-destruction assertion.
169 Copying a derived object into a base value can erase its specialized identity. MeshObject / NamedObject slicing contrasted with a base reference; tested.
170 A backend can implement multiple independent interfaces, creating distinct base views. Multiple inheritance, ambiguity and subobject-adjustment explanation.
171 A diamond may duplicate a common base unless virtual inheritance shares it. Diamond with two paths through a virtual Root; identical subobject address test.
172 Upcasting to a public base is different from a downcast that assumes an actual derived object. static_cast guarantees and the conditions it does not dynamically test.
173 A diagnostic needs to ask whether the runtime backend really has a concrete type. dynamic_cast success and failed pointer cast tested; RTTI and design cautions.
174 Byte reinterpretation must not masquerade as object construction or safe aliasing. reinterpret_cast limitations; byte views and bit_cast alternatives.
175 Removing const qualification is not the same as making a const object writable. const_cast and genuine-const/ownership rules.
176 Operators should communicate a domain operation and preserve invariants. Resource handles versus durations and inappropriate hidden side effects.
177 A handle’s equality includes its generation, not merely a reused slot. Defaulted operator== derived from <=> and two identity assertions.
178 Identifiers need meaningful ordering; NaN can make floating comparison unordered. Strong integer ordering, partial floating ordering and strict-weak-order concerns.
179 Overload selection is a compile-time decision based on arguments and conversions. Integer/double overload calls tested; ambiguity and conversion cautions.
180 Virtual implementation selection and default-argument binding happen at different times. Base default 2 with derived body produces 20; derived default 7 produces 70; tested.

This checksum comparison establishes identical bytes for the compared artifact; the compiler run remains a single compiler/platform witness, not every possible C++ implementation. M012 — Parts 181–200: typed asset requests, deferred callbacks and transactional publication

Original part / exact source title Why the renderer story requires it and where the evidence sits
181 · Implicit conversions and converting constructors A raw integer is not automatically a meaningful byte count; the chapter contrasts implicit construction with deliberate unit conversion.

187 · Callable objects and functors AddBytes::operator() carries state for a progress update; pointer-member lifetime remains a borrow.
188 · Lambdas as generated closure types The closure object combines an operation with stored or referenced captured state; no concrete closure byte layout is claimed.

193 · Strong, basic, and no-throw exception guarantees Prepare privately, publish once, compare stored state and native-handle counts after failure; guarantee is limited to stated observable state.
194 · Error codes versus exceptions in engine code Empty input and operational failure map to typed UploadError; exception categories remain an implementation detail within the bounded example.
195 · Assertions as programmer-error checks The lab’s verify is active under NDEBUG; external input checks and internal invariant failures use distinct policies.
196 · Undefined behavior and optimizer assumptions Invalid lifetime, out-of-bounds, aliasing and data-race examples are explained, never deliberately run as undefined behavior.
197 · Strict aliasing rules A raw file cannot be safely interpreted as a typed struct merely by pointer cast; object type-access and lifetime conditions are explicit.
198 · Object representation, bytes, and std::bit_cast IEEE binary32 bit_cast is tested under platform assertions; a separate little-endian serializer establishes portable file bytes.
199 · Trivial, trivially copyable, and standard-layout properties WireHeader traits are checked without falsely asserting its raw storage is a six-byte file layout; differing type categories are explained.
200 · Designing a resource-owning C++ type from blank memory to safe API Resource develops empty/owning/moved-from states, matching release, deleted copy, noexcept move and a device-outlives-owner contract; AssetStore adds a failure-atomic publication boundary.

M014 — Parts 217–230: one tile planner and its compile-time policy decisions

Original part and authoritative title First-use requirement and inspectable witness

226 · CRTP static polymorphism RecorderBase<CountingRecorder>::record calls record_impl via a derived cast; the derived-object precondition and nonvirtual semantics are explained and tested.

228 · Tag dispatch VerifyPayloadTag and MetadataOnlyTag select overloads that verify real bytes or deliberately produce only a manifest; invalid length is rejected in verified mode.
229 · Empty-base optimization A holder deriving from an empty policy is measured beside an ordinary empty-policy member; observed sizes are toolchain-specific, not promised.
230 · [[no_unique_address]] and zero-size policy storage A policy member eligible for overlap is used in TilePlanner and an isolated holder; local sizeof results and MSVC portability differences are documented.

Evidence limits: the code plans tiles and checks an optional CPU byte span. It does not allocate native graphics memory, enqueue a GPU transfer, validate a device format, establish a real asynchronous transaction, measure speed, or certify a portable ABI layout. Its MetadataOnlyTag deliberately does not check that a payload exists, so the result cannot be represented as a verified upload. constinit supplies no synchronization, CRTP supplies no runtime plugin selection, and local object-size observations cannot be treated as standard-required sizes. No live Kairo/Maveb repository sources were re-inspected. Research and project-code gates remain open.

Language-source anchors: cppreference if constexpr, constexpr, consteval, constinit, empty base optimization, [[no_unique_address]], including implementation notes, and class-template type traits. These clarify specific language rules; they do not stand in for a real cross-compiler benchmark.

M015 — Parts 231–250: growing the asset registry without losing identities

Source status: authored reconstruction from the original integrated 180-chunk / 3,000-part curriculum contract. No received M015 teaching transcript is claimed. Original part — exact authoritative title Where the problem forces its use; evidence
231 · std::vector internal size/capacity/storage model A bounded asset depot begins growing; the lab distinguishes live elements from reserved storage and checks contiguous values.
232 · std::vector geometric growth Derive the geometric relocation sum and amortized append cost; the lab observes capacity 2→4 on its local implementation, not a standard-prescribed factor.
233 · std::vector iterator and pointer invalidation Growth invalidates old element pointers/iterators; the lab checks the growth event without accessing stale addresses.
234 · std::vector reserve versus resize reserve(2) does not create elements; resize(5) constructs new ones with the tested default int values.
235 · std::array fixed contiguous storage Compile-time fixed channel/counter sequences keep their own element storage and do not use vector growth semantics; array indexing tested.
236 · std::deque segmented storage Editor arrival/consumption needs front/back operations without pretending an entire deque is a single contiguous allocation; front/back/index test.
237 · std::list node-based storage Editing work transfers nodes while retaining iterators to unaffected nodes; splice tested.
238 · std::forward_list singly linked storage A singly linked worklist removes a successor using erase_after, needing the predecessor iterator; tested.
239 · std::map balanced-tree semantics Ordered asset names with logarithmic comparison-based operations and ordered iteration; tree shape remains an implementation detail.
240 · std::set ordered unique-key semantics A set of IDs removes duplicates and preserves comparison order; 8,3,8,5 yields three unique values.
241 · std::unordered_map hash-table semantics Persistent name-to-generation-handle index uses owned std::string keys; its hash lookup and rehash rules are explained.
242 · std::unordered_set hash-table semantics Pending-name membership without mapped values; duplicate insertion and contains tested.
243 · Hash function quality and collision behavior A deliberately constant hash places all 24 distinct names in one bucket without corrupting key equality; lookup correctness is tested.
244 · Load factor and hash-table rehashing load_factor=n/b, max_load_factor(0.5) and reserve(96) illustrate the bucket policy; old rehash-invalidated iterators are never dereferenced.
245 · std::priority_queue heap-backed abstraction Uploads require priority selection, plus explicit sequence-number tie-breaking because the adapter alone does not guarantee stability.
246 · std::stack adapter semantics Editor undo/traversal needs LIFO; push 7,8 then pop yields 8 before 7.
247 · std::queue adapter semantics Incoming jobs need FIFO; push 7,8 then pop yields 7 before 8.
248 · std::span as a non-owning contiguous view A checksum consumes byte data synchronously without copying it, with owner lifetime and reallocation constraints explicit.
249 · std::string storage and small-string optimization concept Asset names own characters; locally observed short/long capacities 15/1000 are not portable SSO or allocation guarantees.
250 · std::string_view lifetime rules Borrowed path substring "stone" is copied into an owning string before the source is changed; substring may lack a terminating NUL.

Precisely bounded claims: AssetRegistry is a single-threaded teaching model. It does not prove correct concurrent deletion, GPU fence retirement, persistent identity across sessions, byte-for-byte stable ABI, all custom allocator/hash exception behaviors, uniformly fast worst-case hashing, or measured performance of competing containers. The example is stronger than an append-only depot—it supports removal and generational reuse—but intentionally lacks the full production allocator/threading/hot-reload model. M016 — Parts 251–270: the asset registry becomes a query and transformation pipeline

Provenance: authored reconstruction from the canonical integrated 180-chunk / original 3,000-part contract, not a received M016 lesson transcript. Original part / exact title First-use problem and inspectable evidence
251 · std::optional presence-or-absence semantics find_optional returns a value-copied logical handle for rock.mesh and nullopt for an absent name; it cannot explain an invalid input.
252 · std::variant visitation Inspect, Upload and Evict are closed, distinct request shapes; std::visit and an overload set count each command.
253 · std::any runtime type erasure Open-ended diagnostics hold a copied string, reject any_cast<int> with bad_any_cast and release the value at reset.

256 · Structured bindings auto [..] copies the pair; auto& [..] aliases the original and updates its error count.
257 · Iterators and iterator categories C++20 static assertions distinguish input, forward, bidirectional and random-access capabilities across stream, forward_list, list and deque.
258 · Contiguous iterators and pointer-like optimization Vector iterators are contiguous; deque iterators are random-access but not contiguous; both facts statically checked.

261 · std::stable_sort stability guarantee A descending-priority sort preserves sky.tex before ui.tex and brick.mesh before rock.mesh within equal-priority groups.
262 · std::partition and partition-based algorithms Partition mesh vs nonmesh, validate both sides and recover the boundary with partition_point; no false sorting/stability claim.
263 · std::lower_bound binary search contract Sort by the byte key and find first non-less-than-48 position, index one; note forward-iterator increment cost.
264 · std::upper_bound and equal ranges Upper bound for 48 gives index three, equal_range returns the matching [1,3) interval; a bidirectional heterogeneous comparator is supplied.
265 · std::find and linear search cost One-off name lookup scans an owned name vector without rebuilding an index; compare with the live registry’s maintained hash index.
266 · std::transform data-parallel expression Convert owned asset records into byte counts with a back_inserter to a separate destination; no automatic SIMD/threading claim.
267 · std::accumulate and reduction order Ordered left fold with std::size_t{0} yields the exact small payload total 304; explain why accumulator type matters.
268 · std::reduce and relaxed ordering implications Integer test also yields 304; a binary64 regrouping demonstration produces 3 vs 4, without pretending this library must select one grouping.
269 · std::remove erase idiom remove_if produces a retained logical prefix but leaves vector size six until erase destroys the removed suffix; final IDs are 1,3,5.
270 · std::erase_if modern container erasure C++20 erase_if removes two texture rows from the report copy and separately removes one matching unordered diagnostic entry, without evicting the live registry.

M017 — Parts 271–290: lazy asset queries, allocation lifetimes and compiled API boundaries

M018 — Parts 291–300: the same asset service becomes a typed, hidden and measurable engine API

Canonical boundary: original curriculum Parts 291–300 are taught in one additive continuous chapter at A registry crosses its last C++ boundary. This is an authored reconstruction, not a newly received transcript, independent learner assessment or Kairo implementation audit. The design continues directly from M017’s separately compiled API and M015–M016’s generation-aware registry. The actual multi-translation-unit witness lives in m018_lab.cpp, the public header, the hidden implementation and its build script.

Original part / exact canonical title Integrated teaching and observable proof boundary
291 · PIMPL for compilation and ABI isolation Incomplete Impl in the public header; out-of-line destructor and moves after definition; compiler dependency, deep-const caveat, allocation/indirection cost and ABI limitations are developed.
292 · Strong typedefs and type-safe handles Distinct MeshHandle and TextureHandle, logical slot-generation-catalog identity, invalidation after delete/reuse and cross-catalog rejection; compile-time and runtime checks.
293 · Phantom/tag types for units and spaces WorldSpace/ViewSpace and Meters/Seconds distinguish values at compile time without extra tag fields; actual affine/covector transformations and unit algebra are explained rather than faked by casts.
294 · Generic math types constrained by scalar concepts A deliberately restricted floating-point scalar concept controls Vector and Quantity; limitations for dual, interval and fixed-point scalars and numerical laws are explicit.
295 · Compile-time dimensions versus dynamic dimensions Fixed three-dimensional array/vector comparison with a runtime std::span dot product; mismatched runtime extents throw, and views borrow without owning.
296 · Expression templates and temporary-elimination concepts An eager addition is compared with reference-bearing lazy expression nodes; named inner-node lifetime is tested and temporaries, aliasing and reassociation hazards are explained.
297 · Intrusive versus non-intrusive generic abstractions Caller-owned Task with embedded next pointer, linked-state validation, pop/unlink check and contrast to owning forward_list nodes; no speed claim.
298 · Designing a zero-cost abstraction and verifying its cost Distinguishes compile-time-only tags from PIMPL’s real costs; requires workload, compiler, ISA, allocation count, disassembly and statistically sound benchmark comparisons.

300 · Building a reusable engine container API with explicit ownership and invalidation rules Catalog owns Impl and slot storage, rejects stale/foreign handles, returns owned copies, prepares free-list failure safety, and makes moved-from behavior explicit.

Evidence distinction: the published repository source is real source code, not proof by commentary. Its build script runs GCC release with -DNDEBUG, Clang strict and GCC address/undefined sanitizers on the separately compiled catalog and tests; the tests use a throwing check function rather than assert(), so release checks remain active. It also produces separate optimized assembly for two compilers. Hosted GitHub Actions must be checked for a final passing result; configuring a workflow is not itself evidence that the work ran.

Out of scope and remaining hard requirements: no current KairoMath/Transform.cppm or KairoRenderer/RendererTypes.cppm audit, no full stable binary plugin ABI, no thread-safe catalog, no GPU deferred destruction, no process-persistent handle identity, no exhaustive generation-overflow test or exception-injection matrix, no general expression-template lifetime framework or actual cache/performance benchmark. M001 - Parts 1-20

Part Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
1 Physical and logical binary states: a device maps ranges of a physical measurement to 0/1; thresholds and noise margins let imperfect signals represent stable logical values. Storage retains state, while combinational logic calculates from present inputs.
2 Positional notation: bit bib_i at position ii contributes bi2ib_i2^i. NN independent bits provide 2N2^N patterns, whose unsigned values run from 0 through 2N−12^N-1.
3 Binary conversion by Euclidean division: n=2q+rn=2q+r, r∈{0,1}r\in\{0,1\}. Save rr, repeat on qq, and reverse the saved sequence. For 13, remainders 1,0,1,1 give 1101. Handle zero explicitly.
4 Weighted decoding sums set-bit weights. Horner decoding repeatedly uses v←2v+bv\leftarrow2v+b from left to right. Reading 1101 yields 1,3,6,13, confirming the same value.
5 Hexadecimal has 16 digits; four bits make one nibble and one hex digit. 1010 is A, 1101 is D, so 10101101 is AD.
6 Octal has eight digits and groups three bits. Left-pad 10101101 to 010 101 101, giving octal 255. Leading zero in a C++ integer literal requests octal.
7 Byte and octet: octet means eight bits; C++ byte width is CHAR_BIT. Machine word describes a processing convention, not a fixed unit. Exact format widths need explicit types.
8 Bit mask: a pattern selects owned positions. A low-width mask is 2w−12^w-1 because subtracting one from a power of two fills all lower positions with ones.
9 Bitwise AND filters: x∧0=0x\land0=0, x∧1=xx\land1=x. AD & 07 = 05. Compare the result with zero for any selected flag, or with the full mask for all selected flags.
10 Bitwise OR sets: x∨1=1x\lor1=1, x∨0=xx\lor0=x. AD \| 40 = ED. Repeating the same set operation has no further effect.
11 Bitwise XOR toggles: x⊕1=¬xx\oplus1=\neg x, x⊕0=xx\oplus0=x. AD ^ 08 = A5; toggling again restores AD. XOR of two states marks differing positions.
12 Bitwise NOT inverts all positions at a stated width. Eight-bit NOT(0F)=F0; promoted int-width NOT has more positions. State width before interpreting its value.
13 Shift operations relocate bits. Logical right shift zero-fills; arithmetic right shift sign-fills. Left shift zero-fills low positions; discard behavior and numeric meaning depend on width and language rules.
14 For nonnegative unsigned arithmetic, left shift by kk resembles multiplication by 2k2^k and right shift floor division. Truncation changes the exact answer; signed division toward zero differs from arithmetic right shift for negative odd values.
15 Bit field extraction normalizes with right shift and isolates with a low mask: (AD >> 4) & 03 = 2. Mask-only gives 0x20, still at its original significance.
16 Insertion clears the destination mask, shifts the valid new value, then ORs it into the cleared word. Preserve outside-mask bits. Replacing quality 2 with 1 in AD produces 9D.
17 Bit packing combines disjoint, range-checked fields. OR contributions 05,08,20,00,80 to obtain AD. Packing saves payload bytes but introduces extraction and update work.
18 Unpacking reverses the declared schema. For LSB-first bits use byte ⌊i/8⌋\lfloor i/8\rfloor and offset imod⁡8i\bmod8. Check the requested count, source capacity, and unused padding before indexing.
19 Boolean algebra defines false/true operations by truth tables. Logical versus bitwise operators differ in result domain; built-in logical AND/OR also skip unnecessary operands.
20 De Morgan's laws swap AND and OR when negation crosses the operator. Enumerate four inputs to prove both identities; keep a fixed width for the bitwise versions.

M002 - Parts 21-40

Part Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
21 Unsigned NN-bit range is [0,2N−1][0,2^N-1]. Distinguish state count 256 from maximum eight-bit value 255.
22 Signed magnitude uses one sign bit and N−1N-1 magnitude bits. It has two zeros and requires sign-aware magnitude arithmetic. Eight-bit −5 is 10000101.
23 One's complement encodes negatives by bit inversion. −5 is 11111010. All ones is negative zero; addition returns a final carry to the low end as end-around carry.
24 Two's complement uses the negative residue 2N−x2^N-x and signed top-bit weight −2N−1-2^{N-1}. Decode AD as 173−256=−83. The same adder supports positive and negative residues.
25 Negation follows 2N−x=(2N−1−x)+12^N-x=(2^N-1-x)+1. The first term is the width-limited complement, so −13 is NOT(00001101)+1=11110011.
26 Negating zero gives all ones plus one, leaving low bits zero. Two’s complement has exactly one zero and assigns every pattern a distinct signed integer.
27 Minimum signed value follows the asymmetric range [−2N−1,2N−1−1][-2^{N-1},2^{N-1}-1]. For int minimum, same-type negation, abs, or division by −1 cannot represent the positive result. Narrow storage may promote first.
28 Unsigned modular arithmetic retains residues modulo 2N2^N. 250+10 becomes 4 when narrowed to eight bits; on the usual host the original byte addition expression is int 260.
29 Signed integer overflow is Undefined behavior at the operation type’s width. Check bounds before evaluating, or use a type proved large enough. Evaluating overflow and checking afterward is too late.
30 Unsigned 0−1 wraps to maximum; going below signed minimum is signed overflow. A size_t loop condition i>=0 never becomes false. Prefer reverse iteration or a decrement-before-index pattern with a correct termination guard.
31 Carry and borrow move arithmetic information between digit positions. Four-bit 13+7 gives low 4 with carry 1. Unsigned carry differs from signed range failure. Borrow conventions depend on architecture.
32 Half adder: sum=A XOR B, carry=A AND B. Full adder adds carry-in; sum is three-way parity and carry is the majority of three inputs. A majority function is true when at least two inputs are true.
33 Ripple-carry addition chains full adders. Worst-case circuit delay grows with width; fixed-width software addition remains constant work. Generate/propagate terms permit parallel carry networks.
34 Subtraction through addition uses A+NOT⁡N(B)+1A+\operatorname{NOT}_N(B)+1. Binary 6502-style SBC instead includes C: A−B−(1−C)A-B-(1-C), so C=1 means no borrow.
35 Shift-and-add multiplication sums one shifted multiplicand for every set multiplier bit. 13×11=13+26+104=143. Both the shifting partial value and accumulator must hold the required wider range.
36 Binary long division shifts dividend bits into a partial remainder, then compares and conditionally subtracts the divisor. Check D=Qd+RD=Qd+R and 0≤R<d0\le R<d. For 13/3, Q=4,R=1. Zero division and int-min/−1 are invalid.
37 Saturating arithmetic clamps a widened answer to endpoints: 250+20 becomes 255. Signed saturation is not associative, so evaluation order matters. Do not prematurely clamp an HDR intermediate.
38 Fixed-width integer types define exact widths when available. Least and fast families promise at least the width, with different goals. size_t is for sizes, ptrdiff_t for differences; plain char signedness varies.
39 Integral promotion occurs first; Usual arithmetic conversions then select a common type. Track stored type, promoted type, operation type, and destination conversion separately. ~uint8_t{0} is usually int −1.
40 Mixed signedness can convert negative operands to large unsigned values. Use consistent semantic types or std::cmp_* helpers; valid indexing still requires nonnegative and less-than-size conditions. std::in_range checks conversion representability.

Notation and validity

NN is carrier width, ii a bit position, ww field width, ss offset, and bib_i a 0/1 digit. ∧\land, ∨\lor, ⊕\oplus, and ¬\neg mean AND, OR, XOR, and NOT; integer vectors require a stated width. ≪\ll and ≫\gg denote shifts. Modulo records a residue; floor rounds downward. A bijection pairs every element of one set with exactly one element of the other. An invariant is a property that must remain true across steps. An ALU is an arithmetic and logic unit.

Keep number semantics separate from executable C++ operators. A word-level formula assumes a fixed unsigned carrier; C++ built-in operators act after promotion. For C++23, signed right shift rounds toward negative infinity. Claims about signed overflowing addition remain subject to undefined behavior.

Why these dependencies matter

Representation supplies the weights needed for masks. Boolean operators supply the gates needed for adders. Masks and shifts supply the field operations needed for compact data. Finite width supplies the modular model needed for two’s complement. Promotions and conversions determine the domain in which C++ actually performs each operation. See Dependency Map and each concept’s prerequisites before reconstructing a later mechanism.

M003 - Parts 41-60

Part Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
41 Endianness orders significance bytes at increasing addresses. It does not change the integer value or reverse bits inside each octet. Separate significance, address traversal, and intra-byte packing order.
42 Little endian puts the least-significant byte first: 0x12345678 produces 78 56 34 12. Extract byte i by unsigned right shift by 8i, then narrow to eight bits; reconstruct by shifting each byte into its significance position.
43 Big endian puts the most-significant byte first: 12 34 56 78. Read left-to-right with value←256×value+byte: M001 Horner decoding in base 256.
44 Byte swapping and network order: swapping reverses octet significance; host/network conversion is a no-op when orders already match. Classic Internet fields often use big endian, but each protocol defines its own contract. Serialization fixes widths/order and validates lengths without native padding.
45 Alignment and padding: alignment A restricts starting addresses to multiples of A. C++ alignof reports the requirement; alignas requests a supported stronger alignment. Align-up needs nonzero A and overflow checks; an aligned numeric offset is not automatically a live pointer.
46 Internal and tail padding: internal padding precedes a member to meet its alignment. Under 1/4/1 member alignments, byte–uint32–byte uses offsets 0/4/8, with three internal padding bytes. ABI and object layout determines actual offsets.
47 Tail padding rounds complete-object size for aligned array stride. The same example ends at byte nine and rounds to size 12; the next object’s four-aligned member remains aligned. Never infer sizeof solely by summing payload sizes.
48 Field reordering and AoS versus SoA: order by decreasing alignment can reduce holes. A 1/8/1/4 example commonly shrinks 24→16 bytes. Measure sizeof/alignof/offsetof; ABI compatibility and hot/cold access patterns can outweigh smaller size. AoS stores complete records; SoA has one array per field.
49 Packed structures and misaligned access: packing extensions can remove holes but weaken member alignment. They do not define endianness, versions, or lifetime. A packed native object differs from a specified wire format.
50 Misalignment can cross cache-line/page boundaries, slow access, or fault depending on instruction/platform. C++ access still needs a suitably aligned live object. Reconstruct bytes or copy representation into an existing aligned trivially copyable object; copying alone does not normalize endianness.
51 Pointer arithmetic and provenance: address is a location identifier; a C++ pointer is a constrained typed access path. Within an array, p+i advances i×sizeof(T) bytes; one-past can be formed but not dereferenced. Numeric addresses alone do not establish access rights.
52 Addresses and virtual memory translates process-visible addresses to physical addresses. A contiguous vector buffer can span scattered frames. Virtual and physical contiguity distinguishes address-space adjacency from backing placement.
53 Process isolation and page permissions: each address space has its own mapping context. VA 0x400000 can map to frame 27 in A and frame 913 in B. Shared mappings may select the same frame; read/write/execute/user permissions constrain access.
54 Pages and page offsets: a virtual page is an address block; a frame is corresponding physical storage. For P=2^k, VPN=floor(VA/P), offset=VA mod P. The 4-KiB example uses k=12; actual page size depends on platform/configuration, not universally 4096.
55 Page tables and MMU: entries supply frame identity, permissions, and state; MMU is the translation/protection mechanism. The TLB caches translations, not data. A miss may resolve through page-table walking without a page fault.
56 Page faults and demand paging: OS intervention is needed under current mapping state. Valid demand loading/zero-fill may install a frame and retry; Copy-on-write may copy on first write. Unmapped/forbidden access may fail. A fault does not necessarily imply disk I/O.
57 Call stack and stack frames: calls conventionally use LIFO frames for return state, registers, spills, and some locals. Downward growth is a convention; not every local has a stack slot. Returning a dead-local pointer violates Storage duration and object lifetime, even if bytes remain.
58 Dynamic allocation and heap subdivides OS regions into variable-lifetime blocks. Allocator fragmentation distinguishes slack within allocated blocks (37 requested in a 48-byte class leaves 11) from separated free holes unable to satisfy one request. Allocation cost differs from access latency.
59 Static storage and initialization: namespace/static objects have program-duration storage. Initialized writable data commonly uses data-like regions; zero-initialized storage uses BSS-like zero-fill without literal executable zero payload. Dynamic initialization and cross-unit ordering need later treatment.
60 Read-only data and code: text commonly contains instructions, read-only regions constants. Writable-or-executable policy limits writable executable mappings. Modifying a string literal is undefined behavior; const automatic objects are not forced into read-only segments. Segment names/layout are implementation choices.

Bridges and distinctions that must not be omitted

  • ASLR randomizes mapping locations; a textbook process diagram is not a layout guarantee.
  • Thread storage duration exists alongside automatic, static, and dynamic duration; thread-local storage is not simply the call stack. Storage duration governs available storage; lifetime governs the live object within it.

Clarifications: the layout examples assume stated ABI rules; reordering may break a published ABI. Bounds and lifetime remain necessary even with valid mappings/alignment. Wording cross-checked against the C++ draft alignment, storage duration, and endianness sections.

M004 - Parts 61-76

Part Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
61 IEEE-754 floating point: finite nonuniform representation plus explicitly specified rounding/special-value behavior; formats do not make every C++ float binary32.
62 Binary32: 1/8/23 stored fields, 24-bit normal precision and bias 127; 1.0 has word 3F800000.
63 Binary64: 1/11/52 stored fields, 53-bit normal precision and bias 1023; more precision is distinct from more exponent range.
64 Signed zero: floating sign is separate from magnitude; signbit sees negative zero whereas x<0 does not.
65 Exponent bias: normal stored exponent E=e+B; E=130 decodes to e=3 for binary32; classify reserved fields first.
66 Significand and hidden bit: normal leading binary 1 is implicit; 23 fraction bits plus it give 24 significant bits.
67 Floating-point encoding and decoding: 10.625=1.010101₂×2³ gives S=0,E=130,F=2A0000, word 412A0000.
68 Floating-point encoding and decoding: C1540000 has S=1,E=130,F=540000; reconstruct −1.65625×8=−13.25.
69 Signed zero: 00000000 and 80000000 compare numerically equal but have distinct representations/reciprocals.
70 Floating-point infinities: all-one exponent with zero fraction; distinct from maximum finite and dependent on sign/rounding in overflow.
71 NaNs and payloads: all-one exponent with nonzero fraction; unordered comparisons, quiet/signaling distinction, payload preservation caveats.
72 Subnormals and gradual underflow: E=0 uses no hidden one; binary32 x=(-1)^S F×2^-149, filling the normal-to-zero gap.
73 Machine epsilon: spacing above 1, 2^-23 for binary32, not min(), denorm_min(), or a universal tolerance.
74 ULP and representable spacing: normal binade spacing is 2^(e-23) for binary32; 1 has different immediate lower/upper gaps.
75 Rounding to nearest ties to even: choose nearest neighbor; exact halfway picks even retained significand; guard/round/sticky summarize discarded bits.
76 Directed rounding modes: upward, downward and toward-zero are signed directions; runtime environment changes must be checked and restored.

The continuous chapter contains these definitions and essential traces directly. Numerical reproductions establish supplied-formula behavior, not current repository implementation; see Supplementary/Sources and Code Anchors.

M005 - Parts 77-88

Part Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
77 Terminating fractions and dyadic rationals: a reduced fraction terminates in binary iff its denominator is a power of two; 0.1f stores 13421773/2^27, not 1/10.
78 Floating-point addition and absorption: align exponents, preserve guard/round/sticky, normalize and round; 2^24+1 is a nearest-even tie that stores 2^24.
79 Cancellation and loss of significance: nearly equal operands expose prior error relative to a small difference; sensitivity factor |a|+|b||a−b|\frac{\lvert a\rvert+\lvert b\rvert}{\lvert a-b\rvert}.
80 Sterbenz lemma: nearby nonnegative stored floats satisfying x/2≤y≤2x have an exact representable difference under suitable gradual-underflow rules; input uncertainty remains.
81 Floating-point exception flags: max×2 overflows; min-normal/2 is exact subnormal, while min-subnormal/2 rounds to zero with tiny/inexact behavior in the tested environment.
82 Absolute and relative error: absolute discrepancy carries units; relative discrepancy divides by nonzero reference magnitude. Distinguish forward/backward error and stability from conditioning.
83 Numerical tolerance policies: separate absolute and relative tolerances; validate them and non-finite inputs. Numeric exact equality is not representation equality.
84 Numerical tolerance policies: a global epsilon mixes units, scales, algorithmic error and conditioning; approximate closeness is nontransitive.
85 Fused multiply-add: one-rounding fl(ab+c) differs from fl(fl(ab)+c); the (1+2-23)2 witness yields 2^-46 rather than zero.
86 Floating-point reassociation: (a+b)+c and a+(b+c) can differ; naive, compensated and fixed pairwise reductions have different contracts.
87 Floating-point reassociation: distributive graphs differ: with a=1e10,b=1+2^-23,c=-1, factored result 1192.0928955078125 versus unfused expanded 1024.
88 Numerical reproducibility: precision, ordering, FMA, environment and compiler/math-library settings matter. Atomicity does not fix global order; capped TSDF updates are mathematically history-dependent.

All essential explanations and traces are in the continuous chapter. Repository findings remain supplied-source claims; no live engine experiment is implied. ## M006 - Parts 89-100

Part Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
89 Fixed-point representation: a signed raw integer I at scale S represents I/S; F=16 gives step 2^-16 and raw 212992 for 3.25.
90 Fixed-point range and resolution: require 2^-F≤requested step and M·2F≤2(N-1)-1. A 32-bit domain ±1e6 with step≤0.001 permits F=10 or 11.
91 Fixed-point rescaling: multiply at scale S², then round/divide by S; division uses A·S/B. Prove intermediate width, handle negative ties and zero divisors, and check destination range.
92 Arithmetic policies remain necessary for fixed point. Nearest unclipped absolute error≤1/(2S); near-zero relative error can be large. Controlled integer arithmetic can improve repeatability, not make every operation associative.
93 Affine quantization and zero point maps finite values to codes and reconstructs s(q-z). Groupwise scales cost metadata; source-shaped offset INT4 codes [1,5,8,11,15] pack to 51 B8 0F. One-bit row centroids are not automatically ±1.
94 UNORM and SNORM: UNORM8 reconstructs q/255; SNORM8 clamps q/127 at −1. Quantized normal components can require safe renormalization; sRGB is a separate interpretation.
95 Binary16 uses 1/5/10 fields, bias15, 11 normal precision bits, maximum65504, normal minimum2^-14, subnormal minimum2^-24. Word3E00 encodes1.5.
96 Bfloat16 uses1/8/7 fields, bias127, 8 normal precision bits; it trades detail for wide exponent range. Nearest-even conversion must classify NaNs instead of discarding their low payload into infinity.
97 Bit casting and representation transfers suitable initialized object representation; numeric cast converts a value. Eligibility does not solve byte order, arbitrary valid representations, alignment or mapped-object lifetime.
98 Binary format contracts declare widths/order/representation/version; Checked binary parsing validates products, subtracted bounds, exact lengths and resource limits. Magic/version are not integrity or authenticity.
99 Checksums CRCs and hashes summarize specified content. Additive sums miss byte reordering; CRC requires named parameters; a cryptographic digest needs a trusted reference, MAC or signature for an adversarial trust claim.
100 Memory dump interpretation decodes by offset/schema/byte order. The 2×3 demonstration has a28-byte header and24-byte binary32 payload; identical bytes have different meanings under integer, float or character interpretations.

Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership

Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C010 · Latest development: C010

Definition and mechanism

std::unique_ptr<T, D> is a move-only exclusive owner whose deleter D defines disposal. get() exposes a borrow; release() transfers the responsibility without deleting. std::shared_ptr<T> joins a shared ownership group represented by a control block; the managed object is destroyed when the last strong owner is released. The control block can outlive the object while weak observers remain. The stored pointer and the object whose destruction the control block arranges can differ (for example, aliasing ownership).

Shared ownership is not pointee synchronization. Concurrent operations on distinct smart-pointer handles do not automatically make concurrent access to T safe. Use sharing only when several independent parties truly retain the same lifetime.

Prerequisites

  • Ownership and non-owning views — Access-only views and ownership responsibilities are different contracts.
  • RAII and resource handles — Smart pointers are standard resource owners built around lifetime-bound cleanup.

Used by

  • Weak observation and ownership cycles
  • Placement construction and explicit lifetime management

Recall and next depth

Explain why unique_ptr<Derived> converted to unique_ptr<Base> needs a valid base destruction policy. Pending: allocator/deleter state and atomic shared ownership interfaces.

Source and navigation

Weak observation and ownership cycles

Weak observation and ownership cycles

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C010 · Latest development: C010

Definition and mechanism

std::weak_ptr<T> observes a shared_ptr ownership group without increasing its strong count. lock() atomically attempts to create a temporary strong owner; the result is empty if the managed object is no longer alive. Replacing one edge of an otherwise all-strong ownership cycle with a weak observation can allow the strong count to reach zero. A check with expired() followed later by access is not equivalent to a successful lock().

enable_shared_from_this joins the already-established shared ownership group; it must not create a second shared_ptr control block from this.

Prerequisites

  • Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership — Weak observation belongs to a real shared ownership group.

Used by

  • Deferred captures and borrowed views
  • RAII and resource handles

Placement construction and explicit lifetime management

Placement construction and explicit lifetime management

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C010 · Latest development: C010

Definition and mechanism

Placement new or std::construct_at initializes an object in storage already provided by the caller; it does not allocate that backing storage. The storage must have adequate size and alignment. std::destroy_at ends an object’s lifetime but does not release the storage. A pool/container must track occupancy, partial construction, exactly-once destruction, and when reuse is permitted. Transparent replacement and std::launder have detailed preconditions; launder neither constructs nor revives an object.

Prerequisites

  • Object construction and storage reuse — An object’s lifetime is not the same as backing storage availability.
  • RAII and resource handles — Low-level storage protocols still need one responsible owner.

Used by

  • Object identity and generation handles

Interface contracts and publication

Interface contracts and publication

An interface contract says more than which function name to call. It defines the states in which an operation is valid and what becomes true when it succeeds.

A complete contract should state:

  • valid input domain and units;
  • ownership and lifetime of arguments/results;
  • mutation and aliasing;
  • failure representation and exception/error guarantees;
  • thread/concurrency rules;
  • timing: immediate, deferred or asynchronous;
  • invalidation;
  • observability/publication point.

Publication is a state transition

A producer may construct a resource privately and then publish it so consumers can rely on it. Before publication, partial state can remain invisible. After publication, every documented invariant must hold.

For CPU concurrency, release/acquire synchronization is one possible publication mechanism when the memory model requirements fit the data structure.

For asynchronous assets, “decode finished” does not mean “GPU resource is safe to sample.” A useful state machine may distinguish:

requested → decoded → upload recorded → submitted → GPU-ready → published.

Similarly, an obsolete request must not publish after a newer generation has replaced it. Generation IDs or request tokens protect the destination identity.

Ownership versus readiness

A reference can be alive but not ready. A GPU buffer wrapper can exist while its upload is still in flight. Conversely, a resource can be GPU-ready while the CPU owner is about to destroy it unless retirement is deferred until all GPU use completes.

Lifetime and synchronization are independent axes.

Failure guarantees

If publication is atomic, consumers should observe either the old valid version or the new valid version, not a half-updated mixture. That promise requires implementation evidence appropriate to the domain: atomics/locks for CPU state, transaction/staging for files, semaphore/fence/queue dependencies for GPU work.

Evidence

tools/labs/threaded_asset_publication_lab.cpp and tools/labs/production_pipeline_contract_lab.cpp exercise two different publication domains: concurrent asset decoding/publication and deterministic staged production publication.

Read the connected explanation in Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#An API is a promise about an operation.

Related: Atomic publication and durability, Production manifests and transactional publication, Vulkan synchronization2 and resource transitions.

Definition and mechanism

Matrix row/column semantics are independent of physical row-major or column-major storage. A strided view uses explicit row and column strides, shape, backing extent, and borrow lifetime. Separate named scalar members are not an array eligible for pointer indexing.

Shader buffer ABI

Shader buffer ABI

A shader buffer is a binary interface between independently compiled code. CPU and shader code must agree on member offsets, element widths, alignment, array stride, matrix layout, and total record stride. “These structs have the same fields” is not enough.

Suppose a record logically contains a 3-vector followed by a scalar. The mathematical payload is four floats, but the ABI may impose an alignment boundary for the vector or the containing record. The only safe statement is the one established by the layout rules and, ideally, reflection/compiled shader metadata.

Layout is a function of context

Different interfaces can have different rules: vertex attributes, constant/uniform buffers, storage buffers, argument buffers and push/root constants are not interchangeable contracts. Matrix row/column-major convention is another independent dimension.

On the CPU side, standard C++ object layout also has rules about padding and alignment. Copying bytes from a native struct into a shader buffer is valid only when the native representation is deliberately made compatible or explicit serialization writes the expected offsets.

Verify rather than guess

A robust pipeline should generate or reflect a machine-readable layout description and compare it with CPU declarations:

  • expected offset for every member;
  • expected array stride;
  • matrix stride and orientation;
  • record size/alignment;
  • scalar widths and signedness.

Static assertions can catch CPU layout changes. Shader reflection or compiler metadata catches shader-side changes. A golden byte dump can test the complete bridge.

Failure modes

Common failures include using a 12-byte mental model for a vector type whose ABI slot is 16 bytes, mixing bool widths, assuming packed enums, copying pointer-containing structs, row/column-major disagreement, and updating one side of the interface without rebuilding the other.

Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Make a shader record an explicit binary contract.

Related: Alignment and padding, GPU vertex specification, Tensor runtime layout and views.

Prefix scan and stream compaction

Prefix scan and stream compaction

A prefix scan turns local counts into globally consistent offsets. For an exclusive sum scan of input xx,

y0=0,yi=∑j=0i−1xj. y_0=0, \qquad y_i=\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}x_j.

If each element says how many output records it will emit, yiy_i is the first output slot owned by element ii. This converts a race-prone global append into deterministic non-overlapping regions.

For Boolean compaction, let predicate bi∈{0,1}b_i\in\{0,1\}. Scan bb to obtain offsets. Every active element with bi=1b_i=1 writes itself to output[scan[i]]. The final output count is scan[n-1] + b[n-1].

Parallel structure

The naive parallel scan that repeatedly doubles an offset performs O(nlog⁡n)O(n\log n) work. A work-efficient tree scan performs an up-sweep/reduction followed by a down-sweep and uses O(n)O(n) work with O(log⁡n)O(\log n) depth.

On a GPU, a practical large-array scan normally has several levels:

  1. scan each workgroup block into local output;
  2. record each block total;
  3. scan the block totals;
  4. add each scanned block offset back into that block’s local results.

Every phase has a dependency. Dispatching all phases without establishing visibility/order is not a valid scan merely because each shader is individually correct.

Shared-memory bank conflicts and subgroup width affect performance, while workgroup barriers only synchronize participating invocations in that workgroup.

Stream compaction as an allocation proof

Compaction is useful beyond filtering visible objects. It appears in GPU-driven draw generation, BVH construction, particle survival, tiled light lists, Gaussian tile duplication and sparse work queues.

The scan proves that each surviving producer owns a distinct range before any scatter writes occur.

Evidence boundary

The current repository has CPU-side scan/compaction reasoning in the canonical volumes but does not yet claim a native Vulkan/Metal scan kernel benchmark. The next hardware proof should compare a scalar CPU oracle, a workgroup implementation, multi-workgroup hierarchy, adversarial non-power-of-two sizes, and captured GPU timing.

Primary background: NVIDIA GPU Gems 3, Chapter 39, “Parallel Prefix Sum (Scan) with CUDA.”

Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Scan turns local counts into nonoverlapping output regions.

Related: GPU workgroups and synchronization, BVH build traversal and workload selection.

Build graph usage requirements

Build graph usage requirements

A build target has two interfaces at once. Its source code exposes a programming interface, while its build-system target exposes the information consumers need to compile and link against that interface.

In CMake terminology, PRIVATE, PUBLIC and INTERFACE describe propagation of usage requirements. They do not correspond to private/public members in C++.

A PRIVATE requirement is needed to build the target itself but should not be inherited by ordinary consumers.

A PUBLIC requirement is needed both by the target and by consumers because the target’s public interface depends on it.

An INTERFACE requirement is consumed by downstream targets but is not used to compile the target’s own sources.

Why public headers force propagation

Suppose library EngineMath has a public header that includes ThirdParty/Vec.hpp. A consumer compiling only its own source plus EngineMath’s public include path still needs the third-party include directory. Marking that dependency PRIVATE may let EngineMath build while every independent consumer fails.

The same reasoning applies to compile features, preprocessor definitions, generated headers and transitive link dependencies whose symbols appear in the public ABI.

The test should therefore be from the consumer’s perspective: can a tiny program include the advertised public header and link using only the public target?

Build graph versus include graph

A textual include graph and a target dependency graph answer different questions. A source file can include a header without the build graph correctly propagating its location. Conversely, linking to a library can be required even when no source file directly includes one of its headers.

Imported targets and namespaced targets are preferable to global compiler/linker flags because the dependency becomes attached to the thing that owns it.

Cycles and architecture

A cycle in target dependencies is often an architecture smell. Static-library cycles can also produce linker-order problems. Dependency inversion, interface targets or extracting a lower-level common module can make the ownership direction explicit.

Evidence

A strong build-interface test creates a minimal consumer target in a separate directory, links only the exported target, and compiles with no accidental include directories from the main project. Installation/export tests should repeat this against the installed package so the build tree cannot hide missing usage requirements.

Read the connected explanation in Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#The build graph becomes another interface.

Related: C++ modules and reachability, ABI and object layout, Interface contracts and publication.
