GPU workgroups and synchronization

GPU workgroups and synchronization

GPU execution has several scopes that must not be collapsed into the word “thread.” An invocation executes one logical shader instance. Invocations are grouped into workgroups for explicitly shared local memory and workgroup barriers. Hardware may execute smaller subgroup or SIMD groups inside a workgroup. Many workgroups make up a dispatch.

A workgroup barrier can coordinate invocations that participate in that workgroup. It cannot create a global barrier across arbitrary workgroups in the same dispatch. If an algorithm requires all blocks to finish phase A before any block begins phase B, use a mechanism that establishes that dependency: usually separate dispatches/commands with API synchronization, or a carefully designed device-wide primitive supported by the target model.

Execution barrier versus memory visibility

“Everyone reached the same point” and “everyone can now observe the required writes” are related but distinct contracts. APIs and shading languages expose memory scopes and semantics because a control barrier alone is not a universal cache flush.

The producer/consumer question is always:

  • what operation produced the bytes?
  • what later operation consumes them?
  • which execution scopes must be ordered?
  • which memory accesses must become visible?
  • which resource/subresource is covered?

Subgroups

Subgroup collectives can exchange values and perform ballots, reductions and scans without workgroup shared memory. They are fast but require care around subgroup width, inactive lanes and portability. An algorithm that silently assumes 32 lanes can break on hardware using a different subgroup size.

Shared memory and bank conflicts

Workgroup memory is physically optimized for cooperation but has finite capacity and bank structure. Tiling can reduce global bandwidth, yet an unfortunate address pattern can serialize accesses through bank conflicts. Register pressure and shared-memory allocation also constrain occupancy, so increasing tile size is not free.

Evidence boundary

The canonical notes now distinguish CPU semantic models from native hardware evidence. A CPU prefix-scan or render-graph test can prove dependency logic but cannot prove Vulkan visibility, Metal hazard behavior, subgroup width or driver performance. Hardware claims require validation layers, GPU capture/counters, and device-specific results.

Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Let many invocations cooperate without inventing a global clock.

Related: Prefix scan and stream compaction, Shader buffer ABI.

Tensor runtime layout and views

Tensor runtime layout and views

A tensor runtime does not begin with neural-network vocabulary. It begins with a byte-addressing contract. A tensor value needs an element type, a rank, a shape, a mapping from logical indices to storage offsets, and an ownership/lifetime rule for the backing storage. If any of those are implicit, later operations such as broadcasting, transposition, slicing, matrix multiplication, device transfer, or quantized kernels can silently disagree about what the same bytes mean.

For a contiguous row-major tensor with shape

(d0,d1,…,dr−1), (d_0,d_1,\ldots,d_{r-1}),

the canonical stride of axis ii is

si=∏j=i+1r−1dj, s_i = \prod_{j=i+1}^{r-1} d_j,

so an index (i0,…,ir−1)(i_0,\ldots,i_{r-1}) addresses

offset⁡=∑k=0r−1iksk. \operatorname{offset}=\sum_{k=0}^{r-1} i_k s_k.

Shape describes the logical domain while strides describe the storage map. A transposed or sliced view may have the same elements without being contiguous. A runtime that assumes offset = row × width + column for every two-dimensional tensor will eventually misread a view.

A rank-zero tensor is a scalar and has shape []; it is not the same object shape as a rank-one tensor of shape [1]. A zero-sized dimension is also meaningful: shape [4,0,8] has zero elements but still has rank three. These distinctions matter when importing external graph formats because shape information is part of the interface contract rather than decoration.

Broadcasting is an index transformation

Broadcasting does not physically duplicate the smaller tensor. Align the input and output shapes at the trailing axes. For every aligned axis, the input size must either equal the output size or equal one. If the input size is one, every output index on that axis maps to input index zero.

For a bias of shape [3] applied to a matrix [2,3], output coordinates across both rows map back to bias indices 0,1,2 repeatedly. This is why some runtimes can represent a broadcast axis with a zero stride: advancing the logical output coordinate does not advance the input address.

Views, aliases, and mutation

A view is cheap because it shares storage. That also means it shares lifetime and mutation hazards. A runtime must decide whether an operation accepts arbitrary strided inputs, requests a contiguous materialization, or dispatches to separate kernels. Reshape is metadata-only only when the requested logical order can be represented by the existing storage arrangement; otherwise it requires a copy.

The same question appears on the GPU. A kernel receiving shape and stride metadata can support arbitrary views, but the extra integer arithmetic and irregular memory access can cost more than making a compact copy. The correct choice is workload-dependent and should be measured.

Executable reconstruction

tools/labs/phase29_ml_runtime_lab.cpp contains a standalone C++20 tensor representation with checked element counts, contiguous strides, multi-index addressing, and trailing-axis broadcasting. Its negative test rejects incompatible shapes rather than allowing an accidental indexing interpretation.

The witness is intentionally small enough to rebuild from memory. It does not claim to implement a production tensor allocator, autograd engine, sparse tensor representation, or GPU device-memory manager.

External contract

The ONNX IR specification defines tensors by values plus shape, distinguishes scalar shape [] from a one-element vector, and requires top-level graph inputs and outputs to carry rank information even when individual dimensions are symbolic. When an ONNX model is imported, the internal tensor representation must preserve those distinctions instead of flattening everything into an untyped byte blob.

Primary reference: https://onnx.ai/onnx/repo-docs/IR.html

Failure probes

A tensor-runtime implementation should deliberately test integer overflow while multiplying dimensions, out-of-range indexing, zero-sized dimensions, rank-zero scalars, incompatible broadcasting, views whose strides are not contiguous, aliased mutation, negative or unsupported strides if the API exposes them, and CPU/GPU disagreement over element size or alignment.

The central reconstruction question is: given only shape, strides, element size and an index tuple, can you prove which byte is being accessed and whether that byte remains alive?

Related: Shader buffer ABI, Quantization and compressed weights, ONNX graph import and lowering, Transformer attention and KV cache runtime.

GGUF binary model loading

GGUF binary model loading

GGUF is a binary container used by GGML-family inference runtimes. Treating it as “a file full of weights” is too vague for a safe loader. A loader must first establish a byte-level contract: magic, format version, tensor count, metadata count, typed metadata records, tensor descriptors, alignment, tensor-data offsets, and bounds. Only after those checks can tensor bytes become runtime values.

The first four bytes identify the format as GGUF. Multi-byte fields must be decoded according to the file format instead of reinterpreting an arbitrary file buffer as a C++ struct. Native C++ structs inherit compiler padding, alignment and host-representation assumptions that a binary file does not owe the process reading it.

A useful loading pipeline is:

  1. Read and validate the fixed prefix.
  2. Parse metadata key/value records with checked lengths.
  3. Parse tensor descriptors: name, rank and shape, data type, and relative data offset.
  4. Compute the aligned start of the tensor-data section.
  5. Validate every tensor interval against file length and arithmetic overflow.
  6. Keep file or mapping ownership alive for every lazy tensor view.
  7. Convert the file tensor type into an internal runtime type only after the descriptor is validated.
  8. Dispatch dequantization or quantized kernels from that internal type rather than from filename assumptions.

The official GGUF documentation describes the format as a single-file, extensible model container and defines architecture metadata, tensor data layout information, and attention metadata such as head counts and key/value dimensions. Those metadata values affect runtime shape contracts; they are not merely labels.

Primary reference: https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/blob/master/docs/gguf.md

Prefix witness

tools/labs/phase29_ml_runtime_lab.cpp parses the GGUF magic, version, tensor count and metadata count from an explicit byte vector using checked little-endian reads. It has a negative case for invalid magic.

That witness intentionally stops at the prefix. It proves that the repository now owns the boundary between raw bytes and validated scalar header fields; it does not pretend that the entire GGUF metadata type system or quantized tensor catalog has already been implemented.

What a full loader must prove

A production reader must defend against truncated strings, absurd ranks, shape-product overflow, unsupported quantization types, alignment overflow, tensor intervals outside the file, duplicate or contradictory metadata, offsets that alias unintentionally, and files whose declared architecture cannot be executed by the runtime.

For memory mapping, “the pointer is valid” is not enough. The mapping object and file lifetime must outlive every lazy tensor view. Page faults also become part of performance: a model that technically maps instantly can still stall during first use if access order faults pages unpredictably.

Quantized execution boundary

GGUF storage type and execution type are separate decisions. A block-quantized format normally stores scale or other metadata together with packed codes. A portable reference path should decode or dot-product those blocks in a simple scalar implementation first. SIMD or Metal kernels then have an independent oracle. If the optimized path disagrees, the scalar path is evidence; if both paths share the same unpacking bug, the test is not independent enough.

Related: Tensor runtime layout and views, Quantized matvec and dequantization, Transformer attention and KV cache runtime, Binary format contracts.

Metadata and tensor-descriptor witness

The earlier prefix-only boundary has now been extended by tools/labs/gguf_metadata_tensor_lab.cpp. The subset parser validates GGUF v3 magic and counts, parses typed UINT32 and STRING metadata, consumes general.alignment, reads tensor names/ranks/dimensions/type IDs/relative offsets, computes the aligned tensor-data start, and rejects truncation or invalid alignment.

The parser remains deliberately incomplete rather than permissive. Unsupported metadata types are rejected instead of skipped with guessed sizes. It does not yet implement arrays, every GGUF value type, every GGML quantized tensor block, tokenizer metadata, endian conversion for big-endian files, or payload interval validation for all tensor types. That is the correct boundary for an independent reference: a small loader should fail loudly outside the subset it actually understands.

ONNX graph import and lowering

ONNX graph import and lowering

ONNX is a graph interchange format, not a command stream to execute blindly. Import therefore has two separate responsibilities: decode the normative serialized model, then lower its graph semantics into the engine’s own validated intermediate representation.

The ONNX IR describes a graph as a side-effect-free computation containing model parameters and a topologically ordered list of nodes. Node outputs obey single-static-assignment: an output value name is produced once. Inputs, outputs and initializers have declared types and shapes, and symbolic dimensions can constrain values across the graph.

Primary reference: https://onnx.ai/onnx/repo-docs/IR.html

Import pipeline

Parse. Decode Protocol Buffers into ONNX model objects. Reject malformed serialization before graph reasoning begins.

Validate names and versions. Check IR version, opset imports, graph name, duplicate names and unsupported domains.

Resolve value contracts. Establish element type, rank and known or symbolic dimensions for graph inputs, outputs, initializers and intermediate values.

Validate graph order and SSA. Every consumed value must either be a graph input, initializer or output of an earlier node; every node output must be unique in its namespace.

Normalize operators. Convert ONNX attributes and optional inputs into an internal operator description whose defaults are explicit.

Infer and verify shapes. Propagate shapes where operator rules permit it, while keeping an unknown dimension distinct from an invented concrete dimension.

Lower. Translate supported operators into backend-neutral internal nodes. Unsupported operations must produce a deterministic diagnostic, not fall through to an unrelated kernel.

Plan execution. Topologically schedule nodes, assign storage and lifetimes, select kernels by capabilities, and insert device transfers or fallback boundaries deliberately.

Why an internal IR matters

If Vulkan, Metal and CPU code each interpret ONNX attributes independently, the repository effectively owns multiple importers with multiple chances to disagree. The importer should instead produce one small semantic IR: tensors, operators, attributes, shapes, constants and explicit capability requirements. Backends lower that IR.

This creates a testable seam. A CPU reference kernel and a Metal kernel can receive the same normalized MatMul or Softmax node. Their numerical agreement can then be tested without re-testing protobuf parsing.

Executable graph contract

tools/labs/phase29_ml_runtime_lab.cpp does not parse protobuf and labels that limitation explicitly. It models the post-decode internal graph boundary and verifies that inputs and initializers are available before use and that node outputs satisfy SSA uniqueness. Negative cases reject use-before-definition and duplicate outputs.

That is deliberately narrower than ONNX support. Full support requires actual protobuf decoding, opset semantics, operator-specific validation, shape inference and numerical parity against a trusted runtime.

Related: Tensor runtime layout and views, Transformer attention and KV cache runtime, Interface contracts and publication.

Real protobuf and official reference-runtime witness

The internal graph contract is now complemented by tools/ml/onnx_contract.py, which uses the official ONNX package instead of modeling the interchange format by hand. The witness builds a ModelProto with MatMul → Add → Relu, named initializers and symbolic batch dimension, serializes it to a real .onnx protobuf, reloads it, runs the official model checker, invokes shape inference, and executes the graph with ONNX’s reference evaluator.

The expected numerical result is independently computed with NumPy before comparison. A second deliberately invalid model reuses a node-output name and must be rejected by the official checker, exercising the SSA constraint at the actual interchange boundary.

This changes the evidence level for the ONNX file/IR boundary, not for a production inference backend. Dynamic control flow, nested subgraphs, arbitrary opsets, external tensor data, quantized operators, custom domains, ONNX Runtime/device execution and current KairoONNX lowering still need separate proofs.

Quantized matvec and dequantization

Quantized matvec and dequantization

Quantization trades representation precision for storage and bandwidth. The runtime question is not merely “how many bits per weight?” It is what mathematical value each stored code represents, where its scale or zero-point metadata lives, and how the dot product is accumulated without silently changing the model.

For a simple symmetric per-row signed 8-bit scheme,

s=maxi|wi|127,qi=round⁡(wis), s = \frac{\max_i |w_i|}{127}, \qquad q_i = \operatorname{round}\!\left(\frac{w_i}{s}\right),

with clamping to the representable range. The reconstructed value is

ŵi=sqi. \hat w_i = s q_i.

A reference matrix-vector product can therefore compute

y=∑i(sqi)xi. y = \sum_i (s q_i)x_i.

That scalar implementation is not necessarily fast, but it creates an oracle for SIMD or GPU fused dequantization-and-dot kernels.

Before clamping, the scalar reconstruction error for ordinary round-to-nearest is bounded by roughly half a quantization step. The output error is workload-dependent because the dot product combines weight errors with input magnitudes. An accuracy report therefore needs representative activations or a model-level metric, not only weight reconstruction error.

Zero rows and exceptional values

When all weights in a block are zero, dividing by the maximum absolute value would produce an invalid scale. The format and runtime need an explicit zero-block representation. Non-finite input weights should be rejected or handled by a documented conversion policy instead of entering integer casts accidentally.

Groupwise 4-bit formats add another trade-off. Smaller groups let the scale adapt more locally but spend more bytes on metadata and may increase metadata bandwidth. Larger groups reduce metadata overhead but make each scale describe a wider distribution.

Reference versus optimized execution

tools/labs/phase29_ml_runtime_lab.cpp implements a checked per-row Q8 reference and compares its dot product against the original floating-point row under a stated error budget. The point is not to advertise Q8 as the final format; it is to establish the proof pattern:

stored codes plus metadata → scalar interpretation → reference result → optimized kernel → measured error and performance.

A Metal or SIMD kernel should be judged against that reference on adversarial widths, tails, zero blocks, extreme scales and random vectors. SIMD lane packing is an implementation detail; the dequantized mathematical contract remains the same.

Related: Quantization and compressed weights, GGUF binary model loading, Tensor runtime layout and views.

Transformer attention and KV cache runtime

Transformer attention and KV cache runtime

A transformer runtime becomes understandable when tensor shapes remain visible. For one attention head, let a token representation produce query, key and value vectors

q,k,v∈ℝd. q,k,v \in \mathbb{R}^{d}.

For a query attending to keys kjk_j, the scaled score is

ℓj=qTkjd, \ell_j = \frac{q^T k_j}{\sqrt{d}},

followed by a stable softmax

pj=eℓj−m∑teℓt−m,m=maxtℓt, p_j = \frac{e^{\ell_j-m}}{\sum_t e^{\ell_t-m}}, \qquad m=\max_t \ell_t,

and the output is

o=∑jpjvj. o = \sum_j p_j v_j.

Subtracting mm does not change the distribution because the same factor appears in numerator and denominator, but it prevents overflow when logits are large.

Causal masking

For autoregressive decoding at token position tt, a query must not observe keys and values from future positions. In a batch attention matrix this is represented by a causal mask before softmax. During incremental decoding, a correctly managed KV cache gives the same structural guarantee: only keys and values through the current token have been appended.

The cache exists because recomputing all earlier K/V projections every token is wasteful. If each layer has key/value vectors of head width dhd_h, number of KV heads hkvh_{kv}, sequence length LL, and element size bb, the rough storage per layer is

2Lhkvdhb 2 L h_{kv} d_h b

bytes before allocator and alignment overhead. Cache datatype, paging strategy and maximum context length are therefore memory-system decisions.

Multi-head and grouped-query attention

Multiple heads perform the same mechanism with separate projected subspaces. Grouped-query attention may use fewer key/value heads than query heads; the mapping from query head to KV head must be explicit. GGUF metadata commonly carries head-count and key/value dimension information, so model loading and runtime shape validation meet at this boundary.

Residual, normalization, and feed-forward structure

Attention is only one sublayer. A complete transformer block also needs residual paths, normalization, and a feed-forward network or architecture-specific alternative. The order—pre-norm versus post-norm, RMSNorm versus LayerNorm, activation and gating choice—is part of the model architecture and must come from the model contract rather than a generic “transformer” assumption.

Executable witness

tools/labs/phase29_ml_runtime_lab.cpp implements stable softmax and a small incremental KV cache. Two keys with distinct values make the weighting observable; a single-token case proves that incremental causal attention cannot see a future token that has not been appended.

It intentionally does not claim multi-head batching, rotary position embeddings, grouped-query attention, tokenizer behavior, paged KV caches, fused kernels or production-model parity. Those are separate implementation milestones.

Related: Tensor runtime layout and views, GGUF binary model loading, ONNX graph import and lowering, Quantized matvec and dequantization.

Reciprocal bases and coordinate measurements

Reciprocal bases and coordinate measurements

A basis reconstructs vectors; a reciprocal basis measures their coefficients. Those are different jobs when the basis is not orthonormal.

Let basis vectors b1,…,bnb_1,\ldots,b_n form the columns of matrix BB. Coordinates cc reconstruct a vector by

v=Bc. v=Bc.

Recovering the coordinates means solving

Bc=v,c=B−1v Bc=v, \qquad c=B^{-1}v

when BB is square and nonsingular. The rows of B−1B^{-1} are the coordinate-measurement covectors. In Euclidean coordinates, their vector representatives are the columns of

B−𝖳. B^{-\mathsf T}.

These reciprocal vectors bib^i satisfy

bi⋅bj=δji. b^i\cdot b_j=\delta^i_j.

For the slanted basis b1=(1,0)b_1=(1,0), b2=(1,1)b_2=(1,1) and vector v=(3,2)v=(3,2), directly dotting with the basis vectors gives (3,5)(3,5) and is wrong as a coordinate recovery rule. The reciprocal basis is

b1=(1,−1),b2=(0,1), b^1=(1,-1),\qquad b^2=(0,1),

so the measurements are b1⋅v=1b^1\cdot v=1 and b2⋅v=2b^2\cdot v=2, exactly the coefficients that reconstruct v=b1+2b2v=b_1+2b_2.

A reciprocal basis is therefore a concrete bridge from vectors to covectors. It also explains why normal transformation uses an inverse transpose: normals are measurements that must continue to annihilate tangent directions after the tangent basis changes.

In numerical code, do not build a matrix inverse merely to solve one coordinate problem. Use a factorization or direct solve appropriate to the matrix structure and condition.

Full derivation and worked trace: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Recover a component with the right measuring rule.

Related: Covectors linear functionals and normal transforms, Basis coordinates and dimension, Conditioning and singularity.

Norms, dual norms and error budgets

Norms, dual norms and error budgets

A norm defines a size rule. Its dual norm measures the largest scalar response a linear measurement can produce over the unit ball of that norm.

For a covector represented by coefficients aa,

∥a∥*=max∥e∥≤1a𝖳e, \|a\|_* = \max_{\|e\|\le 1} a^{\mathsf T}e,

and therefore

|a𝖳e|≤∥a∥*∥e∥. |a^{\mathsf T}e|\le \|a\|_*\,\|e\|.

This turns an error budget into a sensitivity bound. The choice of norm matters because different “allowed error shapes” have different worst cases. A Euclidean ball is self-dual: the dual of ℓ2\ell_2 is ℓ2\ell_2. A componentwise box uses ℓ∞\ell_\infty for the error and has ℓ1\ell_1 as the dual measurement norm. An ℓ1\ell_1 error budget has ℓ∞\ell_\infty dual sensitivity.

Example: if a=(2,−3)a=(2,-3) and ∥e∥∞≤0.01\|e\|_\infty\le0.01, then

|a𝖳e|≤(|2|+|−3|)0.01=0.05. |a^{\mathsf T}e| \le (|2|+|{-3}|)0.01 =0.05.

This is more informative than a generic epsilon because it says what perturbations are permitted and what scalar quantity is being protected.

Error budgets in graphics and simulation should also carry units. A state vector mixing metres, radians, exposure values and normalized texture coordinates does not acquire a physically meaningful Euclidean norm merely because the values are stored in one array. The metric or scaling must state what “one unit of error” means in each subspace.

Full derivation and worked trace: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Bound a measurement using a dual norm.

Related: Metric gradients and differential measurements, Forward and backward error, Numerical error budgets.

Metric gradients and differential measurements

Metric gradients and differential measurements

The differential of a scalar function is a linear measurement of displacement. The gradient is the vector that represents that measurement after an inner product or metric has been chosen.

At a point, let coordinate derivative coefficients be collected in gg. Then

df[h]=g𝖳h. df[h]=g^{\mathsf T}h.

If the vector-space inner product is

⟨u,h⟩G=u𝖳Gh \langle u,h\rangle_G=u^{\mathsf T}Gh

for symmetric positive-definite metric matrix GG, the metric gradient is defined by

df[h]=⟨grad⁡Gf,h⟩G df[h]=\langle \operatorname{grad}_G f,h\rangle_G

for every displacement hh. Therefore

Ggrad⁡Gf=g,grad⁡Gf=G−1g. G\operatorname{grad}_G f=g, \qquad \operatorname{grad}_G f=G^{-1}g.

In ordinary orthonormal Euclidean coordinates G=IG=I, so derivative coefficients and gradient-vector coordinates happen to match. That familiar coincidence hides the conceptual distinction.

Example: for f(x,y)=x+yf(x,y)=x+y and

G=[1004], G=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&4\end{bmatrix},

the derivative coefficients are g=(1,1)g=(1,1) but

grad⁡Gf=(1,1/4). \operatorname{grad}_G f=(1,1/4).

The steepest direction depends on the ruler used to constrain step length. This is not merely abstract geometry: weighted optimization, pose parameters mixing translation and rotation, and preconditioned numerical methods all choose an effective metric.

The maximum first-order change over the metric unit ball is the dual norm of the differential:

maxh𝖳Gh≤1g𝖳h=g𝖳G−1g. \max_{h^{\mathsf T}Gh\le1} g^{\mathsf T}h = \sqrt{g^{\mathsf T}G^{-1}g}.

So metric gradients and dual-norm error bounds are two views of the same measurement-versus-vector relationship.

Full derivation and worked trace: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#A derivative measures change; a gradient needs a ruler.

University course development

Extend the existing color note with why image-processing arithmetic must distinguish encoded values from light. A display encoding such as sRGB uses a nonlinear transfer curve so code values allocate precision in a way that suits perception and storage. Averaging or adding those encoded numbers does not generally average or add emitted light. Decode to linear-light RGB before blending, filtering, estimating radiance, or compositing, then encode for display. If two equal-area samples contain linear intensities 00 and 11, their physical average is 0.50.5; averaging their encoded sRGB values and treating that result as light yields a different, brighter answer. Color primaries and a white point also define the coordinate system of RGB, so a numeric triplet is incomplete without its color space. Keep scene-referred radiance, display-referred color, and perceptual appearance separate.

Continuous explanation · Coverage and source gap · Sources and verification

University course development

Computational geometry often decides whether points are left or right of a directed line, whether three points are collinear, or whether a point lies inside a circle. These decisions reduce to determinant signs. For points a,b,ca,b,c in 2D, the signed area determinant classifies orientation. If its exact value is near zero, floating-point rounding can change the sign and make neighboring algorithms disagree, creating flipped triangles or invalid topology. Robust predicates evaluate a fast approximate determinant with an error bound; if the sign is certain they stop, and if uncertain they recompute with higher precision. This adaptive strategy spends extra work only near degeneracy. It does not make constructed intersection coordinates exact, but it protects discrete branching decisions that must be globally consistent in triangulation, mesh repair, and ray-edge intersection.

Pose estimation, transforms, and robust fitting · Visibility queries and ray intersections · Meshes, connectivity, and geometry processing

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase7 · Latest development: University courses

University course development

Extend the existing quaternion note with interpolation and sign handling in animation. A unit quaternion represents a 3D rotation, but qq and −q-q encode the same physical orientation. If two endpoint quaternions have a negative dot product, negate one endpoint before interpolation so the path follows the shorter arc on the unit four-dimensional sphere. Linear interpolation followed by normalization is inexpensive and often adequate for close orientations; spherical linear interpolation travels at constant angular speed for widely separated rotations. Quaternion interpolation acts on orientation, while translation and scale need their own rules. This matters in camera paths and articulated characters: interpolating four components without handling the double cover can create an unnecessary long spin, while interpolating Euler angles can encounter a gimbal singularity. Validate unit length after operations subject to floating-point drift.

Coordinate frames, transformations, and pose · Scene graphs and articulated geometry · Animation curves and motion paths

Cache lines and memory bandwidth

Cache lines and memory bandwidth

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C003

Definition and mechanism

Packing can place more logical values in each transferred cache line, trading arithmetic for lower footprint and traffic.

A cache line is the block moved between cache levels; memory bandwidth is bytes transferred per unit time. With an illustrative 64-byte line, byte-per-bit data stores 64 logical bits, while packed data stores 512. Real line sizes and performance must be measured for the target.

Reordering 24→16-byte records reduces footprint, not necessarily measured traffic or speed. Field reordering and AoS versus SoA separates hot field arrays from full records; TLB caches translations rather than contents.

Atomic operations and write contention

Atomic operations and write contention

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C005

Definition and mechanism

Independently meaningful fields sharing a word can require coordinated read-modify-write and can cause unrelated writers to contend.

An atomic update is indivisible to other participating accesses under its specified memory ordering. Packed independent flags may share one read-modify-write location: writers can overwrite each other without coordination. Contention means accesses compete for ownership or serialization.

Atomic additions can prevent lost writes without fixing addition order. Different valid schedules can produce different rounded sums; deterministic reduction requires a defined tree as well as safe synchronization.

Prerequisites

  • Bit packing — Packing places several constrained values into a carrier.
  • Machine word — A processor’s natural integer processing width is often called its word width, but the term is architecture dependent.

Guest and host integer domains

Guest and host integer domains

Curriculum depth: Forward · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002

Definition and mechanism

An emulator may compute an NN-bit guest operation in a wider host type so carry and other discarded architectural information remain observable.

Guest means the machine being emulated; host means the implementation platform. An eight-bit guest addition can use a host temporary holding 0–511, extract carry, then narrow to 0–255. Host signed overflow must never be used to imitate guest wrap.

Stable probability normalization and log-sum-exp

Stable probability normalization and log-sum-exp

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

To normalize nonnegative weights, divide each by their sum; direct summation can overflow even when the normalized probabilities are representable. Scale by the largest weight before summing. For log weights aia_i, compute m+log⁡∑ieai−mm+\log\sum_i e^{a_i-m}, where m=max⁡iaim=\max_i a_i. Subtracting the maximum prevents exponential overflow, and the result can be used to form softmax probabilities. This assumes at least one finite, valid weight and requires an explicit policy for all-zero, negative, NaN, or infinite inputs. Underflow of very small normalized probabilities is a separate concern from overflow; do not silently equate zero after underflow with mathematically impossible. For log weights (1000,1001,1000)(1000,1001,1000), subtracting 10011001 keeps exponentials bounded while leaving the normalized probabilities unchanged.

Stable quadratic root evaluation

Stable quadratic root evaluation

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

The direct quadratic formula can lose nearly all significant digits in one root when it subtracts nearly equal values. For real coefficients with nonzero leading coefficient and a valid nonnegative discriminant, compute a signed large-magnitude numerator first: q=−12(b+copysign⁡(b2−4ac,b))q=-\frac12(b+\operatorname{copysign}(\sqrt{b^2-4ac},b)), then obtain roots as q/aq/a and c/qc/q. The second root follows from the product relation x1x2=c/ax_1x_2=c/a. This avoids cancellation in the small root, but it does not prevent overflow in the discriminant or cover degenerate coefficients, nonfinite inputs, or q=0q=0; a robust solver also scales inputs and handles those cases explicitly. For example, the small root of x2+108x+1=0x^2+10^8x+1=0 is near −10−8-10^{-8}, exactly the root most endangered by direct subtraction.

ODE integration and stability

ODE integration and stability

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

An ordinary differential equation gives the rate of change of a state over time. Forward Euler uses the current derivative: qk+1=qk+hf(qk,tk)q_{k+1}=q_k+h f(q_k,t_k), where hh is the time step. For decay u̇=−au\dot u=-au, it multiplies each step by 1−ah1-ah; if the magnitude exceeds one, the numerical solution grows even though the true solution decays. Spring systems can be stiff because high-frequency modes force very small stable steps. Backward Euler evaluates the rate at the unknown new state and is more stable for decay but requires solving an equation and may add numerical damping. Symplectic Euler updates velocity then position and often keeps energy bounded for conservative mechanics. Choose an integrator according to stability, accuracy, conservation, and runtime rather than displayed frame rate alone.

Phase 9–10 development

An initial-value problem consists of a differential equation and a specified starting state. A numerical integrator replaces continuous evolution with finite updates, so accuracy and stability depend on both method and step size. Consistency concerns local approximation, stability concerns error growth under repeated steps, and convergence concerns the limiting solution as the step is refined. Stiff systems can force explicit methods to take very small steps even when the visible trajectory changes slowly. Symplectic methods preserve Hamiltonian structure but do not generally preserve exact energy at each step.

Prerequisites

  • Absolute and relative error
  • Conditioning and singularity
  • ODE initial-value problems and stiffness
  • Time integrators and symplectic updates

Used by

  • Implicit differentiation and parameter sensitivities

Finite differences and step-size balance

Finite differences and step-size balance

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

Finite differences estimate derivatives from sampled function values. Forward and backward differences use one-sided samples and have first-order truncation error; central differences use samples on both sides and usually have second-order truncation error for smooth functions. Making the step arbitrarily small is not always better: subtractive cancellation and evaluation noise grow as the step shrinks, while truncation error grows when it is too large. The useful step balances these effects and depends on scale, precision, and function noise. Finite differences are valuable for black-box sensitivities and gradient checks, but they are not automatic differentiation and can fail near discontinuities or branch changes. A numerical gradient check should compare directional derivatives, use scale-aware steps, and avoid interpreting one tolerance pass as proof that every derivative path is correct.

Prerequisites

  • Derivative as a local linear map
  • Absolute and relative error

Numerical quadrature and error

Numerical quadrature and error

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

Quadrature approximates a definite integral from finitely many function evaluations. Left, right, and midpoint rectangle rules use constant local models; the trapezoid rule uses linear interpolation; Simpson’s rule integrates a local quadratic fit over paired intervals. Their errors depend on smoothness, interval size, and rule-specific derivative bounds. Refining the mesh usually improves accuracy for smooth functions, but increases computation and may expose floating-point accumulation error. Adaptive quadrature places more samples where the integrand changes rapidly, provided its error estimator is trustworthy. Quadrature differs from Monte Carlo: deterministic rules have dimension-dependent behavior, while random sampling is attractive in high dimensions but has statistical uncertainty. Report the interval, nodes, weights, stopping tolerance, and error-control method so numerical results can be reproduced.

ODE initial-value problems and stiffness

ODE initial-value problems and stiffness

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

An ordinary differential equation specifies a state’s rate of change as a function of state and time. An initial-value problem adds the starting state; together they define the trajectory when existence and uniqueness conditions hold. Numerical integration advances approximate states through finite time steps. Stability concerns whether numerical errors remain controlled under repeated updates, not just whether one step is accurate. A stiff system contains modes with very different time scales; explicit methods may require impractically small steps to remain stable even when the visible solution changes slowly. Implicit methods can enlarge the stable step region but require solving equations. Consistency, stability, and convergence are distinct properties. A simulator should choose its step and integrator based on the dynamics, not merely the display frame interval or apparent smoothness of one trajectory.

Robust summaries and error metrics

Robust summaries and error metrics

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Histograms, quantiles, medians, and robust scales summarize different features of a finite dataset. Histogram bar area represents probability only when heights are divided by sample count and bin width. Quantile conventions differ across software, so report the interpolation rule. The median minimizes absolute deviation and resists some extreme observations; the mean minimizes squared deviation and is more sensitive to outliers. MAD and trimmed means provide other robustness choices with efficiency tradeoffs. MSE and RMSE emphasize large errors, MAE is less sensitive to them, and relative metrics can become unstable near zero. Aggregating per-scene scores differs from pooling every observation. Choose the metric from the scientific question, units, and failure cost, and report tail behavior when rare large errors matter.

Matrix norms and numerical error

Matrix norms and numerical error

The spectral norm is the largest 2-norm stretch and equals the largest singular value. The Frobenius norm measures aggregate squared entry energy. Residuals, orthogonality errors, and condition numbers need a declared norm and scale; a small residual alone need not imply a sensitive solution is accurate.

Use it when: setting scaled tolerances or interpreting numerical diagnostics.

Developed in Phase 8: The spectral norm measures worst-case amplification, while the Frobenius norm accumulates squared energy across entries. The chapter uses them to scale residuals, reconstruction errors, and orthogonality defects, and separates backward error in a nearby problem from forward error in the requested answer. norms and scale · residuals and error interpretation

A matrix norm can protect a geometry bound

A local sphere under a linear transform is generally an ellipsoid. The Frobenius norm times its original radius gives a safe, possibly loose enclosing radius. Taking only the longest matrix column can fail under shear. The culling example derives the bound, demonstrates the shear counterexample, and links its geometric figure. This connects numerical matrix norms to conservative rejection decisions.

A posteriori error bounds for contractive iteration

A posteriori error bounds for contractive iteration

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

For a fixed-point iteration xn+1=G(xn)x_{n+1}=G(x_n), suppose GG is a contraction with Lipschitz constant q<1q<1 on a region containing the iterates and its fixed point. Then the remaining error is bounded by the next step divided by 1−q1-q: ∥x*−xn∥≤∥xn+1−xn∥/(1−q)\|x^*-x_n\|\le\|x_{n+1}-x_n\|/(1-q). The assumption is essential; a small step alone does not prove convergence because stagnation or a failed update can also make changes tiny. In implementation, report the contraction evidence or a suitable residual bound and keep failure distinct from success. This turns an observed update into a conditional, checkable estimate rather than a guess. If q=1/2q=1/2 and the latest step is 10−610^{-6}, this bound is 2×10−62\times10^{-6}, conditional on the contraction proof.

Algorithmic stability

Algorithmic stability

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

A numerical problem can be sensitive even when an algorithm handles it well. Stability describes whether the finite-precision algorithm introduces only the error expected from rounding, often by showing that its output exactly solves a nearby problem. Backward stability is one useful form; forward stability asks directly how close the computed answer is to the exact answer for the original input. The claim must name its assumptions, arithmetic model, and problem class. For example, a stable linear solver can still have a large forward error on an ill-conditioned matrix. Stability therefore belongs beside conditioning, not in its place. A dot product with a small residual can still conceal an ill-conditioned problem, so report which notion of stability is actually supported.

Numerical error budgets

Numerical error budgets

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

A computed result can differ from a target because of model assumptions, discretization, solver termination, arithmetic, sampling, or uncertain reference data. These contributions may interact, so an additive budget is a diagnostic model rather than a universal identity. First identify which errors are deterministic bounds, which are observed estimates, and which are stochastic uncertainty. For example, a ray-traced pixel can combine approximation of geometry, finite sample variance, floating-point accumulation, and an imperfect reference image. Allocate effort where the dominant contribution lies: extra precision cannot fix model bias, and more samples cannot repair an incorrect PDF. Report units and assumptions with every tolerance.

QR factorization and least squares

QR factorization and least squares

QR writes A=QRA=QR with orthonormal columns in QQ and triangular RR. Orthogonal coordinates preserve Euclidean lengths, so least squares reduces to a triangular solve and a perpendicular residual. Householder QR is a stable dense method; Gram–Schmidt explains the geometry but can lose orthogonality.

Use it when: fitting overdetermined data with known full column rank.

Developed in Phase 8: Orthogonal transformations change coordinates without changing Euclidean lengths. QR therefore separates the fitted component, solved through triangular RR, from the constant perpendicular residual; the Householder construction is the stable dense route, with Gram–Schmidt retained to make the geometry visible. Bracketed and open root solvers

Bracketed and open root solvers

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

A root solver seeks f(x)=0f(x)=0. A bracketed method maintains an interval whose endpoints have opposite signs; continuity then guarantees at least one root remains inside, and bisection provides a predictable shrinking error bound. Open methods such as secant and Newton can converge faster near a well-behaved simple root, but they may diverge, encounter a zero derivative, or leave the relevant domain. A safeguarded hybrid uses a bracket for global protection and accepts fast proposals only when they preserve progress. Residual size alone does not certify root accuracy when the root is poorly conditioned, and discontinuous functions do not satisfy the sign-change guarantee.

Online moments and Welford accumulation

Online moments and Welford accumulation

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Online statistics update a mean and centered sum of squares as observations arrive, using constant storage. Welford’s recurrence computes a new mean from the old mean and one sample, then adds the product of deviations measured before and after that update. The centered form avoids severe cancellation in E[X²]−E[X]² for data with a large offset and small spread. Divide accumulated scatter by n for descriptive population-normalized variance or by n−1 for unbiased sample variance under IID finite-variance assumptions. The recurrence is numerically better behaved, not immune to overflow, count exhaustion, or all rounding error. Parallel workers can merge count, mean, and scatter summaries with a correction term for different means; merge order can change floating-point results.

Discretization, truncation, and roundoff

Discretization, truncation, and roundoff

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Discretization replaces a continuous object or domain with a finite grid; truncation omits terms or limits an iterative expansion; roundoff comes from finite-precision arithmetic. They have different causes and respond to different changes. Refining a spatial grid may reduce discretization error while increasing computation. Adding more terms can reduce truncation error. Increasing precision or reformulating arithmetic can reduce roundoff, though a poor algorithm may still dominate. A signed-distance field sampled too coarsely can lose a thin feature entirely, while an ODE’s Euler step has a local truncation error even under exact arithmetic. An error budget should distinguish these mechanisms instead of calling every disagreement “numerical error.”

Automatic differentiation and backpropagation

Automatic differentiation and backpropagation

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

Automatic differentiation evaluates derivatives by applying the chain rule to the operations in a program. Each operation has a local derivative rule; composing the rules gives the derivative of the complete computation without symbolically expanding it or approximating it by finite differences. Forward mode propagates a tangent perturbation and computes a Jacobian-vector product (JVP), useful when there are few inputs. Reverse mode propagates sensitivities from outputs back to inputs and computes a vector-Jacobian product (VJP), making gradients of one scalar loss with respect to millions of parameters practical. Backpropagation is reverse-mode differentiation through a neural network’s computation graph. It does not remove numerical problems: nondifferentiable operations require conventions, saturated activations can yield tiny gradients, and an incorrect graph or reduction yields an incorrect gradient. Gradients are local sensitivity information, not proof of a global optimum. Finite differences remain a useful small-scale check, but cancellation and step-size tradeoffs make them a poor training method.

Phase 9–10 development

Forward mode propagates an input tangent through local derivatives and computes a Jacobian-vector product. Reverse mode propagates an output sensitivity backward and computes a vector-Jacobian product. These are chain-rule evaluations on the operation graph, distinct from finite differences, which perturb inputs and can suffer cancellation. The reverse pass requires a valid reverse-topological order and storage that remains alive until propagation finishes. Differentiating a converged solution uses an implicit equation and its local Jacobian; it is not automatically the same as differentiating every solver iteration.

Reproducible numerical benchmarking

Reproducible numerical benchmarking

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

A useful numerical benchmark separates sample-level variability from run-level variability and pairs competing methods on the same inputs or seeds. Record the algorithm, precision, compiler/runtime settings, sample count, seed or keyed input, warm-up policy, timing method, and error metric. Compare distributions or paired differences rather than a single favorable run. A speed improvement is meaningful only if accuracy and failure rates remain acceptable for the target workload. For Monte Carlo methods, repeat independent runs and report uncertainty; for deterministic solvers, use analytical or manufactured solutions and measure convergence. Reproducibility is an experimental contract, not merely a fixed random seed. If the workload is stochastic, compare paired seeds and report both runtime and error distributions.

Prerequisites

  • Numerical reproducibility
  • Confidence intervals and sequential evidence
  • Robust summaries and error metrics
  • Numerical error budgets
  • Convergence order and Richardson extrapolation
  • Latin-hypercube sampling

Used by

  • Research validity and ablation

Full teaching explanation

  • Test numerical methods and benchmark reproducibly

Vector storage SIMD and boundary layouts

Vector storage SIMD and boundary layouts

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6

Definition and mechanism

Storage layout, compute lanes and external buffer layout are separate contracts. SIMD may operate within one vector or across objects. AoS, SoA and AoSoA change access patterns. Alignment and padding must be measured; a spare lane is not implicitly valid homogeneous data.

One million twelve-byte vectors occupy four million fewer payload bytes than sixteen-byte vectors. A sixteen-byte load still needs sixteen accessible bytes even if one lane is discarded.

Prerequisites

  • Vector value types and component access — Primitive representation and access rules support layout choices and semantic wrappers.
  • Alignment and padding — Object alignment and array stride constrain storage and boundary conversions.
  • SIMD and GPU data layouts — Lane access and external interface layouts require separate storage contracts.

Named members versus array elements

Named members versus array elements

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C007 · Latest development: C008

Definition and mechanism

The x member’s one-past pointer is not an authorized y access. A span describes an already-valid range; adjacency cannot create that range.

Adjacent x/y/z fields are separate subobjects, not T[3]. A pointer to x supports one-element-array pointer arithmetic; one-past cannot be dereferenced to access y. span(&x,3) does not create an array. Use explicit member dispatch or actual array storage; a ToArray result is a copy.

Prerequisites

  • Pointer arithmetic and provenance — Array-relative pointer bounds explain why adjacency of separate members cannot authorize indexing.

Used by

  • Vector value types and component access — Phase 6 uses this established foundation in its geometry narrative.

GPU vertex specification

GPU vertex specification

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A GPU vertex-input specification explains how bytes in one or more buffers become per-vertex shader inputs. A buffer object owns bytes; a vertex array object records their interpretation: enabled attributes, component count and type, normalization, stride, byte offset, and the buffer binding used for fetch. Stride is the number of bytes between successive vertices; offset is the first component’s byte position. For vertex i, the address is base + offset + i × stride. For interleaved records containing position (3 floats), normal (3), and UV (2), the stride is 8 × 4 = 32 bytes and the UV offset is 24 bytes. Modern binding APIs separate attribute format from the buffer binding; older pointer-style calls can capture the buffer bound at setup time. A wrong stride may still address valid memory, so the symptom is often plausible but scrambled geometry. The contract must agree with CPU packing, shader input types, and the API’s state-capture rules.

Prerequisites

  • Vector storage SIMD and boundary layouts
  • Matrix storage indexing and strides
  • Camera view and clip-space pipeline
  • Pointer arithmetic and provenance

Used by

  • Rasterization, coverage, and depth
  • Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation

Full teaching explanation

  • Rasterization, coverage, and depth

Recall and next depth

  • Trace the fetched address for vertex 3 when stride is 32 bytes and offset is 24 bytes.
  • Why can an incorrect stride produce plausible but scrambled geometry without a memory fault?

HMAC and HKDF

HMAC and HKDF

HMAC authenticates a message under a shared secret key. HKDF uses HMAC to turn input keying material into one or more pseudorandom-looking keys with explicit context separation.

Extract then expand

HKDF has two conceptual stages.

Extract computes a pseudorandom key:

PRK=HMAC⁡salt(IKM). PRK=\operatorname{HMAC}_{salt}(IKM).

Expand derives output keying material in blocks:

T(1)=HMAC⁡PRK(info∥0x01), T(1)=\operatorname{HMAC}_{PRK}(info\,\|\,0x01),

T(i)=HMAC⁡PRK(T(i−1)∥info∥i). T(i)=\operatorname{HMAC}_{PRK}(T(i-1)\,\|\,info\,\|\,i).

Concatenate blocks until the requested output length is reached.

The info field is not decoration. It lets the same root keying material derive separate keys for different purposes, versions, peers or directions. Domain separation reduces accidental cross-protocol key reuse.

A salt can improve extraction and should follow the protocol design. HKDF does not create entropy that is absent from the input keying material.

Evidence

tools/labs/crypto_primitives_lab.cpp validates HMAC-SHA256 against RFC 4231 and HKDF-SHA256 extract/expand against RFC 5869 test vectors.

That proves the bit-level reference on those vectors. It does not establish side-channel resistance, secret erasure, key storage, protocol context selection or application security.

Primary standards: RFC 2104 / RFC 4231 for HMAC testing and RFC 5869 for HKDF.

Related: Integrity and authenticity, Checksums CRCs and hashes.

Merkle trees and authenticated structure

Merkle trees and authenticated structure

A Merkle tree hashes data into leaves and repeatedly hashes child digests into parent digests until one root remains. The root commits to the entire ordered leaf set under the collision-resistance assumptions of the hash and the tree encoding.

A safe design domain-separates leaves from internal nodes, for example:

Li=H(0x00∥datai), L_i=H(0x00\,\|\,data_i),

P=H(0x01∥left∥right). P=H(0x01\,\|\,left\,\|\,right).

Without an unambiguous encoding, different logical tree structures can accidentally serialize to the same byte concatenation before hashing.

Inclusion proof

To prove that one leaf belongs to a tree, provide the sibling hash at each level and the left/right ordering bits. The verifier starts from the leaf hash and reconstructs the root. Proof size is O(log⁡n)O(\log n) for a balanced binary tree.

The trusted root must come from a trusted channel or authenticated record. A Merkle proof checked against an attacker-provided root proves nothing about authenticity.

Odd leaf policy

When a level has an odd number of nodes, the format must specify what happens: duplicate the last node, promote it, or use another encoding. Different policies create different roots.

tools/labs/crypto_primitives_lab.cpp uses an explicit domain-separated construction and duplicates the last digest on odd levels. The test proves determinism and that changing one sample leaf changes the root in the exercised case.

Related: Checksums CRCs and hashes, Integrity and authenticity.

Production manifests and transactional publication

Production manifests and transactional publication

A production manifest is a durable description of what should be built and published. It prevents a pipeline from depending on hidden editor state or on “whatever files happen to be in this directory.”

A useful manifest separates identity from location. A logical asset ID names the thing the project means. Source and output paths say where a particular revision is read and written. A cryptographic digest can identify exact content bytes. A schema version says how to interpret all fields.

Path safety

Normalize paths before planning any write. A production-safe policy normally rejects parent traversal, unexpected absolute paths, ambiguous separators, and paths that escape the declared project root after symlink resolution.

Lexical normalization alone cannot prove symlink safety. The filesystem must be queried at the point where real paths are resolved, and the resolved target must still lie inside the approved root.

Deterministic plans

The same manifest and tool versions should produce the same ordered build plan. Determinism makes logs diffable, cache keys stable and failures reproducible.

Planning should be side-effect free. A dry run should reveal every intended output, overwrite, deletion and dependency before publication begins.

Staging and commit

A safe publication sequence is:

  1. validate the whole request;
  2. write derived outputs to staging names or directories;
  3. validate staged bytes and metadata;
  4. fsync or equivalent when durability is part of the promise;
  5. publish with the platform’s proven atomic replacement mechanism;
  6. update manifest/index state;
  7. retain enough evidence to diagnose rollback or partial failure.

Atomicity and durability are separate. A rename can make a new name appear atomically yet still not guarantee survival across power loss unless the required data and directory metadata were persisted.

Idempotence

Repeating the same publication should either be a no-op or produce the same visible state. A pipeline that appends duplicate records, increments versions accidentally or rewrites unrelated timestamps on every run is harder to cache and reason about.

tools/labs/production_pipeline_contract_lab.cpp models deterministic plan generation and idempotent publication in memory. It intentionally labels real filesystem durability as unproved.

Related: Atomic publication and durability, DCC adapters and engine publication.

Shamir secret sharing

Shamir secret sharing

Shamir secret sharing splits a secret into shares so that any threshold number can reconstruct it while fewer shares reveal no information in the ideal finite-field construction when coefficients are chosen uniformly at random.

Choose a prime field 𝔽p\mathbb F_p containing the secret value and a threshold tt. Construct a random polynomial

f(x)=s+a1x+⋯+at−1xt−1 f(x)=s+a_1x+\cdots+a_{t-1}x^{t-1}

with secret s=f(0)s=f(0). Give participant ii the share (xi,f(xi))(x_i,f(x_i)) for distinct nonzero xix_i.

Any tt shares recover f(0)f(0) through Lagrange interpolation:

s=∑iyi∏j≠i−xjxi−xj(mod⁡p). s= \sum_i y_i \prod_{j\ne i} \frac{-x_j}{x_i-x_j} \pmod p.

Every division is multiplication by a finite-field inverse. Ordinary integer division is wrong.

Security condition

The coefficients must be generated with a cryptographically secure random generator. Deterministic or predictable coefficients destroy the information-theoretic secrecy claim even though interpolation still reconstructs correctly.

Share identifiers also matter: using duplicate x coordinates makes interpolation invalid.

Evidence boundary

tools/labs/crypto_primitives_lab.cpp demonstrates a three-share reconstruction over prime field 257 and reconstructs the same secret from two different three-share subsets.

Its polynomial coefficients are deliberately deterministic so the test is reproducible. Therefore the laboratory proves interpolation arithmetic, not production secrecy.

A production system additionally needs CSPRNG coefficients, authenticated share transport/storage, versioning, participant identity, compromise/recovery policy and secure erasure.

Related: Integrity and authenticity, HMAC and HKDF.

Executable and rendering verification

The original inline runtime_lab.cpp was compiled and run with Homebrew Clang 18.1.8 using -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror; it passed its timing-partition, interpolation, stale-handle, deferred-removal, capacity, overload, and invalid-duration assertions. The exact body also passed Apple Clang 21.0.0 with AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer. An initial Homebrew sanitizer binary did not terminate during observation and was stopped; that run is not reported as passed.

The physics numeric witness checks the stated explicit/semi-implicit/constant-acceleration results and signed impulse/momentum example. These CPU tests are limited to the saved examples. They do not validate a windowed engine, graphics API integration, a complete collision solver, audio deadlines, network behavior, or editor interactions. Final local link, fence, Mermaid, MathJax, and code-body checks are recorded in the checkpoint reports.

Historical review commentary, not a source-code audit.

Coverage gaps preserved

The caption set contains demonstrations and discussion for legacy OpenGL, early Hazel/Sparky input, textures, shaders, fonts, groups, audio setup, C# scripting, and editor workflow. It does not establish current behavior for any named API or engine branch. Several episodes openly end with unfinished work or failed experiments. No video-frame evidence or manual audio inspection is claimed. These sources extend the book’s teaching examples and provenance notes; they do not replace its present-day API boundaries, measured benchmarks, or implementation evidence.

Limits

All eleven group B caption texts were fully read, with canonical word counts and cleaned-file hashes saved in reviews-b.json. This is not frame-by-frame review, source checkout, build reproduction, benchmark verification, or current API research. Some videos are reactions, code reviews, or historic roadmap reports; opinions, narrated observations, and confirmed mechanisms are distinguished in their receipts. The coverage map routes all salient findings, but it is not a literal claim that every utterance has a unique paragraph in the book. Several foundations are already covered under the exact headings above; additions-b.md therefore prioritizes the incremental cold-start investigation, grid-sizing derivation, ownership decision questions, and evidence boundary.

Batch 015 — technical source-to-teaching coverage

This ledger covers the bounded 24-page assignment only. The reading drafts keep conceptual explanations separate from the author’s historical examples and from cautions about apparent code defects.

Source pages (PDF / printed) Distinct source ideas and mechanisms Teaching destination in pdf-additions-a.md
Game Engine Architecture 784–785 / 762–763 A subsystem-oriented frame loop; cache-friendly contiguous subsystem data; once-per-batch global work; reusable frame resources; pipelined processing; coupled multi-body collision resolution as group work “Let dependencies set the update order”
GEA 785–788 / 763–766 Parent/held-object ordering; animation-to-ragdoll and ragdoll-to-animation data flow; subsystem phases; pre/post hooks; multiple per-frame object hooks; per-phase membership lists to avoid useless iteration “Let dependencies set the update order”
GEA 788–790 / 766–768 Dependency forest and tiers; root-first buckets; full phased subsystem passes per bucket; shallow-depth examples; external systems may not accept bucketed calls; the author’s historical Uncharted account “Let dependencies set the update order”
GEA 790–793 / 768–771 Sequential partial updates; consistent states only before/after a loop; wrong-time reads and one-frame lag; old/new state caching and interpolation; memory cost and residual inconsistency; time stamps and same-bucket query guards “Make mixed-time reads visible”
GEA 793–795 / 771–773 Object dependency makes parallel updates hard; direct state peeking vs message passing; serial high-level model and parallel low-level systems as the author’s account; blocking vs non-blocking requests; issue as early as possible and consume as late as possible; tolerable stale results; batch ray requests; page 795 introduces events and notification/response duties “Make mixed-time reads visible”
Game Physics Engine Development 268–272 / 245–249 Insertion descends by child getGrowth; leaf split into existing/new child; ancestor-bound refresh; enclosing but nonminimal sphere; reason for runtime approximation; deletion replaces parent with sibling data, detaches adopted children, and recalculates upward; apparent double-delete typo preserved as a warning “Update the hierarchy without rebuilding all of it”
Physics 273–274 / 250–251 Multiple bounds for awkward sub-objects; level decomposition; box bounds for boxlike spaces; transition from object-dependent hierarchy to world-space partition “Grow a spatial hierarchy around the world’s shape”; “Update the hierarchy without rebuilding all of it”
Physics 274–278 / 251–255 Spatial structure is fixed to the world while a BVH follows its objects; hybrid combinations; BSP plane representation and signed dot-product side test; normalized direction and sphere crossing; nodes/leaves can contain sets; duplicate cross-plane object policy and candidate pairs; optional BVH per leaf; static-level collision leaves; preprocessing cost “Grow a spatial hierarchy around the world’s shape”
Physics 278–279 / 255–256 Quad-tree four-way ground/2D split; oct-tree eight-way 3D split; fixed world axes; coordinate-to-child selection with the source’s example; memory reason for choosing quad-tree in ground-focused 3D; apparent uninitialized child index in printed excerpt “Grow a spatial hierarchy around the world’s shape”

The merged pdf-additions.md additionally contains the separately authored scaled sphere-gap visual and recall prompt. It illustrates the already derived parent/child bound example and makes no claim about new book content. Grids are named as a common spatial structure on PDF p. 274 but their mechanics are outside the assigned range; the teaching text labels that limit. Event dispatch is introduced only at the end of GEA p. 795, so the draft records notification and response responsibilities without inventing a queue design.

Read receipts are in pdf-assignment-a.json and pdf-reviews-a.json for the technical pages, with combined four-book receipts in pdf-assignment.json and pdf-reviews.json. Declarations and definitions

Declarations and definitions

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C007 · Latest development: C007

Definition and mechanism

A declaration introduces or redeclares an entity; a definition provides the entity’s defining information. extern int x is only a declaration; int x=0 defines an object; a function body defines a function. A forward-declared class is incomplete, but a fixed-underlying opaque enum is complete.

Class access and invariants

Class access and invariants

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C007 · Latest development: C009

Definition and mechanism

Constructors establish externally usable state before publication; failed ordinary construction destroys completed subobjects. Generated memberwise moves do not automatically preserve relations such as extent-to-buffer consistency.

struct and class differ in default member and base-class access: public versus private. Either supports methods, inheritance, constructors and hidden data. The record-versus-invariant distinction is design convention; an invariant is a condition each public operation must preserve.

Prerequisites

  • Declarations and definitions — Class declarations establish members and bases whose access must be public or controlled.

Used by

  • Logical constness and mutable caches
  • Constructors and invariant establishment

Matrix multiplication and composition order

Matrix multiplication and composition order

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase7 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

The product AB applies B first for column-vector actions. Its entries sum A(i,k)B(k,j) over the shared dimension. Composition is associative over exact scalars and usually noncommutative; floating-point evaluation orders need not agree bitwise.

Matrix transpose symmetry and trace

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase7 · Latest development: Phase7

Definition and mechanism

Transpose exchanges row and column indices and reverses product order. Symmetric and skew-symmetric parts reconstruct any real square matrix. Trace is the diagonal sum and is invariant under similarity, while cyclic product trace needs compatible dimensions.

Phase 11 camera development

A basis change re-expresses the same physical points and transforms; a reconstruction gauge allows different parameter assignments to produce identical measurements. Fixing one camera pose chooses a world origin and orientation, but adds no image evidence. Monocular scale remains free until a baseline, known length, or metric sensor anchors it. Do not mistake a coordinate convention for an empirical measurement. This distinction matters when defining bundle-adjustment priors and covariance, and assumes a rigid calibrated camera model. Camera view and clip-space pipeline

Camera view and clip-space pipeline

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase7 · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A camera pose maps camera coordinates to world coordinates; its inverse is the view map. Projection produces homogeneous clip coordinates, clipping applies the API-specific inequalities, and valid perspective division produces NDC. Storage order supplies none of these coordinate contracts.

Reconstruction cue: A standard minus-Z perspective example needs a point in front of the camera and a meaningful clip w before division.

Continuous explanation · Coverage and source gap · Sources and verification

University course development

Extend the existing transform pipeline with the clipping and depth-precision decisions that make projection robust. A view frustum is the set of points a camera can see, bounded by near and far planes as well as image sides. Transforming the frustum into a canonical clip cube makes outside tests cheap; partially intersecting triangles must be clipped and triangulated so the rasterizer still receives triangles. The near plane also avoids geometry crossing the eye plane, while the far plane limits depth range. Floating-point depth values are unevenly distributed after perspective division, so an excessively tiny near distance paired with a huge far distance can make two nearby surfaces quantize to the same depth and produce z-fighting. Choose the narrowest useful depth interval and keep the view, clip, normalized, and screen coordinates distinct.

A scene description becomes an image · Cameras, projection, and calibration · Rasterization, coverage, and depth

Phase 11 camera development

A raster-to-ray camera maps a pixel to a geometric sample; In a pinhole model, invert projection and view transforms to recover a camera-space direction, then transform it to world space without applying translation as if it were a point. Pixel-center convention, viewport origin, handedness, clip-depth range, and normalization all affect the result. Offset a pixel to generate differential rays and estimate the surface footprint; that footprint grows with depth and changes with surface orientation. Keep ray generation distinct from raster projection while ensuring their conventions agree. Link: A camera model must close the loop; research: Four deeper links from the TUM lecture review.

Scalars fields and real-number models

Scalars fields and real-number models

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6

Definition and mechanism

A scalar is an element of the field used by a vector space. A field supports addition, multiplication and nonzero division under specified algebraic laws. The reals also supply order and completeness. Floating-point values approximate this model but do not form a mathematical field.

An integer reciprocal need not be an integer; 2−1=1/22^{-1}=1/2. A real scalar can carry metres or seconds. A finite representation cannot preserve every real-number operation.

Complex numbers and planar rotations

Complex numbers and planar rotations

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6

Definition and mechanism

Complex multiplication combines planar rotation and scaling. A unit complex multiplier represents a rotation; its conjugate gives the inverse. A two-component storage tuple is not automatically a rotation.

Multiplication by ii sends (x,y)(x,y) to (−y,x)(-y,x). Zero collapses the plane rather than representing any rotation.

Vectors coordinates and affine points

Vectors coordinates and affine points

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6

Definition and mechanism

A free vector describes movement independently of its starting point. A coordinate tuple describes that vector relative to an ordered basis. An affine point is a location without an intrinsic preferred origin. Point differences produce vectors; point translations produce points.

For the workcell panel, B−A=(4,0,0)B-A=(4,0,0) is a displacement in metres. Changing the origin changes point coordinates but cancels in this difference.

Vector spaces subspaces and span

Vector spaces subspaces and span

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6

Definition and mechanism

A vector space is closed under addition and field-scalar multiplication with coherent algebraic laws. A subspace retains these operations inside a larger space. The span of generators is every finite linear combination of them.

The plane z=0z=0 is a subspace of ℝ3\mathbb R^3; z=1z=1 is an affine translate, not a subspace. The span of (4,0,0)(4,0,0) and (0,3,0)(0,3,0) contains all in-plane movements.

Basis coordinates and dimension

Basis coordinates and dimension

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase7

Definition and mechanism

Phase 7 stores basis images as matrix columns and derives coordinate conversion [v]C=C−1B[v]B[v]_C=C^{-1}B[v]_B. The endpoint bases and whether motion is active or passive determine the product; row-major storage does not. Reconstruction and active/passive example.

A basis is an ordered independent spanning set. Independence makes coordinates unique; spanning makes every vector reachable. Dimension counts basis elements over the chosen field, not stored components or bytes. A basis change alters coordinates without necessarily moving the physical vector.

(3,2)=1(1,0)+2(1,1)(3,2)=1(1,0)+2(1,1), so its slanted-basis coordinates are (1,2)(1,2). A plane inside three-dimensional coordinates still has dimension two.

Norms lengths and induced distances

Norms lengths and induced distances

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6

Definition and mechanism

A norm is nonnegative, definite, absolutely homogeneous and satisfies the triangle inequality. It induces distance by taking the norm of a point difference. Coordinate-defined first, second and infinity norms answer different geometric questions.

For (3,−4)(3,-4), the three norms are 77, 55 and 44. Squared length scales quadratically and is not itself a norm or induced metric.

Dot products and orthogonality

Dot products and orthogonality

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6

Definition and mechanism

An inner product provides a scalar measurement of two vectors. In orthonormal real coordinates the dot is a sum of component products. Its geometric form is length product times angle cosine. Orthogonality means zero inner product; zero itself has no angle.

(3,4,0)⋅(2,0,0)=6(3,4,0)\cdot(2,0,0)=6, while the cosine is 6/(5⋅2)=0.66/(5\cdot2)=0.6. Coordinate dotting assumes the correct metric.

Projection rejection and scalar components

Projection rejection and scalar components

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6

Projection onto a nonzero axis is the along-axis vector whose remainder is orthogonal. Rejection is the remainder. Signed scalar projection measures length; the projection coefficient multiplies the target axis and need not equal that length.

For input (3,4,0)(3,4,0) and target (2,0,0)(2,0,0), coefficient is 1.51.5, scalar projection 33, projection (3,0,0)(3,0,0) and rejection (0,4,0)(0,4,0).
