Gram matrices and coordinate metrics

Gram matrices and coordinate metrics

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6

Definition and mechanism

A Gram matrix stores pairwise basis inner products. Coordinate vectors measure physical dot products through c𝖳Gdc^\mathsf TGd. It is positive semidefinite, and positive definite for independent generators. It records metric geometry but not orientation.

The basis (1,0),(1,1)(1,0),(1,1) has G=(1112)G=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}. Coordinates (1,2)(1,2) give squared length 1313, not 55.

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6

Definition and mechanism

A scalar triple product measures oriented parallelepiped volume. Four-point orientation uses edge differences; tetrahedral volume is one sixth of the absolute result. A vector triple product is a different, vector-valued identity, and cross products are not associative.

The panel with D=(0,0,2)D=(0,0,2) has signed volume 2424 and tetrahedron volume 44. Parenthesis changes can turn a nested cross from a nonzero vector into zero.

Prerequisites

  • Dot products and orthogonality — Inner-product measurements supply the perpendicularity and alignment constraints.

Robust vector angles

Robust vector angles

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6

Definition and mechanism

The unsigned angle uses nonzero finite directions. An atan2 expression combines cross magnitude and dot, retaining sine- and cosine-like information. Scale inputs before evaluating to reduce range failures. A signed angle requires a specified oriented plane.

Parallel directions give zero, antiparallel directions give π\pi, and perpendicular directions give π/2\pi/2. Zero input has no angle.

Reflection refraction and shading directions

Reflection refraction and shading directions

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Plane reflection reverses a direction’s normal component. Refraction scales its tangent component by the incident/transmitted index ratio and solves for a unit normal component. A negative computed discriminant indicates total internal reflection under the stated model. Half-vectors require normalized outward light/view directions.

Incident (0.6,0,−0.8)(0.6,0,-0.8) reflects to (0.6,0,0.8)(0.6,0,0.8) across normal (0,0,1)(0,0,1). Antiparallel light/view directions have no unique half-vector.

University course development

Extend the existing direction note by separating geometric surface orientation from optical ray behavior. The normal vector is perpendicular to a local tangent plane; it determines the cosine term in diffuse shading and the directions of ideal reflection and refraction. For unit incident direction ωi\omega_i and unit normal nn, specular reflection mirrors the direction about the normal, while refraction changes direction according to the ratio of refractive indices and may undergo total internal reflection. Direction conventions matter: some texts define incoming vectors toward the surface, others point away from it, so signs must be checked before applying formulas. A shading normal may differ from the true geometric normal, as in normal mapping, but it cannot change silhouette or visibility. Distinguish shading perturbations from geometry displacement, and use consistent normals when evaluating BRDFs, ray offsets, and medium transitions.

Orthonormal frames and Gram-Schmidt

Orthonormal frames and Gram-Schmidt

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6

Definition and mechanism

An orthonormal frame has unit perpendicular axes, so its Gram matrix is identity. Gram–Schmidt constructs axes by repeated rejection. Modified order uses the updated residual and changes rounding behavior. Frame existence, numerical reliability and output continuity are distinct questions.

For (1,1,0)(1,1,0) and (1,0,0)(1,0,0), rejection produces (1/2,−1/2,0)(1/2,-1/2,0). A least-aligned helper axis avoids a near-parallel cross but can switch discontinuously.

Prerequisites

Barycentric coordinates and interpolation

Barycentric coordinates and interpolation

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Barycentric weights reconstruct a triangle point as an affine combination. The weights sum to one; nonnegative weights describe points inside or on a nondegenerate triangle. Dot-system solves on off-plane inputs describe their projection, not proven surface membership.

The panel sensor (1,1,0)(1,1,0) has weights (5/12,1/4,1/3)(5/12,1/4,1/3) and corner temperatures (20,40,50)(20,40,50) interpolate to 3535.

University course development

Extend the existing interpolation note with the geometric meanings that make triangle rasterization and camera calibration easier to reason about. For triangle vertices p0,p1,p2p_0,p_1,p_2, a point inside can be written p=λ0p0+λ1p1+λ2p2p=\lambda_0p_0+\lambda_1p_1+\lambda_2p_2, where the weights sum to one and are nonnegative. Each weight is the area of the opposite subtriangle divided by the full triangle area; equivalently it is a signed edge-distance normalized by altitude. The weights therefore provide both a point-in-triangle test and attribute interpolation. They also reveal a limitation: screen-space weights do not linearly interpolate a 3D attribute after perspective projection. Interpolate reciprocal depth and attribute divided by depth, then divide the interpolated values to recover perspective-correct texture coordinates or colors.

Convex combinations and convex hulls

Convex combinations and convex hulls

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6

Definition and mechanism

Affine point combinations have weights summing to one. Convex combinations additionally have nonnegative weights. A convex set contains every segment between its members; a convex hull is the smallest such set containing supplied points.

The panel is the convex hull of its corners. A filled disk is convex; its boundary alone is not.

Minkowski sums and support mappings

Minkowski sums and support mappings

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6

Definition and mechanism

Minkowski addition combines pairwise position coordinates of sets in a common frame. Collision difference means A+(−B)A+(-B) here. A support function returns an extreme scalar measurement; a support mapping returns a maximizing point, possibly with ties.

Intervals [2,4][2,4] and [3,5][3,5] have difference [−3,1][-3,1], containing zero. Support of the difference uses a support point of AA minus one of BB queried in the opposite direction.

Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division

Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Phase 7 derives the affine block matrix, distinguishes a singular affine map from an invertible frame, and traces model → view → homogeneous clip → NDC using a declared projection. The worked figure keeps the divisor visible and checks the chosen near/far depth endpoints.

An affine homogeneous point has last coordinate one; a direction has zero. Nonzero common scale defines projective equivalence, while dehomogenization divides by a nonzero final component. Clip representatives and projective classes have related but distinct semantics.

(2,4,6,2)(2,4,6,2) and (1,2,3,1)(1,2,3,1) describe one finite projective point. NDC normalization standardizes ranges, not vector length.

Source and navigation

Teaching narrative · Coverage and source gap · Evidence and limits · Dependency Map

University course development

Extend the existing account with the geometric reason for the final divide. A 3D point is stored as (x,y,z,1)(x,y,z,1); after multiplying by a projective matrix it becomes (X,Y,Z,W)(X,Y,Z,W). Dividing the first three components by WW maps the homogeneous representative to ordinary coordinates. Any nonzero scalar multiple of a homogeneous vector represents the same point, which is why this division is meaningful. For a perspective camera, WW is chosen to depend on depth, so apparent size shrinks with distance. A direction has homogeneous coordinate zero and is not translated like a point. Projection matrices encode the camera frustum before division; afterward, a viewport transform scales and shifts normalized coordinates to pixels and commonly flips the vertical axis because image rows increase downward. Keep clipping before division to avoid unstable behavior around W=0W=0.

Coordinate frames, transformations, and pose · Cameras, projection, and calibration

Phase 11 camera development

Homogeneous image coordinates represent a ray up to nonzero scale; perspective division produces normalized image coordinates. Monocular reconstruction has a separate physical scale gauge: multiplying all scene points and camera translations by the same positive factor preserves projections. Do not confuse representational scale with unknown metric scale. A known object dimension, baseline, or depth measurement can anchor metres; normalizing a homogeneous vector cannot. This assumes calibrated perspective projection without an external scale prior. The distinction explains why a numerically precise reconstruction can still lack physical units. Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: University courses

Source and navigation

Expanded teaching explanation · Independent coverage · Dependency Map

University course development

Radiometry distinguishes total radiant flux Φ\Phi in watts, irradiance EE in watts per square metre, radiant intensity II in watts per steradian, and radiance LL in watts per square metre per steradian measured with projected source area. A spectrum distributes the energy over wavelength; a three-channel RGB value is a measurement in a chosen color system and does not uniquely identify that spectrum. Solid angle measures directional extent rather than physical area. Consequently an area-light sample requires the projected-area and inverse-square Jacobian when expressed as a directional sample. Free-space radiance remains constant along an unobstructed ray, while irradiance from a point-like source changes with geometry. Photometry instead applies standardized visual weighting: luminous flux uses lumens, illuminance lux, and luminous intensity candela. These distinctions prevent treating brightness, exposure, flux and radiance as interchangeable scalar labels.

Reflectance and rendering equation

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: University courses

Source and navigation

Expanded teaching explanation · Independent coverage · Dependency Map

University course development

Extend the existing light-transport note with the distinction between a material’s directional response and the incident illumination it receives. At surface point xx, outgoing radiance depends on emitted radiance plus an integral over incoming directions. The BRDF fr(x,ωi,ωo)f_r(x,\omega_i,\omega_o) is reflected outgoing radiance per incident irradiance, with units of inverse steradians; it depends on incoming direction ωi\omega_i and viewing direction ωo\omega_o. A physically plausible BRDF is nonnegative and conserves energy, but can still have narrow glossy lobes that are difficult to sample. The rendering equation combines this local material response with visibility, incoming radiance, and the cosine foreshortening factor. This form explains why shading, direct lighting, global illumination, and Monte Carlo integration are connected parts of one transport calculation rather than independent image effects.

University course development

Extend the existing frequency-domain treatment with visual interpretation and filtering consequences. A Fourier coefficient records how strongly a sinusoidal basis function occurs at a given frequency and phase. In images, the origin of a two-dimensional spectrum represents slow spatial variation; moving farther from it corresponds to finer variation. A broad bright center indicates low-frequency structure, while energy far from the center often represents edges and texture. Filtering multiplies each frequency by the filter response: a low-pass response suppresses fine detail, and a high-pass response emphasizes it. Aliasing folds unresolved high frequencies into lower ones because sampled sinusoids can share identical sample values. This explains moiré patterns and animated shimmer, and shows why a spectrum is useful for diagnosing sampling problems rather than only for theoretical signal processing.

Sampling continuous signals and image formation · Image sampling, filtering, and efficient reconstruction · Edges, contours, and subpixel localization

Sampling aliasing and reconstruction

Sampling aliasing and reconstruction

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Uniform samples identify frequencies only modulo sample rate and corresponding real-signal equivalences. Strictly band-limited ideal reconstruction needs non-overlapping spectral replicas; exact-Nyquist phase is a boundary hazard. Prefilter before decimation.

Phase 9–10 development

Signal aliasing occurs when distinct signal frequencies produce the same sampled values; reconstruction then cannot recover which signal generated the samples without additional assumptions. Stratification, low-discrepancy sequences, and blue-noise point sets describe where samples are placed, not a guarantee that the signal is band-limited or that an estimator is unbiased. Each strategy still needs a valid support, probability weight, and reconstruction filter.

Prerequisites

  • Fourier analysis and spectral phase — Frequency and phase reveal transfer, sampling ambiguity and structural loss.

University course development

Sampling records measurements of a continuous signal on a discrete grid. Frequencies that differ by integer multiples of the sampling rate can produce the same samples, so the sampled values alone cannot identify which original signal was present. For ideal band-limited reconstruction, the signal must be restricted below half the sampling rate; equality at the limiting frequency needs additional phase and endpoint conditions. A real pixel also integrates light over area and exposure time, making its measurement a filtered sample. Prefiltering attenuates frequencies that would alias, while reconstruction estimates a continuous signal from the stored samples. Ideal sinc reconstruction has infinite support; practical filters trade computation, sharpness, ringing and residual aliasing. More samples reduce integration error only when their placement and weights match the intended pixel or path-space measure.

Convolution and filter footprints

University course development

Extend the current convolution note from a sliding kernel to image formation and resampling. A pixel integrates incoming image energy over a finite footprint; point sampling is only an approximation to that area integral. Convolution combines nearby values with weights whose spatial support is the kernel footprint, and its Fourier transform describes which spatial frequencies survive. Before reducing resolution, low-pass filtering suppresses frequencies the coarser grid cannot represent. In texture mapping, the screen-to-texture Jacobian maps a nearly square screen pixel to a texture-space parallelogram. If the two singular directions have very different lengths, an isotropic mip level blurs one direction too much; anisotropic filters take extra samples along the long axis. This same footprint reasoning links pixel reconstruction, antialiasing, texture filtering, and sensor blur without treating them as unrelated tricks.

Antialiasing and sample allocation

Antialiasing and sample allocation

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

SSAA increases spatial observations; MSAA principally adds coverage-related sampling under its shading conventions. TAA reuses aligned temporal observations. Nonlinear shading makes pre-/post-filtering noncommutative, so coarse rates need appropriate input/output policies.

Phase 9–10 development

Antialiasing combines a sampling pattern with a reconstruction or integration footprint so unresolved variation contributes with controlled error. More samples can reduce Monte Carlo variance, while better placement can reduce structured error; these are different effects. Adaptive allocation based on observed samples changes the sampling procedure and can affect uncertainty estimates. Spatial sample allocation should remain distinct from importance sampling over path or event space.

Phase 11 camera development

Reprojection predicts where a prior sample lands under camera and object motion. Depth agreement tests whether the same visible surface likely occupies that location, but cannot prove stored color remains valid after lighting, exposure, material, or sampling changes. Combine projected position, depth tolerance, and disocclusion checks; reduce history weight when confidence is low. Monocular reconstruction has arbitrary global scale, so metric depth thresholds require an external scale or consistent units. Reprojection success is geometric evidence, not a photometric guarantee. Link: A camera model must close the loop; research: Four deeper links from the TUM lecture review.

Neighborhood clipping and deterministic jitter witness

tools/labs/realtime_effects_reference_lab.cpp now extends history validity into two mechanisms that directly affect temporal stability.

The first is deterministic subpixel jitter generated from Halton bases 2 and 3. The sample lies inside one pixel but changes frame to frame, allowing temporal accumulation to observe different subpixel locations. A jitter sequence must be owned by the camera/projection history contract: if the current and previous transforms disagree about whether jitter is included, the motion vector and reprojection become inconsistent.

The second is neighborhood clipping. A reprojected history value can be geometrically valid yet photometrically stale after disocclusion or fast shading change. The smallest CPU oracle clamps the history sample into the current 3×3 neighborhood min/max interval before blending. Production TAA often uses variance-guided bounds, color-space transforms, reactive masks and velocity-dependent weighting, but the invariant remains: history should not inject values unsupported by the current local evidence.

The laboratory checks known first Halton points, uniqueness over an initial sequence, bright/dark history rejection and preservation of an in-range history value. It remains a semantic oracle rather than a complete production TAA implementation.

Linear systems and fundamental subspaces

Linear systems and fundamental subspaces

A linear system A𝒙=𝒃A\mathbf x=\mathbf b asks which inputs satisfy all row measurements at once. It is consistent exactly when 𝒃\mathbf b lies in the column space. The null space contains input changes invisible to every measurement; rank-nullity counts observable versus free directions.

Use it when: explaining consistency, underdetermination, least squares, parameter observability, or constraints in geometry.

Developed in Phase 8: The expanded treatment connects each row to a hyperplane and the complete matrix to a map: consistency asks whether the target lies in the column space, while the null space describes every invisible change to a solution. Rank then counts constrained directions and determines the dimension of the solution family. constraint geometry · rank and solution families

LU factorization and reusable solves

LU factorization and reusable solves

LU stores elimination as triangular factors. With row pivoting in this vault’s convention, PA=LUPA=LU; apply the same permutation to each right-hand side, then solve one lower- and one upper-triangular system. Factorization cost is amortized across repeated solves.

Use it when: solving square general systems, especially with multiple right-hand sides.

Developed in Phase 8: The multipliers used to eliminate entries become the lower factor, while the remaining upper triangle records the reduced system; with row exchanges the convention is PA=LUPA=LU. The runnable pivoted LU reference traces permutation, factor storage, status, and repeated forward/back substitution on actual values. runnable pivoted LU lab · forward and backward solves

Symmetric positive-definite matrices and Cholesky

Symmetric positive-definite matrices and Cholesky

A real symmetric matrix AA is positive definite if every nonzero xx has positive quadratic energy x𝖳Axx^\mathsf T A x. Then A=LL𝖳A=LL^\mathsf T with nonsingular triangular LL. Positive semidefinite permits zero energy directions and may be singular, so Cholesky’s assumptions and failure status must be respected.

Use it when: covariance, Gram systems, energy minimization, or an SPD solve is established.

Developed in Phase 8: Positive definiteness means every nonzero direction has positive quadratic energy, which permits a Cholesky factor and stable triangular solves. The continuation derives the positive pivots, then broadens to LDL𝖳LDL^\mathsf T when a symmetric matrix is indefinite and explains how a failed pivot reflects the assumptions or numerical scale. Eigenvalues and eigenspaces

Eigenvalues and eigenspaces

An eigenvector is a nonzero direction that a square linear map scales by its eigenvalue. The eigenspace is the null space of A−λIA-\lambda I. Real symmetric matrices have an orthonormal eigenbasis; general matrices may be defective or have sensitive eigenvectors.

Use it when: studying repeated powers, invariant directions, covariance, stability, or matrix functions.

Developed in Phase 8: Eigenanalysis begins with invariant directions, then distinguishes algebraic multiplicity from eigenspace dimension and shows why a defective matrix may not have a full eigenbasis. Power and inverse iteration target selected eigenpairs; QR iteration approaches a Schur form, while residual size and eigenvector sensitivity answer different accuracy questions. eigenspaces and multiplicity · eigenvalue iteration and Schur form

Singular value decomposition

Singular value decomposition

For any real rectangular matrix, A=UΣV𝖳A=U\Sigma V^\mathsf T. Right singular vectors are input directions, left singular vectors are output directions, and nonnegative singular values are principal stretches. Unlike eigenvectors, the two sets live in different spaces.

Use it when: revealing rank and conditioning, solving rank-uncertain least squares, compressing a matrix, or understanding PCA.

Developed in Phase 8: The SVD expresses a rectangular map using orthonormal input and output directions joined by nonnegative stretches. Full, thin, and compact shapes have different dimensions; bidiagonal reduction and Jacobi methods compute the factors, and reconstruction, orthogonality, and triplet residuals check them independently. factor shapes · SVD algorithms and validation

Prerequisites

Matrix multiplication and composition order, Eigenvalues and eigenspaces, Dot products and orthogonality.

Used by

Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse, PCA and covariance eigensystems, Polar decomposition, Matrix factorization choices.

Teaching path: SVD geometry. - Matrix norms and numerical error — Extends this foundation into the Phase 8 dependency spine. - Camera calibration and bundle adjustment - Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics

University course development

Extend the existing factorization note with its role in estimation, conditioning, and geometry. For matrix AA, the decomposition A=UΣVTA=U\Sigma V^T separates orthogonal input directions, axis-aligned scaling, and orthogonal output directions. Singular values on the diagonal of Σ\Sigma quantify how strongly each independent direction is preserved; a zero or tiny value signals rank loss or poor conditioning. Least-squares fitting can use this structure to identify which parameter combinations are well constrained and to avoid amplifying measurement noise along nearly invisible directions. The same analysis explains why a camera calibration or bundle-adjustment system can have gauge freedoms: translating or scaling the entire reconstruction may leave image measurements unchanged. Singular values diagnose these ambiguities, while constraints or fixed reference poses remove them. Thus SVD links linear algebra to robust vision, not just matrix compression.

Pose estimation, transforms, and robust fitting · Stereo, relative orientation, and reconstruction · Optimization, constraints, and inverse kinematics

PCA and covariance eigensystems

PCA and covariance eigensystems

Center sample rows, then find the orthogonal directions of greatest variance. For centered XX, SVD gives directions in VV, scores in UΣU\Sigma, and covariance eigenvalues σi2/(N−1)\sigma_i^2/(N-1). Units and feature scaling change the question; near-equal eigenvalues make individual axes unstable.

Use it when: describing point clouds, reducing dimensions, or estimating a best-fit plane.

Developed in Phase 8: PCA first centers observations so the covariance measures variation around the sample mean. The right singular vectors of centered data give principal directions, UΣU\Sigma gives scores, and squared singular values scaled by sample count give covariance eigenvalues; feature units and small eigengaps affect interpretation. centering and principal axes · plane fits and eigengaps

Phase 9–10 development: For a random vector XX with finite second moments, covariance is Σ=𝔼[(X−μ)(X−μ)T]\Sigma=\mathbb E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T]. For every vector vv, vTΣv=𝔼[(vT(X−μ))2]≥0v^T\Sigma v=\mathbb E[(v^T(X-\mu))^2]\geq0, so covariance is positive semidefinite. Its eigenvectors give uncorrelated principal directions and the eigenvalues give variance along them. Whitening rescales nonzero-variance directions and needs a stated policy for zero or tiny eigenvalues. A Gaussian kernel used to model rendering footprints is a spatial distribution model, not automatically a statement about epistemic uncertainty.

Polar decomposition

Polar decomposition

The right polar form A=QHA=QH separates an orthogonal factor from a positive-semidefinite stretch H=(A𝖳A)1/2H=(A^\mathsf T A)^{1/2}. The orthogonal factor may include reflection; singular matrices can make its completion nonunique. Symmetric stretch can include shear in the chosen coordinates.

Use it when: separating local rigid-like motion from symmetric deformation.

Developed in Phase 8: Polar decomposition factors a map into an orthogonal part and a positive-semidefinite stretch. The SVD constructs both left and right forms, separates reflection from a proper rotation, and gives the nearest orthogonal or special-orthogonal factor when the singular directions allow a unique choice; zero singular values leave completion freedom. left and right stretch · nearest proper rotation and ambiguity

Matrix functions

Matrix functions

For diagonalizable matrices, a scalar function can be applied to eigenvalues in a usable eigenbasis. Stable algorithms such as scaling-and-squaring are distinct from the defining power series.

Use it when: integrating linear dynamics or interpolating structured transforms.

Sparse and iterative solvers

Sparse and iterative solvers

Sparse storage avoids zeros when structure and scale justify its index overhead. Iterative methods replace a dense factorization with matrix-vector products and a convergence process. Conjugate gradient requires symmetric positive definiteness; preconditioning, residual criteria, and a maximum iteration count belong in the contract.

Use it when: large structured systems make dense storage or factorization impractical.

Developed in Phase 8: Sparse storage pays off when zeros and dimensions outweigh indexing overhead, while direct factorization can create fill that destroys sparsity. Iterative methods instead use matrix-vector products and stopping tests; conjugate gradient requires an SPD operator, and preconditioning, a maximum iteration count, and a true residual make convergence reviewable. storage and fill · direct versus iterative solving

Vulkan synchronization2 and resource transitions

Vulkan synchronization2 and resource transitions

Vulkan synchronization is not “put a barrier between two passes.” A dependency has to connect a real producer access to a real consumer access with execution and memory scopes that cover both operations.

Vulkan 1.3 includes the synchronization2 model promoted from VK_KHR_synchronization2. It places stage and access masks together in the version-2 barrier structures and uses commands such as vkCmdPipelineBarrier2 and vkQueueSubmit2.

Primary references: - https://docs.vulkan.org/guide/latest/extensions/VK_KHR_synchronization2.html - https://docs.vulkan.org/spec/latest/chapters/synchronization.html

Producer → consumer reasoning

For every hazard, write the transition in words first.

Example:

A transfer command writes a storage buffer. A later compute shader reads that buffer.

The producer execution stage is transfer. The producer access is transfer write. The consumer execution stage is compute shader. The consumer access is shader storage read.

An abstract memory barrier therefore needs to cover:

source stage = TRANSFER
source access = TRANSFER_WRITE
destination stage = COMPUTE_SHADER
destination access = SHADER_STORAGE_READ.

Using ALL_COMMANDS and MEMORY_READ/WRITE everywhere may accidentally work but destroys precision and can hide misunderstanding. Using a destination stage that never performs the consumer access is not made correct by a broad access mask.

Image transitions add a layout contract

Images have another state dimension: layout. An image memory barrier can both synchronize accesses and transition from oldLayout to newLayout. The old layout must describe the state established by prior use unless the contents are intentionally discarded under the rules that permit that.

A render graph therefore needs more than “read” and “write.” For each image subresource it eventually needs:

  • stage/access usage;
  • required layout;
  • aspect;
  • mip range;
  • array-layer range;
  • queue ownership when queues/families differ.

A whole-image state tracker is a valid early implementation but cannot claim correct independent mip/layer scheduling.

Queue submission and timeline semaphores

Synchronization2 also modernizes queue submission through VkSubmitInfo2 and related structures. Timeline semaphores carry monotonically increasing integer values and are useful for expressing ordered completion points across submissions. A timeline value is not a memory barrier by itself; the signal/wait operations participate in dependencies whose scopes must still match the work.

Native witness now in the repository

tools/native/vulkan_sync_smoke.cpp is compiled and executed in the dedicated native graphics workflow on Ubuntu with a Vulkan implementation and validation layer packages. It:

  • creates a Vulkan 1.3 instance;
  • finds a device exposing synchronization2;
  • creates a queue/device with the feature enabled;
  • records a VkMemoryBarrier2 through vkCmdPipelineBarrier2;
  • submits the command buffer using vkQueueSubmit2;
  • waits for fence completion;
  • fails on validation-layer errors when the layer is available.

That materially raises the evidence level from a CPU-only logical graph.

It still does not prove a resource-specific RAW transition, image layout transition, queue-family transfer, timeline protocol, transient aliasing, physical-GPU performance, or current Kairo/Vulkax integration. Each of those needs its own captured witness.

Related: GPU workgroups and synchronization, Rendering history validity, Render graph barrier lowering.

BVH build traversal and workload selection

BVH build, traversal, and workload selection

A bounding-volume hierarchy is a tree whose nodes bound groups of primitives. Its purpose is not to make intersection magically faster; it is to let a query prove that large groups cannot matter.

For an overlap query Q, traversal follows a simple implication:

if Q does not overlap node.bounds, then Q cannot overlap any primitive below that node.

That pruning claim is only correct when every child primitive is actually contained by every ancestor bound. Tree construction therefore owns an invariant: each internal bound is the union of its children, and each leaf bound contains the primitives assigned to the leaf.

Build choices

A median split sorts or partitions primitive centroids and divides them into similarly sized groups. It is simple and usually avoids catastrophically unbalanced trees, but equal primitive counts do not imply equal traversal cost.

Surface-area heuristic construction estimates expected query/ray work. In the common ray-tracing interpretation, a split cost has the form

C=CT+ALAPNLCI+ARAPNRCI, C = C_T + \frac{A_L}{A_P}N_L C_I + \frac{A_R}{A_P}N_R C_I,

where APA_P is parent surface area, AL,ARA_L,A_R are child areas, NL,NRN_L,N_R are primitive counts, CTC_T is traversal cost and CIC_I is primitive-intersection cost. Binned SAH approximates candidate split positions efficiently.

LBVH chooses hierarchy structure from Morton ordering. It can build quickly and map well to parallel hardware, but tree quality can be worse than a careful SAH build for some scenes. Which strategy wins depends on how often the scene rebuilds and how expensive later queries are.

Traversal representation

A production BVH must choose node layout as deliberately as split policy. Questions include:

  • binary versus wider nodes;
  • array indices versus pointers;
  • parent links or stackless encodings;
  • leaf primitive ranges;
  • AoS versus SoA bounds;
  • quantized bounds;
  • traversal stack depth and overflow behavior;
  • child ordering by query direction or distance.

For GPU traversal, divergence and memory coalescing can dominate the nominal tree complexity.

Dynamic scenes

Refitting recomputes ancestor bounds without changing topology. It is cheap when objects move modestly, but tree quality can decay. Rebuilding restores quality at higher cost. A useful dynamic policy measures a quality proxy and rebuilds when continued bad traversal is more expensive than reconstruction.

Dynamic AABB trees instead maintain a mutable hierarchy and often enlarge leaf bounds by a motion margin. The margin trades fewer reinserts for more false candidates.

Executable reference

tools/labs/spatial_index_lab.cpp builds a median-split BVH over deterministic random AABBs and compares 250 overlap queries against a brute-force oracle. Any missed or extra primitive is a test failure. The same laboratory also contains A* graph search with relaxation, reinsertion and unreachable-goal handling.

The witness does not claim SAH quality, LBVH construction, dynamic updates, SIMD traversal, ray packet behavior, navmesh construction, or KairoSpatial parity. Those remain separate evidence layers.

Related: AABB overlap and containment, Prefix scan and stream compaction, Field reordering and AoS versus SoA.

SAH, Morton and refit witness

tools/labs/bvh_sah_refit_lab.cpp advances the construction side beyond the earlier median-split query oracle. It computes prefix/suffix bounds for candidate partitions and minimizes the surface-area-weighted primitive cost, verifies that two separated three-object clusters split between the clusters, tests 3D Morton bit interleaving on a controlled monotone coordinate sweep, and refits a parent bound after one child moves.

This is enough to make the equations executable, but not enough to call the builder a production binned SAH or LBVH. A complete next layer needs fixed-bin accumulation, stable primitive partitioning, LBVH range/split construction from Morton prefixes, dynamic-tree rotations or reinsertion, and measured build-versus-query trade-offs on real workloads.

Rigid Contact - Persistent Manifolds and Solver Reconstruction

Rigid contacts: from point velocity to a persistent contact manifold

Scope: original, independently reconstructed teaching for the existing engine collision-response narrative. The executable witnesses are rigid_contact_lab.cpp and persistent_contact_lab.cpp. These are 2D velocity-level CPU witnesses; they do not claim to be Kairo’s engine implementation, 3D production manifold generation, or continuous collision detection. Symbols and sign conventions below follow those two witnesses.

Why a contact is a constraint rather than a force chosen by eye

Imagine a box descending onto a static floor. The collision detector reports that the geometry is touching or overlapping, but it does not say which velocities are physically admissible. With body A as the floor and body B as the box, define the contact normal n to point from A toward B. At contact position p, the lever arms measured from each body’s centre of mass are r_A = p − x_A and r_B = p − x_B. For a planar rigid body, its point velocity is v(p) = v_com + ω × r, where planar scalar angular speed ω produces ω × (r_x,r_y) = (−ω r_y, ω r_x). This matters because an object rotating toward the floor can be closing at a corner even when the centre of mass is moving away.

The relative velocity of the two material points is u = (v_B + ω_B × r_B) − (v_A + ω_A × r_A). The normal component u_n = u · n tells us whether those two points are closing (u_n < 0) or separating (u_n > 0). For a non-penetrating unilateral contact without restitution, the desired post-solve condition is u_n ≥ 0, with a nonnegative accumulated contact impulse λ_n ≥ 0. Their complementarity condition is λ_n u_n = 0 at an exact solution: either the contact carries a positive separating-prevention impulse and reaches zero normal speed, or the bodies separate freely and the contact carries no impulse. Finite-iteration solvers only approximate this coupled condition.

Deriving effective inverse mass, rather than memorizing its denominator

The impulse on B is +λ n and the reaction on A is −λ n. Newton’s linear momentum law gives Δv_B = +λ m_B⁻¹ n and Δv_A = −λ m_A⁻¹ n. Angular impulse about the centre of mass gives Δω_B = +λ I_B⁻¹ (r_B × n) and Δω_A = −λ I_A⁻¹ (r_A × n), where the planar cross product of vectors is the scalar r_x n_y − r_y n_x. A rotation changes point velocity through Δω × r, and its projection onto n adds an angular term proportional to the squared lever arm.

Consequently the normal relative velocity changes by Δu_n = k_n λ, where

kn=mA−1+mB−1+IA−1(rA×n)2+IB−1(rB×n)2. k_n = m_A^{-1} + m_B^{-1} + I_A^{-1}(r_A \times n)^2 + I_B^{-1}(r_B \times n)^2.

Here k_n is inverse effective mass in the contact direction, not mass itself. The same physical impulse changes normal speed less when the effective mass is large. The equation follows from the full point-velocity update; it is not valid to omit rotational terms whenever the contact is off-centre. A static body uses zero inverse mass and inertia, but two completely unresponsive bodies yield k_n = 0 and must not be divided by. The corresponding tangential value k_t is obtained by substituting the perpendicular unit tangent t = (−n_y, n_x) for n.

For a desired post-impact normal speed b, one unconstrained correction is Δλ = (b − u_n)/k_n. A real contact cannot pull the bodies together, so the accumulated normal multiplier is projected:

λnnew=max⁡(0,λnold+b−unkn). \lambda_n^{new}=\max\left(0,\lambda_n^{old} + \frac{b-u_n}{k_n}\right).

Apply only the difference, Δλ_n = λ_n^{new} − λ_n^{old}, to body velocities. Applying the whole accumulated value every iteration would add the same historical impulse repeatedly, making motion energy grow artificially. Conversely, resetting the accumulator on every sweep defeats the projected Gauss–Seidel interpretation and prevents reliable friction bounds.

Restitution is a contact-creation decision, not a new bounce each iteration

For an impact with pre-solve normal speed u_n^before < −v_threshold, the outgoing speed target in this simplified solver is b = −e u_n^before, with restitution coefficient e ∈ [0,1]. This target must be sampled before contact impulses change the velocity and then held fixed during the iteration. If a solver recomputes b from the current velocity at every visit, a persistent resting point can acquire artificial new bounce energy. The witness distinguishes a new impact from a persistent contact through an explicit newImpact argument; a production engine requires an actual contact-state machine and impact detection so the decision is not left to a careless caller.

For the central collision test, both bodies have mass 1 kg, A starts at 2 m/s, B at 0 m/s, and the normal is +x. Their relative closing speed is −2 m/s; with e=1 and k_n=2 kg⁻¹, we need Δλ_n = (2 − (−2))/2 = 2 kg·m/s. The resulting velocities are 0 m/s and 2 m/s. Linear momentum remains 2 kg·m/s, and the kinetic energy remains 2 joules. This equality is specific to the elastic, frictionless, central, idealized two-body case—not a conservation promise for frictional or inelastic impacts.

Why friction depends on the normal impulse

For the upward normal n=(0,1) the laboratory chooses the tangent t=(−1,0). The sliding box initially moves at +3 m/s in x, so its tangent-coordinate velocity is u_t = −3 m/s. The unconstrained tangent impulse is −u_t/k_t; here k_t=1 kg⁻¹, giving +3 kg·m/s. The normal collision supplies λ_n=2 kg·m/s. With coefficient μ=0.5, the Coulomb limit is μλ_n=1 kg·m/s, so the stored tangent impulse is +1, not −1. Multiplying +1 × (−1,0) produces an x-directed impulse of (−1,0), reducing the box’s x velocity from +3 to +2 m/s. The sign of the stored scalar is relative to the chosen tangent direction; it cannot be interpreted without that basis.

The projected update is λ_t^{new} = clamp(λ_t^{old} − u_t/k_t, −μλ_n, +μλ_n). This is a scalar tangent model for 2D; real 3D contact has a two-dimensional tangent plane and requires a disk-cone constraint or a chosen approximation. The witness applies a single coefficient and does not model static-versus-dynamic friction transition, anisotropy, rolling friction, torsional friction or compliant materials.

Why a manifold needs persistent identity and sequential sweeps

A wide box can contact a floor at two corners. Both rows modify the same centre-of-mass velocity and angular velocity. Solving one row therefore changes the velocity seen by the next row. A one-pass independent pair of impulses is not equivalent to solving their coupled system. The reference witness stores two world-space contact points, evaluates each row in sequence, and repeats sweeps. The residual normal speeds and angular velocity are checked after twenty sweeps. Its iteration result is deterministic for its fixed row order but should not be advertised as an order-independent exact solution.

On the next frame, a geometry matcher must identify whether each physical contact feature persisted. If the same feature, body pair, contact orientation, and compatible basis survive, previously accumulated impulses are useful initial guesses. Warm-start once by applying the cached impulses to the newly constructed pre-solve velocities before iteration. Never warm-start twice, and never reuse a tangential scalar after rotating the tangent basis without transforming it. A changed feature ID, reversed A/B order, altered normal, teleport, or discontinuous mass/inertia change may invalidate the cache. The witness includes a feature ID as data but does not implement feature matching; that is a separate production requirement.

Caches may also require dt-aware scaling when timestep changes, and a true contact solver must decide how speculative contacts and missed or sleeping frames are handled. Warm-starting can improve convergence, but it is not a substitute for manifold quality.

Contact identity: why matching by memory address or contact index is insufficient

The physical reaction at a point can be reused between frames only if the cache still refers to the same interacting surface features. When two faces touch, clipping may produce two manifold points whose array order changes as the bodies rotate. If we cache impulse #0 against array position #0, a later reordering can accidentally apply the left-corner impulse at the right corner, creating a torque that was never physically demanded. A robust narrow phase should assign each contact a stable feature pair, for example an incident vertex/edge identifier and reference face identifier, with deterministic canonicalization of body ordering. These identifiers are geometric facts maintained by collision generation, not sequential indices assigned by a container.

The executable contact-cache witness concentrates on the subsequent policy rather than inventing a complete polygon clipper. The Key holds canonical body IDs plus two feature identifiers. The map stores the previously accepted normal and tangent impulse, its local normal direction, the previous friction coefficient, timestep, and last-seen frame. The cache is valid only if the same key was seen on the immediately preceding frame, the normal has changed by no more than 15 degrees, and the new timestep is between half and twice the cached timestep. These are documented laboratory thresholds, not universally optimal thresholds or engine-wide facts. The code rejects reversed body order because reversing A and B changes the sign of the normal and impulse convention.

A tangent impulse is a vector in world space, although this 2D solver stores it as one scalar relative to a perpendicular tangent. When the normal rotates from n_old to n_new, the tangent axes t_old=(-n_old.y,n_old.x) and t_new=(-n_new.y,n_new.x) also rotate. The old physical friction impulse is P_t_old=λ_t_old t_old. The scalar along the new tangent is its dot projection:

$ {t,new}^{seed} = ({t,old},t_{old}t_{new}). $

The normal cache receives the same heuristic timestep ratio, and the tangent is clamped to ± μ_new λ_n_new. With an old upward normal (0,1), the old tangent is (-1,0). If the normal turns 10 degrees, the tangent projection of a previous scalar impulse 0.5 is 0.5 cos(10°) ≈ 0.492404, while the world impulse direction has changed consistently. Reusing 0.5 unchanged would preserve the scalar but not the intended projection onto the new contact tangent. This linear projection is a warm-start heuristic, not an exact solution of the new contact constraint; the subsequent iterative solver must still correct its residual.

An edit to the friction coefficient clears only the tangential cached impulse in this experiment, retaining the normal impulse if all other validity rules pass. A material change in restitution, velocity discontinuity, teleport, substantial mass/inertia change, sleeping transition, or topology discontinuity may also require cache rejection in a production system and is not automatically detected by this small input type. Impulse scaling by timestep ratio is similarly a common starting heuristic, not an unconditional physical identity; the test exercises ratios 0.5, 1, and 4 and rejects the last. A caller must invoke begin_frame, use lookup to seed each new manifold row, warm-start those rows once, run velocity iterations, store each final impulse exactly once, and prune stale entries. Pruning at the wrong moment can erase still-needed contacts; storing duplicate feature keys silently makes iteration results depend on array ordering, so the witness rejects duplicates.

The implementation has a testable boundary: it assumes a reliable feature matcher has already produced identifiers, that contact validity has been established by the geometry system, and that stable body IDs are never prematurely recycled. A generation-counted body handle would be safer than an integer object index alone. The cache does not detect 3D tangent-frame rotation, it does not calculate a physically accurate contact point, and its ordered map is a reference implementation rather than a measured real-time allocation strategy. A production engine should benchmark a preallocated flat hash map or per-pair cache with explicit frame ownership and deterministic iteration requirements.

Velocity correction is not penetration correction

The equations above change velocities. They do not, by themselves, repair existing overlaps in positions. A production pipeline generally needs a distinct and carefully scoped policy: geometry generation and signed separation, speculative contact margins, split impulses or position-level stabilization, and consistent timestep handling. Naively adding a large position-error velocity bias can inject energy, make stacks jitter, or break restitution. This CPU witness intentionally has no position integrator, no Baumgarte term, no split impulse and no continuous collision detection. Therefore its passing tests cannot establish the correctness of CCD tunneling prevention or deep-overlap recovery.

From end-of-frame overlap to continuous time of impact

The contact solver described above only acts on contacts it has been given. A fast-moving disk can start to the left of a thin obstacle and finish to the right of it without overlapping at the end of a fixed simulation step. If collision detection samples positions only at the step boundary, it sees no collision, so even a mathematically perfect impulse solver cannot prevent tunneling. This is the reason continuous collision detection (CCD) is a separate geometric question: what is the first time, within the proposed integration interval, when the moving shapes touch?

For two disks with initial centres x_A and x_B, constant velocities v_A and v_B, and radii r_A, r_B, define the relative centre separation p = x_B - x_A, relative velocity v = v_B - v_A, and sum of radii R = r_A + r_B. Their separation at time t is p(t) = p + tv. They first touch when the squared centre distance equals the squared radius sum:

$ p+tv2=R2. $

Expanding the dot product gives the quadratic

$ at^2+bt+c=0, a=vv, b=2pv, c=pp-R^2. $

The meaning of the coefficients is crucial. c is the initial squared-distance gap: c<0 means the disks are already overlapping and this witness returns t=0, assigning overlap correction to a separate solver; c=0 means initial touching. If a=0, the relative geometry never moves during the interval. For initially separated disks, b≥0 means squared distance is not initially decreasing, so a collision cannot occur under these constant velocities. A discriminant D=b²−4ac<0 means the motion line misses the expanded-radius disk. D=0 gives a tangent or grazing touch, which counts as a contact in this laboratory.

The familiar quadratic expression (-b−sqrt(D))/(2a) can lose precision when nearly equal quantities are subtracted. The swept-disk CPU witness instead computes a stable intermediate q = -0.5(b − sqrt(D)) in its restricted b<0 branch, then evaluates the roots as t_near = c/q and t_far = q/a. Their product remains c/a, and the smaller root is tested against 0≤t≤Δt. The code uses std::fma in the discriminant to avoid one rounding step, but this is still finite-precision arithmetic; reliable collision detection across extreme dynamic ranges needs scale-aware error analysis or a more robust predicate policy.

Consider a disk of radius 1 m stationary at the origin and another radius-1 disk initially at x=10 m moving left at 100 m/s. Its centre must move 8 m before touching, so the time of impact is 0.08 s. At Δt=0.1 s, the moving disk would end at the origin and overlap if sampled; for an even faster moving disk it could end past the obstacle and be missed entirely. An analytical time-of-impact query reports the 0.08 s encounter regardless of the end position. During a simulation step, a practical engine can advance up to this impact, generate a contact normal, solve or schedule the event, and then advance the remaining time, with a bounded substep count and an explicit policy for simultaneous events and resting contacts.

The event’s collision normal is the normalized relative separation n(t) = (p+tv)/|p+tv|, pointing A to B. When initial centres coincide, there is no unique geometric normal; the witness uses a deterministic velocity-based fallback or +x if relative velocity is zero. This fallback is a test policy rather than a geometrically determined surface normal. The tests explicitly examine grazing touch, no-hit trajectories, hits outside the requested frame, existing overlap, coincident centres, invalid parameters, a high-dynamic-range trajectory, and Galilean invariance under equal velocity added to both bodies. The latter should not change relative motion or time of impact.

What this does not solve: disk CCD assumes translational linear motion throughout the interval and fixed radii. It does not include forces or acceleration changing the trajectory, rotation of polygons, concave meshes, vertex-edge events, general convex support functions, conservative advancement, broadphase swept bounds, contact island rescheduling, stable substep integration, or CCD after multiple impulses. It also does not prove the absence of false misses at all floating-point scales. These exclusions must be explicit when moving from a CPU analytic oracle to the engine’s full collision pipeline.

A complete impact event: geometry, first time, impulse and remaining interval

The earlier swept-disk query identifies an impact but does not evolve a scene. The independent disk event pipeline laboratory connects geometry, state integration, simultaneous constraints and the remainder of the frame. It does not claim to be Kairo’s actual world step. The model assumes fixed-radius, non-spinning disks, piecewise constant velocities, instantaneous frictionless impulses, and linear motion between impacts. There are no forces, torque, resting-contact stabilization, soft contacts or arbitrary polygons.

The entire algorithm follows from keeping one variable: remaining time. At each iteration, query all unordered disk pairs for their first collision in that remaining interval. If no pair collides, advance every position by its current velocity times the entire remaining interval. If collisions exist, find the earliest time, move all disks to that instant, collect other impacts at approximately the same time, freeze each event’s incoming normal velocity and restitution target, solve their normal impulses, then repeat the time-of-impact scan because the impulses have changed the future motion.

The numerical trace is visible in the first laboratory test. A radius-1 stationary disk is at x=0. Another radius-1 disk starts at x=10 with velocity −100 m/s, and the requested frame duration is 0.10 s. The moving disk must travel 8 m before the two surfaces meet, giving TOI=0.08 s. The world advances both disks through 0.08 s, then an elastic impulse against the infinite-mass disk reverses its incoming velocity to +100 m/s. The remaining time is 0.02 s, so its centre ends at x=4 m. An end-of-frame overlap test cannot reconstruct this physically meaningful trajectory by merely reversing the velocity at t=0.10 s.

For non-spinning disk collisions along the line of centres, the inverse effective mass is the sum of inverse masses, k = m_A⁻¹ + m_B⁻¹. With unit collision normal n pointing from A to B, relative normal speed u_n=(v_B−v_A)·n, and fixed impact target b=−e u_n_before, the solver’s unilateral accumulated impulse is

$ {next}=(0,{previous} + {m_A{-1}+m_B{-1}}). $

Only the difference Δλ = λ_next − λ_previous changes velocities. In a simultaneous batch, multiple contact rows may share a disk, so each row modifies the velocities seen by subsequent rows. The laboratory runs 32 sequential sweeps, freezing the original bounce target rather than repeatedly inventing a new restitution event. A symmetric three-disk scene tests two simultaneous impacts; another three-disk scene tests two impacts at different times in one frame.

The discovery procedure is O(n²) for each rescan because it checks every unordered pair, with no spatial acceleration. The same-time grouping threshold and near-touch geometry threshold are explicit finite-precision policies, not robust computational-geometry predicates. Grazing trajectories with zero closing normal speed are skipped. Deep initial overlaps are rejected rather than repaired. An event budget throws when exhausted, preventing an infinite event loop from masquerading as successful advancement. Importantly, a thrown exception can leave the input scene partly advanced: a production caller needs a rollback snapshot or transactional step if partial state mutation is unacceptable.

The nine deterministic tests exercise fast impacts, isolated elastic momentum and energy conservation, simultaneous row coupling, separating pairs, initial overlap rejection, event-budget exhaustion, chained events, ideal inelastic energy loss, and zero-duration/duplicate-ID validation. These tests establish a small analytic oracle, not a general proof of energy or convergence for arbitrary many-body simultaneous collisions, a guarantee against floating-point tunneling, support for rotating convex objects, or a persistent resting-contact engine. For an impact against an externally fixed body, momentum conservation of the two displayed disks alone is not the correct closed-system invariant; the stationary environment receives the reaction.

Reducing collision search without losing collisions: conservative swept bounds

The event-step laboratory above asks every pair of disks whether they will collide during the remaining time interval. With n bodies, this examines n(n−1)/2 unordered pairs after each event. For 1,000 disks, that is 499,500 expensive exact pair-time queries per scan—even if almost every disk is far away from the others. A broad phase exists to reject pairs that cannot possibly interact using a cheaper geometric test; it is not allowed to reject a true collision merely to be fast. This is why the central proof obligation is conservative coverage, not an attractive benchmark on one scene.

For a disk of radius r, initial centre p=(p_x,p_y), velocity v=(v_x,v_y) and remaining interval Δt, its centre under constant velocity travels along the segment from p to p+vΔt. Every possible disk position lies inside its swept axis-aligned rectangle. Its x bounds are min(p_x,p_x+v_xΔt)−r and max(p_x,p_x+v_xΔt)+r; y is analogous. The swept-broadphase reference lab conservatively rounds each boundary one representable floating-point value outward with std::nextafter. The exact continuous disk shape is a capsule around the segment, while its swept AABB is a larger rectangle: the rectangle admits extra pairs but must not discard any collision, provided the endpoints and bounds are correctly represented.

The algorithm sorts these rectangles by their minimum x coordinate, breaking ties by stable disk ID. As it visits each new rectangle, it removes from an active set any earlier rectangle whose maximum x lies strictly before the current minimum x. Every remaining active rectangle overlaps along x; the algorithm then compares their y intervals. Pairs that pass both checks are returned in deterministic lexicographically sorted index order, with a duplicate assertion. A true disk impact at time t∈[0,Δt] means the two disk regions intersect at that time; their swept AABBs must both contain the intersection point. Therefore their AABBs overlap in x and y and the pair must survive the broad-phase filtering. The reverse implication is false: AABBs may overlap even when the disks pass at different times or miss geometrically. The exact TOI narrow phase must therefore test every candidate before scheduling an event.

The laboratory compares its candidate set with an independent analytic disk TOI predicate, rather than comparing the broad phase against itself. Each true TOI pair must appear in the returned set. It tests a high-speed crossing, 100 stationary well-spaced disks with zero candidates, 200 seeded randomized scenes containing 35 disks each, and malformed identity/time inputs. The random scenes therefore examine up to 119,000 unordered pairs for conservative coverage, because each 35-disk scene contains 595 pairs. These are useful regression witnesses, not a proof against all finite-precision failures.

Sorting has O(n log n) comparison cost. Maintaining the simple active vector has potentially O(n²) scanning and removal cost when many broad AABBs overlap; the output itself can contain O(n²) candidate pairs in a dense scene. A scalable production version may use a better interval structure, broadphase BVH, grid, or incremental pair cache, and should benchmark temporally coherent motion rather than assuming this sample has production throughput. The original broadphase witness remains independently testable; the event stepper now has an optional swept-candidate mode alongside its exhaustive reference mode. Both generate candidate pairs for the current remaining interval, and the event stepper rebuilds candidates after each velocity-changing impact. A differential test source is committed to compare complete outcomes, but its successful GitHub-hosted execution remains unverified. This code-level integration is not yet native Kairo runtime integration or evidence of speedup.

How to reconstruct and verify the witness

Read the Row fields as a prepared contact Jacobian in compressed form: ra/rb are the lever arms, n/t are the constraint axes, kn/kt are scalar rows of the matrix J M⁻¹ Jᵀ. The method relative_velocity computes Jv, inverse_effective_mass computes a row’s inverse effective mass, solve_one projects impulse increments, and warm_start applies an already-owned cache once. make_row validates data and freezes the impact target. The six tests cover central momentum/energy, friction orientation, angular impulse, separating and static degeneracies, coupled two-contact iteration/next-frame cache, and nonfinite-input rejection.

Run strict compilation and execution, then run a sanitizer build. Expected output is persistent-contact witness: 6 suites PASS. This verifies only the tested cases on the compiling environment; the repository GitHub Actions workflow repeats strict and undefined-behavior checks, with remote status to be verified separately.

A reconstruction exercise is to add two bodies with unequal masses and an off-centre contact, compute kn by hand and compare every intermediate u_n, Δλ_n, Δv and Δω. A stronger follow-up exercise is to implement real feature matching, deliberately reverse normals between frames, and demonstrate that incorrectly reused cached tangential impulses generate artificial energy. Neither extension is presently claimed as implemented.

Verified boundary and research questions

The lab does not verify Kairo’s current renderer or physics engine, broadphase pair generation, narrowphase contact topology, 3D Jacobians, static/dynamic island management, precise multi-contact complementarity, numerical convergence across arbitrary scenes, determinism across compilers, robust CCD, or real-time performance. Before a research claim about stability or speed, define independent scene families, error metrics (maximum penetration, residual closing speed, drift, energy increase), iteration budgets, timestep families and order-randomization trials. Compare warm versus cold starts without changing geometry, feature matching or tolerances at the same time.

Implementation-depth contract for every developed concept

A reader should be able to close the book and build the mechanism. Therefore a concept is not “done” until its first meaningful use provides: the forcing engineering problem; definitions of every symbol, convention and unit; the derivation and its assumptions; the concrete memory/state representation and ownership; the full algorithm and decision branches; a complete documented implementation or a clearly labeled API-specific implementation; a numerical trace with inspectable intermediate state; failure/degeneracy and alternatives; proof of invariants and bounded behavior; and reproducible positive, negative and metamorphic tests. The note itself must contain these, not just a heading, a pointer to a video, or a code file that the reader must discover elsewhere.

Witness categories must remain distinct. A CPU-only pedagogical model can prove logic, arithmetic and expected rejection cases. It cannot prove production GPU memory visibility or Apple/NVIDIA driver behavior. A reference engine test cannot establish the current Kairo integration unless the exact Kairo commit and reproducible build are inspected. A mathematically derived assumption is not an observed result; a video transcript’s claim is not verified code; the 3,000-part route map is an ownership assignment rather than 3,000 completed reconstructions.

It does not emit stage/access masks, image layout transitions, queue-family ownership, timeline waits, transient aliasing or device-loss recovery. Those remain first-class milestones, not implicit features of this passing laboratory. See the Vulkan synchronization specification for the separate memory-model obligations.

Robust geometric predicates

Robust geometric predicates

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6

Definition and mechanism

A geometric predicate decides a category from a sign, such as orientation. Near cancellation, ordinary floating arithmetic may not certify that sign. Adaptive arithmetic adds work only when justified error bounds leave uncertainty. Exact stored-input decisions cannot restore rounded-away physical information.

A triangle can have an accurately small area estimate yet an uncertified orientation sign. Declaring every small value zero changes topology instead of proving a decision.

Prerequisites

  • Cross products and oriented area — Oriented area supplies face normals, frame signs and geometric determinants.
  • Dot and cross-product rounding — Cancellation and rounded inputs explain when a determinant sign or finite measurement is uncertain.

Used by

  • Collision barriers and continuous detection ## Recall and next depth

Distinguish tolerance-based geometry, measurements and certified predicates; the Phase 6 lab implements only ordinary tests. Full production proofs, target-specific integration and learner mastery require further evidence.

Phase 11 camera development

Adaptive orientation and incircle predicates protect discrete sign decisions from floating-point error by refining arithmetic when an error bound cannot certify the result. Camera estimation has a different uncertainty: noisy pixels and weak observability can leave pose uncertain even when every sign is exact. Predicate robustness does not improve measurement accuracy, and a low reprojection residual does not guarantee every combinatorial decision was reliable. Keep layers distinct: use robust predicates for topology, uncertainty weights for image residuals, and Jacobian spectra for weak directions. Jacobians, pushforwards, and pullbacks

Jacobians, pushforwards, and pullbacks

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

The Jacobian is the matrix of first derivatives of a vector-valued function. It maps a small input displacement to a first-order output displacement, a forward sensitivity often called a pushforward or Jacobian-vector product. Gradients transform in the reverse direction by the transpose Jacobian, the pullback used in reverse-mode differentiation. These operations differ because vectors and covectors have different transformation rules. Jacobians compose by matrix multiplication and their determinants describe local volume changes. A Jacobian is local: it does not replace a nonlinear transformation globally. At singular points it can lose rank or become ill-conditioned, affecting inverse sensitivity, uncertainty propagation, and optimizer steps. State coordinate ordering and column-vector conventions before interpreting signs or multiplication order.

Prerequisites

  • Derivative as a local linear map
  • Matrix multiplication and composition order
  • Probability density and change of measure

Used by

  • Automatic differentiation and backpropagation
  • Hessians and local curvature
  • Nonlinear least squares: Gauss-Newton and Levenberg-Marquardt

Hessians and local curvature

Hessians and local curvature

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

The Hessian collects second partial derivatives of a scalar objective. It describes how the gradient changes and supplies the quadratic term in a local Taylor model. For a smooth scalar field, the Hessian is symmetric under the usual equality-of-mixed-partials assumptions. Its eigenvectors indicate local curvature directions: positive eigenvalues give upward curvature, negative values downward curvature, and near-zero values weakly constrained directions. A positive-definite Hessian supports a strict local minimum in the unconstrained setting, while an indefinite Hessian signals a saddle-like local model. The Hessian is not the same as the curvature of an embedded geometric surface, though both involve second-order change. In optimization, exact Newton steps solve with the Hessian; practical methods may regularize or approximate it because conditioning, cost, or indefiniteness can make direct steps unreliable.

Prerequisites

  • Jacobians, pushforwards, and pullbacks
  • Symmetric positive-definite matrices and Cholesky

Used by

  • Newton and quasi-Newton optimization
  • Nonlinear least squares: Gauss-Newton and Levenberg-Marquardt
  • Taylor models and approximation error

Exposure and sensor response

Exposure and sensor response

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A camera sensor converts arriving photons into electrical measurements. Exposure depends on scene radiance, lens transmission, aperture, shutter duration, and sensor sensitivity; changing these settings trades motion blur, depth of field, noise, and saturation. A pixel integrates light over a finite area and exposure interval before quantization. Sensor wells have finite capacity, so highlights clip, while low photon counts have shot noise and readout adds electronic noise. ISO gain amplifies the signal and its noise rather than collecting additional photons. The recorded raw values are not yet display colors: white balance, color transforms, tone curves, and transfer encoding turn measurements into an image. A camera model must distinguish photon capture, sensor response, and display rendering to explain dynamic range and exposure choices.

Prerequisites

  • Lens optics and depth of field
  • Color encoding and linear-light operations

Probability density and change of measure

Probability density and change of measure

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

A probability density describes probability per unit of a chosen measure, not probability at a point. A density pA(a)p_A(a) over area differs from a density pω(ω)p_\omega(\omega) over solid angle. When a mapping changes variables, its Jacobian converts density so total probability remains one: pB(b)=pA(a)|da/db|p_B(b)=p_A(a)|da/db| in one dimension, with the determinant of the inverse Jacobian in multiple dimensions. In rendering, choosing a point on a light and using its direction from a shading point requires an area-to-solid-angle conversion involving distance squared and the light’s projected cosine. Estimator formulas are only correct when the sampling density and integral use the same measure. This concept prevents missing factors in importance sampling, environment-map sampling, and camera-lens integration.

Phase 9–10 development

A density is meaningful relative to a measure and its support; its value at a point is not itself an event probability. For a continuous scalar variable, an interval probability is the integral of the density over that interval. Under a differentiable one-to-one change of variables, the transformed density includes the absolute determinant of the inverse Jacobian. Values outside the transformed support have zero probability. A mixed law can contain both point masses and a continuous part, so one PDF alone cannot describe every distribution. When a renderer changes a surface-area density into a solid-angle density, the geometric Jacobian must preserve the same probability.

Prerequisites

  • Light spectra and radiometry
  • Random variables and probability laws

Monte Carlo rendering estimators and variance

Monte Carlo rendering estimators and variance

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Monte Carlo integration estimates an integral by averaging random samples with importance weights. For target integral I=∫f(x)dxI=\int f(x)dx and samples drawn from density p(x)p(x), the estimator is Î=N−1∑k=1Nf(xk)/p(xk)\hat I=N^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^N f(x_k)/p(x_k). It is unbiased when samples cover every region where ff is nonzero and the density is correct. Its variance falls approximately as 1/N1/N, so halving standard error takes about four times as many samples. Importance sampling chooses pp to follow the magnitude of the integrand; multiple importance sampling combines strategies such as light sampling and BSDF sampling with weights that avoid overtrusting a strategy that rarely finds a contribution. Path tracing applies these estimators to light paths, while rare caustics and narrow visibility openings remain high-variance cases.

Phase 9–10 development

For independent samples from density pp, the sample average estimates the integral using terms f(Xi)/p(Xi)f(X_i)/p(X_i) where pp is positive on the integrand support. Unbiasedness requires the support condition and integrability; finite variance additionally requires a finite second moment of f/pf/p. A variance estimate describes sampling spread, not systematic bias. Dependent samples add covariance terms, and multiple-importance weights combine proposal densities while preserving mixture support. A confidence interval is justified only when its sampling and moment assumptions are stated.

Prerequisites

Time integrators and symplectic updates

Time integrators and symplectic updates

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

A time integrator turns a differential equation into a discrete state update. Explicit Euler uses the current slope; midpoint and Runge–Kutta methods combine several slope evaluations to improve local accuracy; semi-implicit Euler updates velocity before position and can behave better for mechanical systems. Symplectic methods preserve the geometric structure of Hamiltonian dynamics, often keeping long-run energy error bounded rather than allowing systematic drift. No method is universally best: order, stability region, cost, conservation, and stiffness all matter. A higher formal order does not guarantee better behavior at an unsuitable step size or under discontinuous forces. Compare integrators on the same problem, step policy, and error target. Update order is part of the algorithm: changing it can change stability and physical behavior, not merely code style.

Prerequisites

  • ODE initial-value problems and stiffness

Used by

  • ODE integration and stability

Implicit differentiation and parameter sensitivities

Implicit differentiation and parameter sensitivities

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

Implicit differentiation obtains how a solution changes when it is defined by an equation rather than an explicit formula. If a state satisfies F(y,θ)=0 and the Jacobian with respect to y is invertible, differentiating gives dy/dθ=−(∂F/∂y)⁻¹(∂F/∂θ). This can differentiate equilibrium states, constrained optima, and roots without unrolling every solver iteration. For a converged optimizer, differentiating stationarity and constraint conditions yields sensitivity equations, but active-set changes, nonunique solutions, singular Jacobians, and imperfect convergence complicate the result. Continuous sensitivity equations propagate derivatives alongside an ODE; adjoint methods can reduce cost when there are many parameters and few scalar outputs. These are modeling tools with assumptions, not a guarantee that every algorithmic branch is differentiable.

Prerequisites

  • Automatic differentiation and backpropagation
  • Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics

Derivative as a local linear map

Derivative as a local linear map

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

The derivative measures first-order change. In one variable it is the limit of the difference quotient; in several variables it is the linear map that best predicts small output changes near a point. For a scalar function, this local model is the tangent line. For a vector-valued function, it is a matrix acting on an input perturbation. The derivative is local: its approximation error becomes small relative to the perturbation as the step shrinks, but the linear model need not remain accurate over a large region. This view unifies instantaneous velocity, gradients, Jacobians, and optimization directions. It also gives a practical check: compare a small finite perturbation with the derivative’s predicted change, while remembering that floating-point rounding and curvature limit how small or large the perturbation should be.

Convergence order and Richardson extrapolation

Convergence order and Richardson extrapolation

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

If an approximation has leading error Qh=Q*+Chp+O(hp+1)Q_h=Q^*+Ch^p+O(h^{p+1}), halving the step reduces that term by about 2p2^p. Comparing results at hh, h/2h/2, and h/4h/4 estimates the observed order; Richardson extrapolation combines two resolutions to cancel the leading term when the assumed order is valid. The method is diagnostic, not magic: measurements must be in the asymptotic regime, the same mathematical quantity must be computed at each resolution, and roundoff or stochastic noise must not dominate. For Euler integration, first-order refinement predicts the leading error to halve. Record the sequence and residuals rather than reporting an order from one pair alone. Ratios near an expected power provide evidence, but one noisy ratio is not a convergence study.

Prerequisites

  • Discretization, truncation, and roundoff
  • Finite differences and step-size balance
  • Numerical quadrature and error
