Definite integrals and the fundamental theorem

Definite integrals and the fundamental theorem

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

A definite integral accumulates a quantity over an interval, with sign and units determined by the integrand and integration variable. Riemann sums approximate this accumulation by weighted samples; under suitable regularity conditions their limit defines the integral. The fundamental theorem connects accumulation and differentiation: an antiderivative evaluates the net integral, and the derivative of an accumulated integral recovers its integrand when continuity conditions hold. This link explains why integrating velocity gives displacement and why a variable upper-limit integral solves a simple differential equation. Definite integral, indefinite antiderivative, and geometric area are related but not interchangeable ideas. The integration variable is a dummy variable, so name it distinctly from the endpoint. Integrals also form the target of Monte Carlo estimators, where measure and sampling density must match.

Prerequisites

  • Derivative as a local linear map

Expectation, covariance, and dependence

Expectation, covariance, and dependence

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Expectation is the probability-weighted average of a random quantity, and variance is the expected squared deviation from that average. Covariance measures how two centered quantities vary together; correlation scales it to a unitless linear-association measure. For a random vector, the covariance matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite because every directional quadratic form equals a variance. Zero covariance does not usually imply independence, except under special joint Gaussian conditions. Conditional expectation and total-variance identities decompose uncertainty into within-group spread and variation between group means. These moments drive Monte Carlo error analysis, Gaussian geometry, and linear uncertainty propagation. An empirical covariance depends on sample convention and denominator; Bessel correction concerns unbiased population-variance estimation under IID sampling, not a universal change to descriptive covariance.

Prerequisites

  • Probability spaces, events, and conditioning
  • Random variables and probability laws

Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse

Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse

The exact SVD defines A+A^+ by reciprocating every positive singular value and transposing the orthogonal factors. A+bA^+b minimizes residual first and Euclidean solution norm among minimizers second. A numerical cutoff instead produces Aτ+A_\tau^+: if it discards a positive singular value, it solves a retained-rank approximation and can increase the residual of the original system. The cutoff makes the treatment of weak directions explicit.

Use it when: rectangular or rank-deficient least squares needs a minimum-norm answer.

Developed in Phase 8: The exact pseudoinverse reciprocates every positive singular value, yielding the least-squares solution with minimum Euclidean norm. A practical cutoff defines a different, truncated operator: discarding even a positive singular value can increase the residual for the original system, so the tolerance and retained rank are part of the mathematical answer. the exact pseudoinverse · truncation and regularization

Prerequisites

Used by

Position reconstruction from depth

Position reconstruction from depth

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11

Definition and mechanism

Given a pixel and an axial depth value, reconstruct a view-space point by converting the pixel to NDC, forming its camera ray, and scaling that ray so its forward-axis component equals the measured depth. Alternatively, transform the corresponding homogeneous clip point through an inverse projection matrix and divide by its resulting homogeneous coordinate. To obtain world position, apply the inverse view transform. These routes must share the actual viewport, pixel-centre, NDC-depth, and projection conventions used to render the image. In large worlds, subtract camera-relative origins before reducing precision; converting an already-rounded coordinate cannot restore lost detail. In a camera-relative renderer, reconstruct near the camera origin before adding a large global offset.

Prerequisites

  • Axial depth and Euclidean range
  • Hardware depth-buffer linearization
  • Camera calibration and bundle adjustment
  • Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division

Used by

Conditional Gaussians and Schur complements

Conditional Gaussians and Schur complements

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Conditioning one block of a jointly Gaussian vector on another produces a Gaussian conditional law under the usual nonsingular assumptions. Its mean shifts by the cross-covariance times the inverse observed-block covariance, while its covariance is the Schur complement Σbb−ΣbaΣaa⁻¹Σab. That conditional covariance is positive semidefinite: insert the vector (−Σaa⁻¹Σabv,v) into the joint covariance quadratic form. If the joint covariance is positive definite, the Schur complement is positive definite. The conditional covariance does not depend on the observed value, although the conditional mean does. This formula links Bayesian updating, Gaussian elimination, and block linear systems. Singular observed blocks require a compatible degenerate-Gaussian treatment or a rank-revealing method; blindly applying an inverse is invalid.

Prerequisites

  • Multivariate Gaussian distributions and whitening
  • Gaussian elimination and pivoting

Taylor models and approximation error

Taylor models and approximation error

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

A Taylor model approximates a smooth function near a reference point using its value, derivatives, and higher-order terms. The first-order model is the derivative’s linear map; the second-order model adds curvature through the Hessian. A remainder term describes what the finite truncation omits, so local accuracy depends on step size and higher derivatives over the region. Big-O notation gives an asymptotic scale, while a concrete error bound needs assumptions such as bounded derivatives. Taylor models power local optimization, camera Jacobian updates, uncertainty propagation, and numerical error analysis. They are not reliable far from the expansion point merely because the polynomial is easy to evaluate. When the input distribution is broad or crosses a singularity, first-order covariance propagation can miss bias and tail behavior; validate or replace the local model.

Prerequisites

  • Derivative as a local linear map
  • Hessians and local curvature

Axial depth and Euclidean range

Axial depth and Euclidean range

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11

Definition and mechanism

Axial depth measures distance along the camera’s forward axis; Euclidean range measures distance from the camera centre along the viewing ray. With a right-handed view frame looking along −Z-Z, positive axial depth is d=−zd=-z, while range is r=x2+y2+z2r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}. They agree only on the optical axis. For a unit ray direction qq with qz<0q_z<0, a range measurement converts to axial depth as d=−rqzd=-rq_z. A range sensor and a perspective depth buffer may therefore encode different quantities. Applying a depth-buffer formula directly to a range image distorts reconstructed geometry away from the image centre. At view point (3,4,−12)(3,4,-12), axial depth is 1212 while range is 1313, a visible distinction off-axis.

Prerequisites

Omnidirectional camera projections

Omnidirectional camera projections

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11

Definition and mechanism

Cubemaps, equirectangular panoramas, and fisheye lenses map unit directions onto different image domains. A cubemap selects one of six faces and projects two direction components; equirectangular coordinates map longitude and latitude to a rectangle; fisheye mappings use a radial function of angular distance. These parameterizations are not equal-area: uniform pixel sampling does not imply uniform solid-angle sampling. Choose the mapping that matches capture or rendering needs, define face orientation and seam rules, and measure reconstruction with angular error between unit vectors. Fisheye formulas also differ (equidistant, equisolid, orthographic, stereographic), so name the model before interpreting pixels. At the poles, longitude is undefined, so seam and pole handling need explicit sampling rules.

  • Visual angle and calibrated rays

Screen-space ray generation and mouse picking

Screen-space ray generation and mouse picking

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11

Definition and mechanism

A screen ray begins with a pixel location mapped through the viewport to NDC, then through inverse projection and camera pose into a world-space origin and direction. For perspective cameras, rays usually share the eye origin; orthographic rays have parallel directions but different origins across the image. Mouse picking must use the same high-DPI scaling, viewport offset, origin, and Y convention as rendering. Near and far unprojection can define a ray segment, but a point at infinity or an infinite far plane needs an explicit direction construction. Picking then intersects that ray with scene geometry or uses an object-ID buffer.

Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics

Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

Optimization chooses parameters to minimize an objective while satisfying constraints. Gradient descent steps opposite the gradient; Newton’s method also uses curvature, while quasi-Newton methods estimate curvature from gradient changes. Constraints may be enforced by parameterization, penalty terms, projection, or constrained solvers. In inverse kinematics, the parameters are joint angles and the objective measures distance between an end effector and its target. Forward kinematics maps angles to a hand or foot position; its Jacobian maps small joint changes to small endpoint changes. A damped least-squares step solves a stabilized linear system to reduce target error without exploding near singular poses. Joint limits, collisions, and multiple valid solutions make initialization and constraints important. The same framework applies to fitting cameras, deforming meshes, or matching image observations.

Phase 9–10 development

An optimization problem specifies an objective, variables, and equality or inequality constraints before an algorithm is selected. A gradient step uses first-order information; Newton and quasi-Newton steps add curvature, while line searches or trust regions control how far a local model is trusted. For nonlinear least squares, Gauss-Newton approximates curvature from the residual Jacobian and Levenberg-Marquardt damps the resulting system. Lagrange multipliers and KKT conditions describe constrained stationary points under their regularity assumptions. These local conditions do not by themselves prove global optimality.

Prerequisites

  • Singular value decomposition
  • Coordinate frames and change of basis

Learned image features and CNNs

Learned image features and CNNs

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A convolutional neural network (CNN) learns filters that detect useful image patterns from data. A convolution layer applies the same small kernel at many image locations, so a feature such as an edge can be recognized wherever it appears. Early layers often respond to local contrast or texture; later layers combine these responses into task-specific patterns. Stride and pooling reduce spatial resolution, trading detail for computation and larger receptive fields. Training adjusts filter values by gradient descent using backpropagation and labeled or self-supervised objectives. Weight sharing gives translation equivariance: shifting an input shifts the feature map, but does not guarantee full translation invariance or robustness to scale, viewpoint, lighting, or distribution change. Padding and stride determine border behavior and output size; too much downsampling can erase small objects. A learned feature is a representation useful for a training objective, not a human-interpretable semantic guarantee. Performance depends on data coverage, augmentation, architecture, optimization, and honest held-out evaluation.

Attention and visual transformers

Attention and visual transformers

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Self-attention lets each token build a context-dependent mixture of other tokens. A learned linear map produces queries QQ, keys KK, and values VV; scaled dot products compare each query with all keys, softmax converts scores to weights, and those weights combine values. Multiple heads learn different relationships, while positional information tells the model where patches or words came from. Vision transformers split an image into patches, embed them as tokens, and process the sequence with attention and feed-forward blocks. Unlike a small convolution, global attention can relate distant regions in one layer, but its pairwise score matrix grows roughly as the square of token count. Patch size trades spatial detail for compute; positional encodings and training data affect transfer. Attention weights are a mechanism for mixing information, not an explanation of causal importance. A transformer still needs a task objective, data, optimization, and validation, and can fail under distribution shift or poor spatial grounding.

Latent-variable models and generative flows

Latent-variable models and generative flows

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Generative models describe how data could be produced, often by first sampling a latent variable zz and mapping it to an observation xx. A variational autoencoder (VAE) learns an encoder distribution q(z|x)q(z|x) and decoder p(x|z)p(x|z); its evidence lower bound balances reconstruction likelihood against a KL penalty that keeps the latent distribution tractable. A generative adversarial network (GAN) trains a generator against a discriminator, creating a game that can produce sharp samples but may be unstable or collapse to limited modes. Normalizing flows use invertible transformations so the data density can be computed with a change-of-variables Jacobian determinant. These methods solve different tradeoffs among likelihood, sample quality, latent structure, and optimization stability. Their assumptions matter: a VAE’s posterior family may be too simple, a GAN score is not a calibrated density, and a flow’s invertibility constrains architecture. Generated samples are not evidence that the model has learned the true causal process.

Prerequisites

  • Probability density and change of measure

Radiance fields and Gaussian splatting

Radiance fields and Gaussian splatting

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A radiance field represents a scene by the color and density seen along each 3D viewing ray. NeRF maps a position and viewing direction through a learned function, then volume-renders samples using transmittance and opacity weights; multiple calibrated photographs supervise the result. This representation handles view-dependent appearance but can require many ray samples and careful camera alignment. 3D Gaussian splatting instead stores anisotropic colored Gaussian primitives in space and projects them to screen, sorting and blending their footprints for fast interactive views. 2D Gaussian splatting uses oriented surface-like splats to improve geometric consistency. These methods trade continuous function evaluation for explicit primitives and rasterization. Sparse or biased views leave unseen regions unconstrained; floaters, blur, aliasing, incorrect transparency ordering, or poor geometry can remain even when training views look convincing. Novel-view quality is not equivalent to a watertight mesh or physically correct material. Reconstruction quality depends on camera poses, coverage, calibration, and the scene’s changing illumination.

Perception feedback and robot learning

Perception feedback and robot learning

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A robot learning system closes a loop: sensors produce observations, a policy chooses an action, the world changes, and new observations arrive. A policy maps states or observations to actions; a value function estimates expected future return and can help compare actions. Reinforcement learning updates behavior from outcomes, while imitation learning fits demonstrations. In visual robotics, the observation pipeline may include cameras, learned features, pose estimates, and spatial grounding; errors then affect movement rather than only a label. The training and deployment distributions can differ because the robot’s own actions change what it sees. Small perception errors can compound into different states and larger future errors, a form of covariate or distribution shift. Stable deployment therefore needs calibrated sensing, feedback timing, safety constraints, and evaluation on physical conditions. Demonstrations in simulation do not establish robust real-world manipulation; embodiment, contact, latency, and unmodeled dynamics matter. A successful policy is evidence for a task and setting, not general intelligence.

Confidence intervals and sequential evidence

Confidence intervals and sequential evidence

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

A confidence interval is a procedure with repeated-sample coverage under stated assumptions; it is not a posterior probability assigned to a fixed parameter. A normal interval for a mean uses a known population standard deviation or an approximation justified by the central limit theorem. With unknown scale and IID normal observations, the Student t distribution accounts for estimating the standard deviation. Heavy tails, sample dependence, multiple comparisons, and optional stopping can invalidate simple textbook guarantees. Adaptive algorithms that stop when a fixed-sample interval looks narrow need sequentially valid methods or a separately justified stopping rule. Report the target, sampling unit, dependence structure, estimator bias, interval procedure, stopping policy, and independent-run count. A narrow interval around a biased estimator measures precision about its expectation, not correctness of the target.

Prerequisites

  • Common probability distributions and their assumptions
  • Expectation, covariance, and dependence
  • Monte Carlo rendering estimators and variance

Latin-hypercube sampling

Latin-hypercube sampling

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Latin-hypercube sampling divides each coordinate axis into NN equal strata and uses a permutation so every sample occupies one stratum per dimension. With randomized within-stratum positions and randomized permutations, each sample has uniform marginal coordinates; samples are dependent by design. This can improve coverage for some integrands at arbitrary sample counts, including counts that do not form a square grid. It does not guarantee lower variance for every function, and IID variance formulas cannot be applied without accounting for dependence. Test exact stratum coverage deterministically, then compare estimator error over repeated randomized trials for the intended integrand. For N=5N=5, each axis still receives five strata, avoiding the missing-cell bias of taking five cells from a 3×33\times3 grid.

Prerequisites

  • Uniform shuffling without replacement
  • Sampling quality: stratification, quasi-Monte Carlo, and blue noise
  • Probability density and change of measure

Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation

Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

After a vertex is transformed, its clip-space coordinate is (xc,yc,zc,wc)(x_c,y_c,z_c,w_c). Clip primitives against the view volume before perspective division; under the conventional OpenGL clip convention the inequalities are −wc≤xc,yc,zc≤wc-w_c\le x_c,y_c,z_c\le w_c. A crossing edge is split by interpolating its homogeneous endpoints, which preserves the projective line and avoids dividing by a small or negative ww too early. Only surviving points are divided by wcw_c to enter normalized device coordinates. Attributes then need perspective-correct interpolation: screen-space barycentric weights interpolate a/wa/w and 1/w1/w, and the fragment value is their ratio. For a triangle with weights λi\lambda_i, a=(∑iλiai/wi)/(∑iλi/wi)a=(\sum_i\lambda_i a_i/w_i)/(\sum_i\lambda_i/w_i). Direct linear interpolation in screen space is correct only for affine quantities or equal depth; otherwise textures warp. Clip-space depth conventions and the near/far interval vary by API and projection setup, so the inequalities must match the active pipeline.

Phase 11 camera development

Clipping and perspective-correct interpolation preserve projective geometry, while texture filtering asks how much surface area maps to a pixel. Neighboring camera rays approximate the image-to-surface footprint. At grazing angles one pixel can cover a long, thin region; a center-only texel lookup may alias detail even when attributes interpolate correctly. Use footprint estimates to select mip levels or anisotropic filters, while respecting visibility edges where derivatives jump. Ray differentials aid sampling but do not replace clipping or multisample coverage. Source basis: PBRT differential-ray texture filtering. Link: A camera model must close the loop; research: Four deeper links from the TUM lecture review.

Worked clip-plane trace beside the shader explanation

For clip endpoints (0,0,0,1)(0,0,0,1) and (6,0,0,2)(6,0,0,2), the right-plane intersection uses homogeneous edge parameter 1/51/5; interpolating the already divided endpoints would use 1/31/3. The worked trace and pipeline figure also explain negative fourth components, the zero-divisor limit and declared depth conventions. This is used by the shader-stage teaching before program compilation and linking are discussed.

Executable raster-state continuation

The project now carries two complementary CPU witnesses. tools/labs/raster_reference_lab.cpp owns edge coverage, barycentrics, perspective-correct interpolation and depth ordering. tools/labs/raster_pipeline_state_lab.cpp continues the same pipeline through a homogeneous clip-plane intersection, an explicit four-sample coverage mask, stencil compare/pass update and premultiplied source-over blending.

That separation is deliberate: clipping happens in homogeneous coordinates before divide-by-ww; sample ownership happens after screen mapping; stencil/depth are stateful per-fragment/sample decisions; blending combines a surviving source with an existing destination. Treating all of them as “rasterization” without preserving these boundaries makes debugging nearly impossible.

DCC adapters and engine publication

DCC adapters and engine publication

A production pipeline should not let every DCC application define a different engine truth. Blender, Maya, Houdini and Nuke expose different object models, dependency systems and scripting APIs, but the engine-facing publication contract can remain host-neutral.

The useful separation is:

Host adapter → normalized asset description → validation → deterministic build plan → staged publication → engine-side verification.

The host adapter owns how to read the authoring application. The normalized core owns what the engine requires. Publication owns filesystem and identity guarantees. Engine verification proves that the published result can actually be consumed.

Blender boundary

Blender’s Python API exposes application data through the bpy module, including data access, context, operators, types, utilities and path helpers. A production exporter should prefer direct data access for deterministic inspection and use context-sensitive operators only when their context requirements are understood.

An adapter should establish which evaluated scene state it exports, how collections and object visibility are interpreted, which transforms are baked, and which external dependencies are copied or referenced. Exporting the editable authoring graph and exporting evaluated geometry are different contracts.

Primary reference: https://docs.blender.org/api/main/index.html

Maya boundary

Maya exposes both scripting commands and C++/Python APIs, with explicit dependency-graph and DAG plug-in concepts. A Maya adapter should distinguish scene hierarchy from dependency relationships and should make attribute/default/reference semantics explicit rather than flattening everything into names.

Primary reference: https://help.autodesk.com/view/MAYADEV/2026/ENU/

Houdini boundary

Houdini’s Object Model exposes nodes and geometry through the hou package. SOP networks generate geometry, while ROP networks can describe render/output dependencies. Geometry references can also depend on node cook state, so an adapter must decide when data is evaluated and copied into the host-neutral representation.

SideFX documentation explicitly distinguishes node families such as SOP geometry, LOP/USD scene description, ROP output networks and TOP task workflows. A pipeline should use those semantics instead of treating every node graph as the same kind of data.

Primary references: - https://www.sidefx.com/docs/houdini/hom/ - https://www.sidefx.com/docs/houdini/

Nuke boundary

Nuke publication often involves image nodes, knobs, file paths and frame ranges rather than mesh topology. The engine-neutral contract should therefore represent sequence ranges and missing-frame policy explicitly. Frame range syntax can represent contiguous and stepped ranges, so “first and last frame exist” is not sufficient validation.

Primary reference: https://learn.foundry.com/nuke/content/getting_started/managing_scripts/defining_frame_ranges.html

Host-neutral core

A normalized publication record should carry at least:

  • logical asset identity;
  • schema version;
  • source provenance;
  • normalized relative input/output paths;
  • declared coordinate/unit/color-space conventions where relevant;
  • dependencies;
  • content identity or cryptographic digest;
  • frame range or subresource inventory;
  • tool/version information when reproducibility depends on it;
  • deterministic diagnostics.

The core should not contain live bpy, Maya, hou or Nuke objects. Those are host-lifetime objects. Convert them into owned normalized data before asynchronous work or engine publication.

Validation before mutation

A dry-run plan should be complete before writing outputs. Validate path traversal, duplicate output destinations, missing dependencies, unsupported schema versions, frame gaps and identity collisions first.

Then write to staging locations. Only after every staged artifact passes validation should publication become visible. On filesystems where atomic replacement is relied upon, that property needs an actual platform/filesystem test; a logical transaction model does not prove disk semantics.

Executable witness

tools/labs/production_pipeline_contract_lab.cpp implements the host-neutral part of this design. It validates a portable relative-path grammar, rejects parent traversal, checks schema and SHA-256 string shape, produces a deterministic sorted publication plan, checks output collisions, models idempotent publication, and verifies contiguous frame sequences.

It deliberately does not claim real Blender/Maya/Houdini/Nuke execution, SHA-256 computation, symlink resolution, atomic rename behavior or render-farm integration.

Related: Atomic publication and durability, Binary format contracts, Interface contracts and publication.

Executed Blender boundary

The host-neutral adapter contract now has one real DCC execution path. tools/dcc/blender_contract.py runs inside Blender in background mode, creates mesh/collection/object datablocks without UI interaction, attaches logical publication metadata, saves a .blend, exports a binary glTF/GLB with extras, validates the GLB header/JSON chunk, resets Blender, re-imports the GLB and verifies mesh identity plus custom publication fields.

The GitHub workflow .github/workflows/blender-dcc-contract.yml installs Blender on Linux and executes that round trip headlessly. This changes the Blender portion from “API described” to “host executed in CI.” It does not upgrade Maya, Houdini or Nuke: their adapters remain host-neutral contracts until a licensed/current host can execute them. It also does not prove arbitrary production scenes, armatures, materials, texture packaging or current Kairo import parity.

Current Blender documentation explicitly supports background Python execution and glTF export; the repository test treats those host APIs as an external boundary and validates the exported artifact rather than assuming an operator call succeeded.

Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure

Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A polygon mesh is a combinatorial surface made of vertices, edges, and faces plus an embedding that assigns each vertex a position. Manifoldness is a local connectivity condition: an interior edge belongs to two faces, and the faces around each interior vertex form one cycle or fan. At a boundary, an edge belongs to one face and the vertex neighborhood forms one open chain; each boundary component closes into a loop. A bow-tie vertex with two disconnected fans is nonmanifold even if every face is an ordinary triangle. These conditions let algorithms define an unambiguous local tangent neighborhood, traversal, and surface orientation. Connectivity validity does not guarantee good geometry: valid topology can still self-intersect, collapse to a point, or contain poor skinny triangles. Keep topological and geometric quality checks separate.

Camera gauge freedoms and observability

Camera gauge freedoms and observability

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11

Definition and mechanism

A gauge freedom is a coordinated change to unknown scene and camera parameters that leaves every measured image unchanged. In calibrated monocular structure from motion, translating and rotating the entire reconstruction changes only the chosen world frame, while a common scale change of points and camera translations preserves projections; absolute metric scale therefore needs an external reference. Observability asks which local parameter changes produce distinguishable measurements. Linearizing reprojection residuals gives a Jacobian; its weighted information tensor or matrix J𝖳WJJ^{\mathsf T}WJ reveals weak parameter combinations through small eigenvalues after gauge directions are fixed. Example: adding more points to one planar, nearly fronto-parallel view may reduce pixel noise while focal length and distance remain strongly coupled. These conclusions assume a stated camera/scene model, correctly associated observations, and local linearization; the information matrix diagnoses local constraints, not global uniqueness. Report uncertainty only after fixing the gauge and specifying the observation noise model.

Example: A monocular map can be uniformly enlarged with all camera translations enlarged by the same factor and render the same images; a known baseline or measured object length fixes that scale gauge.

Assumptions: The gauge statement assumes calibrated monocular perspective cameras and no metric prior.; The information-matrix interpretation is local and depends on residual weighting and parameterization.

Depth buffering and visibility order

Depth buffering and visibility order

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A depth buffer stores the nearest depth seen so far for each image sample. When rasterizing a fragment, compare its depth with the stored value; if it is closer, update both depth and color, otherwise discard it. This per-sample test resolves opaque visibility without sorting all triangles. Perspective projection maps view-space depth nonlinearly, so the near and far clipping planes affect how floating-point precision is distributed. If they span an unnecessarily huge ratio, nearly coplanar surfaces may quantize to equal or inconsistent depths and flicker as the camera moves; this is z-fighting. Alpha-blended surfaces need additional ordering or order-independent methods because color composition is not commutative. Depth establishes visibility, while transparency determines how multiple visible layers contribute.

Depth gives ordering or camera-relative distance under a specific projection convention; it does not identify the surface that produced a sample. Reprojecting old color and depth can place history behind a newly visible surface. Validate with current depth, normal, object identity, or neighborhood checks; reject disocclusions and large reprojection errors. Reversed-Z and nonlinear perspective depth require consistent reconstruction before threshold comparisons. Valid visibility does not guarantee photometric stability after lighting, exposure, or material changes. Link depth semantics to temporal history validation. Lens optics and depth of field

Lens optics and depth of field

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A pinhole camera maps every scene point to one image point through a single center, but a real lens has a finite aperture. Rays from one object point pass through different parts of the aperture and meet at a focused image point only for the chosen focus distance. Points nearer or farther from that plane form a blur disk called the circle of confusion. Stopping down the aperture narrows the cone of rays and increases depth of field, but reduces collected light and may require longer exposure or higher sensor gain. Focal length and focus distance also affect field of view and perspective magnification. A thin-lens model is an approximation; real lenses add aberrations and vignetting. The model helps explain why depth of field is both an optical effect and a sampling/integration process over aperture positions.

Lens optics, focus, and image formation · Photographic composition, history, and communication · Photographic workflow and integrated decisions

Phase 11 camera development

A pinhole camera emits one ideal ray per image location. A finite-aperture lens samples a family of rays whose intersections form a blur disk away from the focal plane. A thin-lens camera therefore samples film and lens position, then aims through a focal point. Differentials from film offsets alone omit aperture variation unless the model includes it. Monte Carlo PDFs and camera weights must match the sampled film/aperture measure. The thin-lens model approximates real optics; aberrations and bokeh shape require richer models. Hardware depth-buffer linearization

Hardware depth-buffer linearization

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11

Definition and mechanism

Perspective projection maps axial distance nonlinearly into NDC depth. For a declared projection depth row q=−A+B/dq=-A+B/d, solve d=B/(q+A)d=B/(q+A); finite conventional, finite reversed, infinite reversed, and OpenGL-style conventions have different coefficients or NDC conversions. The depth sample must first be interpreted in the same range and direction used by the projection matrix. This is why a single generic formula without an API and projection contract is unsafe. Verify near and far endpoints, test round trips over a range of distances, and handle an infinite-far endpoint such as reversed depth q=0q=0 explicitly. Near/far endpoint checks catch sign mistakes immediately; interior round trips then test scaling and finite precision.

Ray differentials and camera sampling measures

Ray differentials and camera sampling measures

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11

Definition and mechanism

A camera sample selects a film location and usually a shutter time, then maps that sample to a weighted ray or path contribution. Ray differentials approximate how neighboring pixel samples change the generated ray; after intersection they estimate the surface footprint covered by a pixel and help choose a texture filter level. A sampling measure states which quantity is sampled and therefore which probability density belongs in a Monte Carlo estimator; area, solid angle, image-plane area, and discrete pixel measures are not interchangeable without a Jacobian. Example: two adjacent pixels generate rays whose intersection points span a large patch on a distant oblique surface, so filtering should average that footprint rather than use a single high-frequency texel. Differential rays are local first-order approximations and can fail at discontinuities or complex lens mappings; the weight and PDF must match the camera model and chosen measure.

Example: For a pinhole camera, offset the raster sample by one pixel in x and y, generate neighboring rays, and intersect them with a textured plane; the resulting parallelogram estimates the pixel footprint for texture filtering.

Assumptions: Differentials approximate nearby rays locally and are not exact at visibility or lens discontinuities.; Importance weights/PDFs are valid only when defined in the same measure as the estimator.

Additive energy and approximate structure

Additive energy and approximate structure

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Additive energy measures how often two pairs from a set have the same sum: E(A)=|{(a,b,c,d)∈A4:a+b=c+d}|E(A)=|\{(a,b,c,d)\in A^4:a+b=c+d\}|. A random-like set has relatively few repeated sums; a set with many additive coincidences often contains a structured subset. The Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers principle turns high energy into a large subset with small doubling, while Ruzsa-style inequalities and Freiman-type theorems describe how small doubling constrains approximate additive structure. In finite fields, sum-product results show that a set cannot remain simultaneously additively and multiplicatively concentrated unless it has special algebraic structure, such as subfield behavior. These implications are quantitative and depend on group or field hypotheses, subset size, and constants. High energy does not mean the entire set is a subgroup, and a small-doubling conclusion may apply only after discarding many elements. Energy is a counting diagnostic that guides structure theorems, not a complete classification by itself.

Exceptional projections and dimension

Exceptional projections and dimension

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Projection usually lowers dimension, but a finite or fractal set may collapse unusually many points in special directions. For a finite planar set XX, count pairs whose orthogonal projections coincide in direction θ\theta; such pairs lie on lines parallel to the projection fibers. Averaging over directions gives a baseline, while exceptional directions produce larger fibers and encode geometric structure. For a density, the related transform integrates along each fiber, as in tomography; the Fourier-slice identity connects the transform of a projection to a slice of the original Fourier transform. Dimension and separation assumptions matter: finite point sets, thickened sets, measures, and finite-field analogues have different statements. A highly structured set can defeat naive random-grid intuition, and subfield examples in finite fields create strong obstructions. Results are estimates with hypotheses, not universal formulas for every dimension or projection family. This node connects geometric projection to incidence counting and harmonic analysis.

Spline bases and curve evaluation

Spline bases and curve evaluation

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A spline is a piecewise polynomial curve whose neighboring pieces join under explicit continuity constraints. A cubic Bézier segment uses four control points and Bernstein weights; the weights sum to one, so the curve lies in their convex hull. A B-spline uses local basis functions so moving one control point changes only nearby spans rather than the whole curve. Knots mark where polynomial pieces meet; repeated knots reduce continuity. Catmull–Rom curves interpolate their control points and can be convenient for motion paths, while Bézier curves expose endpoint tangents through their handles. To evaluate a curve, compute basis weights at parameter tt and take their weighted sum of control points. Position, first derivative, and parameterization speed matter separately: even a smooth path may speed up or slow down unless its parameter is adjusted.

Collision barriers and continuous detection

Collision barriers and continuous detection

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A collision barrier turns a geometric safety condition into an optimization energy that rises sharply as bodies approach contact. Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) combines barrier terms for vertex-face and edge-edge separations with a time-step formulation that prevents interpenetration while a deformable object moves. Continuous collision detection (CCD) asks whether two moving primitives touch at any time during a step, not only at its endpoints; a pair can cross and separate between discrete samples. Robust CCD therefore needs conservative root bounds and careful handling of near-degenerate geometry. The barrier does not replace a correct collision set: missing pairs, invalid orientations, or a nonconservative CCD test can still allow tunneling. Very stiff barriers also make optimization ill-conditioned and require line search or step restrictions. IPC’s guarantees depend on assumptions about the initial configuration, collision constraints, and numerical tolerances. The core distinction is discrete overlap testing versus continuous-in-time contact prevention.

Local rigidity and mesh orientation fields

Local rigidity and mesh orientation fields

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) deformation seeks vertex positions that change as little as possible from a preferred local rigid transform. For each vertex neighborhood, fit a rotation to the deformed edge vectors, then minimize residuals between transformed rest edges and current edges. Alternating between local rotations and a global position solve makes a nonlinear shape-editing problem tractable, but the result depends on constraints, initialization, mesh quality, and rotation fitting. Instant Meshes uses direction or orientation fields over a surface to guide a quad-dominant remeshing; field singularities encode where a globally consistent direction cannot exist. A mesh’s half-edge connectivity, boundary structure, and orientation determine valid neighborhoods and field transport. Poor triangles, seams, boundary conditions, or inconsistent orientation can create artifacts. ARAP is a local preservation objective, not exact rigidity of the whole shape; a direction field guides topology but does not uniquely determine a good mesh without sizing and feature constraints.

Triangle rasterization and coverage tests

Triangle rasterization and coverage tests

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Rasterization converts triangle geometry into a finite set of image samples. A pixel’s ideal coverage is the area fraction inside the triangle; a center test approximates this integral with one binary answer and therefore creates jagged edges. A directed edge defines an inside half-plane, so three signed edge tests classify a point against a triangle. A consistent tie rule assigns samples exactly on shared edges to one triangle, preventing cracks and double coverage. Supersampling tests several locations per pixel and averages their coverage, trading cost for a better area estimate. Hardware often checks candidate samples in parallel within a bounding box, then rejects or accepts coarse blocks that are wholly outside or inside. Triangle coverage is also the basis for interpolating depth, color, normals, and texture coordinates.

Ray-triangle intersection

Ray-triangle intersection

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A ray is a parametric half-line r(t)=o+tdr(t)=o+td, where oo is its origin, dd is its direction, and only t≥0t\ge0 lies ahead of the ray. To intersect a triangle, first intersect the ray with its plane, then express the hit point in barycentric coordinates and accept it only if the weights lie inside the triangle. An equivalent determinant test solves for ray distance and two barycentric coordinates together. The hit record should state whether the result is nearest, any, or all intersections; those are different query contracts. Parallel or nearly parallel rays, degenerate triangles, and hits near edges require care because small floating-point errors can change classification. Scale-aware tolerances and consistent orientation predicates reduce cracks and self-intersection artifacts.

Stereo correspondence and epipolar geometry

Stereo correspondence and epipolar geometry

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Stereo reconstruction uses two or more views to infer depth from corresponding image features. A 3D point and the two camera centers define an epipolar plane; its intersection with each image plane is an epipolar line. Thus a feature in one image should match along a one-dimensional line in the other, reducing a 2D search to a constrained search. With calibrated cameras, triangulation intersects the two viewing rays; noise means they are skew, so estimate the 3D point minimizing reprojection or ray distance. Depth uncertainty grows rapidly when the viewing rays are nearly parallel, which happens for distant points or small baselines. Rectification rotates images so epipolar lines become horizontal scanlines. Occlusion, repetitive texture, and calibration error can still produce mismatches, so confidence and consistency checks are essential.

Interpolation versus approximation

Interpolation versus approximation

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Interpolation reproduces every prescribed sample exactly, while approximation minimizes or controls an error criterion and may miss the observations. The distinction matters when data are noisy: a high-degree interpolant can fit measurement noise and oscillate between samples, while a lower-complexity approximation can better represent the underlying trend. In texture reconstruction, the samples themselves often define the represented signal, so interpolation is an appropriate reconstruction rule. In calibration, observations have uncertainty, so fitting a model may be more defensible. Neither method is automatically superior; choose based on the meaning of the data, the error measure, and whether evaluation stays within or extrapolates beyond the sampled domain.

Subdivision surface masks

Subdivision surface masks

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Subdivision refines a control mesh and updates old and newly inserted vertices with local masks, producing a sequence that approaches a smooth limit surface. Loop subdivision targets triangle meshes: for an interior edge with endpoints a,ba,b and opposite vertices c,dc,d, its new point is 3(a+b)/8+(c+d)/83(a+b)/8+(c+d)/8. An old vertex of degree nn becomes (1−nβ)S+β∑iPi(1-n\beta)S+\beta\sum_iP_i, with the lecture’s simple weight β=3/16\beta=3/16 for n=3n=3 and 3/(8n)3/(8n) otherwise. Catmull–Clark targets polygon meshes: face points are face-vertex averages, interior edge points average endpoints and two adjacent face points, and old vertices use face-average, edge-midpoint-average, and original-position terms. Boundary rules differ from interior masks and must be stated. Extraordinary vertices have nonregular valence and need deliberate treatment.

Camera calibration and bundle adjustment

Camera calibration and bundle adjustment

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Camera calibration estimates parameters that map 3D points to image coordinates. Intrinsics describe focal scale, principal point, and lens distortion; extrinsics describe camera pose relative to the scene. Known calibration targets provide 3D-to-2D correspondences, and a nonlinear least-squares objective minimizes reprojection error. Bundle adjustment jointly refines many camera poses and 3D feature points by minimizing all observed image residuals. The problem is sparse because each image sees only a subset of points. It also has gauge freedoms: translating or scaling the entire reconstruction may leave projections unchanged, so fix a reference pose or scale. Robust loss functions reduce the effect of mismatched features. Good initialization, parameter scaling, and Jacobian structure determine whether optimization converges.

Surface orientation from image brightness

Surface orientation from image brightness

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Shape-from-illumination methods infer surface orientation or depth from how light changes across an image. Photometric stereo observes a fixed camera view under multiple known light directions; for a Lambertian surface, measured intensity is proportional to albedo times the dot product between light direction and surface normal. Solving several such equations estimates the scaled normal, then integration recovers height up to boundary and scale ambiguities. A reflectance map plots brightness as a function of surface normal under fixed illumination and can reveal which orientations are visible. The extended Gaussian image maps each surface area to its normal on the unit sphere; its distribution summarizes orientation and convex shape properties. Shape-from-shading uses one image and must jointly reason about unknown lighting, albedo, and depth, so it is more ambiguous. Each method needs assumptions stated explicitly.

Reservoir resampling and ReSTIR

Reservoir resampling and ReSTIR

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Reservoir sampling keeps a compact candidate for a weighted distribution without storing every sample. When candidate yiy_i has target weight wiw_i, maintain a running weight sum and replace the stored candidate with probability proportional to wiw_i; the reservoir records enough normalization information to estimate the desired integral without bias under stated assumptions. ReSTIR reuses candidates across pixels and frames, which is valuable when direct lighting has many possible lights or paths but only a few can be evaluated per pixel. Reuse requires correcting for the source and target distributions, accounting for visibility changes, and managing temporal history. If weights or normalization are wrong, the image may be biased; stale reuse causes trails or light leaks when geometry or illumination moves. The method reduces expensive samples rather than making sampling free. It depends on a valid estimator, careful normalization, and an understanding of whether correlated reused samples preserve the intended expectation.

Edge localization and subpixel contours

Edge localization and subpixel contours

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

An edge is a rapid image-intensity change, often associated with a material or depth boundary. Differentiating a noisy image amplifies high-frequency noise, so edge detectors first smooth with a Gaussian-like filter and then compute a gradient. Gradient magnitude estimates edge strength; gradient direction estimates the local normal. Nonmaximum suppression keeps a candidate only if it is a local maximum along that normal, thinning a broad response to a contour. Thresholding and hysteresis connect strong responses through weaker neighboring pixels. Subpixel localization fits a local peak to gradient samples, estimating a contour position between pixel centers. Accuracy depends on sampling, blur, contrast, and the assumed edge profile. This makes edge detection a measurement problem whose output uncertainty should propagate into later line, pose, or shape fitting.

Prerequisites

  • Convolution and filter footprints
  • Sampling aliasing and reconstruction

PDE fields and discrete Laplacians

PDE fields and discrete Laplacians

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A partial differential equation constrains a field through spatial and temporal derivatives. Laplace’s equation Δu=0\Delta u=0 seeks a harmonic field whose value matches its neighborhood average; Poisson’s equation adds a source term. On a regular grid, finite differences produce the five-point stencil with four neighbor weights and a negative center weight. On a triangle mesh, cotangent weights encode angles and a mass matrix normalizes by vertex area. Boundary conditions supply essential data: Dirichlet fixes values, Neumann fixes normal flux, and Robin combines them. Neumann Laplace systems require zero net flux and a pinned value or mean because constants lie in the nullspace. Explicit heat updates have a stability-limited time step; implicit updates solve a sparse system. PDE algorithms separate field representation, spatial operator, boundary conditions, and time integration.

Prerequisites

  • Sampling aliasing and reconstruction
  • Convolution and filter footprints

Used by

  • Worlds, Images and Inference

  • Collision barriers and continuous detection ## Full teaching explanation

A valid finite-element cotangent stiffness can have negative edge weights while retaining nonnegative quadratic energy. Energy contraction, conservation and positivity of the evolving samples are separate requirements. The single-triangle derivation shows the distinction; the heat-step trace gives a negative sample while energy decreases.

Sampling quality: stratification, quasi-Monte Carlo, and blue noise

Sampling quality: stratification, quasi-Monte Carlo, and blue noise

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Sampling quality concerns the arrangement of points across dimensions used by an estimator, not only each coordinate’s one-dimensional histogram. Stratification partitions a domain and allocates points across cells, reducing large gaps for suitable integrands. Quasi-Monte Carlo sequences such as Sobol aim for low discrepancy and often improve integration of smooth, structured functions, though their samples are dependent and error estimates differ from IID Monte Carlo. Blue-noise point sets suppress low-frequency clumping while retaining local separation; they are useful in image sampling and spatial placement but do not automatically minimize every integral’s variance. Scrambling, domain mapping, dimensional ordering, and discontinuities affect performance. Compare methods against a clear target function and measure. The supplied probability narrative introduces stratification and Sobol but not blue-noise constructions; that part is an explicit teaching addition, not a received source claim.

Tensor-product interpolation

Tensor-product interpolation

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Bilinear and trilinear interpolation apply one-dimensional linear weights independently along each coordinate axis. In a rectangular cell, each corner contributes the product of its axis weights; the weights are nonnegative and sum to one for coordinates inside the cell. This preserves the range of scalar corner values, but the interpolated surface can be twisted rather than planar, and derivatives may jump across cell boundaries. For a voxel field, trilinear interpolation provides a continuous in-cell estimate; differentiating it yields a local gradient, which need not have unit length even when samples approximate signed distance. Keep coordinates normalized to the cell and define behavior outside the sampled grid explicitly.

Prerequisites

  • Interpolation versus approximation
  • Sampling aliasing and reconstruction

Optical flow and time to contact

Optical flow and time to contact

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Optical flow is the apparent 2D motion of image features between frames. Under brightness constancy, a tracked point keeps approximately the same intensity as it moves, yielding the constraint Ixu+Iyv+It=0I_xu+I_yv+I_t=0, where spatial derivatives Ix,IyI_x,I_y and temporal derivative ItI_t are measured from the image and (u,v)(u,v) is image velocity. One equation cannot determine two unknown components at a single pixel, so algorithms add neighborhood smoothness, feature tracking, or multiple scales. Flow can reveal camera motion, object motion, and looming. For an object approaching at speed VV, its image size grows at a rate related to depth; the ratio of size to its time derivative estimates time to contact without separately knowing absolute scale under simplifying assumptions. Texture, occlusion, and illumination changes violate brightness constancy.

Prerequisites

  • Spatiotemporal sampling and retinal motion

Template matching and distance transforms

Template matching and distance transforms

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Template matching searches an image for a known pattern by comparing a small reference patch at candidate positions. Sum of squared differences penalizes intensity mismatch; normalized correlation compensates for brightness scale and offset. Direct search costs work proportional to image area times template area, while convolution or Fourier methods can accelerate broad searches. Rotation and scale changes require transforming the template or searching additional parameters. For contour-based matching, a distance transform stores each pixel’s distance to the nearest edge. A template edge point then receives a low cost when it lands near an observed contour even if the exact pixels do not align. The chamfer score sums these distances over template points. These methods suit industrial inspection where the target geometry is known, but need explicit thresholds for occlusion, deformation, and false positives.

Prerequisites

  • Convolution and filter footprints
  • Edge localization and subpixel contours

Contrastive vision and image-language alignment

Contrastive vision and image-language alignment

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Contrastive image-language learning trains an image encoder and a text encoder to place matching descriptions near their images in a shared feature space. For a batch of paired examples, cosine similarities between normalized embeddings form a score matrix; a temperature scales the scores, and an InfoNCE-style cross-entropy treats the matching pair as the positive while other batch items act as negatives. The objective makes retrieval and zero-shot label comparison possible by encoding class names as text. It learns statistical alignment, not a guarantee that every phrase is grounded in the pixels. Batch composition, duplicate or semantically similar negatives, captions, and web-data biases all shape the representation. A model may associate a prompt with correlated context rather than the requested object, and similarity scores are not calibrated probabilities. Evaluation must distinguish retrieval, classification, localization, and reasoning rather than treating one score as general visual understanding.

Multivariate Gaussian distributions and whitening

Multivariate Gaussian distributions and whitening

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

A multivariate Gaussian is determined by a mean vector and a symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance matrix. When the covariance is positive definite, its density is an elliptical bell whose principal directions are covariance eigenvectors. Cholesky factorization maps independent standard-normal samples into correlated samples; whitening applies an inverse factor to express observations in unit-variance coordinates. Singular covariance instead confines the distribution to a lower-dimensional affine subspace and has no ordinary density with respect to full-dimensional volume. Covariance transforms as AΣAᵀ under a linear map and approximately as JΣJᵀ through a nonlinear map near a reference point. These equations support sensor fusion and projected uncertainty, but a Gaussian rendering kernel is not automatically a normalized probability density or epistemic uncertainty model.

  • Expectation, covariance, and dependence
  • Symmetric positive-definite matrices and Cholesky

Nonlinear least squares: Gauss-Newton and Levenberg-Marquardt

Nonlinear least squares: Gauss-Newton and Levenberg-Marquardt

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

Nonlinear least squares minimizes one half the squared norm of a residual vector. Its gradient and Hessian involve the residual Jacobian; the exact Hessian also contains second derivatives of each residual. Gauss–Newton drops those latter terms, producing a positive-semidefinite normal matrix and an efficient local step when residuals are small or the model is close to linear. Levenberg–Marquardt adds damping to control ill-conditioned or overly aggressive steps, blending Gauss–Newton with gradient descent. These algorithms are useful for camera calibration, bundle adjustment, and geometric fitting. Residual scaling, parameter units, rank deficiency, and gauge freedoms influence the solution. Normal equations can square the condition number, so QR or other structured solves may be safer. A small residual does not prove parameters are identifiable or physically correct.

Prerequisites

  • Jacobians, pushforwards, and pullbacks
  • Hessians and local curvature
  • Symmetric positive-definite matrices and Cholesky

Rendering history validity

Rendering history validity

A temporal renderer reuses information from earlier frames only if that information still estimates the same target quantity at the reprojected location. “Previous frame exists” is therefore not enough. History needs a validity contract.

A history sample may become invalid because of:

  • camera cuts or projection changes;
  • resize or dynamic-resolution changes;
  • object transform discontinuities;
  • newly visible or disoccluded surfaces;
  • material or lighting changes;
  • estimator changes such as sample pattern, exposure domain or denoiser configuration;
  • resource reallocation or version replacement.

Reprojection is a hypothesis

Motion vectors or previous transforms propose a correspondence from current sample to previous sample. The renderer should test that hypothesis with available evidence such as depth, normal, object/material identity, velocity magnitude or neighborhood statistics.

A common failure is using a valid coordinate that points to the wrong surface. Bounds checking prevents memory errors, not temporal ghosting.

Versioned history

Treat history like a cache with a key. Relevant state changes advance a version or invalidate specific history resources. The render graph can then express that a temporal pass consumes history version N and produces version N+1.

This is also important for progressive path tracing. Accumulation belongs to a camera/scene/material/light/estimator state. If any target-defining state changes and old samples remain, the output converges to a mixture of different images.

Failure-oriented tests

Useful temporal tests include a hard camera cut, a moving foreground object revealing background, an emissive material changing abruptly, resize, FOV change, jitter-sequence restart, and an object whose ID remains but geometry changes. For each case, record which history samples should survive and why.

The existing render-graph witness proves logical resource dependencies, not temporal validity itself. Native renderer evidence should capture motion/depth/ID buffers and show the acceptance/rejection mask.

Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/Game Engine - From First Frame to Living Worlds#Let a renderer evolve without losing resource ownership.

Related: Temporal reprojection and history validation, Reversed-Z depth contracts.

Render graph barrier lowering

Render graph barrier lowering

A logical render graph and an API synchronization plan are different layers.

The logical graph answers:

  • which pass reads or writes each resource;
  • which hazards create ordering edges;
  • whether the pass dependency graph is acyclic;
  • when a logical resource is first and last used.

API lowering answers:

  • what concrete stage/access state each use requires;
  • what image layout or resource state is required;
  • which subresources are affected;
  • which queue executes each pass;
  • what barrier, semaphore, fence/event, or encoder boundary realizes the dependency.

The repository already has tools/labs/render_graph_contract_lab.cpp for the first layer. That CPU witness proves RAW/WAR/WAW edge construction, deterministic topological order and several invalid-graph cases. It does not prove Vulkan or Metal memory visibility.

State machine per resource version

A practical compiler treats each write as producing a new logical version. A read consumes a particular version. For every concrete resource/subresource, track the last known backend state:

producer pass
queue
stage/access
layout or storage state
version.

When the next use requires an incompatible state, emit a transition whose source scope covers the prior access and whose destination scope covers the next access.

This versioned model prevents an important bug: a pass can read “history texture” while the graph accidentally associates it with the current-frame version rather than the previous-frame version.

Subresource granularity

Whole-resource tracking is simple but can over-synchronize. Independent mip levels, array layers or depth/stencil aspects may be used by different passes. Moving to subresource tracking requires interval/range splitting and merging so that state for mip 0 does not overwrite the state of mip 5.

The first correct implementation should prefer conservative whole-resource barriers over an incorrect fine-grained optimizer. Fine granularity is an optimization after invariants are tested.

Vulkan lowering

For Vulkan synchronization2, a transition record eventually becomes VkBufferMemoryBarrier2, VkImageMemoryBarrier2 or VkMemoryBarrier2 inside VkDependencyInfo, possibly combined with queue submission dependencies.

See Vulkan synchronization2 and resource transitions.

Metal lowering

Metal does not mirror Vulkan’s barrier vocabulary one-for-one. The backend should lower the same logical dependency into Metal’s encoder ordering, resource hazard mode, fences/events where required, and heap/lifetime rules rather than forcing Metal to imitate Vulkan object names.

See Metal heaps memoryless resources and hazards.

Verification ladder

A render-graph compiler should be verified in layers:

  1. dependency graph against a CPU oracle;
  2. resource-state transition plan against hand-written traces;
  3. Vulkan execution with validation enabled;
  4. Metal execution with GPU capture;
  5. cross-backend image/data parity;
  6. transient aliasing stress with deliberately overlapping and non-overlapping lifetimes;
  7. current production-engine integration.

The current branch now has stages 1 and a minimal Vulkan synchronization2 execution/Metal compile boundary. The deeper stages remain explicit rather than implied.

Newton and quasi-Newton optimization

Newton and quasi-Newton optimization

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

Newton’s method builds a local quadratic model of an objective from its gradient and Hessian, then solves for the model’s stationary point. Near a well-conditioned solution with suitable smoothness and curvature, it can converge faster than gradient descent. Away from that regime, the Hessian may be indefinite, poorly scaled, or a poor model over the proposed step. Line searches and trust regions control step acceptance. Quasi-Newton methods such as BFGS estimate curvature from successive parameter and gradient changes, avoiding repeated exact Hessian construction. Their guarantees depend on assumptions and update safeguards. Optimization should monitor objective change, gradient norm, step size, constraints, and numerical failures; a small step alone can indicate stagnation rather than success. The method’s result is a local solution unless global structure proves more.

  • Hessians and local curvature
  • Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics

Random variables and probability laws

Random variables and probability laws

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

A random variable is a measurable mapping from outcomes to numerical values; its probability law describes how those values are distributed. Discrete laws assign probability mass to points, while continuous laws use densities relative to a chosen measure. A cumulative distribution function exists for either kind and records probability accumulated up to a threshold. Mixed distributions can contain both atoms and continuous parts. Density is not probability at an exact point, and it changes with coordinates according to a Jacobian. Expectation integrates a function against the law, whether the variable is represented by a PMF or PDF. These distinctions matter in sampling APIs: returned value, support, endpoint behavior, and reported density must refer to the same measure. A finite computer sampler approximates a continuous law with finitely many representable outputs.

  • Probability spaces, events, and conditioning

Inverse, rejection, and importance sampling

Inverse, rejection, and importance sampling

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Sampling transforms convert simpler random inputs into a target law. Inverse-CDF sampling maps a uniform value through a quantile function; rejection sampling accepts proposal draws according to a bounded target-to-proposal ratio; importance sampling estimates an integral by dividing each sampled integrand by the actual proposal density. Each method requires correct support and endpoint handling. Importance sampling is unbiased when the proposal covers every contributing region and the weighted contribution is integrable; finite variance additionally requires the integral of f²/p to be finite. Rejection sampling needs a valid finite envelope. Discrete floating-point inputs can hit boundaries that have zero probability in an ideal continuous model. Report the density with its measure and use the same measure in the estimator. A proposal that misses target support cannot be repaired by a larger weight.

  • Random variables and probability laws
  • Probability density and change of measure

Directional and total derivatives

Directional and total derivatives

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

A directional derivative measures first-order change along a chosen direction. For a differentiable scalar field, it is the gradient paired with that direction; for a vector map, the Jacobian acts on the direction. The total derivative accounts for every input coordinate changing according to a path, combining partial derivatives with the rates of the coordinates themselves. A direction need not be normalized: normalization changes whether the derivative is per unit distance or per unit parameter. This distinction matters in signed-distance queries, motion paths, and parameterized camera projections. The total derivative clarifies the chain rule: if a state depends on time and an output depends on that state, the time rate is the local derivative composed with the state velocity. These are local statements, not global linearity claims.

Prerequisites

  • Partial derivatives and gradients
  • Derivative as a local linear map

Partial derivatives and gradients

Partial derivatives and gradients

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

For a function of several inputs, a partial derivative varies one coordinate while holding the others fixed. Collecting these derivatives gives the gradient for a scalar-valued function. The gradient is a covector of first-order sensitivities: its pairing with a small displacement predicts the scalar change. Under the Euclidean inner product, the gradient vector points in the direction of steepest ascent, and its negative gives steepest local descent. Coordinate scaling changes derivative magnitudes and can therefore change optimization behavior. A partial derivative is not generally the full effect when inputs move together; that requires the total derivative or directional derivative. In graphics, gradients describe image sensitivity to geometry or material parameters, while their coordinates must be interpreted with the parameter units and basis used by the model.

  • Function contracts: domains, codomains, and images
  • Derivative as a local linear map

Probability spaces, events, and conditioning

Probability spaces, events, and conditioning

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

A probability model consists of a sample space, a collection of measurable events, and a probability measure assigning values to those events. Conditional probability renormalizes the measure within an event of positive probability; Bayes’ theorem reverses conditioning by combining likelihood with prior probability. Independence is a factorization property, not a synonym for disjointness or zero correlation. Conditioning on a zero-probability event cannot use the ordinary ratio directly; continuous models need density-based or regular conditional formulations. This framework keeps possible outcomes separate from distributions placed on them and clarifies what information an experiment provides. A random model can describe a deterministic pseudorandom generator over a distribution of seeds, but one fixed seed produces a fixed sequence. State the event model and conditioning assumptions before interpreting probability as evidence.

Common probability distributions and their assumptions

Common probability distributions and their assumptions

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Distribution families encode different experiment structures. Bernoulli models one binary trial; binomial counts independent trials with the same success probability; uniform assigns constant density or mass over a specified support; Gaussian models a bell-shaped law through mean and covariance; exponential describes memoryless waiting under a constant event rate; Poisson counts events in a fixed exposure under independent, stationary event assumptions. Their formulas are not interchangeable labels: each relies on support and sampling assumptions. Moments summarize center and spread but may fail to exist for heavy-tailed laws. Multivariate Gaussian models also require a symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance, with positive definiteness needed for an ordinary full-dimensional density. Identify the experiment, parameter meanings, and dependence structure before selecting a distribution. The same family can model measurement noise, a prior, or a sampling proposal, which are different roles.

Prerequisites

Off-axis stereo projection and disparity

Off-axis stereo projection and disparity

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11

Definition and mechanism

Stereo cameras use two eye centres separated by a baseline, while each projection frustum is shifted so a chosen zero-parallax plane aligns in the images. Parallel eye orientations with asymmetric frusta avoid the vertical mismatch and discomfort often introduced by toe-in cameras. For rectified pinhole cameras, disparity is approximately Δx=fxB/Z\Delta x=f_xB/Z, so inferred depth is Z=fxB/ΔxZ=f_xB/\Delta x under the calibration and rectification assumptions. Depth uncertainty grows roughly with Z2Z^2 for fixed pixel disparity error. Distinguish interpupillary distance from lens and display-centre spacing; the rendered baseline is an optical/comfort design decision. Use consistent pixel units for focal length, baseline, and disparity before computing metric depth.
