Bounding volume hierarchies

Bounding volume hierarchies

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) organizes primitives into a tree of enclosing boxes. An internal node’s box contains the boxes of its children; a leaf stores a small set of triangles. To trace a ray, test the root box, recurse only into intersected children, and compare triangle hits in reached leaves. A box miss safely rejects every primitive beneath it, so the hierarchy reduces expensive exact tests when geometry is spatially coherent. Construction chooses how to group primitives and where to split; a surface-area heuristic estimates expected traversal work, while simpler median splits are faster to build. Dynamic scenes may refit boxes after deformation or rebuild the hierarchy when overlap grows. Correctness requires every primitive to remain enclosed; performance depends on tree quality and ray distribution.

Prerequisites

  • Ray-triangle intersection
  • Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure

Uniform shuffling without replacement

Uniform shuffling without replacement

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Fisher–Yates generates a uniform permutation by walking from the last array element downward and choosing an index uniformly from the unshuffled prefix. Each permutation has probability 1/n!1/n! if every bounded integer choice is unbiased and the random source meets its assumptions. A common error is to use a random integer routine with modulo bias; another is to draw from the wrong interval and omit permutations. For a fixed input array, test that the output contains every original element once; statistical tests can supplement, but not replace, deterministic checks of bounds and uniqueness. The same primitive supports uniform sample subsets and randomized stratification.

Half-edge mesh connectivity

Half-edge mesh connectivity

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

A half-edge data structure stores each undirected edge as two opposite directed records. Each record points to its twin, the next directed edge around its face, its origin vertex, its edge, and its face; vertices, edges, and faces keep one representative half-edge. Repeatedly following next visits a face boundary. Following twin then next walks around a vertex fan. This makes local neighborhoods and edits proportional to local degree rather than requiring a scan of every face. Correctness depends on invariants: twin of twin returns to the original, a half-edge is not its own twin, and next pointers form closed face cycles. The representation naturally assumes manifold connectivity; it can encode flips, splits, and collapses by changing a bounded set of pointers, but careless updates can break the cycles and corrupt subsequent traversal.

Quadric error mesh simplification

Quadric error mesh simplification

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

Quadric error simplification greedily collapses the edge with the least predicted geometric error. For each triangle plane with unit normal nn and offset dd, form v=(nx,ny,nz,d)Tv=(n_x,n_y,n_z,d)^T and K=vvTK=vv^T. A homogeneous point U=(x,y,z,1)TU=(x,y,z,1)^T has squared point-to-plane error UTKUU^TKU. Sum the matrices of incident planes at each vertex; an edge candidate combines endpoint matrices. Partitioning the combined quadratic gives Q(x)=xTAx+2bTx+cQ(x)=x^TAx+2b^Tx+c, whose stationary point solves Ax=−bAx=-b. If the system is singular or indefinite, test endpoints and midpoint and keep the least-cost candidate. After selecting a location, reject collapses that flip incident face normals. The metric is a local approximation, so topology preconditions and orientation checks remain necessary.

Bézier curves and De Casteljau evaluation

Bézier curves and De Casteljau evaluation

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

A Bézier curve blends control points with Bernstein basis weights. The weights are nonnegative and sum to one on [0,1][0,1], so the curve remains in the control points’ convex hull and reaches its first and last control points at the endpoints. De Casteljau’s repeated linear interpolation evaluates the curve using numerically straightforward convex combinations; the intermediate levels also reveal subdivision geometry. A cubic Bézier’s endpoint tangents depend on its first and last control-polygon edges, so moving a handle changes direction and scale. The convex-hull guarantee applies to the curve parameter interval; extrapolation outside it loses that containment property. Subdivide the curve before tessellation when screen-space curvature changes rapidly; parameter steps alone do not guarantee uniform pixel error.

Cubic Hermite interpolation

Cubic Hermite interpolation

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

A cubic Hermite segment is determined by endpoint values and endpoint tangent data. With normalized t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], its four basis polynomials blend the two endpoint positions and two tangents. Tangents are derivatives with respect to the parameter, so physical-time derivatives must be scaled by segment duration: a velocity in units per second is not interchangeable with a tangent per normalized parameter. Hermite curves are useful when a camera path or animation must pass through known positions while exposing direct control over its entry and exit directions. The endpoint constraints determine one cubic polynomial; continuity between adjacent segments still requires compatible endpoint tangents.

Hough transform and geometric voting

Hough transform and geometric voting

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses

Definition and mechanism

The Hough transform detects a parametric shape by letting each image feature vote for compatible shape parameters. A line can be represented by normal angle θ\theta and signed distance ρ\rho, avoiding the vertical-line singularity of slope-intercept form. Each edge point votes along a curve in (ρ,θ)(\rho,\theta) space; a bin with many votes indicates a line supported by many image points. Circle detection adds center and radius parameters, increasing accumulator dimension and cost. Quantization controls a tradeoff: coarse bins merge nearby hypotheses but reduce precision; fine bins need more votes and memory. Gradient direction can restrict votes and reduce clutter. The transform tolerates missing edge segments because evidence accumulates globally, but unrelated edges can also create peaks, so candidates need geometric validation and robust fitting.

Stateless keyed sampling and reproducibility

Stateless keyed sampling and reproducibility

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

Stateless sampling derives an output from explicit coordinates such as a master seed, pixel, sample index, and dimension. The same key can be recomputed without replaying prior generator calls, which makes debugging and parallel scheduling easier. A hash mixer can provide deterministic, well-dispersed values, but reproducibility does not prove IID behavior or statistical quality. Counter-based generators use designed mixing rounds and can provide stronger parallel-stream properties under their analyzed models. Distinct sampling dimensions reduce accidental reuse, yet a dimension map must remain stable when code changes. Record the key layout, algorithm, version, and conversion to floating point. Test multidimensional patterns and estimator convergence; a good one-dimensional histogram does not establish good joint behavior.

Reversed-Z depth contracts

Reversed-Z depth contracts

A depth buffer stores an ordering coordinate, not Euclidean distance. Reversed-Z changes the mapping so near geometry receives larger depth values and far geometry approaches zero. The precision advantage comes from combining the reciprocal structure of perspective depth with floating-point numbers whose representable values are denser near zero.

The entire renderer has to agree on the convention. Reversing only the projection matrix while keeping old clear/comparison assumptions creates a system that is internally contradictory.

Contract checklist

For a conventional zero-to-one API depth range, a common reversed-Z setup uses:

  • near plane mapped near 1;
  • far distance mapped toward 0;
  • depth buffer cleared to 0;
  • comparison set to GREATER or GREATER_EQUAL;
  • hierarchical depth/occlusion reductions defined consistently with “larger is nearer”;
  • screen-space reconstruction derived from the exact projection convention.

Infinite-far reversed projection can remove an explicit far-plane distance from the perspective matrix, but frustum/culling policy still needs a practical world-space bound when the application cannot process infinite geometry.

Why floating point helps

Perspective depth is approximately affine in 1/z1/z. Conventional mapping spends many floating-point representable values near depth one, where far geometry is crowded. Reversed-Z places far geometry near zero, where floating-point exponent scaling gives much more useful relative spacing.

With integer/fixed-point depth, reversal alone does not create the same dramatic distribution advantage; the floating-point representation is part of the argument.

Reconstruction must use the actual matrix

Do not paste a “linearize depth” formula from another API. Different clip-space ranges, handedness, finite/infinite far planes and reversed mappings change the coefficients.

A robust reconstruction derives camera-space position from the same projection matrix or stores explicit projection parameters and tests known near/far points.

Occlusion and temporal systems

Hierarchical Z, SSAO, SSR, clustered depth slicing, picking and temporal rejection all consume depth meaning. Every reduction or comparison must be audited when the convention changes. A min-reduction hierarchy written for standard depth may need a max-reduction interpretation under reversed-Z.

Tests

Project known camera-space depths, confirm monotonic ordering, quantize them to the real depth format, reconstruct them, and measure relative world-space error over logarithmically spaced distances. Also test clear-value behavior with an empty frame and a near geometry sample.

Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#Give depth an explicit meaning.

Related: Hardware depth-buffer linearization, Rendering history validity.

Metal heaps memoryless resources and hazards

Metal heaps, memoryless resources, and hazards

Metal exposes several resource-lifetime tools that matter directly to an engine render graph. Their purpose is not just API convenience; they let the engine state when storage must exist, when bytes may be reused, and who is responsible for synchronization.

Apple documents MTLHeap as a way to create resources from a larger allocation and to alias memory among resources whose lifetimes do not overlap. Apple also documents memoryless textures for temporary render targets whose contents can remain in tile memory rather than occupying ordinary persistent system/GPU memory.

Primary references: - https://developer.apple.com/documentation/metal/memory-heaps - https://developer.apple.com/documentation/metal/reducing-the-memory-footprint-of-metal-apps

Heap aliasing is a lifetime proof

If resources A and B use overlapping heap memory, the engine must prove that A is dead before B begins using the same bytes. “They are in different render passes” is not enough when command encoding/execution overlap or when a resource is consumed asynchronously later.

A render graph can perform interval analysis:

A lifetime = [first use, last use]
B lifetime = [first use, last use].

Only non-overlapping lifetimes are candidates for aliasing, and compatibility constraints such as size/alignment/storage mode still apply.

The allocator also needs to keep the heap itself alive for every resource created from it.

Hazard tracking mode

Metal heap resources can use tracked or untracked hazard behavior. Apple’s heap documentation explicitly notes that Metal synchronizes heap-created resources when their hazard tracking mode is tracked. Choosing untracked mode transfers more responsibility to the application. That decision should therefore exist in the backend state model rather than being an incidental resource flag.

Memoryless attachments

Memoryless texture storage is suited to temporary render-target contents that do not need to survive beyond the render-pass/tile use for which they are created. A later pass that samples the image needs persistent storage; marking such a resource memoryless would contradict the data-flow graph.

The render graph can infer memoryless eligibility only after it understands whether the produced contents escape the render-pass lifetime.

Argument buffers and residency

Argument buffers can reduce CPU binding overhead and can reference many resources. That also makes lifetime/residency reasoning more indirect: the resource referenced by an argument buffer must remain valid for the encoded GPU work even if the CPU-side wrapper is no longer visible.

Current evidence

tools/native/metal_compile_smoke.metal is compiled to AIR and metallib on the macOS CI job. This proves that the repository owns a real MSL compile boundary instead of only pseudocode.

Compile success is not GPU execution evidence. It does not prove heap aliasing, tracked/untracked hazard behavior, memoryless attachment correctness, argument-buffer residency, command-buffer timing or Apple-GPU performance. Those require a Metal execution/capture on suitable hardware.

Related: GPU workgroups and synchronization, Render graph barrier lowering, Interface contracts and publication.

Stateful pseudorandom generators and stream state

Stateful pseudorandom generators and stream state

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10

Definition and mechanism

A pseudorandom-number generator is a deterministic state transition plus an output rule. With a fixed engine, seed, and call order, its integer sequence is reproducible; it is not a source of mathematical independence by itself. Linear congruential generators are compact but have lattice and low-bit structure that can make multidimensional samples poor. Larger-state engines trade memory for period and other statistical properties. Parallel programs need an explicit stream strategy: shared state couples samples to thread scheduling, while copied seeds can duplicate streams. Reproducibility requires recording algorithm version, state, seed derivation, distribution mapping, and sampling order. Standard-library distributions may not yield identical transformed sequences across implementations. Simulation generators are not cryptographically secure unless specifically designed for that purpose.

Function contracts: domains, codomains, and images

Function contracts: domains, codomains, and images

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

A function is a rule that assigns exactly one output to every allowed input. Its domain states which inputs are valid; its codomain states the declared output set; its image is the subset actually reached. These sets affect whether an inverse exists and whether a formula is defined at a boundary. For example, squaring maps the real line into nonnegative outputs but is not one-to-one until its domain is restricted to nonnegative values. In a camera map, division by depth makes zero depth invalid, while a positive-forward convention further restricts visible points. Treating these as contracts makes composition safer: the output of one function must lie in the next function’s domain. A typed implementation can encode some, but not all, of these mathematical restrictions.

Differentiation rules and chain rule

Differentiation rules and chain rule

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

Differentiation rules let us build derivatives from simpler functions. Linearity handles sums and constant factors; the product and quotient rules account for both factors changing; the chain rule handles nested mappings. For a composition, the derivative of the outer function is evaluated at the inner output and multiplied by the derivative of the inner function. In multiple dimensions, this becomes matrix multiplication of Jacobians in composition order. Elementary rules for powers, exponentials, logarithms, trigonometric functions, and inverse trigonometric functions follow from limits and implicit relations. These rules are the local sensitivity algebra used by automatic differentiation and gradient-based fitting. Each rule has a domain: quotient denominators must be nonzero, logarithms require positive arguments, and inverse trigonometric derivatives can become singular at boundary values.

Limits and continuity

Limits and continuity

Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9

Definition and mechanism

A limit describes the value a function approaches as its input approaches a point, even when the function is undefined or assigned a different value there. Continuity at a point adds the requirement that the function value equal that limit. Epsilon-delta language makes this precise: every requested output tolerance can be met by choosing a sufficiently small input neighborhood. Continuity rules out finite jumps but does not guarantee a derivative; the absolute-value function is continuous at zero yet has a corner there. Limits expose removable singularities such as a cancelled factor, while one-sided limits reveal boundaries and discontinuities. In numerical software, local smoothness matters because derivative-based approximations rely on nearby inputs producing controlled output changes. Domain restrictions, branch conditions, and singular denominators must be checked before applying derivative formulas.

How to use this desk

Cover the visual, sketch it from memory, answer the numbered prompts, then expand the answer key. Score each prompt 0 (missing/wrong), 1 (correct label but weak explanation), or 2 (can reconstruct an example and its limits). Revisit weak prompts in the linked teaching section. Do not turn recognition of a diagram into a mastery claim.

Mermaid shows relationships; byte strips show placement; tables show exact distinctions; state/sequence diagrams show what changes over time. Diagrams are conceptual models, not fixed CPU/OS layouts. Answer keys use collapsible Obsidian callouts.

Short-form recall — the whole route

Pattern is not meaning. A representation contract assigns weights and interpretation. → Bits become decisions. Masks select fields; packing needs widths, ranges, and a policy. → Arithmetic is finite. Choose wrap, saturation, rejection, or widening before calculation. → Real values use a ruler. Floating point trades spacing against range; fixed point chooses a scale. → Operations expose error. Rounding, cancellation, conditioning, and reproducibility matter. → Keep the needed information. Quantization/codebooks spend precision deliberately. → Bytes occupy places. Alignment, lifetime, ownership, and virtual mapping are distinct. → Files are agreements. Define schema, validate lengths, then decode and check integrity.

[!answer]- Reveal 1–3 Noise margin tolerates disturbances within a logical range. A bit has two logical states; octet means exactly eight bits; C++ byte has CHAR_BIT bits and sizeof(char)=1. A word is architecture-specific; a character can need multiple bytes. Historical byte sizes varied.

Low mask L=2w−1L=2^w-1, positioned mask M=L2sM=L2^s. Extract is right-shift then AND L; insert clears M and ORs the shifted valid field. Any tests nonzero; all compares with the whole mask. Use independent golden bytes, preservation/range checks and boundary/invalid cases: encoder and decoder can share one bug.

Integer division truncates toward zero (−1); arithmetic right shift rounds downward (−2). Promotions determine the operation width, including the width of NOT; a narrow stored type does not force a narrow expression.

3 - The adder is simple; the policy is not

Repair finite arithmetic · Full adder · Arithmetic policies

flowchart LR
    A["A, B, carry-in"] --> S["Sum = three-way XOR"]
    A --> C["Carry-out = majority"]
    C --> N["Next full adder"]
    C --> U
    S --> R["Low N result bits"]
    R --> U["Unsigned carry or borrow question"]
    R --> V["Signed representability question"]
Calculation Exact/wide result Eight-bit destination policy
250+20 270 Wrap14 / saturate255 / reject
127+1 128 Signed eight-bit overflow; no legal wrapping assumption
0−1 unsigned −1 mathematically Residue255
13×11 13+26+104 143
13÷3 13=4(3)+113=4(3)+1 Quotient4, remainder1 
stored type → promotion → common operation type → calculation → destination conversion

signed overflow    must be prevented BEFORE evaluating the expression

Recall

  1. Derive a half adder, add carry-in, and explain ripple delay versus generate/propagate carry networks. Distinguish carry, overflow, negative and zero flags.
  2. Rebuild shift-and-add multiplication and long division. What intermediate width and invalid inputs must be handled?
  3. Choose wrap/saturate/reject/widen for a counter, image sample and size calculation. Why can saturation break associativity?
  4. Explain signed minimum/−1, unsigned reverse-loop failure, plain-char signedness, exact/least/fast widths, and mixed-sign comparisons.

[!answer]- Reveal 7–10 Half-adder sum=A XOR B, carry=A AND B. Full-adder carry is true when at least two of its three inputs are true. Ripple chains carry dependencies; prefix designs combine generate/propagate information. Carry answers an unsigned question; overflow a signed-range question; N observes a result sign bit; Z observes all-zero result. Borrow conventions vary: binary6502 SBC uses A−B−(1−C), with C=1 meaning no borrow.

Set multiplier bits select shifted partial products. Division shifts bits into a remainder, conditionally subtracts, and satisfies D=Qd+R with0≤R<d. Prove partial/intermediate ranges. Reject division by0 and same-type signed-min/−1.

Policies follow meaning: bounded samples may clamp, modular counters may wrap, sizes usually need checked arithmetic. Signed overflow remains undefined behavior; widening after the overflowing expression is too late. Saturation and capped updates are order-dependent.

An unsigned i≥0 never terminates a reverse loop. char signedness varies; exact-width aliases are optional, least/fast may be wider. Promotions/common-type conversions can turn a negative operand into a large unsigned value. Track all five stages, not only storage width.

Repair floating representation · IEEE-754 floating point

binary32: [ sign:1 ][ stored exponent:8 ][ fraction:23 ]  normal precision24
binary64: [ sign:1 ][ stored exponent:11][ fraction:52 ]  normal precision53

x=(−1)S(1+F/223)2E−127. x=(-1)^S(1+F/2^{23})2^{E-127}.

Here S is sign0/1, E stored exponent, F the unsigned23-bit fraction. Subnormal value is (−1)SF2−149(-1)^SF2^{-149}.

Visual checkpoint Reconstruct
10.625 1.0101012×231.010101_2\times2^3 → word412A0000
C1540000 Sign1, exponent130, significand1.65625 → −13.25
Above1 binary32 spacing 2−232^{-23}

Recall

  1. Decode the class before the normal formula. Why do +0 and −0 compare equal but differ as representations?
  2. Reconstruct both words above and explain bias127/1023 and hidden precision24/53.
  3. Distinguish epsilon, min-normal, min-subnormal and local ULP. Explain guard/round/sticky and all four rounding directions.

[!answer]- Reveal 11–13 Reserved exponent fields alter the interpretation. Zero has E=F=0 and a separate sign; infinities have all-one E,F=0; NaNs have all-one E,F≠0. Signed-zero reciprocals can differ under IEEE behavior; signbit sees the sign even when x<0 does not. NaN comparisons are unordered; payload/signaling behavior needs a declared policy.

Normal exponent is E−bias and significand is1+F/2^fractionBits. Subnormals remove the hidden one and keep a fixed tiny grid. A C++ float is not universally required to be binary32.

Epsilon is spacing above1, not a universal comparison tolerance. Binary32 min-normal=2−1262^{-126}; min-subnormal=2−1492^{-149}. Normal binade exponent e gives step 2e−232^{e-23}. Guard/round/sticky summarize discarded information. Nearest-even picks the even retained significand at an exact tie; upward/downward/toward-zero are signed directions. Check and restore runtime rounding state.

5 - Follow the rounding points, not algebra alone

Repair numerical reasoning · Cancellation and loss of significance · Numerical reproducibility

flowchart LR
    A["Inputs<br/>Intended to stored"] --> B["Evaluation<br/>Order and rounding or FMA"]
    B --> C["Output<br/>Stored result"]
    C --> D["Decision<br/>Tolerance and conditioning"]
Witness What it exposes
0.1 Reduced denominator10 is not a power of two: repeating binary fraction
binary32 224+12^{24}+1 Nearest-even stores 2242^{24}: absorption
Nearby stored x−y Subtraction can be exact while intended inputs remain uncertain
min-normal/2 Exact subnormal is not automatically an underflow flag
FMA versus multiply then add One final rounding versus two rounding points
Atomic floating sum Race-free update does not fix update order

Recall

  1. When does a rational terminate in binary? Why can cancellation magnify relative input error even when subtraction itself is exact?
  2. Classify overflow, tiny exact results, tiny inexact results, invalid operations and division-by-zero flags.
  3. Distinguish absolute/relative and forward/backward error; stability versus conditioning. Why is approximate closeness not equality?
  4. Draw factored/distributed and FMA/unfused evaluation graphs. What do pairwise/compensated sums, wider accumulation and fixed order solve—and not solve?

[!answer]- Reveal 14–17 A reduced rational terminates iff its denominator is a power of two. Sterbenz’s nearby-float condition x/2≤y≤2x for nonnegative stored values can give exact subtraction under the stated gradual-underflow conditions. A small difference can still expose earlier input uncertainty; sensitivity scales with (|x|+|y|)/|x−y|.

Tiny and underflow are not synonyms. Flags also include inexact, overflow, divide-by-zero and invalid; classify the actual operation/environment.

Absolute error has units; relative error needs a nonzero reference. Forward error measures output discrepancy; backward error asks how perturbed inputs explain the output. Conditioning belongs to the problem, stability to the algorithm. Validate tolerances and non-finite inputs first; pairwise closeness need not be transitive.

FMA rounds ab+c once; unfused arithmetic rounds the product too. Reassociation/distribution move rounding points. Pairwise and compensated algorithms can reduce error but do not reconstruct lost input bits or guarantee identical cross-platform execution. Wider transient arithmetic does not preserve a repeatedly narrowed state. Determinism needs order, precision, compiler/environment and algorithm contracts; capped TSDF-style weighted updates can remain history-dependent mathematically.

fixed F=8:    1.5 → raw384     2.25 → raw576

Recall

  1. Choose F for a signed32-bit fixed domain ±10^6 with step≤0.001. Derive multiply/divide rescaling and nearest unclipped error.
  2. Encode1.5 in FP16; compare FP16/BF16 near1 and at large magnitude. Why can truncating a NaN payload accidentally produce infinity?
  3. Explain affine q/z/scale, outlier effects, group metadata, learned one-bit centroids, RMSE/MAE and normalized graphics/color-space distinctions.

[!answer]- Reveal 18–20 Require 2−F≤0.0012^{-F}\le0.001 and 1062F≤231−110^6 2^F\le2^{31}-1: F=10 or11. Multiply raw operands at scale S² then round AB/S; quotient rounds AS/B for B≠0. Prove intermediate capacity before calculating, check destination range, and define negative ties. Nearest unclipped error≤1/(2S); relative error can explode nearzero.

FP16 1.5→3E00; bias15, normal min2^-14, subnormal min2^-24. BF16 bias127, normal spacing above1 is2^-7 versus FP16’s2^-10. Dropping a nonzero discarded NaN fraction can leave all-one exponent and zero fraction: infinity. Classify first; canonicalization is a policy.

Affine reconstruction is scale×(q−z), with positive valid scale; nearest unclipped ideal error≤scale/2. A max-absolute outlier can erase small values. INT4 payload costs ceil(N/2)+4ceil(N/G) bytes with float32 scales, not four bits/value universally. At N=5,G=32 it costs7 bytes. One-bit labels can select learned means rather than±1. RMSE squares errors; MAE takes magnitudes; neither proves application quality. UNORM is not sRGB; quantized normals may need safe renormalization and still lose direction.

7 - Placement, translation and lifetime are separate

Repair memory reasoning · Endianness · Alignment and padding · Page tables and MMU

offset 0: [a][pad][pad][pad][b b b b][c][tail][tail][tail]
member offsets0,4,8; size12; alignment4; array stride12

    A["Virtual address plus process context"] --> B["Split page number and offset"]
    B --> C{"TLB translation available?"}
    C -->|Yes| D["Check permitted mapping"]
    C -->|No| E["Walk page tables"]

stateDiagram-v2
    state "Storage available" as StorageAvailable
    state "Live object" as LiveObject
    state "Lifetime ended" as LifetimeEnded
    state "Storage released" as StorageReleased

Recall

  1. Why does swapping bytes not reverse bits? Derive aligned offsets and tail padding; compare packing, reordering, AoS/SoA and CPU/GPU layouts.
  2. Reconstruct the address translation. Distinguish process isolation, shared mappings, TLB/data-cache misses, faults, COW, virtual/physical contiguity and huge-page tradeoffs.
  3. Separate stack/heap/static regions from storage duration and object lifetime. Explain fragmentation, dangling views, mapped files, const, W^X and ASLR.

[!answer]- Reveal 21–23 Endianness orders significance bytes, not bits within an octet. Align each member under stated ABI requirements; round total extent for aligned array stride. Reordering can reduce holes but change ABI. Packing may misalign; smaller is not automatically faster. AoS groups records, SoA fields; hot access patterns and backend layout contracts decide.

For page size P, VPN=floor(VA/P), offset=VA mod P; PA=PFN×P+offset. Context/permissions matter. TLB caches translations; data cache caches contents. COW copies a shared backing page when a permitted write needs a private copy. Consecutive virtual pages may use scattered frames. Larger pages increase simplified TLB reach entries×pageSize but reduce granularity/flexibility.

Automatic objects often use stack frames, but optimization/ABI can differ; heap allocation manages variable-lifetime blocks. Static duration can still need runtime initialization. Internal fragmentation is allocated slack; external fragmentation is separated holes. A span does not own/extend backing life. A mapped file needs bounds, permissions and access/lifetime validity. const does not force a read-only segment; W^X concerns mapping permissions; ASLR varies locations. Old bytes do not prove a live object.

Recall

  1. State bit-cast preconditions; distinguish native ABI from external schema. Give safe multiplication and range checks before parsing.
  2. Explain checksum blind spots, specified CRC parameters, hash collisions, authenticity and durability. Decode the mini-dump below.

[!answer]- Reveal 24–25 Bit-cast needs same size, trivially copyable types and valid initialized representations under the applicable rules. It is not numeric conversion, endian conversion or permission for arbitrary typed access.

Before unsigned a×b check a=0 or b≤MAX/a. Before reading n bytes at o in length L, check o≤L then n≤L−o. Check header≤length, exact payload length, size_t representability and practical resource limits before allocation.

Additive byte sums miss reorderings. A CRC needs polynomial, initial/final operations, reflection/order and covered range. CRC-32/ISO-HDLC check string123456789 gives CBF43926. Finite digests necessarily have collisions over unrestricted messages. A hostile replacement requires trusted digest/key policy; valid decoding, integrity, authenticity, publication and durability are different claims.

Magic, dimensions and file length can remain plausible; structural validation alone misses this substitution. This is a teaching schema, not a freshly verified production format.

02 - C++ - Objects, Ownership and Lifetime - Visual Recall

C++: Objects, Ownership and Lifetime — Visual Recall

Scope: Companion to Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs. A compact teaching board, not a substitute for the worked chapter. Draw each model from memory; explain every arrow and state its preconditions.

One-page short notes

Story stop Shortest useful note Open the explanation / figure
Build Translation makes declarations visible, definitions executable, and linking joins program pieces. Build pipeline · Modules
Object Storage is the place; lifetime is the interval; identity is the occupant. Same address does not promise same object. Storage/object figure · Generation handle
Borrow A pointer/reference/view grants access, not ownership. Validity depends on the referent, lifetime, mutation, and invalidation contract. Borrow hazards · Deferred views
Value Construction creates; assignment replaces; move may transfer responsibility while source remains alive. Rule of Zero composes tested owners. Construction/destruction · Rule of Zero
Resource RAII binds cleanup to an owner lifetime; external users may require deferred release. Four-lifetime figure and full story
Smart owner unique_ptr = one duty; shared_ptr = shared lifetime; weak_ptr = observe, then lock() to try. Shared ownership does not synchronize the pointee. Exclusive ownership · Shared ownership · Weak observation
Raw storage Allocation obtains bytes; construction starts an object; destruction ends its life; deallocation returns bytes. Placement construction does not allocate. Allocation versus construction · Placement/lifetime figure

Board in one breath: source → object → borrow/owner → value transfer → RAII cleanup → safe external reclamation. At every arrow ask: who owns it, how long is it valid, and what ends use?

The notes above target a single landscape page when rendered at ordinary study-note scale. The diagrams and answer keys below remain the linked detail, not required reading for every review pass.

One story: from source text to responsibly released resource

flowchart LR
    A["Build: translate + link"] --> B["Objects: storage + lifetime"]
    B --> C["Access: borrow or own"] --> D["Transfer: copy or move"]
    D --> E["RAII release protocol"] --> F["Reclaim after external completion"]

Caption: Resource safety starts with the object model but ends only when the external-use contract permits release. A C++ destructor is not a GPU completion fence.

Four figure briefs

Use one row as a small revision card. Open its figure to see the caption and the surrounding worked example. The four cards supplement the existing notes and ownership boards.

Card Short note Figure and explanation Check yourself
Build Declare to compile a call; supply the definition to link it. Header guards act inside one translation unit. CPP-01 · two build lanes Why can a call compile yet fail at link time?
Borrow Reallocation can dangle a path; slot assignment can keep it live while changing the entity. Validate, then reacquire. CPP-02 · lifetime versus identity Can the same address still reach the wrong entity?
Move Construction creates a destination; a move operation may transfer duty. The source remains alive under its type’s contract. CPP-03 · two live objects, one duty Why does std::move(x) alone release nothing?
GPU release RAII triggers the selected cleanup protocol; GPU completion governs when native release is safe. CPP-04 · deferred reclamation Which owner keeps the device and pending release queue alive?

Answers: translation sees a usable declaration but linking still needs the definition; yes, semantic invalidation can preserve a live slot; std::move changes expression category and requires a consuming operation; the renderer must explicitly own the queue/device until all pending duties complete.

Ownership decision board

flowchart LR
    Q{Who must keep this alive?}
    Q -- no ownership transfer --> B[Borrow: T& / T* / view]
    Q -- exactly one owner --> U[std::unique_ptr or domain owner]
    Q -- multiple independent owners --> S[std::shared_ptr]
    S --> W{Observer must extend lifetime?}
    W -- no --> WP[std::weak_ptr; lock to try]
    W -- yes --> S

Caption: Pick semantics first, syntax second. A raw pointer usually borrows; it does not extend lifetime. Shared ownership is a relationship, not a generic safety upgrade.

Need Recall Common trap
Borrow briefly T&, T*, span Caller must preserve lifetime and validity.

RAII: move cleanup from branches into scope

sequenceDiagram
    participant F as Function
    participant O as RAII owner
    participant R as Resource
    F->>R: acquire
    R-->>F: handle
    F->>O: immediately adopt handle
    alt normal return
        F->>O: scope ends
    else early return or exception
        F->>O: scope unwinds
    end
    O->>R: matching release exactly once

Caption: Partial construction is safe only for responsibilities already held by fully constructed members/guards. A naked raw handle between acquire and adoption is a leak window.

Storage, object and occupant are different states

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> StorageReserved
    StorageReserved --> ObjectAAlive: construct A / construct_at
    ObjectAAlive --> StorageReserved: destroy A / destroy_at
    StorageReserved --> ObjectBAlive: construct B in same suitable storage
    ObjectBAlive --> StorageReserved: destroy B
    StorageReserved --> StorageReleased: allocator releases bytes
    StorageReleased --> [*]

Caption: Destroying an occupant does not necessarily free its storage. Same address does not mean same object. Correct alignment, size, construction, destruction and replacement rules still apply; std::launder does not construct or revive anything.

The four questions to ask at a resource boundary

Layer Ask Example
Storage Which bytes, with what size/alignment? Arena slot large and aligned enough for Widget.
Object Which live typed occupant? Widget has completed construction.
Ownership Who ends its lifetime/releases the handle? Move-only GpuBuffer owner.
External use When is reclamation safe? GPU completion fence/timeline.

Retrieval prompts

  1. Why can a stack object own heap or GPU resources?
  2. What does RAII automate, and what release timing must a GPU wrapper still know?
  3. Why is shared_ptr copying not a synchronization policy for the pointed-to object?
  4. Why does weak_ptr::lock() give a stronger test than checking expired() first?
  5. How can a weak_ptr keep control-block storage allocated after object destruction?
  6. What is the difference among new T, ::operator new, construct_at, destroy_at, and deallocation?
  7. Why does unique_ptr<Derived> converting to unique_ptr<Base> require a correct base destruction contract?
  8. What exactly does std::launder not do?

[!answer]- Compact key Scope-based owners run cleanup on normal exit and unwinding. External completion is a separate condition. Shared-pointer thread safety concerns ownership bookkeeping, not arbitrary pointee mutation. lock() atomically attempts to obtain a strong owner. Weak observers can keep the control block, but not the managed object’s lifetime, alive. A new-expression combines storage allocation and initialization; allocation functions alone only acquire storage; construction starts an object lifetime; destruction ends it; deallocation returns storage. Base deletion needs a valid virtual destructor or a deleter retaining the concrete type. launder can obtain a pointer to an already-live object only under its rules; it is no general repair tool.

Teach the full ownership story · Part coverage · Dependency Map

Added retrieval prompt

Borrow: T& or const T&. Consume: unique_ptr<T> by value. Retain shared lifetime: shared_ptr<T> by value. Borrow an existing shared handle: const shared_ptr<T>& only for that call. Use a matching deleter for non-memory resources. Rebuild the API lab.

Requests and replaceable backends — M011 retrieval experiment

A renderer’s command is one of several known shapes; the runtime backend is one implementation of a common contract. These are two different decisions, so redraw the story without looking: command value → active alternative → borrowed submit call → virtual override → checked visitor → logical result → correctly destroyed owner. Then explain what remains separate from the story: the GPU’s completion and native-resource release rules.

From memory, reconstruct the situation What the answer must account for
Why can a union’s storage not be treated as several simultaneously live objects? One active member and the correct lifetime transitions; a byte pattern is not a type tag.
How does a request prove its form? variant discriminant, checked get_if / visit, and possible exceptional valueless state.
Why does a base reference call the derived implementation but a copied base value not preserve it? Static type, dynamic type, subobjects, virtual dispatch and slicing.
Why is the interface destructor virtual? Destruction through an owning base pointer must reach the derived destructor; external GPU use has its own completion rule.
What does a diamond with a virtual common base mean? Two inheritance paths reach one most-derived common-base subobject, not a mandated memory offset.
What can each cast prove? static_cast follows a statically permitted conversion; dynamic_cast can runtime-check polymorphic relationships; reinterpret_cast does not create objects; const_cast does not legalize writing to genuinely const storage.
Why must two handles with the same slot but different generations compare unequal? Identity includes the occupant generation; equality still does not prove current liveness.
Why does the overridden reserve body see 2 through a base view but 7 through a derived view? Default argument from static type; virtual body from dynamic type.
Can <=> always produce a total order? Integer ID fields can support strong ordering; NaN yields unordered floating comparisons and demands an explicit container key policy.
Can we claim this is the fastest dispatch architecture? No: compare allocation, memory layout, branch behavior and optimizer effects on the same workload.

Blank-file reconstruction: Recreate Clear, DrawMesh, Upload, Request, Backend and CountingBackend with a single exclusive owner; verify command counts, derived destructor execution, failed runtime cast, slicing, shared virtual base, generation-aware equality, NaN’s unordered comparison, overload selection and static default-argument binding. Full code and the checked build command are in the M011 C++20 laboratory; complete derivations and failure explanations are in the continuous narrative. Do not infer Kairo or GPU execution from this standalone test.

One request, one transaction, callbacks that may outlive their caller — M012 reconstruction

Read the complete M012 narrative only after attempting this recall route. The important picture begins with an editor requesting a resource and ends with either a fully published asset or the original published store unchanged.

flowchart LR
    U["Upload request: bytes, label"] --> V["Validate units, format and bounds"]
    V --> P["Privately acquire and prepare"]
    P --> C{"Preparation succeeds?"}
    C -->|no| R["Unwind owners; typed failure"]
    C -->|yes| S["Commit complete AssetRecord"]
    S --> N["Notify only under safe callback lifetime"]

The first thing to reconstruct is why each arrow is necessary. The request’s count must be distinct from an asset index, because identical raw integer types do not carry the same domain meaning. The file must be decoded as checked bytes, not by assuming any pointer cast creates a live WireHeader. Preparation must be private because callbacks or render systems must never observe half-constructed state. Every acquired handle must have one owner before a throwing operation can intervene. Publication needs a precise boundary: an exception before the commit must not modify existing records under the stated guarantee; a callback that throws afterward is a different event requiring its own policy.

Reconstruction question Minimum evidence the reader must produce
Why is a raw std::size_t a dangerous API for bytes? Show accidental unit mixing; write explicit ByteCount with explicit conversion back.
Can a function pointer close over a local variable? No: a plain pointer carries a callable identity; extra state needs a context, whose lifetime is separately guaranteed.
Why is a member-function pointer not an ordinary callback address? Explain the required instance and demonstrate object.*member invocation.
What does a functor or lambda actually store? Draw state fields or references; contrast capture of an integer, pointer, view and this.
How do value and reference captures differ after mutation? Predict snapshot 10 and live view 20; explain why a deferred reference may dangle.
What changes when a lambda is stored in std::function? Type erasure, copyable target, possible storage cost, empty-call error; no guaranteed inline capacity.
Which exceptions cause cleanup, and what cannot be rolled back? Distinguish stack unwinding/local RAII from preexisting external side effects.
What are the basic, strong and no-throw guarantees? State valid-but-changed, unchanged observable state, and non-escaping exceptions; give each an example.
Why must the native resource move be non-throwing? Trace vector growth, element relocation, and the relevant strong-guarantee conditions.
Why can’t input validation live only in assert? NDEBUG can remove it; show typed invalid-input errors separately from programmer invariant failures.
What do bit_cast and trivially copyable prove? A constrained representation-value operation, not a portable six-byte disk schema.
Why is a typed pointer into an arbitrary file unsafe? Length, alignment, lifetime, alias rules, endian and padding are independent checks.
How do we demonstrate rollback? Reproduce counts: (0,0,0), (1,1,0), (1,2,1), (2,3,1), then 0 live at destruction.

Blank-file laboratory: Rebuild ByteCount; the fake device; the move-only Resource; the private AssetRecord; AssetStore::upload returning a typed result; function/member/functor callbacks; value/reference and owning-lifetime lambda captures; and a six-byte little-endian serializer. Compile under C++20 and warnings as errors, execute the deliberate failure after handle acquisition, then repeat under -DNDEBUG. The tested reference and exact commands are in the M012 lab and the source/evidence record. Do not classify this exercise as complete learner mastery until it can be reconstructed and explained independently.

One asset pipeline, many types — M013 retrieval

The preceding recall exercise ended with a safe, published asset. Now the editor wants the same preparation and publication guarantees for meshes, textures with different channel counts, and shader records. We must avoid duplicating stores without erasing type safety. Redraw this path from memory, then justify every boundary rather than reciting template vocabulary:

flowchart LR
  A["Mesh / Texture / CheckedShader"] --> B{"Uploadable<T> satisfied?"}
  B -->|no| X["Constrained API unavailable at compile time"]
  B -->|yes| T["AssetTraits<T> selects size policy"]
  T --> F["Args&&... + std::forward preserve caller's argument category"]
  F --> C{"Construct next unpublished slot"}
  C -->|throws| R["Published prefix unchanged"]
  C -->|succeeds| P["Increment published count; AssetId returned"]
  P --> S["Checked heterogeneous batch accounting"]

Imagine one Mesh containing three unsigned indices, one Texture<4> containing twelve texels, and one Texture<3> containing five texels. Explain why a trait gives 12, 48 and 15 source bytes, then derive why the checked batch accumulator returns 75. Show why a bound such as texel_count > max/Channels must be checked before multiplication. Finally explain why none of these counts establishes the actual GPU allocation size.

Now reconstruct the implementation without opening the reference. Start with template<class T> function-template deduction. Build template<class T, size_t Capacity> with fixed optional slots and explain why the non-type capacity changes the class specialization. Provide the full AssetTraits<Mesh> specialization and the partial AssetTraits<Texture<Channels>> specialization, then contrast class-template specialization with function overloading. Derive U& & → U&, U& && → U&, U&& & → U&, and U&& && → U&&. Use those results to show why meshes.emplace(input) makes a copy while meshes.emplace(std::move(input)) selects a move path; do not assume the moved-from vector must be empty.

The next reconstruction must connect a heterogeneous parameter pack to a checked fold. Show what happens for zero arguments and why a fold’s grouping is not itself a universal left-to-right side-effect guarantee. Then implement the earlier std::void_t SFINAE detection pattern and a clearer Uploadable concept with compound requirements. State exactly what a requires expression checks and what it does not execute. Constrain emplace with std::constructible_from and show why the overload route(const T&) selects the constrained path for supported assets and the generic fallback for UnknownAsset.

Finally prove publication. If the published count is c, slots [0,c) are live and slots [c,Capacity) are empty. When the constructor throws in slot c, the count is not incremented. Reconstruct the deliberately failed CheckedShader(-1) attempt and show why the previously published version 3 remains valid and version 4 can use the next slot. Explain what would break if we supported deletion, stored raw references after the depot’s lifetime, invoked the API concurrently or replaced the CPU-only record with an asynchronously used GPU buffer without retirement bookkeeping.

Evidence and full explanation: the M013 narrative, the tested C++20 laboratory and the 16-part coverage map. The test checks representative semantics, not the learner’s independent ability to reconstruct these decisions or current Kairo implementation details.

The tile planner makes a choice — M014 reconstruction

This recall path belongs after the full M014 narrative and the C++20 lab. Its purpose is to rebuild the decision chain from memory, not to duplicate an encyclopedia of template keywords.

Picture one 8×2 RGBA texture tile, a budget of 64 bytes, a 64-byte CPU buffer, and a counting recorder. Before the renderer tries to use it, the planning layer must establish what is known from the type and what still depends on the incoming data. Draw this path, then explain each transition and its failure condition:

flowchart LR
    A["PixelFormat chosen in type"] --> B["PixelTraits: channels as compile-time value"]
    B --> C["checked width × height × channels"]
    C --> D{"Policy budget allows bytes?"}
    D -->|no| R["Reject; recorder unchanged"]
    D -->|yes| E{"Payload tag"}
    E -->|Verify| F["Require exact source span length"]
    E -->|Metadata only| G["Mark plan, not ready resource"]
    F --> H["Alpha branch + Morton table"]
    G --> H
    H --> I["CRTP recorder accepts plan"]

A correct reconstruction should derive (8=64) bytes from the uncompressed source representation, then explain why (8=96) fails the budget. It should show why a 4×4 RGBA request with no buffer fails only when the verification tag demands a real payload. The metadata-only 4×4 RGB path may report 48 planned bytes, but it has not proved any upload complete. Show how overflow is rejected by checking (x > /y) before multiplication, not by multiplying and inspecting the wrapped result.

Rebuild PixelTraits<Format> using std::integral_constant and distinguish the fact that a type is empty from an assertion that it costs zero bytes in every containing object. Demonstrate an if constexpr RGBA branch and contrast it with a normal runtime if. Write a constexpr function that accepts either compile-time or runtime arguments; then change the problem so that a consteval function demands a valid compile-time tile definition. Explain why constinit permits a mutable, single-threaded diagnostic counter but does not make it const or atomic.

Derive the four-bit Morton lookup without memorizing its answer. Spread (x=3) to binary 00000101 and (y=5) to 00010001. Shift the second pattern and OR the results to recover decimal 39. Construct the sixteen-entry table during constant evaluation. Then explain when a small lookup table might lose to shift/mask arithmetic because memory traffic and locality matter.

From that setup, implement a stateless policy and a stateful budget policy with the same validate operation. Use TilePlanner<Format,Policy,Recorder> to compose the behavior without a runtime backend switch. Show why RecorderBase<Derived> may call Derived::record_impl only when it is genuinely part of an appropriately derived object; compare this static dispatch with a runtime-selected std::function target. Construct VerifyPayloadTag and MetadataOnlyTag and explain exactly how overload resolution chooses a validation path from the caller’s tag type. Finally compare normal empty-policy membership, private empty-base inheritance, and [[no_unique_address]] membership. On the tested Linux compilers their respective sizes were 16, 8 and 8 bytes; the rule is a permitted optimization, not a universal numeric contract, and compilers can treat the attribute differently.

A complete blank-screen test recreates the accepted 64-byte RGBA plan, rejected 96-byte budget attempt, rejected empty verified payload, accepted 48-byte metadata-only RGB plan, and rejected overflowing extent. The recorder receives exactly two plans in the demonstrated sequence; failed requests do not reach it. Then state why this is not a real GPU resource, performance benchmark, atomic transaction for arbitrary throwing recorders, or proof of thread safety. The evidence ledger preserves the exact compiled commands and original fourteen-part mapping: M014 traceability · verification record.

A growing asset store must preserve its promises — M015 retrieval

A previously working fixed-capacity asset depot now grows, removes assets, accepts work in different scheduling orders, and lets the editor find items by name. Do not use the following as a replacement for the derivations in the complete M015 chapter. Start with this diagram and explain why its arrows and lifetime boundaries exist:

flowchart LR
    A["Editor requests rocks.mesh"] --> B["Prepare owning name + byte vector"]
    B --> C["vector of optional slots"]
    C --> D["Publish name in unordered_map"]
    D --> E["AssetHandle: slot + generation"]
    E --> F["Resolve current live occupant"]
    F --> G["Borrow span for synchronous checksum"]
    F --> H["Erase: destroy occupant + advance generation"]
    H --> I["Reuse slot under new generation"]
    I --> J["Stale old handle must fail"]

First distinguish size from capacity, and prove why reserve(2) creates zero live elements whereas resize(5) creates five. With a geometric capacity sequence 1,g,g²,..., derive the sum of relocation work and explain why an individual append can still have linear latency while amortized append cost remains constant. State the operations that invalidate vector pointers and the difference between an append with spare capacity, one requiring reallocation, a middle erase and reserve that does or does not change capacity. A pointer does not move itself when the vector relocates.

Then reconstruct the identity protocol. Slot zero holds generation one; a handle {0,1} reaches it. After erase, that occupant is destroyed, its generation advances, and a new asset occupies slot zero at generation two. Draw why {0,1} no longer resolves. Explain what happens if generation wraps, if a raw Asset* or span was retained across reallocation, or if the renderer still has an asynchronous GPU read in flight. Distinguish a CPU identity check from the device-completion requirement.

Show the two injected publication failures: one before any slot change, another after a new slot has been populated but before the name index becomes discoverable. Prove why the rollback resets the candidate and removes a newly appended unpublished slot; explain why the test’s successful outcome is not an unrestricted claim about arbitrary throwing user callbacks or all allocator behaviors.

Now change the workload. A fixed-size channel array needs std::array, not vector growth. A front/back event stream makes deque attractive, but its iterator stability differs from that of its existing element references. A list can transfer a node with splice while keeping an iterator to an unaffected node; a forward_list needs the predecessor for erase_after. Explain what those guarantees cost in nodes, pointer chasing and cache locality compared with a contiguous vector scan.

Next give two lookup problems. For ordered traversal and range queries, consider std::map / std::set, with logarithmic comparison-based behavior. For name-to-handle lookup or membership, use std::unordered_map / std::unordered_set and explain expected versus worst-case complexity. Write a hash that returns zero for every string; twenty-four distinct names now collide in the same bucket without becoming equal. Derive load_factor = size/bucket_count, explain what max_load_factor(0.5) and reserve(96) request, and state why rehash invalidates unordered iterators but does not generally invalidate references to surviving elements.

Finally build the scheduling choices from user needs: a FIFO queue, LIFO stack, and a priority_queue whose comparator orders priority 3 before priority 1 and earlier sequence numbers before later ones within equal priority. Explain why priority_queue does not promise tie stability unless the comparator defines it.

Finish by distinguishing borrow from ownership. A span<const uint8_t> carries a range while its byte vector remains alive and stable; it does not own the bytes. A string_view may point into only the middle of a stored string and need not be NUL-terminated at its end. Copy "stone" into std::string before destroying or modifying the source. Describe why the local observed short-string capacity of 15 cannot be advertised as a portable SSO specification.

Actual reconstruction witness: M015 C++20 lab, compiled and run with GCC sanitizers, Clang, and a GCC release-style build. A learner should be able to recreate the sequence of checks without the reference and explain every failure. Original 20-part mapping · Exact test and provenance ledger. Do not claim personal mastery or real Kairo/GPU verification merely because this standalone model passes.

Query the registry without confusing identity and a snapshot — M016 reconstruction

The previous M015 exercise produced a generation-checked asset registry. The new problem is to report on assets without changing their live ownership and without assuming that a handle stays current forever. Read the full M016 narrative before testing recall; the questions below should be reconstructed as one processing story, not as twenty memorized API names.

flowchart LR
  A["Live registry + generational handles"] --> B["Capture owned metadata snapshot"]
  B --> C["Optional result or typed query error"]
  C --> D["Variant command handling / open diagnostic any"]
  D --> E["Sort, stable-sort or partition by the intended key"]
  E --> F["Search only with its required ordering"]
  F --> G["Transform records into sizes"]
  G --> H["Accumulate/reduce with numeric contract"]
  H --> I["Erase from report copy, not live registry"]

Starting with the five records brick.mesh (48 bytes, priority 2), sky.tex (64, priority 3), ui.tex (16, priority 3), terrain.mesh (128, priority 1) and rock.mesh (48, priority 2), answer each part in coherent explanations:

  1. Describe each result’s meaning. Why does optional<AssetHandle> mean “possibly absent” but fail to distinguish an empty query from a missing name? Build ExpectedLike<AssetHandle,LookupError> as a C++20 model. Explain exactly what its has_value() contract requires before value() is accessed and why it is not a full replacement for C++23 std::expected. Then distinguish that result from an Inspect/Upload/Evict variant and from a diagnostic any. Predict a wrong any_cast.

  2. Rebuild the report shape. Group count and error count in a pair and three report fields in a tuple. Show that auto [a,b] = pair copies this pair, while auto& [a,b] = pair aliases it. Explain why a named struct can be clearer at a long-lived public API boundary and why a borrowed structured binding needs an owner that outlives it.

  3. Prove the traversal capabilities before selecting the algorithm. Classify istream_iterator<int>, forward_list<int>::iterator, list<int>::iterator, deque<int>::iterator and vector<int>::iterator according to input, forward, bidirectional, random-access and contiguous iterator concepts. Why can std::sort operate on the vector’s random-access iterators but not directly on list iterators? Why may binary search over forward iterators have logarithmic comparison count but linear iterator advances?

  4. Choose ordering by what the editor needs. Write a comparator that first orders byte counts, then asset names so equal byte counts have deterministic tie breaking. Explain why std::sort need not preserve the order of comparator-equivalent records and why common introsort-like implementations are not mandated by the C++ standard. For descending priorities, write stable_sort and predict the relative order of sky.tex vs ui.tex and brick.mesh vs rock.mesh. State the strict-weak-ordering requirements the comparator must satisfy.

  5. Partition only when the task is binary membership. Use std::partition to put mesh records before non-mesh records; verify both halves and use partition_point on the resulting already-partitioned range. Explain why the two groups are not automatically sorted and why partitioning does not promise to retain original relative order. Say when stable_partition would be appropriate.

  6. Derive the binary-search boundaries. Once the byte-count ordering is [16,48,48,64,128], prove that lower_bound(48) returns index 1 and upper_bound(48) returns index 3. Explain why equal_range gives [1,3) and why lower_bound(50) points to index 3 despite having no match. Supply comparator overloads in both element/value and value/element orders. Describe why using a priority-sorted sequence here would violate the precondition.

  7. Compare one-off scanning with a maintained index. Use std::find to look for sky.tex in an unsorted name snapshot. Explain when this simple linear scan is preferable to building a fresh hash index, and when repeated lookups should instead use the registry’s already maintained name index.

  8. Transform and reduce with the correct numeric meaning. Derive [48,64,16,128,48] using std::transform and an output back inserter, then calculate 304 using an explicit std::size_t{0} initial accumulator. Write the ordered std::accumulate fold and explain why std::reduce may regroup operations, even if a particular run happens to use one thread. Use (10{20},1,-10{20},3) to derive both 3 and 4 from different floating-point groupings. State separate overflow, accuracy and deterministic-reproducibility policies.

  9. Erase at the correct ownership boundary. Starting with {1,2,3,4,5,6}, use remove_if to keep odd IDs but demonstrate that the vector still reports size six until erase destroys the suffix. Then use C++20 std::erase_if to remove the two texture records from an owned report snapshot, leaving three rows. Explain why the live asset registry has not evicted those assets and what additional generation validation, index cleanup and GPU retirement a real eviction would require.

Blank-file witness: reconstruct the program in asset_query_algorithm_lab.cpp with active failure checks, compile under C++20 with warnings as errors, then rerun with -DNDEBUG and sanitizers. The reference was actually run with GCC 14.2 ASan/UBSan, Clang 17 and GCC release flags. Reconstruct the expected values before running it; a passing executable is not a substitute for understanding the data/iterator/lifetime contracts.

Audit: the original 20-part mapping and the source and verification ledger. The registry’s live concurrency, the separately named Kairo implementations and the learner’s independent reconstruction remain unverified here.

From borrowed reports to module boundaries — M017 reconstruction

The Phase 6 report used an owned snapshot so that sorting and erasing metadata did not mutate live engine state. The next problem is making that report composable without accidentally copying intermediates, choosing where its scratch allocations live, and sharing its API with separately compiled consumers. The full explanation is the M017 continuous chapter. Reconstruct the mechanism below from the problem, not by reciting the names of its twenty C++ features.

flowchart LR
    A["Owned snapshot: five live + one retired"] --> B["Custom forward iterator skips tombstone"]
    B --> C["Lazy filter | transform view"]
    C --> D["Borrowed or owning view?"]
    D --> E["Ranges algorithms with projections"]
    E --> F["Owned output: custom allocator / PMR"]
    F --> G["Monotonic arena lifetime and overflow"]
    G --> H["Named C++ module interface and partition"]
    H --> I["Separate implementation and importers"]
    I --> J["Versioned C ABI wrapper for C11 caller"]

First reconstruct what the loop means. Draw the hidden range variable, begin iterator, end sentinel and increment/compare/dereference sequence behind a range-for. Define a cursor that holds a borrowed pointer to the snapshot vector and a numeric index, and makes operator++ skip retired slots. State the invariants for normal, end and default-created iterators; do not dereference the end. Explain why your cursor models std::forward_iterator and why it does not model random access or contiguity. With one 512-byte retired texture and live byte counts 48,64,16,128,48, predict exactly five visits and total 304.

Next reconstruct laziness and lifetime. Compose views::all(rows) | views::filter(...) | views::transform(...) to obtain four names from those live rows with at least 48 bytes. Explain why merely forming the pipeline does not copy all four names into a vector and why iterating it later can call the predicate again. Predict why it is wrong to rely on a precise predicate invocation count for arbitrary repeat traversals. Compare views::all(lvalue_vector) with views::all(rvalue_vector) and explain how a ref_view can satisfy borrowed_range without keeping the vector itself alive. Conversely, explain why an owning view storing the vector need not qualify as a borrowed range when the view’s own destruction destroys the data.

Use a projection only when the search needs one property. Without constructing a separate names vector, use std::ranges::find(rows, "sky.tex", &Row::name) and predict the record’s byte count. Sort an owned copy by &Row::bytes and state why the 512-byte retired row will still appear at the end unless you filtered it first. Discuss why the source vector’s contiguity does not make a filter view a writable random-access container. Compare AtLeastBytes{48} against an equivalent threshold-capturing lambda, giving a plan for benchmarking actual instruction and allocation costs instead of asserting one form is always faster.

Now choose who owns allocation. Build a typed TrackingAllocator<T> that shares statistics across copies and rebindings, uses proper alignment and pairs successful storage acquisitions with deallocation. Explain why allocation is not the same as constructing a T object, and why allocator equality/propagation matter when a container moves or swaps. Then replace the compile-time allocator type with a std::pmr::vector and a std::pmr::unordered_map, both pointing to a counting memory_resource. Explain how unordered buckets/nodes and nested PMR strings may require allocator propagation, and why the resource must outlive both containers.

Derive the arena lifetime, not just its common-case speed. Give a 128-byte aligned scratch buffer to a monotonic resource, then allocate 2,048 64-bit values. Explain why the initial buffer cannot contain the entire request; the resource must obtain upstream blocks. Predict why destroying the vector does not immediately free those blocks and why destroying/releasing the arena later can. Repeat with a 64-byte buffer and null_memory_resource upstream and predict std::bad_alloc. State the difference between a frame scratch lifetime and staging memory still held by an asynchronous GPU operation; neither the presence of PMR nor a move-only vector resolves the missing completion fence.

Finally build an actual module graph. In separate files, put a :rules partition containing an exported 1,024-byte preview budget, a primary export module allmight.asset_query interface that re-exports that partition, and a module allmight.asset_query; implementation unit defining make_preview. Compile in dependency order. Write two separate importing translation units that use an exported inline function, link them with the implementation, and explain which declarations are exported and why that is distinct from C++ namespace naming or C language linkage. Build asset_query_interop.hpp as a header unit before using import "asset_query_interop.hpp";; compare this with an ordinary #include and explain macro/toolchain implications. Then expose a small versioned C header declaring int allmight_asset_approved_v1(uint64_t); build a C11 consumer using gcc and link it with the C++ wrapper and module objects. Explain exactly what this test establishes about the chosen GCC14 toolchain, and why it does not certify ABI stability across unrelated compilers or plugin versions.

The real sources are the tested C++20 CPU lab and the executable module graph script. The local runtime lab passed GCC14 ASan/UBSan, Clang17 and GCC14 release; the module graph passed GCC14’s ordered module/header-unit build with three linked consumers. The original twenty-title coverage map and verification ledger distinguish that evidence from external Kairo audits and unmeasured performance. Personal mastery is earned only after independent explanation, tests and failure-case reconstruction; the authored lesson and one passing lab cannot grant it automatically.

Preserve an asset while the engine changes — M018 reconstruction

The editor selected a teapot before the asset service started deleting, reallocating and reusing storage. The renderer has independently compiled clients, several classes of resource handles and mathematical values from different coordinate frames. Reconstruct the API by starting with the event, not with a memorized list of PIMPL, concepts and expression templates. The complete reasoning lives in the M018 continuous chapter. The actually compiled service and its test program are in the test laboratory and the multi-TU build.

Reconstruction 1 — identity, storage, and ABI. A mesh occupies slot zero in catalog A at generation one, and the client retains a handle. The vector reallocates, the mesh is erased, and a second mesh occupies the same slot. Explain precisely why a pointer might become invalid on reallocation, why a stale index could identify the wrong mesh, why a generation alone does not distinguish two separate catalogs, and why a MeshTag prevents a texture handle being silently passed to a mesh operation. The correct handle is a value containing a type-level kind and catalog/slot/generation runtime identity. A valid lookup compares all required fields and checks that the slot still holds a live value. After erase, the old generation must fail even when the slot is reused. The returned optional MeshInfo is a copy, so keeping it after erase cannot dangle, although its description is now stale. Confirm with the executable’s delete/reuse and cross-catalog tests.

Reconstruction 2 — the public header is not the implementation. Write a declaration of an asset service that contains only an incomplete Impl and a unique pointer to that implementation. Explain why the destructor and move assignment must be defined where Impl is complete. Identify which client recompilations PIMPL can avoid and which ABI questions remain. Then identify the actual costs: one implementation allocation in the constructed design, pointer indirection and possible out-of-line call overhead. PIMPL is appropriate for a relatively cold service boundary, not automatically for every inner-loop vector, task or splat. Name the deep-const hazard: an owning pointer stored in a const public object does not in itself make the pointee immutable.

Reconstruction 3 — three floats are not automatically the same mathematical value. Demonstrate why a world-space displacement and a camera-space displacement must be different C++ types, while also explaining the actual linear or affine transform that converts between them. Show why a point requires translation but a direction does not, why a normal may require inverse-transpose transformation, and why a quantity in meters cannot simply be added to a quantity in seconds. The phantom marker constrains type checking without adding a stored tag field; the underlying numeric representation does not perform a coordinate transform. Compare a fixed-size Vector<float,3,WorldSpace> with a runtime span requiring an explicit extent check. Explain why the supplied RealScalar concept intentionally rejects integers and user-defined autodiff scalars.

Reconstruction 4 — materialization is both a performance and a lifetime decision. Trace eager a+b+c. Then trace a SumExpr storing references and evaluating operator[](i) on demand. Construct the dangerous saved outer expression that refers to a destroyed temporary inner node, and explain why its later evaluation is undefined behavior. Rewrite the example so the inner expression outlives evaluation. Explain how aliasing, SIMD, floating-point reassociation and compiler optimization affect the claim that lazy evaluation must be faster. The tested vectors produce (12,15,18); matching output is necessary but cannot alone establish absence of hidden allocations or the safety of every expression tree.

Reconstruction 5 — own storage or embed links? Compare an intrusive task stack, where the task contains its next pointer and must outlive its membership, against a forward_list owning its elements. Show what breaks when a linked Task is destroyed, moved or inserted twice. The tested stack rejects duplicate membership and unlinks on pop. That is not a safe general-purpose ownership scheme for arbitrary user destruction. Predict how allocation, locality and mutation patterns could make either representation preferable.

Reconstruction 6 — interrogate the machine rather than assuming zero cost. Compile the assembly probe with optimized GCC and Clang. Find the named externally visible function. Decide whether the templated addition was inlined and whether there are calls or unnecessary transfers on that compiler/target. Explain why a different ISA, link-time optimization, compiler flags or fast-math setting can produce different machine code and numerical results. State a fair baseline and define actual comparable workloads before declaring one catalog representation faster. A successful presence check for an assembly symbol is a build witness, not a timing benchmark.

Final synthesis. Draw the lifetime sequence from editor selection to catalog erase and eventual GPU retirement. Distinguish three independently necessary guarantees: the CPU logical handle remains validated, the public C++ representation remains insulated as promised, and a GPU resource stays alive while submitted work may still read it. The M018 sample tests the first two in a limited CPU setting and does not implement the third. Compile under release -DNDEBUG and explain why the test program uses throwing checks instead of ordinary asserts. Then independently implement an asset handle with one additional version or session policy, state its invariants and design negative tests that could falsify those invariants.

Mastery criterion: without looking up the code, reconstruct the public header, its out-of-line implementation, the validation predicate, an exception-safe reuse transition, a typed fixed/dynamic math interface, a lifetime-safe lazy expression evaluation, and a falsifiable compiler-cost experiment. Reading the answers is not evidence of independent reconstruction.
