GPU interfaces and cooperation — shortest useful recall

Prompt Recall answer Expand immediately
Size, alignment, stride? Payload extent, legal start addresses, distance between elements. A 12-byte vec3 can require 16-byte start alignment. [[Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Make a shader record an explicit binary contract
Is a texture-table index ownership? No. Keep its referenced generation and allocation alive through pending uses. [[Continuous Notes/Game Engine - From First Frame to Living Worlds#Let a renderer evolve without losing resource ownership
Workgroup versus subgroup? Workgroups cooperate with shared storage and barriers; subgroups expose a smaller execution collective. Width is not universally 32. [[Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Let many invocations cooperate without inventing a global clock
What does scan allocate? Nonoverlapping output ranges: counts (2,0,3,1)(2,0,3,1) become offsets (0,2,2,5)(0,2,2,5). [[Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Scan turns local counts into nonoverlapping output regions
Atomic, ordering, barrier? Protect an operation; govern visibility/order; rendezvous with specified memory effects. These are different contracts. [[Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Scan turns local counts into nonoverlapping output regions
Can out-of-range lanes return before a required group barrier? Generally no. Supply neutral values while preserving the barrier participation contract. [[Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Scan turns local counts into nonoverlapping output regions

Explain the two barriers in tiled matrix multiplication: one protects complete tile loading; one protects reuse after every consumer finishes. Explain why a later dispatch still needs the API’s execution and memory dependency, rather than assuming a dispatch boundary flushes everything.

API resource stages

A name, initialized API object, allocated storage, initialized bytes and completed use are different states. glCreateBuffers establishes the object; a storage command establishes capacity; null initial data does not mean zero-filled bytes. Open the worked API distinction. A nonzero integer alone proves neither a safe draw range nor safe retirement.

Phase 8 - From constraints to spectra

Read prerequisite → dependent. Phase 8 reuses the vector, matrix, metric, storage, and conditioning foundations from Phases 6–7; those connections are kept explicit here.

Prerequisites Dependent Why the dependency exists
Matrices as linear maps and basis images, Basis coordinates and dimension Linear systems and fundamental subspaces Rows measure inputs; columns span reachable outputs, while rank-nullity counts invisible input changes.
Linear systems and fundamental subspaces, Conditioning and singularity Gaussian elimination and pivoting Elimination exposes equivalent constraints; pivot choices control division risk but cannot cure sensitivity.
Gaussian elimination and pivoting, Matrix storage indexing and strides LU factorization and reusable solves Elimination multipliers and triangular entries become reusable factors in an explicit storage layout.
Matrix transpose symmetry and trace, Gram matrices and coordinate metrics Symmetric positive-definite matrices and Cholesky Symmetry and positive quadratic energy justify the triangular square-root factorization.
Linear systems and fundamental subspaces, Dot products and orthogonality, Conditioning and singularity QR factorization and least squares Orthogonal coordinates preserve residual length and separate fitted from perpendicular components.
Matrices as linear maps and basis images, Linear systems and fundamental subspaces Eigenvalues and eigenspaces An invariant direction is the null-space solution of A−λIA-\lambda I.
Matrix multiplication and composition order, Eigenvalues and eigenspaces, Dot products and orthogonality Singular value decomposition SVD pairs distinct input and output orthonormal directions for any rectangular map.
Singular value decomposition, Linear systems and fundamental subspaces, Matrix norms and numerical error Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse Reciprocating selected singular values gives least-squares and minimum-norm solutions while exposing sensitivity.
Eigenvalues and eigenspaces, Singular value decomposition PCA and covariance eigensystems Centered data covariance eigenvectors and data-matrix singular vectors encode the same principal directions.
Singular value decomposition, Eigenvalues and eigenspaces, Determinants orientation and volume Polar decomposition SVD assembles an orthogonal factor and a positive-semidefinite stretch; determinant exposes reflection.
Norms lengths and induced distances, Singular value decomposition, Forward and backward error Matrix norms and numerical error Norm choice defines residual scale, maximum stretch, and error amplification.
Eigenvalues and eigenspaces, Matrix multiplication and composition order, Matrix norms and numerical error Matrix functions Spectral decompositions explain scalar functions of a matrix; norms and branches constrain computation.
Linear systems and fundamental subspaces, Symmetric positive-definite matrices and Cholesky, Matrix norms and numerical error Sparse and iterative solvers Large sparse structure motivates matrix-vector iteration, with convergence and residual contracts.
Gaussian elimination and pivoting, LU factorization and reusable solves, Symmetric positive-definite matrices and Cholesky, QR factorization and least squares, Singular value decomposition Matrix factorization choices The task and verified matrix structure determine a method; no one factorization fits every case.
Matrix storage indexing and strides, Sparse and iterative solvers Matrix factorization choices Sparse algorithms and their storage/convergence costs inform workload selection.

Phase 7 - From basis images to moving worlds

Read prerequisite → dependent. Storage layout does not determine algebraic action, and quaternion component order does not determine multiplication convention.

Prerequisites Dependent Why
Basis coordinates and dimension Matrices as linear maps and basis images A matrix is a rectangular scalar array.
Matrices as linear maps and basis images Matrix multiplication and composition order The product AB applies B first for column-vector actions.
Matrix multiplication and composition order Matrix transpose symmetry and trace Transpose exchanges row and column indices and reverses product order.
Cross products and oriented area, Matrices as linear maps and basis images Determinants orientation and volume A square matrix determinant measures oriented volume scale.
Determinants orientation and volume, Conditioning and singularity Matrix inversion pivoting and residuals Inversion reconstructs input coordinates from output for an invertible square map.
Matrices as linear maps and basis images, Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division Linear affine and projective transformations Linear maps preserve linear combinations and fix zero.
Linear affine and projective transformations, Matrix inversion pivoting and residuals Coordinate frames and change of basis A frame gives an origin and independent axes relative to another frame.
Coordinate frames and change of basis Camera view and clip-space pipeline A camera pose maps camera coordinates to world coordinates; its inverse is the view map.
ABI and object layout, Pointer arithmetic and provenance, Matrices as linear maps and basis images Matrix storage indexing and strides Matrix row/column semantics are independent of physical row-major or column-major storage.
Matrix storage indexing and strides, Floating-point reassociation Matrix SIMD tiling and cache reuse Loop ordering and tiling change memory traffic and reuse while preserving the exact scalar algebra.
Dot products and orthogonality, Cross products and oriented area Quaternion algebra and Hamilton product A quaternion has scalar w and vector u.
Quaternion algebra and Hamilton product Quaternion rotation and double cover For a unit quaternion q, the sandwich q(0,v)conjugate(q) rotates v.
Quaternion rotation and double cover, Matrices as linear maps and basis images Quaternion matrix and axis-angle conversion A unit axis and angle give q=(cos(theta/2),axis sin(theta/2)).
Quaternion rotation and double cover Quaternion interpolation and shortest paths Quaternion interpolation must account for the double cover.
Quaternion matrix and axis-angle conversion, Matrix multiplication and composition order Euler angles and gimbal singularity Euler/Tait-Bryan angles are coordinates for rotation with a specified axis/order convention.
Quaternion algebra and Hamilton product, Linear affine and projective transformations Dual quaternions and rigid motion A rigid dual quaternion consists of a unit real quaternion and a dual quaternion part satisfying real dot dual equals zero.
Coordinate frames and change of basis, Quaternion matrix and axis-angle conversion, Dual quaternions and rigid motion Transform hierarchies TRS and shear A TRS transform stores translation, rotation and diagonal scale, with an explicit application order.

Validated finite unit directions establish the preconditions for simplified geometry formulas. Removing an unwanted component creates residuals, tangent axes and mirror decompositions.
Surface tangents normals and bitangents, Gram matrices and coordinate metrics Orthonormal frames and Gram-Schmidt The surface tangent plane gives the axes that orthogonalization must preserve. Pairwise basis measurements define the systems and metric used in reconstruction.
Projection rejection and scalar components, Unit directions and safe normalization Reflection refraction and shading directions Removing an unwanted component creates residuals, tangent axes and mirror decompositions. Validated finite unit directions establish the preconditions for simplified geometry formulas.
Gram matrices and coordinate metrics, Vectors coordinates and affine points Barycentric coordinates and interpolation Pairwise basis measurements define the systems and metric used in reconstruction. Point, displacement and coordinate roles determine which geometric operations are meaningful.
Cross products and oriented area, Dot and cross-product rounding Robust geometric predicates Oriented area supplies face normals, frame signs and geometric determinants. Cancellation and rounded inputs explain when a determinant sign or finite measurement is uncertain.
Barycentric coordinates and interpolation Convex combinations and convex hulls Affine weights establish origin-independent combinations and inside-hull restrictions.
Convex combinations and convex hulls, Dot products and orthogonality Minkowski sums and support mappings Convex set geometry is the domain for hull support and collision constructions. Inner-product measurements supply the perpendicularity and alignment constraints.
Vectors coordinates and affine points Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division Point, displacement and coordinate roles determine which geometric operations are meaningful.
Basis coordinates and dimension, Dot products and orthogonality Covectors linear functionals and normal transforms An ordered basis fixes coordinate meaning and the space whose geometry is measured. Inner-product measurements supply the perpendicularity and alignment constraints.
Cross products and oriented area, Triple products and signed volume Exterior products and geometric algebra Oriented area supplies face normals, frame signs and geometric determinants. Oriented volume connects exterior grades and determinant-based geometry.
Vectors coordinates and affine points, Named members versus array elements Vector value types and component access Point, displacement and coordinate roles determine which geometric operations are meaningful. Array-relative pointer rules constrain safe named-component access.
Vector value types and component access, Alignment and padding, SIMD and GPU data layouts Vector storage SIMD and boundary layouts Primitive representation and access rules support layout choices and semantic wrappers. Phase 6-10 mathematical learning route

Phase 6 establishes vectors, coordinates, and geometry; Phase 7 treats matrices as maps and changes of basis; Phase 8 develops solves, decompositions, and matrix functions; Phase 9 models change with derivatives, integrals, ODEs, and optimization; Phase 10 uses probability and statistics to reason about uncertain samples.

Narrative order and source coverage

The first six sources cover Parts 1–100. Volume 01 follows physical state → interpretation → decisions/fields → finite arithmetic → floating representation/error → deliberate precision choices → placement/lifetime → serialization/integrity/dump. Source order remains in Foundations. M007–M010 now cover C++ Parts 101–160; exact source ranges remain in Foundations.

Future connections already have definitions: IEEE-754 floating point, Cache lines and memory bandwidth, Atomic operations and write contention, SIMD and GPU data layouts, Quantization and compressed weights, Compiler IR and machine instructions, and Guest and host integer domains. M004 - Representation and rounding learning spine

Prerequisites Dependent Why these steps are needed
IEEE-754 floating point, Bit field Binary32 A 32-bit binary interchange format with one sign bit, eight exponent bits and 23 fraction bits. Normal precision is 24 bits; exponent bias is 127. Word 3F800000 has E=127,F=0 and means 1.
Binary32 Binary64 A 64-bit binary interchange format with 1/11/52 fields, 53 significant normal bits and bias 1023. Normal exponent range is −1022 through 1023. Word 3FF0000000000000 means 1.
Binary32 Exponent bias Normal exponents are encoded as unsigned E=e+B. Binary32 B=127, so exponent 3 stores 130. Field zero and all-ones are reserved; classify before subtracting bias.
Binary32, Positional notation Significand and hidden bit The significand supplies significant digits; the exponent supplies scale. A normal binary value begins 1.f, so its leading one is implied, not stored. Binary32 fraction F contributes F/2^23; subnormals instead begin 0.f.
Exponent bias, Significand and hidden bit, Hexadecimal Floating-point encoding and decoding Encoding chooses fields for a value; decoding classifies fields and reconstructs their meaning. 10.625 normalizes to 1.010101₂×2³, giving 412A0000. C1540000 decodes to −13.25.
Binary32 Signed zero Exponent and fraction zero permit either sign. 00000000 and 80000000 compare numerically equal, but signbit and reciprocal distinguish them. Ordinary x<0 does not detect negative zero.
Binary32 Floating-point infinities All-one exponent and zero fraction encode signed infinity. This is not maximum finite. Infinity minus itself is NaN; overflow’s result also depends on rounding direction.
Binary32 NaNs and payloads All-one exponent with nonzero fraction encodes a non-numerical, unordered NaN. Quiet and signaling classes differ; fraction bits can carry payload information. Ordinary NaN equality is false; use isnan. Raw words can be classified without consuming signaling NaNs as floating values.
Exponent bias, Significand and hidden bit Subnormals and gradual underflow Exponent zero and nonzero fraction remove the hidden one and hold the effective exponent at the normal minimum. Binary32 values are F×2^-149, connecting smoothly to 2^-126. Absolute spacing stays fixed while relative precision degrades.
Significand and hidden bit Machine epsilon For these binary types epsilon is upward spacing at 1: 2^-23 for binary32 and 2^-52 for binary64. It is neither minimum positive value nor a physical threshold.
Machine epsilon, Exponent bias, Subnormals and gradual underflow ULP and representable spacing A unit in the last place describes local spacing. Inside normal binade [2e,2(e+1)), p-bit precision gives spacing 2^(e-(p-1)). Immediately above 1 the binary32 gap is twice the gap below it.
ULP and representable spacing Rounding to nearest ties to even Choose the nearest representable value; exactly halfway choose the even retained significand integer. At toy precision three bits, 1.125→1 and 1.375→1.5. std::round uses halfway-away-from-zero instead.
ULP and representable spacing, Rounding to nearest ties to even Unit roundoff Under nearest binary rounding the conventional relative bound for normal-range results is u=2^-p, half upward epsilon. For binary32 this is 2^-24. The bound has range/rounding assumptions.
Boolean algebra, Rounding to nearest ties to even Guard round and sticky bits Guard is first discarded bit, round the next, sticky ORs all remaining bits. With retained low bit L, nearest-even increments when G AND (R OR sticky OR L). Sticky summarizes any nonzero tail.
Rounding to nearest ties to even Directed rounding modes Upward means toward positive infinity, downward toward negative infinity, and toward-zero truncates magnitude. Upward rounding of −2.1 to an integer gives −2, not −3.
Directed rounding modes, NaNs and payloads Floating-point environment and compiler modes The environment includes rounding direction and exception status. Runtime mode changes can fail and must restore prior state. Strict compiler settings are needed; fast-math may discard required special-value or environment assumptions.
IEEE-754 floating point, Subnormals and gradual underflow Floating-point exception flags Invalid, divide-by-zero, overflow, underflow and inexact are status conditions, not C++ throw exceptions. Exact subnormal results need not signal underflow. Flag/trap behavior depends on the environment.
Subnormals and gradual underflow, Floating-point environment and compiler modes Flush-to-zero and denormals-are-zero FTZ flushes certain tiny results to zero; DAZ treats subnormal inputs as zero in supporting environments. They change gradual-underflow behavior. Cost and support are target/mode-specific.
Fixed-width integer types, Interpretation contract, IEEE-754 floating point Bit casting and representation A same-size eligible bit_cast transfers representation, not numeric value. On the checked binary32 host, bit_cast<uint32_t>(1.0f)=3F800000, whereas a numeric cast gives 1. Pointer punning is not an equivalent legal operation.
ULP and representable spacing, Signed zero, NaNs and payloads ULP distance policies Distance counts representable steps under a declared ordering/equality policy. The finite-only laboratory collapses both zeros to one key and rejects NaNs/infinities. Across negative minimum subnormal to positive minimum subnormal distance is two.
Machine epsilon, ULP and representable spacing, Floating-point infinities, NaNs and payloads Numerical tolerance policies Tolerance is a task-chosen allowed discrepancy: absolute in original units, relative to scale, or representable-step based. Machine epsilon is not automatically a norm cutoff. Handle non-finite values and validate tolerances before formulas.
IEEE-754 floating point, Floating-point infinities Robust norm and intermediate range A final representable answer can be lost to overflowing intermediates. Squaring 1e20f overflows before a finite norm could be formed. Scale by maximum component or use hypot to avoid unnecessary squared overflow.
Numerical tolerance policies Conditioning and singularity Conditioning measures sensitivity to input perturbation. A=1e-4 I has determinant 1e-8 but condition number one in the 2-norm. Uniform scaling changes determinant magnitude without changing this conditioning measure.
Signed zero, NaNs and payloads, Serialization, Bit casting and representation Floating-point canonicalization Canonicalization deliberately merges encodings: both zeros to positive zero, all NaNs to one quiet pattern. Raw preservation instead keeps sign/payload distinctions. Neither is universally correct; this is a file/hash contract choice.
Directed rounding modes, Floating-point environment and compiler modes Interval arithmetic An interval encloses a possible exact value between lower and upper bounds. Correct outward rounding can preserve containment when the whole algorithm honors necessary assumptions.

The first volume covers all Parts 1–100. Prerequisites explain the story’s dependencies; they do not require leaving the continuous volume to learn an essential definition.

Prerequisites Dependent Why these steps are needed

Cancellation and loss of significance, Subnormals and gradual underflow Sterbenz lemma Nearby stored operands can subtract exactly even though their original inputs were rounded.
Cancellation and loss of significance Stable reformulation Change intermediates to avoid unnecessary loss while preserving the mathematical target.
IEEE-754 floating point, Rounding to nearest ties to even Fused multiply-add One final rounding differs from separate product and sum roundings.
Floating-point addition and absorption, Fused multiply-add Floating-point reassociation Expression grouping changes rounded intermediates.

Absolute and relative error, Directed rounding modes Numerical decision boundaries Small numeric changes can cross pixel, sign or threshold decisions.
Cancellation and loss of significance, Fused multiply-add, Compensated and pairwise summation Dot and cross-product rounding Input representation, product rounding and summation are separate sources of error.

Representation choices and external contracts

Prerequisites Dependent Why these steps are needed
Two's complement, Interpretation contract Fixed-point representation A raw integer I represents I/S for an agreed positive scale S and units. With S=2^16, raw 212992 means 3.25. The integer has no built-in fractional point.
Fixed-point representation Fixed-point range and resolution For signed N-bit raw storage and F fraction bits, step is 2^-F and the positive endpoint is (2(N-1)-1)/2F. Required step 0.001 and magnitude 1e6 in 32 bits allow F=10 or 11.
Fixed-point representation, Minimum signed value, Arithmetic policies Fixed-point rescaling Raw multiplication changes scale S to S²; divide the wide product by S with a declared rounding rule. Raw division uses A*S/B. Check the destination after widening, and handle divisor zero and signed minima.
Fixed-point representation, Absolute and relative error Affine quantization and zero point A positive step s, integer zero point z and bounded code q reconstruct x̂=s(q-z). Nearest encode uses clamp(round(x/s)+z). Half-step error assumes no clipping and ideal parameters.
Affine quantization and zero point, Bit packing Groupwise quantization and metadata Local groups share a scale, improving adaptation at a metadata cost. Symmetric INT4 calibration maxAbs/7 reconstructs codes around [-7,7]; float scales add about 32/G bits per value for full groups.
Quantization and compressed weights One-bit centroid quantization One sign label selects one of two row means. Row [-1,-3,2,4] reconstructs [-2,-2,3,3], with RMSE one. Two float32 centroids cost 64 additional bits per row.
Affine quantization and zero point UNORM and SNORM UNORM decodes q/(2^n-1); UNORM8 code128 gives128/255. SNORM commonly clamps q/(2^(n-1)-1) at -1, so -128 and -127 both map to -1 for eight bits.
IEEE-754 floating point, Rounding to nearest ties to even Binary16 IEEE binary16 has 1/5/10 fields, bias15 and11 normal precision bits. Word3E00 is1.5; maximum finite65504; normal minimum2^-14 and subnormal minimum2^-24.
IEEE-754 floating point, Rounding to nearest ties to even Bfloat16 BF16 has1/8/7 fields, bias127 and8 normal precision bits. It keeps broad exponent range at coarse spacing2^-7 above1. A nearest-even conversion must handle NaNs separately from finite rounding.
Unsigned modular arithmetic, Interpretation contract Offset-binary coding A bias turns signed levels into unsigned codes. For the source-shaped INT4 convention c=q+8, -3 becomes nibble0101, not the two’s-complement nibble1101.
Absolute and relative error, Quantization and compressed weights Quantization error metrics For N>0, RMSE is sqrt(sum squared discrepancies/N), MAE is mean absolute discrepancy, and max error is the largest observed magnitude. Promote float operands before subtraction when measuring in double.
Serialization, Bit casting and representation Binary format contracts A schema declares field widths/order, byte order, numeric representation, valid values, lengths, version, padding and identity policy. Magic identifies a candidate format; version chooses a schema, neither authenticates content.
Binary format contracts, Unsigned modular arithmetic, Short-circuit evaluation Checked binary parsing Validate products before size calculation, ranges with offset≤size and length≤size-offset, and practical resource limits before allocation. Mapping/alignment does not itself establish valid typed object access.
Bitwise XOR, Serialization Checksums CRCs and hashes Checksums/digests summarize specified bytes. Additive checksums miss reorderings; CRCs use GF(2) polynomial remainders and declared parameters. Cryptographic hashes need a trusted reference to support integrity claims against substitution.
Checksums CRCs and hashes, Interpretation contract Integrity and authenticity Integrity compares content with a declared reference; authenticity requires a trust mechanism such as a MAC or signature. Replacing both file and untrusted digest defeats a simple hash comparison.
Endianness, Bit casting and representation, Binary format contracts Memory dump interpretation Raw octets gain meaning from offsets, width, encoding and byte order. Bytes00 00 80 3F mean integer1065353216 or binary32 one under different little-endian contracts. A dump does not prove a typed object is live.

Calculus and optimization — visual recall

One-page quick recall

  • Scalar change: f(a+h)=f(a)+f′(a)h+o(|h|)f(a+h)=f(a)+f'(a)h+o(|h|).
  • Vector output: F(x+h)=F(x)+JF(x)h+o(∥h∥)F(x+h)=F(x)+J_F(x)h+o(\|h\|); JJ has output rows and input columns.
  • Scalar curvature: f(x+h)≈f(x)+∇fTh+12hTHhf(x+h)\approx f(x)+\nabla f^T h+\tfrac12h^THh.
  • Accumulation: y(t)=y0+∫t0tf(s,y(s))dsy(t)=y_0+\int_{t_0}^t f(s,y(s))\,ds; a numerical solver approximates this evolution.
  • Forward sensitivity: JvJv; reverse sensitivity: JTλJ^T\lambda.
  • Least squares: E=12∥r∥2E=\tfrac12\|r\|^2, ∇E=JTr\nabla E=J^Tr, HE=JTJ+∑iriHriH_E=J^TJ+\sum_i r_iH_{r_i}.
  • Gauss–Newton: JTJp=−JTrJ^TJp=-J^Tr; LM: (JTJ+λD)p=−JTr(J^TJ+\lambda D)p=-J^Tr.
  • Constrained stationarity: use KKT/projected-gradient conditions, not a raw zero-gradient test.
  • Always diagnose: domains, units/scales, coordinate frames, conditioning, nonfinite values, line-search/solver status, and whether the derivative exists.

Figure guide

  1. Local change ladder (horizontal): secant slopes converge to derivative; derivative defines tangent prediction; multivariate derivative becomes JΔxJ\Delta x; Hessian adds quadratic curvature. Annotate the remainder orders and assumptions.
  2. Camera differential frame map: object-space perturbation → world → camera → perspective projection → pixel change, with multiplication order JπRAJ_\pi R A and a coordinate-convention callout. Include the ideal positive-forward projection Jacobian only as a declared convention.
  3. Integration comparison strip: left/right rectangle, midpoint, trapezoid, Simpson over x2x^2 on [0,2][0,2], showing the exact 8/38/3 and the four-subinterval estimates.
  4. ODE stability plane: Euler amplification R(z)=1+zR(z)=1+z disk, damped scalar eigenvalue on negative real axis, oscillator eigenvalues on imaginary axis; contrast explicit Euler growth and semi-implicit bounded regime.
  5. AD graph: forward primal/tangent arrows and reverse adjoint arrows for (xy+sin⁡x)2(xy+\sin x)^2; shared xx paths merge by addition.
  6. Solver decision map: objective/residual structure → gradient descent, Newton/BFGS, Gauss–Newton/LM; wrap each with scaling, globalization, constraints and explicit termination statuses.

10 - Probability and Monte Carlo - Visual Recall

Probability and uncertainty — visual recall

flowchart LR
 M["Model and data scale"] --> D["Discretization choice"] --> A["Stable arithmetic"] --> S["Sampling and reduction"] --> E["Error budget and tests"]
 K["Problem conditioning"] -. "limits attainable accuracy" .-> E

classDef blue fill:#e5eff9,stroke:#2463a6,color:#18354c;
classDef green fill:#e3f3ed,stroke:#16806a,color:#174b3c;
classDef amber fill:#fff0dc,stroke:#c57820,color:#64400d;

Shortest route: start with a model of outcomes, then ask what distribution the computer actually sampled, how it weighted each sample, and what evidence supports the estimate.

Reconstruct the chain

(Ω, F, P) describes outcomes, measurable events, and their probabilities. A random variable maps outcomes into numbers; a random vector preserves their joint behavior. A PMF assigns point mass to discrete values; a PDF gives density relative to a stated measure; a CDF accumulates probability and exists even when no PDF does.

Conditioning changes the information available. Independence means joint probability factors, not merely that events are disjoint. Bayes reverses the conditioning direction by multiplying likelihood by prior and normalizing over alternatives.

Expectation is a probability-weighted center. Variance is mean squared spread. Covariance records coupled variation; correlation divides it by both standard deviations but only captures linear association. For a vector, covariance is symmetric PSD because aᵀΣa = Var(aᵀX) ≥ 0.

Bernoulli describes one binary outcome; binomial counts IID Bernoulli successes. Uniform has constant density in its declared measure. Gaussian describes a quadratic-distance bell shape. Exponential waiting times are memoryless; Poisson counts belong to the corresponding constant-rate process. A multivariate Gaussian’s covariance sets ellipse/ellipsoid orientation and scale.

The computational chain is:

seed/state or keyed input → finite random bits → sample transform → actual PDF and measure
                              → weighted contribution f(X)/p(X) → average → uncertainty/error report

Every arrow carries assumptions. A wrong PDF or measure can bias the result. A low-variance estimator can still be biased. Correlated observations change the standard error. Confidence intervals do not repair a wrong expectation.

Formula prompts

Prompt Reconstruct
Conditioning P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B); chain rule multiplies successive conditional probabilities.
Bayes P(H|E)=P(E|H)P(H)/ΣᵢP(E|Hᵢ)P(Hᵢ).
Expected transform E[g(X)] = Σg(x)p(x) or ∫g(x)p(x)dx.
Variance/covariance Var(X)=E[X²]−E[X]²; Cov(X,Y)=E[XY]−E[X]E[Y].
Linear propagation E[AX+b]=Aμ+b; Cov(AX+b)=AΣAᵀ; local nonlinear approximation uses JΣJᵀ.
Importance estimate I=∫f dx=Eₚ[f(X)/p(X)]; average contributions and divide by the actual sampling density.
Monte Carlo error IID finite-variance mean has Var(Ȳ)=σ²/N, SE=σ/√N; four times samples halves SE.
Estimator quality MSE = variance + bias².
Bessel/Welford Unbiased sample variance uses M₂/(n−1); update with δ=x−μ, μ←μ+δ/n, M₂←M₂+δ(x−μ).
Error metrics MSE squares; RMSE returns original units; MAE uses absolute error; relative metrics fail or need policy near zero.

Fast error checks

  • Does a density integrate to one in the stated coordinate measure? Is its unit inverse measure?
  • Are the samples distributed according to the PDF used in the weight?
  • Is a stated confidence interval fixed-sample, and are IID/normal or approximation assumptions plausible?
  • Is covariance symmetric PSD? Does singular mean invalid, or valid but lower-rank?
  • Are sample and population variance being confused? Is a single run being mistaken for evidence of variance reduction?
  • Is a “Gaussian” a normalized probability model or merely a rendering kernel?

Source-provided recall and compact formula reference

Supplied concise recall summary

The mathematical core is the probability space (Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega,\mathcal F,P), random variables defined on that space, and probability laws for their values.

Conditional probability changes the reference information. Independence is a factorization property. PMFs assign masses to discrete values, while PDFs assign density relative to a measure. CDFs accumulate probability and exist for every real-valued random variable.

Expected value describes the weighted centre. Variance describes squared spread. Covariance describes coupled spread. Correlation standardizes covariance but does not measure every form of dependence.

Bernoulli models one binary trial. Binomial models the count of successes in independent identically distributed Bernoulli trials. Uniform models constant density over a region. Gaussian models a particular smooth bell-shaped distribution. Exponential models memoryless waiting times. Poisson models event counts under its defining assumptions.

A multivariate Gaussian combines mean, covariance, and correlations into a joint distribution. Positive-definite covariance permits a full-dimensional nonsingular Gaussian density. Singular PSD covariance describes a distribution confined to a lower-dimensional affine subspace.

Key engineering invariants: all probabilities are valid and normalized; PDF units match the integration measure; covariance is symmetric PSD; Gaussian density evaluation avoids unnecessary inversion; nonfinite inputs and singular cases are explicit; sampling tests use statistical tolerances rather than exact equality.

Cholesky whitening

From Sigma=LL transpose and x=mu+Lz, solve z=inverse(L)(x-mu); then Mahalanobis squared distance is z transpose z. A singular covariance is supported on a lower-dimensional affine subspace.

Rebuild the numerical witness.

Six figures

F10-1. Ordered outcomes and the exact two-dice sum PMF. The supplied lesson already derives this example; the figure is a visual check of the 36 ordered pairs. PMF numerators sum to 36 and P(S=7)=1/6.

F10-2. Zero covariance need not mean independence. For standard normal X, Cov(X,X squared)=0 by symmetry although X and X squared are dependent. Sample covariance is a finite-run witness.

F10-3. Uniform area sampling requires a square-root radial transform. The theoretical mean radius is 2/3 for uniform area in the unit disk and 1/2 for uniform radius; plotted sample means are finite-run illustrations.

F10-4. Monte Carlo random error and a fixed bias floor. For the stated integral, unbiased RMSE falls with sample count while the biased estimator retains its offset.

F10-5. A matched importance proposal can make contributions constant. For the stated nonnegative integrand and support, the matched proposal gives constant contributions; uniform-proposal variance is 4/45. This does not generalize to arbitrary signed integrands.

F10-6. A full-period toy LCG can still have a simple low-bit pattern. For m=16, a=5, c=1, all 16 states are visited but the least-significant bit alternates. Full period does not imply good multidimensional quality. The keyed-input sketch indicates deterministic indexing only: a different key does not establish statistical independence or collision freedom.

The chain

Input uncertainty is amplified by conditioning; finite-precision algorithms add their own error. Keep problem sensitivity, algorithm stability, approximation error, and sampling uncertainty distinct. A small residual or update is evidence only when assumptions provide an error bound.

Checks before trusting a result

  • State arithmetic assumptions (normal/subnormal, overflow, rounding mode) and data scale.
  • Check both residual/backward error and conditioning before interpreting forward accuracy.
  • Verify interpolation range, boundary policy, and parameter units.
  • Separate discretization, truncation, roundoff, and sampling error.
  • Fix a reproducible reduction tree or record seed, sample design, and uncertainty.
  • Test exact identities, invariants, edge cases, convergence order, and randomized strata.

Numerical reliability figures and their explanations

  • N10-7 · Summation is an algorithm, not just a plus sign — Exact real sum is 10000. The three-term counterexample shows why Kahan is not an exact-arithmetic guarantee. Strict IEEE-style evaluation is assumed; reassociation can invalidate compensation.

  • N10-8 · More polynomial degree does not guarantee a better picture — Both interpolants match every node. Their behaviour between nodes differs. Chebyshev extrema reduce this example’s endpoint oscillation; this comparison is not a universal interpolation error bound.

  • N10-9 · Bézier and Hermite can tell the same curve story — Use Hermite tangents 3(P1−P0) and 3(P3−P2) for this cubic Bézier curve. The control polygon bounds the curve through nonnegative weights summing to one; inner control points need not lie on the curve.

  • N10-10 · A root solver needs both progress and a safety argument — The error comparison uses cos(x)−x with specified starting values. Bisection has a shrinking bracket; Newton and secant need additional hypotheses. The plotting floor is explicitly shown rather than interpreted as continuing convergence.

  • N10-11 · Arbitrary sample counts need full-domain support — Left: choosing the first five of nine equal cells and averaging equally gives E[y] = 0.3, while the uniform-square value is 0.5. Right: one point per marginal bin is a midpoint illustration; randomized LHS jitters and permutes appropriately, and is not full multidimensional stratification.

  • N10-12 · Algebraically equal formulas can have unequal numerical error — The reference uses 90-digit Decimal arithmetic and compares binary64 formulas for b from 100 to 10¹⁶. This bounded example illustrates cancellation, not a complete robust quadratic solver.

Frames and transforms

  • A coordinate needs a frame: p=o+BpFp=o+Bp_F. Camera world-to-view is pV=RT(pW−c)p_V=R^T(p_W-c); points use homogeneous w=1w=1, directions use w=0w=0, and normals use A−TA^{-T}.
  • Frames and coordinate meaning · Camera pose and view transform

Projection, depth, raster, and culling

  • For RH view space looking down −Z-Z, axial depth is d=−zvd=-z_v and perspective clip w=dw=d. Projection and depth mapping are separate choices; declare NDC range, depth direction, viewport origin, and Y orientation.
  • Recover positions using the rendered projection and matching pixel centre, viewport, and depth convention. A frustum plane test is conservative: sphere reject if s<−rs<-r; AABB reject if s<−∑i|ni|eis<-\sum_i|n_i|e_i.
  • Perspective-correct attributes interpolate as ∑iλi(ai/wi)/∑iλi/wi\sum_i\lambda_i(a_i/w_i)/\sum_i\lambda_i/w_i; depth has its own projected interpolation rule.
  • Projection derivation · Depth precision · Raster mapping · Frustum culling · Interpolation

Time and calibrated image formation

  • Track jittered and unjittered projection state. Intrinsics map optical-camera rays to pixels; extrinsics map between world and optical camera. Lens distortion is a separate nonlinear map with a valid domain and inversion method.
  • Thin-lens rays originate across the aperture and converge on the focus plane. CoC and depth-of-field limits depend on an explicit sensor blur criterion. Aperture and shutter affect collected light; ISO-like gain does not add photons.
  • Stereo depth follows Z=fxB/ΔxZ=f_xB/\Delta x for a rectified pinhole pair. Equal image areas on a sphere do not imply equal solid angles.
  • Temporal camera state · Intrinsics · Extrinsics · Lens distortion

Figures and their full explanations

  • C11-1 · Depth mapping and floating-point spacing work together — RH camera looks down −Z, zero-to-one depth, n=0.1 and finite conventional far=100000; reversed curve uses infinite far. Right: error after rounding depth to binary32 and moving to its next representable value, including rounding and inversion effects. This is not a complete GPU transform-error model.

  • C11-2 · Culling is a conservative half-space test — This s–x cross-section has near=1, far=5 and ±45° side planes. For an inward unit plane normal, a sphere is outside only when signed centre distance < −radius. For an AABB use r = |nx|ex + |ny|ey + |nz|ez. Passing each plane does not prove exact intersection with the whole frustum.

  • C11-3 · Attributes follow reciprocal clip w — Vertex clip w values are (1,4,4); attribute values are (0,1,1). At the screen centroid the affine value is 2/3 and the corrected value is 1/3. Use sum(λ a/w) / sum(λ/w); depth-buffer interpolation has its own projected-depth rule.

  • C11-4 · Stereo turns pixel uncertainty into depth uncertainty — Rectified pinhole pair: focal length 800 pixels, baseline 0.064 m, disparity noise σd=0.25 pixel. Z=fB/d and σZ≈Z²σd/(fB). This local propagation assumes corresponding points, small noise and valid calibration; it is not a perception model.

  • C11-5 · Focus distance, focal length and aperture are different controls — Paraxial 50 mm lens at f/2 focused at 2 m: 1/F=1/u+1/v and c=D|v0/v−1|, with D=F/N. The 0.03 mm threshold is an explicitly chosen viewing criterion. This excludes diffraction, aberrations and sensor processing.

  • C11-6 · Distortion is a map with a domain, not just a coefficient list — Normalized Brown-style radial example xd=x(1+k₁r²), yd=y(1+k₁r²). This displayed domain has positive radial derivative 1+3k₁r², so the local radial map remains monotone. Larger radii can fold; numerical undistortion requires domain and convergence checks.

  • C11-7 · Image coordinates need a sampling-measure conversion — For longitude λ and latitude φ, dω=cosφ dλ dφ. Equal-width equirectangular image rows shrink toward the poles. Ray-differential Jacobians generalize the local image-area-to-solid-angle conversion; they do not by themselves specify lens-area or shutter-time probability.

  • C11-8 · Residual count does not guarantee observable motion — Toy Lucas–Kanade information matrices H=sum(∇I∇Iᵀ): repeated horizontal gradients give eigenvalues (0,3); diverse gradients give (1,3). Small eigenvalues expose weak directions. Camera-calibration gauge freedoms require a larger Jacobian model and explicit constraints.

Worlds, Images and Inference — Fast Recall

Fast route

Start with a world description and follow it through the physical and computational steps that form an image. Then ask what the measurements let us recover about the world. Each step changes representation and may discard information.

flowchart LR
    W["Represent geometry and motion"] --> C["Pose the scene and define camera"]
    C --> O["Form an optical image"]
    O --> L["Resolve visibility and light"]
    L --> S["Sample and filter image signals"]
    S --> D["Encode color and display"]
    D --> V["Infer shape, motion, pose"]
  1. Represent points, curves, surfaces, and meshes with the data each operation needs.
  2. Place and move geometry with coordinate frames, hierarchies, animation, and simulation.
  3. Measure the scene through optics, exposure, sensors, and camera projection.
  4. Render visible surfaces, material response, and light transport; rasterization and ray queries organize the work differently.
  5. Sample the continuous image with filters and finite pixels, then encode color for a device.
  6. Infer hidden motion, orientation, shape, or object pose from measurements, stating ambiguities and assumptions.

For the core visual anchors, open Figure U1; Figure U2; Figure U3; Figure U4; and Figure U5.

Thirty-five retrieval briefs

Each brief gives a mechanism to recall, the condition that matters, and a concrete question to use when reopening that section. The links target the matching chapter in the main note.

  1. A scene description becomes an image — Graphics maps a scene description to image measurements; vision works backward from measurements to constraints on the scene. Both depend on camera, geometry, light, and sampling assumptions. Ask: In a ray renderer and a rasterizer, which direction does the visibility query travel?

  2. Mathematical language: points, vectors, and derivatives — A point locates; a vector displaces. In a skew basis, geometric squared length is cTGcc^T Gc, with G=BTBG=B^TB. A Jacobian predicts local change; the Hessian records curvature. Ask: Why does summing squared coordinates fail when basis vectors are not orthogonal?

  3. Coordinate frames, transformations, and pose — Homogeneous coordinates let one matrix translate points while leaving direction vectors unchanged. For column vectors, TSTS means scale first, then translate; order matters. Normals use inverse-transpose under nonuniform scale. Ask: What result does STST produce for a point when translation is accidentally scaled too?

  4. Curves as controllable functions — A cubic has four degrees of freedom: endpoint positions and endpoint tangents fit Hermite data. Bézier controls expose tangents; de Casteljau evaluates and subdivides exactly. C1C^1 matches parameter speed as well as direction; G1G^1 only matches tangent direction. Ask: Why can a visually tangent join still have a speed jump?

  5. Surfaces, patches, topology, and parameterization — A chart maps a parameter domain onto a surface; its partial derivatives span the tangent plane. A chart can distort or become singular even if the surface itself is regular. Ask: What condition on the two tangent vectors makes a parameterization lose a local direction?

  6. Meshes, connectivity, and geometry processing — A mesh stores geometry plus adjacency. Half-edges encode directed edge pairs and make face and vertex neighborhoods traversable. Edits must preserve required topology and orientation. See Figure U2. Ask: After an edge flip, which adjacent face can become inverted if the new diagonal is geometrically invalid?

  7. Lens optics, focus, and image formation — A thin lens maps object distance to image distance; defocus spreads a point into a blur circle. Acceptable focus depends on the blur tolerance and output scale, not a universal depth-of-field boundary. The added derivation estimates a focus interval of about 2.34–4.19 m for its stated setup. Ask: Which chosen circle-of-confusion threshold changes that interval?

  8. Exposure, sensors, and dynamic range — Exposure controls collected photons through aperture, shutter time, and sensitivity; equivalent brightness does not imply equivalent motion blur, depth of field, noise, or highlight headroom. Sensor readout and saturation add limits. Ask: If shutter time is halved and aperture widened one stop, what changes besides image brightness?

  9. Cameras, projection, and calibration — Pinhole projection x=fX/Zx=fX/Z couples image scale to depth. Vanishing points constrain parallel directions; calibration estimates internal parameters and pose from known geometry. Orthographic projection is useful when depth variation is negligible or should not affect measured scale. Ask: Why can three orthogonal vanishing directions still leave a mirror-related calibration solution?

  10. Sampling continuous signals and image formation — Sampling records finite values of a continuous signal. Frequencies above half the sample rate can alias to a lower pattern; prefilter before reducing resolution. Pixel-area averaging is already a weak low-pass filter. See Figure U3. Ask: How can two different sinusoids produce identical samples on one grid?

  11. Image sampling, filtering, and efficient reconstruction — Reconstruction filters trade alias suppression, blur, and ringing. A texture Jacobian maps a pixel footprint into texture space; mipmaps suit near-isotropic footprints, anisotropic filters suit elongated ones. Integral images turn any axis-aligned box sum into four table reads after one cumulative pass. Ask: Why does an integral image not make an arbitrary convolution constant-time?

  12. Color perception, encoding, and display — Cone responses compress a spectrum into three values, so distinct spectra can be metamers. Display codes are often nonlinear: decode to linear light before averaging or compositing, then encode for display. Gamut bounds which responses a device can reproduce. Ask: Why does encoded midpoint 0.5 represent roughly 0.22 linear intensity under gamma 2.2?

  13. Light measurement and radiometry — Flux, irradiance, intensity, and radiance use different measures. For an area-light element, conversion from area density to solid-angle density uses |ny⋅(−ω)|/r2|n_y\cdot(-\omega)|/r^2. Use the same measure as the integral. Ask: Why does sampling an area light require both the inverse-square factor and the light-normal cosine?

  14. Reflectance, BRDFs, and shading — A BRDF describes how incoming direction becomes outgoing radiance. Lambertian reflectance is constant at ρ/π\rho/\pi; mirrors are delta-like and glossy materials form lobes. Ask: Why can a smooth directional sampler fail to hit an ideal mirror reflection?

  15. The rendering equation and light transport — Outgoing radiance is emitted light plus visible reflected incoming radiance integrated over a hemisphere. Since incoming radiance comes from other surfaces, transport is coupled. A renderer makes this executable with visibility, BRDF, light, and accumulation. See Figure U5. Ask: Which term becomes zero when geometry blocks a sampled direction?

  16. Numerical integration and Monte Carlo estimation — For samples X∼pX\sim p, estimate ∫f(x)dx\int f(x)dx with the mean of f(X)/p(X)f(X)/p(X). Importance sampling reduces estimator variance only when the density covers every contributing region. Ask: Why does quadrupling independent samples usually halve standard error rather than quarter it?

  17. Rasterization, coverage, and depth — Rasterization tests projected primitives at pixel sample locations, interpolates attributes, then depth-tests. Exact edge coverage is an area integral; multisampling estimates it with subpixel tests. Perspective-correct interpolation compensates for the projection divide. Ask: What artifact appears if a checkerboard floor is linearly interpolated in screen space?

  18. Textures and surface detail — Texture is a signal over surface coordinates. Charts introduce seams and distortion; filtering must follow how that domain projects into each pixel. Ask: Why can one square mip level overblur a floor receding toward the horizon?

  19. Visibility queries and ray intersections — A ray query asks which geometry intersects a path from an origin; hit parameters, barycentric coordinates, and surface orientation answer different parts of the intersection contract. Ask: What additional bound distinguishes a ray from a finite line segment?

  20. Acceleration structures and robust queries — A BVH groups geometry in nested bounds. Traversal skips a node only when its bound cannot intersect the query, so bounds must conservatively contain descendants. Robust predicates matter near tangencies and degenerate geometry. Ask: What correctness failure follows from rounding a bound inward?

  21. Scene graphs and articulated geometry — A node’s world transform composes parent and local transforms; skinning blends posed bone candidates using per-vertex weights. Linear blends can collapse volume when averaging opposing rotations. Ask: Why does applying the inverse bind transform preserve a vertex when current pose equals rest pose?

  22. Animation curves and motion paths — A moving camera needs position and orientation, plus a valid up direction. Smooth position does not guarantee smooth orientation; rotation interpolation and time parameterization are separate choices. Ask: What makes the camera frame singular when view and up vectors align?

  23. Dynamics, forces, and numerical integration — Dynamics evolves state from forces or interaction rules; an integrator approximates continuous time with steps. Large steps can inject energy or destabilize springs and cloth. Ask: Why can explicit Euler make a spring oscillation grow even when the physical model conserves energy?

  24. Optimization, constraints, and inverse kinematics — Define variables, objective, constraints, and derivatives before solving. IK linearizes forward kinematics with a Jacobian; feasibility and conditioning govern whether a target is reachable and stable. Ask: What changes when the end-effector Jacobian loses rank?

  25. PDEs, fields, and discrete solvers — A PDE, spatial discretization, and boundary conditions together define a numerical problem. Choosing a mesh or basis changes the system matrix; boundary data is part of the model. Ask: Why can two solvers using the same interior equation produce different solutions at the boundary?

  26. Optical flow and motion from images — Brightness constancy yields one equation, Ixu+Iyv+It=0I_xu+I_yv+I_t=0, for two flow components. A local aperture therefore leaves motion along an edge ambiguous. Ask: What does a single straight edge constrain well, and which motion component remains unobserved?

  27. Edges, contours, and subpixel localization — Blur spreads an ideal edge; fitting a response profile can estimate its center between pixels. Hough voting accumulates weak local evidence into a global line or shape hypothesis. Ask: Why can an edge’s subpixel estimate shift when the blur model is wrong?

  28. Recognition, templates, and industrial matching — Template matching searches over pose and transformation with a score chosen for expected noise and deformation. Coarse-to-fine search reduces cost; thresholds set tolerance, not truth. Ask: Why should an edge alignment score treat normal displacement differently from tangent displacement?

  29. Pose estimation, transforms, and robust fitting — Estimate rigid pose from correspondences, enforce a proper rotation, and use robust fitting when outliers contaminate matches. RANSAC trial count depends on inlier rate and sample size. Ask: Why does lowering the assumed inlier fraction sharply increase the number of RANSAC trials?

  30. Stereo, relative orientation, and reconstruction — Two views constrain rays and relative pose; triangulation recovers structure up to gauge freedoms such as global scale. Critical surfaces make the geometry ill-conditioned. Ask: Why can perfect image correspondences still leave metric scale unknown?

  31. Surface orientation from illumination — Photometric stereo uses several known light directions to solve for scaled normal from brightness measurements. The lighting matrix must span the components being estimated. See Figure U4. Ask: Which normal component becomes unobservable if every light direction lies in one plane?

  32. Shape from shading and reflectance — A single shading image gives a nonlinear relation among surface normal, reflectance, and illumination; integration into height requires boundary conditions and extra assumptions. Ask: Why does a locally valid normal field fail to guarantee one globally consistent surface?

  33. Surface descriptions and Gaussian images — A Gaussian image maps surface area to normal directions. Its directional mass distribution summarizes orientation and curvature patterns but can be shared by geometrically different surfaces. Ask: Why does the zero-centroid condition hold for a closed surface, and what does it rule out?

  34. Photographic composition, history, and communication — Viewpoint, crop, sequence, and caption shape how a photograph functions as evidence or argument. A recorded scene is selected and framed, not a neutral inventory. Ask: What does a wide frame reveal that a close crop hides in the same documentary image?

  35. Photographic workflow and integrated decisions — Trace a capture from scene spectrum through optics, exposure, sampling, processing, and display. Each stage can discard information or add artifacts; choose settings around the intended output. Ask: Which stage caused a moiré pattern, and what evidence distinguishes it from JPEG blocking?

Evidence and scope

The source ledger covers 88 entries: 70 requested lectures and 18 added sources. Its evidence includes 86 published English automatic-caption tracks, one locally generated Whisper transcript for a technical lecture, one sampled showcase video, and 70 lecture PDFs matched to their course years. Captions, notes, and sampled visuals support different claims; the legend records which evidence supports each entry.

These briefs are deliberately compact retrieval notes for a 35-chapter continuous treatment. They are not a transcript, a substitute for the worked derivations, or a claim that the entire companion fits on one physical page.

Four more figures to redraw from memory

New mechanisms to retrieve

A vertex buffer is a byte array interpreted by a draw command. The stride says how many bytes separate successive vertices; the attribute offset says where one field begins inside a vertex. Rasterization and vertex layout · U10. Ask: For 24-byte float32 vertices with RGB after XYZ, what are the position stride and color offset?

A mathematical projection of a finite point set is a map to a line. Small image size means many collisions. Scale, spacing, and additive structure determine whether many directions can compress the same set. This is separate from a camera’s projection matrix. Finite-field collisions · Real projection scales · U11. Ask: Is the obstruction arithmetic, spatial clustering, or an incidence pattern?

A classifier maps an image representation to scores; a loss compares those scores with the target. The gradient sends a local change backward through each operation by the chain rule. Convolution shares a local filter over the image; attention instead builds content-dependent weights between tokens. Learning basics · CNNs · Attention. Ask: Which shape changes at each layer, and where does the chain rule multiply upstream and local derivatives?

Dense prediction assigns an output to every pixel; detection also predicts object locations and categories. Video adds temporal alignment, motion, and compute cost. Dense prediction and detection · Video. Ask: Does the evaluation measure pixel accuracy, object matching, or temporal consistency?

Self-supervision creates training targets from the data; generative objectives instead define how a model represents or samples possible outputs. Evaluation must match the claim: reconstruction quality, likelihood, sample quality, and downstream usefulness are different measurements. Self-supervision · Generative models. Ask: What observable target trains the model, and what test would falsify the capability claim?

NeRF represents a scene with a learned field queried along rays; Gaussian splatting stores explicit 3D elements and composites their projected contributions. A planar Gaussian gives a direct local surface normal, while 3D Gaussian splats need geometric regularization to recover reliable surfaces. Learned 3D representations · research methods · U12 · U13. Ask: Which representation is queried per ray and which is explicitly rasterized?

An environment map supplies incoming illumination by direction. ReSTIR uses weighted reservoirs to reuse light candidates, but the final estimator still needs correct proposal support and normalization. LoD changes also change geometry, so reused paths need a surface correspondence and its area Jacobian. Image-based lighting · Monte Carlo reuse · U14. Ask: What distribution was each candidate drawn from, and what normalization makes reuse valid?

Mitsuba 2 shows how a renderer can change execution mode and differentiate through image formation. It is a 2019 Enoki-based system; its API details are historical and should not be treated as Mitsuba 3 guidance. Differentiable rendering. Ask: Which quantities are differentiated and which sampling decisions are held fixed?

ARAP editing alternates local rigid rotations with a global sparse position solve. Field-aligned remeshing uses orientation and position fields to guide edge direction and placement. Mesh processing. Ask: Which part is local per vertex and which system is solved globally?

IPC combines a contact barrier with continuous collision detection and a feasibility-preserving line search. A positive barrier alone is not a proof that a finite time step cannot cross a contact. Contact dynamics · U15. Ask: What checks the entire path between the current and proposed configurations?

    E -->|failure analysis| R

Read the loop as a diagnostic map: representation, forward model, objective, and evaluation can each limit the result. It is not a single training algorithm; Monte Carlo rendering and supervised learning use different estimators and losses.

Rendering, materials, transport — retrieve the reasons

The left panel explains projective interpolation; the middle separates encoded storage from linear light; the right proves that a missing sampling region can create bias. These are numerical witnesses, not rendered screenshots from a working engine.

Recall prompt Short answer Full teaching / figure explanation
Why clip before dividing? A primitive can cross the camera plane; division near zero creates unbounded coordinates. Clip the homogeneous primitive first. [[Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#Decide which samples a triangle owns
Which barycentrics recover a texture coordinate? Screen weights need reciprocal-ww correction. Already-divided depth instead interpolates affinely on screen. [[Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#Decide which samples a triangle owns
Why does reversed depth help? Reciprocal distance pairs well with floating-point spacing near zero; every depth consumer must agree on ordering. [[Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#Give depth an explicit meaning
Why is encoded midpoint 0.50.5 too dark? It decodes to about 0.2140.214 linear light. Average linear values first. [[Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#Make every color number carry a meaning
What do D,F,GD,F,G mean? Facet distribution, interface reflection, and geometric visibility. The NDF normalizes with projected area. [[Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#Ask a surface where incoming energy can go
Why can a PDF exceed one? It is density per unit measure. Its integral is one; its pointwise value need not be bounded by one. [[Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#Follow one path without losing its probability

[[Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#Follow one path without losing its probability
Does more sampling remove every error? It reduces stochastic error under the estimator’s assumptions. Missing-domain and transport-model bias can remain. [[Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#A missing region cannot be repaired by taking more samples there

Then point to where each assumption appears in the implementation.

Explicit rendering, captured kernels and animated surfaces - retrieval briefs

  • Covariance to pixels — A Jacobian is a local linear prediction. Transform covariance as JΣJTJ\Sigma J^T, then invert the 2D covariance for the conic. Near-plane rejection and a finite footprint policy are prerequisites. Why is this only a local perspective approximation?

  • Allocate tile work — Count references, exclusive-scan counts, scatter to disjoint slices, sort by tile/depth, then composite. Counts [4,2,5,1][4,2,5,1] give offsets [0,4,6,11][0,4,6,11]. Why must an unstable final tile sort not destroy depth order?

  • Composite in order — Contribution is TαcT\alpha c and new transmittance is T(1−α)T(1-\alpha). Two half-opaque layers leave T=0.25T=0.25. A transmittance threshold is an approximation budget, not a universal reference constant.

  • Validate separate outputs — Compare color in a declared space, depth with units, and IDs as discrete values. Average error, peak error and changed-pixel fraction answer different questions. CPU/GPU agreement does not establish antialiasing quality.

  • Reuse the right object — A slot fence proves slot work completed. It does not prove a presentation wait consumed its semaphore. Frame-slot and acquired-image indices are separate domains. What resolves an acquisition followed by recording failure?

  • Retire across queues — Every required queue counter must be reached. (10,4,100)(10,4,100) does not cover required (9,5,3)(9,5,3). Ownership preserves the payload; completion permits destruction.

  • Compile the graph — Versions identify values, dependencies order producers/consumers, and lifetimes constrain storage aliasing. A list position does not prove that independent queues have stopped using memory.

  • Turn capture into editable world — Persistent identity survives sorting; physical support supplies deformation. For affine motion, μ′=Fμ+t\mu'=F\mu+t and Σ′=FΣFT\Sigma'=F\Sigma F^T. Appearance kernels alone supply neither mass nor colliders.

  • Animate in a declared space — Sample pose, resolve the hierarchy, morph before skinning, and build matching current/previous transforms. A global-joint palette already outputs world space. Why does adding the mesh world transform again break it?

  • Image-change bounds need assumptions — An opacity-only bound misses a red-to-blue edit at fixed opacity and a depth-order swap. State color range, evaluated per-pixel alpha changes, contributor order, color/background changes, and termination policy before calling an estimate a certificate.
